Gradle starts ndk-build with the script that you tell it to use

  APP_BUILD_SCRIPT=E:\Dhruvin kheni\Backup\Backup\Pancard_pe_loan\Pancard_pe_loan\app\src\main\jni\Android.mk

ndk-build immediately checks whether that file really exists:

  Android NDK: Your APP_BUILD_SCRIPT points to an unknown file …

and stops because it cannot find it.

So either

1. The file is really missing, or is in a different place / has a different
   name (for example you renamed jni → cpp, or deleted the native code).

2. You are pointing Gradle at the wrong place in build.gradle.

What to do

A. If you still use ndk-build

   • Put your Android.mk (and, if you have one, Application.mk) into the
     directory that Gradle is pointing at, or

   • Change the path in build.gradle so that it matches the real location.

   Example:

   android {
       externalNativeBuild {
           ndkBuild {
               path "src/main/cpp/Android.mk"     // <-- adjust to the real path
           }
       }
   }

   Use a forward-slash, relative path; Gradle will expand it to the absolute
   one.

B. If you no longer have any native code

   Simply remove the externalNativeBuild / ndkBuild stanza from your
   module-level build.gradle, clean the project, and build again. Gradle will
   stop invoking ndk-build and the error disappears.

C. Typical “file exists but still not found” reasons to check

   • The file name is Android.mk.txt (because Windows hid its extension).  
   • There is an uppercase / lowercase mismatch (Android.mk vs android.mk).  
   • The directory contains spaces and you did not quote the path (Gradle
     already does quote it in your case, so this is unlikely).  

Once the path in build.gradle matches a real Android.mk file (or you delete
the ndkBuild configuration if you no longer need it) the CXX1429 error is
resolved.

instruction:
User
I am an Android developer. When running my ONNX runtime application, the CPU utilisation is ~40% . How can I increase the CPU usage for my app?
output:
Why you only see ~40 %  

•  The Android AAR that ships with ONNX Runtime is built for “mobile-friendly” behaviour:  
  – XNNPACK is the default CPU execution provider and it is initialised with only 1–4 worker
    threads (depending on the build).  
  – ExecutionMode is SEQUENTIAL.  
  – The library is compiled with the pthread-pool runtime, so no other operator will create more
    threads for you.  
•  40 % in Android Studio usually means “40 % of all logical cores”.  
   On an 8-core big.LITTLE device that may already be 100 % of the three or four big cores.  
•  If the phone is in a “balanced” or “powersave” governor the kernel will deliberately
   down-clock or migrate the threads to the small cores when it can.  
•  Thermal throttling can reduce the maximum frequency after a few seconds of sustained load.  

If you really want to drive the CPU harder you have to (1) allow ONNX Runtime to spawn more
threads and (2) make sure Android does not keep clock frequencies low.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Let ONNX Runtime use more threads
----------------------------------------------------------------
Java / Kotlin
─────────────
import ai.onnxruntime.*;

OrtEnvironment env = OrtEnvironment.getEnvironment();
SessionOptions so = new SessionOptions();

/* 1.  Parallel execution of different nodes */
so.setExecutionMode(SessionOptions.ExecutionMode.PARALLEL);

/* 2.  Threads that an individual operator may use          */
/*    Usually “#big cores” is the sweet spot                */
int nThreads = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); // or e.g. 6
so.setIntraOpNumThreads(nThreads);

/* 3.  Threads for inter-operator parallelism (optional) */
so.setInterOpNumThreads(nThreads);

/* 4.  Tell XNNPACK to obey the same thread count          */
so.addConfigEntry("session.intra_op_num_threads",
                  Integer.toString(nThreads));

/* 5.  If you are not interested in NNAPI/GPU, keep only the CPU EP */
so.disablePerSessionThreads();          // remove thread pools created per session
so.addDisableCpuMemArena(false);        // leave cpu arena enabled

OrtSession session = env.createSession("model.onnx", so);

C / C++
───────
Ort::SessionOptions so;
so.SetExecutionMode(ORT_PARALLEL);
so.SetIntraOpNumThreads(nThreads);
so.SetInterOpNumThreads(nThreads);

/* XNNPACK specific */
Ort::ThrowOnError(
    OrtSessionOptionsAppendExecutionProvider_XNNPACK(so,
        nThreads  /* = intra_op_num_threads */
));

----------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Build or pick the right binary
----------------------------------------------------------------
The pre-built “onnxruntime-mobile-x.y.z.aar” is compiled with a small thread pool.  
If you need more than ~4 threads:

1. Clone the repo and build the “full” Android package:

   ./build.sh \
     --android \
     --android_abi=arm64-v8a \
     --parallel \
     --build_shared_lib \
     --config Release \
     --cmake_extra_defines \
        onnxruntime_ENABLE_BITCODE=OFF \
        onnxruntime_BUILD_UNIT_TESTS=OFF \
        onnxruntime_THREADPOOL_ALLOW_GLOBAL_CONFIG=ON \
        onnxruntime_USE_OPENMP=ON   # optional

   This produces libonnxruntime.so that can use as many threads as you ask for.

2. Or use the nightly “onnxruntime-gpu” AAR; even if you run on CPU it is
   compiled with the global pthread-pool code path.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Keep Android from scaling you down
----------------------------------------------------------------
•  Tell the scheduler that your inference thread is important:

    Thread.currentThread().setPriority(
        android.os.Process.THREAD_PRIORITY_DISPLAY);  // or URGENT_DISPLAY

•  Acquire a “performance” hint when you start NN inference (API 31+):

    val perf = PerformanceHintManager.create(context)
    val handle = perf.reportActualWorkDuration(
                    Duration.ofMillis(predictedDurationMs))

•  Put the device in “perf” governor during benchmarking only:

    adb shell "echo performance > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_governor"

•  Stay within thermal limits: keep batches small or insert short sleeps if you
   do many back-to-back inferences.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Verify that it worked
----------------------------------------------------------------
$ adb shell top -p <pid> -H                 # see individual threads
$ adb shell taskset -p <pid>                # make sure you are not bound to little cores
Android Studio › Profiler › CPU             # should show ~80-100 %

----------------------------------------------------------------
5.  When more CPU no longer helps
----------------------------------------------------------------
•  Move compute to NNAPI or GPU EP – zero CPU utilisation.  
•  Quantise the model (INT8) – same threads, fewer cycles.  
•  Use model-specific optimisation (operator fusion, custom EP, etc.).

----------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Create the session with ExecutionMode.PARALLEL.  
2. Set both intra-op and inter-op thread counts to the number of cores you want.  
3. Use an ORT build that allows >4 threads (self-build if necessary).  
4. Raise the Android thread priority / performance hints to stop the
   governor from parking or down-clocking your cores.

After those changes you will usually see CPU utilisation climb to 80-100 %
(= all big cores + some small ones) and wall-clock inference time drop
accordingly.

instruction: Provide 15 attack  vectors in Manufacturing sector and methods to mitigate the identied risks
output:
Below is a concise, security-focused list of common attack vectors that threaten manufacturing environments, followed by proven defensive measures for each.  The recommendations combine information-technology (IT) and operational-technology (OT) practices, because modern plants rely on both.

1.  Compromised Remote Access (e.g., VPN or RDP)
    • Mitigation:
      – Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on all remote connections.  
      – Restrict access to jump-servers placed in a DMZ; disable direct RDP to shop-floor devices.  
      – Monitor and log all remote sessions; alert on anomalous activity.

2.  Phishing & Business-Email Compromise
    • Mitigation:
      – Continuous user-awareness training with realistic simulations.  
      – Email-gateway filtering for malicious links/attachments.  
      – DMARC, DKIM, SPF to reduce spoofed email.  
      – Segregated approval workflows for purchase orders, wire transfers, etc.

3.  Malware via Removable Media (USB drives used by maintenance staff or vendors)
    • Mitigation:
      – Implement technical controls that block unauthorized media or force them into read-only mode.  
      – Provide dedicated, scanned “clean USBs” for firmware updates.  
      – Maintain a locked, monitored media-drop station on-site.

4.  Outdated PLC / ICS Firmware & Software
    • Mitigation:
      – Maintain an asset inventory with current firmware versions.  
      – Apply vendor patches during scheduled maintenance windows.  
      – Use testbeds to validate updates before plant deployment.  

5.  Poor Network Segmentation Between IT & OT
    • Mitigation:
      – Adopt the ISA/IEC 62443 “zones & conduits” model.  
      – Deploy firewalls with strict allow-listing between corporate, DMZ, and control networks.  
      – Disable “flat” Layer-2 spanning across production and office networks.

6.  Insecure Industrial IoT Devices (sensors, smart cameras, AGVs)
    • Mitigation:
      – Change default credentials and disable unused services.  
      – Place IIoT devices on micro-segmented VLANs with outbound-only internet rules when possible.  
      – Apply manufacturer security patches or compensating controls (e.g., reverse proxies).

7.  Supply-Chain Compromise of Software or Equipment
    • Mitigation:
      – Require SBOMs (Software Bills of Materials) from vendors.  
      – Digitally sign and verify firmware and software before installation.  
      – Establish vendor-risk scoring and periodic security assessments.

8.  Insider Threat (disgruntled employee or contractor)
    • Mitigation:
      – Principle of least privilege; role-based access control for MES/SCADA systems.  
      – Continuous behavioral analytics on badge swipes, logins, and machine commands.  
      – Immediate revocation of credentials upon termination; formal off-boarding checklist.

9.  Wireless Network Exploits (rogue APs, weak encryption on shop-floor Wi-Fi)
    • Mitigation:
      – Use WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X authentication.  
      – Perform regular RF sweeps for rogue access points.  
      – Apply network access control (NAC) to enforce posture checks on wireless hosts.

10. Physical Intrusion into Control Rooms or Cabinets
    • Mitigation:
      – Badge-plus-PIN or biometric access to critical areas.  
      – Tamper-evident seals on cabinets; cabinet-door open sensors tied to the SOC.  
      – CCTV coverage with storage retention aligned to incident-response timelines.

11.  Denial-of-Service on Production Servers or HMIs
    • Mitigation:
      – Redundant HMIs and historians on separate power and network paths.  
      – Rate-limiting and deep-packet inspection on inbound traffic from external networks.  
      – Capacity planning and DoS scrubbing service for internet-facing portals (e.g., supplier portals).

12.  Credential Stuffing / Brute-Force on Legacy Accounts
    • Mitigation:
      – Centralized identity provider with password-less or MFA options.  
      – Enforce account lockout thresholds and use CAPTCHA on user portals.  
      – Periodic audits to delete dormant or default accounts.

13.  Unauthorized Configuration Changes (via engineering workstations)
    • Mitigation:
      – Implement change-management workflow requiring supervisor approval and digital signatures.  
      – Version-control PLC logic and back up daily to immutable storage.  
      – Deploy host-based application whitelisting on engineering laptops.

14.  Exploitation of Cloud-Connected MES / ERP APIs
    • Mitigation:
      – Use API gateways with OAuth2/OIDC tokens and mutual TLS.  
      – Apply least-privilege scopes and continuous monitoring for anomalous API calls.  
      – Conduct regular penetration tests and code reviews of custom integrations.

15.  Ransomware Propagation Across Shared Resources
    • Mitigation:
      – Immutable, offline backups of controllers, recipes, and quality data.  
      – Network-level segmentation plus lateral-movement detection (e.g., East-West traffic analytics).  
      – Endpoint detection & response (EDR) tuned for OT-friendly policies; routinely test restoration procedures.

Cross-Cutting Best Practices
• Develop and rehearse an OT-specific incident-response plan that includes safety shut-down criteria.  
• Align with standards such as NIST CSF, IEC 62443, and ISO 27001, mapping controls to each attack vector above.  
• Conduct regular red-team/blue-team exercises to evaluate both technical defenses and human procedures.

Applied together, these mitigations significantly reduce the attack surface of modern manufacturing plants while improving resilience and safety.

instruction: In what order should I learn Deep Learning from the foundations such as matrices and vectors all the way to transformers?
output:
Below is a practical, dependency-aware road-map that starts with the bare mathematical minimum and ends with modern transformer architectures.  Each stage states (1) the new ideas you should master, (2) what you should already know before starting it, (3) typical hands-on exercises, and (4) a short list of well-regarded, free or low-cost resources.  Treat the stages as checkpoints; the exact time you spend at each one depends on your background.

────────────────────────
0.  Programming & Tooling Bootstrap  (optional if you are already fluent)
────────────────────────
• Goal Write, debug and profile basic scientific Python (or Julia) code.  
• Prereqs General programming experience.  
• Do Solve ~20 Project Euler/LeetCode problems; re-implement numpy dot product for vectors; manipulate CSVs with pandas.  
• Resources  
  – Automate the Boring Stuff with Python (Al Sweigart) – ch. 1-10  
  – Real Python’s “NumPy Foundations” tutorial  
  – Anaconda / JupyterLab set-up guide  

────────────────────────
1.  Math Foundations for Deep Learning
────────────────────────
1A Linear Algebra (vectors, matrices, norms, eigen-stuff)  
1B Multivariable Calculus (partials, gradients, Jacobians)  
1C Probability & Statistics (random variables, expectation, common dists, Bayes rule)  
1D Numerical Optimization basics (gradient descent, line search, convexity)  

• Prereqs High-school algebra/trig.  
• Do Derive the gradient of ‖Ax − b‖²; implement gradient descent for linear regression from scratch in numpy.  
• Resources  
  – Linear Algebra: 3Blue1Brown “Essence of Linear Algebra” videos (free)  
  – Convex Optimization, chap. 1-5 (Boyd & Vandenberghe ‑ PDF)  
  – Khan Academy multivariate calculus playlists  
  – Stanford CS230 notes “Math for ML” (Shen, Ng)  

────────────────────────
2.  Classical Machine Learning
────────────────────────
• Ideas Train/validation/test split, bias-variance, overfitting, regularization, logistic regression, SVMs, decision trees, ensemble methods.  
• Prereqs Stage 1 math + basic Python.  
• Do Compete in a Kaggle “Titanic” or “House Prices” competition; perform 5-fold CV; plot ROC curves.  
• Resources  
  – Andrew Ng’s original Coursera ML course (weeks 1-7)  
  – “Hands-On ML with Scikit-Learn, Keras, & TensorFlow,” ch. 1-2, 4-9  
  – fast.ai Machine Learning course, lessons 1-3  

────────────────────────
3.  Neural-Network Fundamentals
────────────────────────
• Ideas Neuron, activation functions, forward pass, loss functions, back-propagation (automatic differentiation), weight initialization, gradient vanishing/exploding, optimization tricks (momentum, Adam).  
• Prereqs Stage 2.  
• Do Implement a 2-layer perceptron in pure numpy to classify MNIST digits to 92%+ test accuracy.  
• Resources  
  – CS231n (Stanford) lecture 2-4 notes + assignments  
  – Deep Learning (Goodfellow et al.), chap. 6-8  
  – fast.ai Part 1, lessons 1-4 (for a high-level framework view)  

────────────────────────
4.  Regularization, Generalization & Training Engineering
────────────────────────
• Ideas Dropout, batch normalization, data augmentation, early stopping, learning-rate schedules, hyper-parameter tuning (random search, Bayesian search).  
• Prereqs Stage 3.  
• Do Push CIFAR-10 accuracy beyond a known baseline by systematic experiment tracking (e.g., using Weights & Biases).  
• Resources  
  – CS231n lecture 5-7  
  – “Neural Networks and Deep Learning” (Nielsen) chap. 6  
  – Google’s “Rules of ML” document (first 20 rules)  

────────────────────────
5.  Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
────────────────────────
• Ideas Convolutions, receptive fields, pooling, architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet).  
• Prereqs Stage 4.  
• Do Re-implement a tiny CNN from scratch; fine-tune a pre-trained ResNet on your own image dataset.  
• Resources  
  – CS231n lecture 8-11 + assignment 2  
  – fast.ai Part 1, lessons 5-7  
  – “Deep Learning for Computer Vision with PyTorch” (free book by F. Chollet — Keras code, but concepts transfer)  

────────────────────────
6.  Sequence Modeling: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs
────────────────────────
• Ideas Sequential data, teacher forcing, gradient clipping, hidden state, gated units, bidirectionality.  
• Prereqs Stage 3–4 math and back-prop familiarity.  
• Do Build an LSTM character-level language model that writes Shakespeare-like text; train a GRU for IMDB sentiment classification.  
• Resources  
  – Stanford CS224n 2021 lecture 5-9  
  – Andrej Karpathy’s “The Unreasonable Effectiveness of RNNs” blog post  
  – “Dive into Deep Learning” (Zhang et al.), chap. 8-10  

────────────────────────
7.  Attention Mechanisms & Seq2Seq
────────────────────────
• Ideas Encoder-decoder, Bahdanau & Luong attention, translation, pointer networks, coverage.  
• Prereqs Stage 6.  
• Do Translate short English→French sentences with an attention-equipped seq2seq model from scratch.  
• Resources  
  – CS224n 2021 lecture 10-12  
  – “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate” (Bahdanau et al., 2014)  
  – TensorFlow or PyTorch NMT tutorial with attention  

────────────────────────
8.  Transformers
────────────────────────
• Ideas Multi-head self-attention, positional encodings, layer normalization, residual connections, pre-training vs fine-tuning, masking, BERT, GPT, T5.  
• Prereqs Solid understanding of Stage 7 attention and matrix calculus.  
• Do (1) Re-implement scaled dot-product attention & a single Transformer block in PyTorch; (2) fine-tune BERT for question answering; (3) train a small GPT-2 on domain-specific text.  
• Resources  
  – “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al., 2017) – read with the Illustrated Transformer blog side-by-side.  
  – Hugging Face “Transformer Course” (free)  
  – CS25: Stanford “Transformers United” lecture series (R. Socher et al.)  
  – nanoGPT (Karpathy) – minimal standalone GPT training code (great for reading)  

────────────────────────
9.  Scaling & Advanced Topics  (optional specialization)
────────────────────────
• Ideas Distributed data-parallel training, mixed-precision, sparsity, MoE, retrieval-augmented generation, diffusion models, RLHF, multimodal transformers (CLIP, BLIP-2), vision transformers, graph neural nets.  
• Resources  
  – DeepSpeed & Megatron-LM tutorials; OpenAI’s Scaling Laws paper  
  – Berkeley’s “Full-Stack Deep Learning” course  
  – Annotated diffusion models (Yang Song’s notes)  

────────────────────────
10.  MLOps, Ethics & Deployment
────────────────────────
• Ideas Model serving (ONNX, TorchServe), monitoring drift, reproducibility, fairness, privacy (federated learning, differential privacy).  
• Prereqs Any stage after 4.  
• Resources  
  – “Machine Learning Design Patterns” (Lakshmanan et al.)  
  – “Practical MLOps” (Noah Gift)  
  – “Responsible AI” docs by Google, Microsoft  

────────────────────────
Study Tactics & Time Allocation
────────────────────────
• Parallelize wisely: you can learn basic math, Python and classical ML together; but don’t start transformers until you can derive and implement back-prop on paper.  
• Projects > passive learning.  Allocate ≥50 % of time to coding, debugging, visualizing.  
• Build a portfolio: post each stage’s best notebook on GitHub; write short blog explains; enter small Kaggle or PapersWithCode contests.  
• Reading papers: after Stage 6 pick one seminal paper/month; use the “reproduce & explain” method.  
• Community: join a study group (Discord, fast.ai forums, or local meet-up); teaching others cements knowledge.  

Follow this ladder, be relentless about hands-on practice, and you’ll move from dot-products to state-of-the-art transformers with conceptual clarity and practical skill.

instruction: Write a complete Python program to archive files in a specified folder into separate zip files on Linux.
output:
Below is a self-contained Python 3 program that will create one .zip file for every regular file found in a specified directory.  The script is written for Linux (works the same on any POSIX-like system) and relies only on the Python standard library.

Save the code as, e.g.,  zip_each.py, make it executable (chmod +x zip_each.py) or run it with python3 zip_each.py …​

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
zip_each.py –- Archive every file in a directory into its own ZIP file.

Usage
=====
  python3 zip_each.py SOURCE_DIR [options]

Positional arguments
--------------------
  SOURCE_DIR            Directory that contains the files to archive.

Options
-------
  -o, --output DIR      Destination directory for the created .zip files.
                        (Default: SOURCE_DIR)
  -r, --recursive       Recurse into sub-directories.
  -f, --force           Overwrite existing .zip files that have the same name.
  -v, --verbose         Print progress information.

Example
-------
  # Zip every file in ~/Downloads into ~/archives, scanning sub-folders too
  python3 zip_each.py ~/Downloads --output ~/archives --recursive
"""

import argparse
import os
import sys
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path


def zip_single_file(src_path: Path, dst_zip: Path, overwrite: bool = False) -> None:
    """
    Create a ZIP file containing a single source file.

    Parameters
    ----------
    src_path : pathlib.Path
        File that will be archived.
    dst_zip : pathlib.Path
        Path to the resulting .zip file.
    overwrite : bool
        If False (default) the function raises FileExistsError when the
        destination ZIP already exists; if True it is replaced.
    """
    mode = "w" if overwrite else "x"   # "x" = exclusive creation
    with zipfile.ZipFile(dst_zip, mode, compression=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zf:
        # The file is stored in the ZIP by its base name (no directories inside)
        zf.write(src_path, arcname=src_path.name)


def collect_files(root: Path, recursive: bool) -> list[Path]:
    """
    Return a list of all regular files inside *root*.

    Parameters
    ----------
    root : pathlib.Path
        Directory to scan.
    recursive : bool
        If True walk sub-directories; otherwise look at the top level only.
    """
    if recursive:
        files = [Path(dirpath) / file
                 for dirpath, _, filenames in os.walk(root)
                 for file in filenames]
    else:
        files = [p for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_file()]

    return files


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter,
        description=__doc__.split("Usage")[0].strip()
    )
    parser.add_argument("source", help="Directory whose files will be archived.")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", metavar="DIR",
                        help="Where to put the resulting ZIPs (default: SOURCE).")
    parser.add_argument("-r", "--recursive", action="store_true",
                        help="Recurse into sub-directories.")
    parser.add_argument("-f", "--force", action="store_true",
                        help="Overwrite existing ZIP files.")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true",
                        help="Show progress.")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    src_dir = Path(args.source).expanduser().resolve()
    if not src_dir.is_dir():
        parser.error(f"Source directory '{src_dir}' does not exist or is not a directory.")

    out_dir = Path(args.output).expanduser().resolve() if args.output else src_dir
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    # Gather the files to process
    files_to_zip = collect_files(src_dir, args.recursive)

    if not files_to_zip:
        print("No files found – nothing to do.")
        return

    for src_file in files_to_zip:
        # Determine where the ZIP file will be written
        if args.recursive and src_file.parent != src_dir:
            # Mirror the sub-directory structure in the output path
            rel_subdir = src_file.parent.relative_to(src_dir)
            zip_path = out_dir / rel_subdir / f"{src_file.name}.zip"
            zip_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        else:
            zip_path = out_dir / f"{src_file.name}.zip"

        if args.verbose:
            print(f"{src_file}  →  {zip_path}")

        try:
            zip_single_file(src_file, zip_path, overwrite=args.force)
        except FileExistsError:
            print(f"Skip (already exists): {zip_path}", file=sys.stderr)
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"FAILED: {src_file}  →  {exc}", file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

How it works
------------
1. The script parses command-line arguments with argparse.
2. It gathers all regular files inside the source directory (optionally walking sub-directories).
3. For each file it builds an output path `filename.zip` (replicating the sub-folder hierarchy when `-r` is used).
4. It creates a new ZIP file (`zipfile.ZipFile` with `ZIP_DEFLATED` compression) that contains exactly that one file.
5. Optional flags let you overwrite existing ZIPs (`-f`) and display progress messages (`-v`).

instruction: I have a backup of my Linux Mint system from last month in a set of .gz (zipped tar) files. What arguments can I use with tar to update any files that have changed, without re-archiving unchanged files?
output:
tar has an “update” function (-u or --update) that will look inside an existing archive and only append files whose copy on the disk is newer-than (or missing from) the one already stored.  
Syntax (for an uncompressed archive):

    tar -uvf backup.tar  /path/you/want/to/save …

where  
 -u  (--update)  = append only newer / missing files  
 -v             = verbose (optional)  
 -f             = name of tar archive to act on  

The catch: tar cannot modify a compressed archive in place.  
Therefore, with a *.tar.gz you must:

    gunzip  backup.tar.gz                # 1. un-compress the archive
    tar -uvf backup.tar  / …             # 2. run the update
    gzip  backup.tar                     # 3. re-compress it

If you would rather avoid unpack-update-repack each time, use tar’s
incremental mode instead and keep the old archive untouched:

    tar -cvzf mint-`date +%F`.tar.gz \
        --listed-incremental=/var/backups/mint.snar  /

The first run (no mint.snar yet) makes a full backup; subsequent runs
write only the files that have changed since the last run, creating small
“incremental” archives.

Summary  
• To “update” an archive in place:  -u (or -r to append regardless of
  date) – but the archive must be uncompressed.  
• For compressed archives keep the original .tar.gz, unpack it, update,
  and compress again, or switch to incremental backups with
  --listed-incremental.

instruction:
Given a binary array 'nums', you are required to find the maximum length of a contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.

Explanation:

A binary array is an array that contains only 0s and 1s.
A subarray is any subset of the indices of the original array.
A contiguous subarray is a subarray in which all the elements are consecutive, i.e., any element between the first and last element of the subarray is also part of it.
Examples:
Input :nums = [0, 1]
Output : 2
Explanation: The longest contiguous subarray with an equal number of 0s and 1s is [0, 1] with a length of 2.
Input : nums = [0, 1, 0]
Output : 2
Explanation: The longest contiguous subarray with an equal number of 0s and 1s is either [0, 1] or [1, 0], both with a length of 2.
Input : nums = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]
Output : 6
Explanation: The longest contiguous subarray with an equal number of 0s and 1s is [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1] with a length of 6.
The problem requires finding the maximum length of a contiguous subarray in the binary array 'nums' that contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.
output:
Solution Idea  
Turn the array into a running “balance” between the number of 1s and 0s you have seen so far:

• Read 1 as  +1  
• Read 0 as  –1  

If two positions i and j ( i < j ) have the same running balance, the segment (i + 1 … j) must contain exactly the same amount of 0s and 1s, because everything that happened between i and j did not change the balance.

So:

1. Walk once through the array, updating a prefix-sum (=balance).  
2. Remember, in a hash table, the first index at which each balance value occurs.  
3. Whenever the same balance is seen again, compute the distance to that first index – that distance is the length of a balanced subarray.  
4. Keep the maximum of those distances.

Implementation  
• Time-complexity: O(n)  
• Space-complexity: O(n) – the hash table of first-seen balances.

Python code

```python
def findMaxLength(nums):
    first_index = {0: -1}          # balance 0 is seen before the array starts
    balance = 0
    best = 0

    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        balance += 1 if num == 1 else -1

        if balance in first_index:
            best = max(best, i - first_index[balance])
        else:
            first_index[balance] = i

    return best
```

Examples  

```
findMaxLength([0,1])                 -> 2
findMaxLength([0,1,0])               -> 2
findMaxLength([0,0,0,1,1,1])         -> 6
```

The algorithm reports 2, 2, 6 respectively, matching the required results.

instruction:
Help me solve the following qn. Please provide a intuitive easy to understand step by step solution:

Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays.
output:
Step–by–step, from the most naïve idea to the “text-book” O(log (min(m,n))) solution.

────────────────────────
1.  What is a median?
────────────────────────
• If a collection has odd length → the middle number after sorting.
• If it has even length → the average of the two middle numbers.

So for the combined list of size  m+n :
    middle index (0-based) = (m+n-1)/2   (if total is odd)
    two middle indices       = (m+n)/2 –1  and (m+n)/2   (if total is even)

────────────────────────
2.  Slow-but-simple way (merge until the middle)
────────────────────────
Imagine the two arrays lying next to each other.  
We could “merge” them exactly like the merge step of MergeSort and stop as soon as we have produced the first ⌈(m+n)/2⌉+1 items.  
That costs O(m+n) time and O(1) extra memory, which is usually accepted in interviews if m and n are small.

Pseudo-code

    i = j = 0                 # pointers in nums1 and nums2
    prev = cur = None
    for k in range((m+n)//2 + 1):   # walk only to the middle
        prev = cur
        if j == n or (i < m and nums1[i] < nums2[j]):
            cur = nums1[i];  i += 1
        else:
            cur = nums2[j];  j += 1

    if (m+n) is odd:  return cur
    else:             return (prev + cur)/2

Why we stop early  
We never need elements past the two middle positions, so walking farther is wasted work.

Drawback → O(m+n) can be too slow if arrays are huge (e.g. 10⁶ each).

────────────────────────
3.  Fast way (binary search on the shorter array)
────────────────────────
Key observation  
Cut the two arrays somewhere so that:

    • the total number of elements on the left side = the number on the right (±1)  
    • everything on the left ≤ everything on the right

If we manage that, the median is simply:
    odd total → max(left)  
    even total → (max(left) + min(right)) / 2

Because both arrays are already sorted, the only real work is to decide *how many* items to take from the first array; the second array is then forced (it must provide the remaining left-side elements).  
“How many” can be found with a binary search → O(log(min(m,n))).

Let
    A = shorter array  (length = a)
    B = longer  array  (length = b)
    total = a + b
    leftSize = (total + 1)//2   # size of the left half; the +1 handles odd totals nicely

We binary-search a cut index i in A   (0 … a)
Then j = leftSize – i  is the matching cut in B.

Picture of the cut (‖):

        A:  …  A[i-1] ‖ A[i] …
        B:  …  B[j-1] ‖ B[j] …

We need

        A[i-1] ≤ B[j]          (1)
        B[j-1] ≤ A[i]          (2)

If (1) fails   → A[i-1] is too big -> take fewer from A → move high = i-1  
If (2) fails   → we took too few from A     → move low  = i+1  
Otherwise the cuts are perfect.

Edge handling  
If i = 0 there is no A[i-1] (use −∞).  
If i = a there is no A[i]   (use  +∞).  
Same for B and j.

Algorithm

    A, B = nums1, nums2
    if len(A) > len(B):  A, B = B, A        # A is the shorter
    a, b = len(A), len(B)
    low, high = 0, a
    leftSize = (a+b+1)//2

    while low <= high:
        i = (low+high)//2
        j = leftSize - i

        Aleft  = -inf if i == 0 else A[i-1]
        Aright =  inf if i == a else A[i]
        Bleft  = -inf if j == 0 else B[j-1]
        Bright =  inf if j == b else B[j]

        if Aleft <= Bright and Bleft <= Aright:     # perfect cut
            if (a+b) % 2:               # odd total
                return max(Aleft, Bleft)
            else:                        # even total
                return (max(Aleft,Bleft) + min(Aright,Bright)) / 2
        elif Aleft > Bright:             # too many from A, go left
            high = i - 1
        else:                            # too few from A, go right
            low  = i + 1

Time complexity  → O(log(min(m,n)))  
Space            → O(1)

────────────────────────
4.  Tiny worked example
────────────────────────
nums1 = [1, 3, 8]           (A)  
nums2 = [7, 9, 10, 11]      (B)

total = 7, leftSize = 4
Search space for i : 0 … 3

• try i=1 → j = 3
      Aleft =1,  Aright =3
      Bleft =10, Bright =11
  Aleft ≤ Bright  ✓
  Bleft ≤ Aright  ✗   (10 > 3) → i too small → move right

• try i=2 → j = 2
      Aleft =3,  Aright =8
      Bleft =9,  Bright =10
  Aleft ≤ Bright  ✓
  Bleft ≤ Aright  ✗   (9 > 8) → i too small → move right

• try i=3 → j = 1
      Aleft =8,  Aright =+∞
      Bleft =7,  Bright =9
  Both conditions now ✓

Odd total → median = max(Aleft,Bleft) = max(8,7) = 8

────────────────────────
5.  Take-aways
────────────────────────
1. Think “cut/partition” rather than “merge”.
2. Only binary search the shorter array to keep complexity O(log min).
3. Handle edges by pretending the arrays are padded with −∞/+∞.

instruction: In GAMS, assume I have s parameters which is indexed over two sets P1(A,B), and I have another one-to-one-mapping that maps exactly each element of B to each element of C. How can I create a new parameter P2(A,C) such that each value of P2 takes the mapped value from P1?

I have a set of examples (that is assignments of $n$ variables $x_1 ... x_n$ that are labeled as solution (+) or non-solution (-). The goal is to find the minimum subset of variables in  $x_1 ... x_n$  such that it is possible to split between (+) and (-) by seeing only theses variables.
output:
Let  

 E = {e1 , … , em }, ei = (ei1 , … , ein ) , yi ∈ {+, –}  

be the sample.  
A subset of indices S ⊆ {1,…,n} “works” if by looking only at the
coordinates in S every positive example can be distinguished from every
negative one, i.e.  

 ∀ ei , ej with yi = + , yj = – ∃ k ∈ S : eik ≠ ejk.        (1)

Equivalently: for every (+,–)-pair at least one of the chosen variables
takes different values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Reformulation as a Hitting-Set / Set-Cover problem
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For every conflicting pair (i , j) with yi = +, yj = – define  

 Dij = { k | eik ≠ ejk } ⊆ {1,…,n}.                 (the variables that
                                                    separate this pair)

Condition (1) says that S must “hit’’ every set Dij:

 ∀ (i , j) : S ∩ Dij ≠ ∅.

So we have the classic minimum hitting-set problem:

 Minimise |S|  
 subject to S hits all sets Dij .

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Complexity
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Minimum hitting set (== minimum set cover) is NP-hard and cannot be
approximated better than O(log m) unless P = NP.  
Therefore an exact, polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary data is not
expected.  Two classes of algorithms are normally used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Exact algorithms (when n or m is small)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.1  Complete enumeration  
 for k = 1 … n  
  for every subset S of size k  
   if (1) holds return S.

Time: O(2^n · m^2) in the worst case (because there are ≈m^2 conflicting
pairs), but feasible when n ≤ 30–35.

3.2  Integer Linear Programming  
Introduce binary variable zk for each attribute k.

 min  Σk zk  
 s.t. Σk∈Dij zk  ≥ 1     for every (+,–) pair (i , j)  
 zk ∈ {0,1}.

Feed this ILP to any solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, CBC…).  Branch-and-bound
with cutting planes often solves instances with hundreds of variables
quickly if the data are not too pathological.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Approximate (polynomial) algorithms
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Greedy Set-Cover (Johnson 1974):

 U ← set of all (+,–) pairs not yet separated  
 S ← ∅  
 while U ≠ ∅  
  pick attribute k that separates the largest number of pairs in U  
  S ← S ∪ {k}  
  remove from U all pairs separated by k  
 return S.

This runs in O(n·|U|) and is guaranteed to pick at most  
⌈ ln |U| ⌉ + 1 times as many attributes as the optimum.

Other heuristics used in feature-selection and rough-set literature:
• hill climbing / forward–backward elimination  
• genetic algorithms, simulated annealing  
• hit-set specific local search (Chvátal, 1979).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Connection with Rough-Set Theory
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The problem is identical to finding a minimum “reduct’’ of an
information system.  The discernibility matrix of Pawlak is exactly the
collection {Dij}.  All results above (NP-hardness, greedy approximation,
ILP formulations) were obtained independently in that community as
well.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Simple pseudocode for the test “does a subset S work?”
--------------------------------------------------------------------
works(S):
 for each positive ei  
  for each negative ej  
   if ei and ej coincide on all k ∈ S  →  return false  
 return true

Running this test is O(|S|·(#pos)·(#neg)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Reduce the data set to the collection of differing attributes for each
  (+,–) pair.  
• The minimum separating subset of variables is the minimum
  hitting-set of these collections.  
• Finding it exactly is NP-hard; use exhaustive search or ILP for small
  instances, greedy or other heuristics for large ones.

instruction: You are a data scientist, output a Python script in OOP for a contextual multi armed bandit sampling from 3 models
output:
```python
"""
Contextual multi-armed bandit (CMAB) demo in pure Python.

We have three “models” (arms).  
Each arm generates a reward that is a noisy linear function of the
context.  
The learner does NOT know the arm parameters in advance and must learn
online which arm to pull for every context.

Learner = Contextual Thompson Sampling (one Bayesian linear regression
per arm).

Author : <your name>
"""

from __future__ import annotations
import abc
import numpy as np
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Tuple


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#  ENVIRONMENT
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class Arm:
    """
    One arm / model in the environment.
    The true reward is  x · w  +  N(0, σ²)
    """

    def __init__(self, name: str, weight: np.ndarray, noise_std: float = 0.1):
        """
        weight : (d,) latent coefficient vector
        """
        self.name = name
        self._w = weight.reshape(-1, 1)          # column vector
        self._noise_std = noise_std

    def draw(self, context: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Sample a reward for a given context.
        """
        mean = float(context @ self._w)          # scalar
        reward = np.random.normal(mean, self._noise_std)
        return reward

    # --- purely for inspection ------------------------------------------------
    @property
    def weight(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._w.flatten()


class ContextualBandit:
    """
    The simulator that provides a new context and a reward every round.
    """

    def __init__(self, arms: List[Arm], ctx_dim: int, ctx_sampler=None):
        self.arms = arms
        self.K = len(arms)
        self.d = ctx_dim

        # Context distribution – can be replaced by any callable
        if ctx_sampler is None:
            self._ctx_sampler = lambda: np.random.uniform(-1, 1, self.d)
        else:
            self._ctx_sampler = ctx_sampler

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def get_context(self) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Returns a fresh context vector x   shape (d,)
        """
        return self._ctx_sampler()

    def pull(self, arm_index: int, context: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Execute the chosen arm and return the realised reward.
        """
        return self.arms[arm_index].draw(context)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#  POLICIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class Policy(abc.ABC):
    """
    Abstract base class for CMAB policies.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_arms: int, context_dim: int):
        self.K = n_arms
        self.d = context_dim

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def choose(self, context: np.ndarray) -> int:
        """
        Return the index of the arm to pull.
        """

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def update(self, arm_index: int, context: np.ndarray, reward: float):
        """
        Observe (x, a, r) and update internal state.
        """


class ContextualThompsonSampling(Policy):
    """
    Thompson Sampling with a separate Bayesian linear regression model
    per arm (a.k.a. “Linear Thompson Sampling”).
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        n_arms: int,
        context_dim: int,
        v: float = 1.0,               # exploration parameter
        lambda_prior: float = 1.0,    # ridge / prior precision
    ):
        super().__init__(n_arms, context_dim)

        self.v = v

        # Posterior parameters for each arm:
        #   A_a  =  XᵀX + λ I      (d × d)
        #   b_a  =  Xᵀy            (d × 1)
        self.A = [lambda_prior * np.eye(self.d) for _ in range(self.K)]
        self.b = [np.zeros((self.d, 1)) for _ in range(self.K)]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def choose(self, context: np.ndarray) -> int:
        """
        Sample θ_a ~ N(Â⁻¹ b, v² Â⁻¹)  and pick argmax xᵀ θ_a
        """
        x = context.reshape(-1, 1)
        sampled_values = []

        for a in range(self.K):
            A_inv = np.linalg.inv(self.A[a])
            mu = A_inv @ self.b[a]                       # posterior mean
            cov = (self.v ** 2) * A_inv

            theta = np.random.multivariate_normal(
                mean=mu.flatten(), cov=cov
            ).reshape(-1, 1)
            sampled_values.append(float(x.T @ theta))

        return int(np.argmax(sampled_values))

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def update(self, arm_index: int, context: np.ndarray, reward: float):
        """
        Bayesian linear regression update.
        """
        x = context.reshape(-1, 1)
        a = arm_index

        self.A[a] += x @ x.T
        self.b[a] += reward * x


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#  DRIVER
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@dataclass
class RoundOutcome:
    t: int
    arm: int
    reward: float
    cumulative_reward: float


def run_bandit(
    bandit: ContextualBandit,
    policy: Policy,
    n_rounds: int,
) -> List[RoundOutcome]:
    """
    Play `n_rounds` of the bandit and return the trajectory.
    """
    history: List[RoundOutcome] = []
    cum_reward = 0.0

    for t in range(1, n_rounds + 1):
        x_t = bandit.get_context()
        a_t = policy.choose(x_t)
        r_t = bandit.pull(a_t, x_t)

        policy.update(a_t, x_t, r_t)

        cum_reward += r_t
        history.append(RoundOutcome(t, a_t, r_t, cum_reward))

    return history


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#  MAIN (demo)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(0)

    D = 5                     # context dimension
    K = 3                     # number of models/arms
    N_ROUNDS = 5_000

    # Create three arms with random latent weights
    arms = [
        Arm("Model-A", weight=np.random.randn(D), noise_std=0.3),
        Arm("Model-B", weight=np.random.randn(D), noise_std=0.3),
        Arm("Model-C", weight=np.random.randn(D), noise_std=0.3),
    ]

    env = ContextualBandit(arms, ctx_dim=D)

    learner = ContextualThompsonSampling(
        n_arms=K,
        context_dim=D,
        v=0.2,               # smaller = greedier
        lambda_prior=1.0,
    )

    # Run the online interaction
    trajectory = run_bandit(env, learner, N_ROUNDS)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #  Quick analytics
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    final_score = trajectory[-1].cumulative_reward
    pulls_per_arm = np.bincount([o.arm for o in trajectory], minlength=K)

    print("\n=== finished ===")
    print(f"Total reward collected : {final_score:,.2f}")
    for k, arm in enumerate(arms):
        print(
            f"Arm {k}  ({arm.name}) was chosen {pulls_per_arm[k]} times. "
            f"True weight = {arm.weight}"
        )
```

How to use the script
---------------------
Simply run:

    python contextual_bandit.py

You should see the learner increasingly favour the arm whose hidden
weight vector produces the highest expected reward given the contexts.

Extending / customizing
-----------------------
• Replace `Arm.draw` with any reward mechanism (e.g., accuracy of a
  real ML model on live data).  
• Implement new policies by inheriting from `Policy` and overriding
  `choose` and `update` (e.g., Lin-UCB, ε-greedy).  
• Swap in your own context generator via the `ctx_sampler` argument of
  `ContextualBandit`.

instruction: What is the most successful go to market strategy for a managed services business?
output:
There isn’t a single, one-size-fits-all “silver bullet,” but when you study the MSPs and broader managed-services firms that reach $10 M-$100 M ARR fastest, their go-to-market (GTM) playbooks share the same backbone. Below is that backbone distilled into a practical, step-by-step strategy you can adapt to your geography, technical focus, and growth stage.

────────────────────────
1. Nail the WHERE and the WHO
────────────────────────
A. Hyper-specific Ideal Customer Profile (ICP)
   • Revenue band & IT maturity: e.g., 50-500 employees, no in-house CISO, cloud-first posture.  
   • Vertical pains: healthcare (HIPAA compliance), legal (data-loss prevention), manufacturing (OT/IoT uptime).  
   • Psychographics: CFO/COO hates unpredictable cap-ex; IT director drowning in tickets.  
   • Buying triggers: merger, cyber-insurance renewal, Microsoft EA expiration, recent breach.

B. Choose 1–2 beach-head verticals
   Depth beats breadth—“We secure 200-bed regional hospitals” resonates far more than “We do managed services for anyone.” The specialization reduces CAC, increases ASP, and fuels referrals.

────────────────────────
2. Package and Price for Recurring Revenue
────────────────────────
A. Productize, don’t “menu-ize”
   • Good / Better / Best bundles tied to outcomes (not tasks):  
     – Essentials: 24×7 monitoring + patching + help desk SLA.  
     – Professional: Essentials + security stack + compliance reporting.  
     – Premium: Pro + vCIO/vCISO + DRaaS + quarterly roadmap.  

B. Land & Expand entry offers
   • Low-friction assessment (security gap analysis, cloud cost audit) priced low or free → converts 25-40 % to full MSP contract in 90 days.

C. Value-based pricing
   • Peg to seats, workloads, or device count with thresholds—easy for the CFO to model and for you to scale.

────────────────────────
3. Build a Two-Track Demand Engine
────────────────────────
Track 1: Inbound / Thought-Leadership
   • Content hubs for EACH vertical: playbooks, compliance checklists, breach post-mortems.  
   • SEO around “HIPAA managed SOC,” “NIST 800-171 MSP,” etc.  
   • Webinars with ISVs (Microsoft, Fortinet) to borrow their brand and MDF (market-development funds).  
   • Paid LinkedIn ads targeted to job titles in ICP + retargeting.

Track 2: Outbound / ABM (Account-Based Marketing)
   • 200-to-300 named accounts per sales pod.  
   • 12-touch, 30-day sequences (email + LinkedIn + phone) keyed to a trigger: “Your cyber-insurance premium is rising 40 %—here’s why.”  
   • Physical lumpy-mail or invite-only C-suite dinners to move Tier-1 prospects.

────────────────────────
4. Leverage the Channel (Co-Sell and Marketplaces)
────────────────────────
A. Cloud marketplaces (AWS, Azure, GCP)  
   • List your packaged managed service; transact on your partners’ paper so procurement friction vanishes.  

B. Technology Alliance Programs  
   • Microsoft Solution Partner, Cisco Partner, CrowdStrike Elevate, etc. earn you leads, MDF, and credibility.

C. VAR & Boutique Integrator partnerships  
   • Offer white-label NOC/SOC to smaller VARs → you grab scale, they retain customer.

────────────────────────
5. Run a Consultative, Process-Driven Sales Motion
────────────────────────
Stage 1 – Discovery: 30-minute exec call → document business risks, not firewalls.  
Stage 2 – Assessment/pilot: fixed-fee or free, automated tooling produces board-ready gap report.  
Stage 3 – Roadmap & ROI: vCIO workshop converts findings to 12-month managed-service plan (TCO vs. DIY).  
Stage 4 – Close: 36-month MSA with auto-renew, CPI escalator, and project change-order template baked in.

KPIs to watch
   • First-meeting-to-demo rate ≥ 60 %  
   • Assessment-to-MSA close rate ≥ 30 %  
   • Average contract term > 30 months  
   • Gross margin > 50 % on recurring dollars

────────────────────────
6. Obsess over Onboarding & Customer Success
────────────────────────
A. 30-60-90-day onboarding runbook: asset discovery, tool deployment, user comms, executive checkpoint.  
B. Dedicated CSM or vCIO holds QBRs aligned to business outcomes (e.g., “reduced MFA push fraud by 78 %”).  
C. NPS campaign at day 120 → identify advocates → feed referral loop and case studies.

────────────────────────
7. Expand, Upsell, and Renew
────────────────────────
• Attach advanced security (MDR, XDR, Zero-Trust), cloud FinOps, or modern workplace add-ons at QBRs.  
• Aim for net revenue retention (NRR) > 110 %.  
• 6 months pre-renewal, trigger multi-year renewal bundle with price-lock + new feature roadmap.

────────────────────────
8. Measure, Iterate, and Automate
────────────────────────
Core Metrics: MRR growth, CAC payback < 12 months, logo churn < 8 %, service desk CSAT > 95 %.  
Tooling: HubSpot or Salesforce + MSP-specific PSA (ConnectWise, Kaseya, Halo) for data hygiene.  
Quarterly GTM retrospectives to drop low-yield verticals, shift MDF, and tweak bundles.

────────────────────────
Key Takeaways
────────────────────────
1. Specialize—vertical + outcome positioning wins over generic “IT outsourcing.”  
2. Productize—recurring, easy-to-buy bundles beat bespoke SOWs.  
3. Dual engine—inbound thought-leadership plus targeted outbound keeps pipeline balanced.  
4. Partner up—cloud marketplaces and vendor programs shorten sales cycles and elevate trust.  
5. Land & expand—low-risk entry offers drive fast closes; QBRs and CSMs fuel long-term margin.

Follow these principles, adapt the details to your market, and you’ll be using the same fundamentals the fastest-growing MSPs rely on to reach 20 %+ year-over-year recurring-revenue growth with healthy margins.

Overall impression  
The function is short, easy to follow and avoids delay(), so it is already better than many “first day” Arduino sketches.  
Nevertheless you can do a little better on three axes that matter in a small-MCU project:

1. Correctness / robustness (especially with the millis() timer)  
2. Readability / maintainability  
3. Code size and execution speed (they usually improve together)

The remarks below are deliberately “micro” because the function is small; each point shaves a few bytes or a few cycles or makes the intent clearer.

──────────────────────────────────
1. Timer handling
──────────────────────────────────
• Use the canonical “subtraction” idiom to make the code immune to the 49-day
  millis() roll-over:

    if ((millis() - lastChange) >= intervalAbs) { … }

  where intervalAbs is the positive (unsigned) delay.  
  That works even when millis() wraps to 0 because unsigned subtraction is well
  defined.

• Accept the delay as a signed value only to find the direction.  
  After that, store its absolute value in an unsigned long so the compiler does
  not insert sign-extension code on every comparison.

──────────────────────────────────
2. Index arithmetic
──────────────────────────────────
Modulo arithmetic is shorter and clearer than the if cascade:

    currIndex = (currIndex + direction + nOutPins) % nOutPins;

No separate nextIndex variable is needed; you can compute it after currIndex is
updated or drive the “old” and “new” pin directly in two statements.

──────────────────────────────────
3. Drive only the pins that change
──────────────────────────────────
You currently loop over every LED at every step.  
If there are many outputs, that adds latency and code size.  
Only two LEDs actually change state:

    digitalWrite(outPins[currIndex], LOW);      // old one off
    currIndex = (currIndex + direction + nOutPins) % nOutPins;
    digitalWrite(outPins[currIndex], HIGH);     // new one on

(The order LOW then HIGH avoids a brief moment when both LEDs are on, but you
 can swap it if you want the opposite visual effect.)

──────────────────────────────────
4. Avoid recomputing nOutPins
──────────────────────────────────
`nOutPins` depends only on the static array; compute it once at file scope:

    const uint8_t nOutPins = sizeof(outPins) / sizeof(outPins[0]);

`uint8_t` is enough for up to 255 pins and saves a couple of bytes per
instruction that uses it.

──────────────────────────────────
5. Types and names
──────────────────────────────────
• Use `size_t` or `uint8_t` for indexes, `int8_t` for the direction, and
  `uint32_t`/`unsigned long` for millis values.

• The function name suggests forward motion only (“cycleLEDs”).  
  If reverse motion (-interval) is important, a name like
  `stepChaser(int signedIntervalMs)` may convey that better.

• Add a short Doxygen-style comment that states “positive interval ⇒ clockwise,
  negative ⇒ counter-clockwise; magnitude ⇒ milliseconds per step”.

──────────────────────────────────
6. Resulting code
──────────────────────────────────
//  Assumes `outPins[]` is a global pin list
const uint8_t nOutPins = sizeof(outPins) / sizeof(outPins[0]);

void cycleLEDs(int interval)
{
    static uint32_t lastChange = 0;
    static uint8_t  currIndex  = 0;

    int8_t   direction    = (interval < 0) ? -1 : 1;
    uint32_t delayMs      = (interval < 0) ? -interval : interval;

    if ((millis() - lastChange) >= delayMs)
    {
        // turn OFF the current LED
        digitalWrite(outPins[currIndex], LOW);

        // advance index with wrap-around
        currIndex = (currIndex + direction + nOutPins) % nOutPins;

        // turn ON the next LED
        digitalWrite(outPins[currIndex], HIGH);

        lastChange = millis();
    }
}

Compared with the original, this version

• is a few dozen bytes smaller (no loop, fewer temporaries)  
• executes faster (two digitalWrites instead of nOutPins)  
• is rollover-safe  
• has one place where the wrap-around logic lives, thus less chance for error

──────────────────────────────────
7. If even more speed/size is needed
──────────────────────────────────
• Keep track of the current LED level in a byte and use direct port
  manipulation (`PORTx`, `bitSet`, `bitClear`) instead of digitalWrite().  
  That removes the function-call overhead of digitalWrite() and can let you
  drive all LEDs in one instruction with a bitfield.

• Precompute the pin masks for each step and just write them to the port.

For most hobby projects the version shown in section 6 is already small,
readable and “tight” enough.

`ledAny()` receives a pointer to a DigitalOut object:

```cpp
void ledAny (DigitalOut *ledA)
```

Inside the function you dereference that pointer and pass the object itself to `printf()`:

```cpp
printf("My pointer is %p\n", *ledA);   // <-- wrong
```

`%p` expects a pointer (a `void *`).  
`*ledA` is **not** a pointer, it is the `DigitalOut` object that the
pointer refers to, so the types don’t match and you will either get a
compiler error or undefined behaviour.

Replace the line with one that actually passes the pointer:

```cpp
printf("My pointer is %p\n", ledA);               // OK – prints address
// or, explicitly:
printf("My pointer is %p\n", static_cast<void*>(ledA));
```

(If you wanted to print the pin’s logic value you would use
`ledA->read()`.)

That single-character change fixes the issue.

instruction: Is there an early stop out method (to control for multiple testing problem in hypothesis tests) for a dataset with initial probabilities of passing. For example, I have a set of financial market strategies with initial probability of skill using the probabilistic sharpe ratio. I want to test these strategies for a different dataset but I also want to control for multiple testing. Testing all available strategies will lead to multiple testing problems. So, I only want to test a subset of my strategies. Is there an early stop-out method for this application?
output:
Yes.  In the multiple-testing literature there are several “sequential” or “ordered” procedures that let you work through the hypotheses one-by-one, stop as soon as it is no longer worthwhile, and still keep the agreed‐upon family-wise error rate (FWER) or false-discovery rate (FDR) under control.  
The idea is very simple:

1.  Put the strategies in a fixed order before you look at the second data set.  
   •  In your case a natural ordering is decreasing “prior credibility”, e.g. the
      Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR) you estimated on the first sample.  

2.  Walk through the ordered list and “spend” a little of your overall type-I error
    budget α every time you test a hypothesis on the new data.  
    •  If you reject the null for that strategy, you may continue;  
    •  if you fail to reject (i.e. the p-value is too large), you stop and do not look at the
      remaining strategies.  

Because the order is fixed in advance, you can adjust the individual α-levels so that the overall error control is guaranteed even though you may stop early.  Below are the most commonly used variants.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Fixed-sequence procedure (controls FWER)

Let the ordered p-values be p(1), p(2), … , p(m).  
Choose the per-test levels  

          α(1)=α,           α(2)=α,           …,  α(m)=α

and test consecutively.  **The moment you encounter p(i)>α(i) you stop.**  
Since no further tests are performed, strong FWER control at level α is retained (Maurer & Bretz, 2013).  Although simple, this already gives you an “early stop-out”, because the procedure ends as soon as the first candidate fails.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Holm / weighted-Holm step-down (FWER)

A slightly more powerful rule is to tighten the thresholds as you go down the list:

          α(1)=α/m ,  α(2)=α/(m−1), … ,  α(m)=α.

If the hypotheses are ordered by credibility you can combine this with *weights* wi that encode the PSR evidence (Genovese, Roeder & Wasserman, 2006):

          α(i)=wi·α/∑j≥i wj.

Again you test in that order and stop at the first non-rejection.  Holm’s step-down procedure guarantees FWER ≤ α, while the weights let you devote more type-I error to strategies that looked better ex-ante.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Alpha-investing / alpha-spending rules (controls FDR or mFDR)

Foster & Stine (2008) introduced “alpha-investing” for exactly the situation in which hypotheses arrive sequentially and we may never get through the whole list.  You start with an “α-wealth” W0=α.  
For the ith test you decide on a stake γi ≤ Wi-1, perform the test at level γi, and then

    Wi = Wi-1 − γi + R_i·κ,

where Ri=1 if you rejected, 0 otherwise, and κ is a reward parameter (≤ γi) that you collect when you discover a real effect.  As long as Wi stays non-negative you can keep testing; once it hits zero you must stop.  The rule guarantees mFDR ≤ α while letting you “earn back” error budget whenever you find a truly skilled strategy.

Ramdas et al. (2018) give easier “alpha-spending with rewards” formulas and software (R package ‘sae’ and Python package ‘alphainvesting’).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Select‐decision two-stage methods (“replicability” control)

If you want to *select* a subset with the first sample and *confirm* them with a second sample, procedures by Bogomolov & Heller (2013), Benjamini & Bogomolov (2014) or the more recent AdaPT algorithm (Lei & Fithian, 2018) guarantee that the FWER/FDR among *discoveries that replicate* is controlled:

    a) Use the first sample to form scores (PSR) and pick the k most promising
       strategies.  
    b) Apply a multiplicity correction on this reduced family only, but adjust the
       thresholds to account for the fact that selection was data-driven.

For example, if k strategies out of m were forwarded, a simple Bonferroni level
α/k in the confirmation stage keeps the *family-wise* error over the two stages ≤ α.
More powerful weighted or empirical-Bayes versions exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
How you would implement it in practice
--------------------------------------
Assume you have m=200 candidate trading rules.

1.  Compute the PSR for each rule on a pre-2000 data set and order the rules
    from highest to lowest PSR.

2.  Pick a procedure:

    •  Want simple, strong FWER control? Use fixed-sequence or weighted Holm.  
    •  Willing to tolerate a few false discoveries and want more power? Use
      alpha-investing to control (modified) FDR.  
    •  Prefer a strict two-stage “discover-and-replicate” paradigm? Use a selection
      method followed by Bonferroni/BH on the confirmatory sample.

3.  Start testing on the 2000-2024 data set in the pre-committed order.
    Stop automatically as soon as the rule dictated by the chosen procedure tells you to.

Because you never even look at the p-values of the rules that come after the first non-rejection (or after your alpha-wealth runs out), those tests do not inflate your error rate.  Hence you have a principled, statistically valid “early stop-out” mechanism that saves you from evaluating every single strategy on the new sample.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
References (starting points)

•  Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure.  
•  Foster, D. P., & Stine, R. A. (2008). α-investing. JASA, 103(482).  
•  Genovese, C., Roeder, K., & Wasserman, L. (2006). False discovery control with p-value weighting. Biometrika.  
•  Bogomolov, M., & Heller, R. (2013). Discovering findings that replicate. Biometrika.  
•  Ramdas, A. et al. (2018). SAFFRON: an adaptive procedure for FDR control on streams.  
•  Lei, L., & Fithian, W. (2018). AdaPT: An interactive procedure for multiple testing…  

Any of the above gives you a statistically sound way to test only a subset of your strategies while keeping the multiple-testing problem under control.

instruction: Give me a recipe for making 5L of strawberry and blackberry melomel. Use metric measurements.
output:
Strawberry & Blackberry Melomel  
Batch size: 5 L (finished volume)  
Target ABV: ~11–12 %  
Fermentation temperature: 18-22 °C  
Style: Still or lightly sparkling (your choice at bottling)

INGREDIENTS  

Fermentables & fruit  
• Wild-flower or clover honey – 1.35 kg  
  (gives ~110 g fermentable sugars / L; OG ≈ 1.090)  
• Strawberries (frozen or fresh, hulled) – 900 g  
• Blackberries (frozen or fresh) – 900 g  

Adjuncts  
• Water (de-chlorinated) – to 5 L total must volume  
• Yeast nutrient – 4 g (DAP-based or Fermaid-O)  
• Pectic enzyme – 2 g (prevents haze)  
• Potassium metabisulfite (campden) – 1 × 0.44 g tablet, crushed (optional but recommended for fruit sanitising)  
• Potassium sorbate – 2 g (only if backsweetening)  
• Acid blend (citric/malic/tartaric) – 1–3 g to taste after fermentation (optional)  

Yeast  
• Lalvin 71B-1122 (Narbonne) – 5 g rehydrated  
  (Fruit-friendly, good ester profile, metabolises some malic acid)  

EQUIPMENT  

• 10 L stock pot or saucepan  
• 6–7 L food-grade fermenter (PET carboy or glass demijohn) with airlock  
• Fine-mesh bag or nylon “brew bag” for fruit  
• Hydrometer & test jar (or refractometer)  
• Kitchen scale, thermometer, siphon/racking cane  
• Sanitiser (e.g., Star-San / Chemipro)  
• Bottles (still: wine bottles + corker; sparkling: flip-top beer bottles or champagne bottles)  

DAY-BY-DAY PROCESS  

1) Fruit prep (Day -1 to 0)  
   • If using frozen fruit, simply thaw in a sanitised bowl; freezing ruptures cells for better juice release.  
   • If using fresh fruit, wash, hull/cap berries, cut large berries in half, then freeze overnight and thaw.  
   • OPTIONAL sulphite: Dissolve the crushed campden tablet in 50 mL warm water, pour over fruit, cover, and rest 12 h. This suppresses wild microbes.  

2) Must creation (Brew Day, Day 0)  
   a) Warm 2 L of water to ~45 °C, turn off heat, stir in all honey until dissolved (do NOT boil honey—aroma loss).  
   b) Add room-temp water to make 4.5 L. Check temperature; it should be <30 °C.  
   c) Measure OG (target ≈1.088–1.094). Adjust with more honey or water if needed.  
   d) Add 4 g yeast nutrient, stir to aerate.  
   e) Place fruit in sanitised mesh bag; tie off and submerge in the must.  
   f) Add pectic enzyme (2 g) and stir gently. Wait 6–12 h if you sulphited; otherwise proceed.  

3) Yeast pitch (Day 0)  
   • Rehydrate 5 g 71B-1122 in 50 mL 37 °C water for 15 min, then add a little must to temper.  
   • Pour yeast into fermenter, seal with air-lock. Shake or rock for 30 s to oxygenate.  

4) Primary fermentation (Days 1–7)  
   • Keep at 18–22 °C. Expect vigorous fermentation within 12–24 h.  
   • Stir or rock gently once daily for the first 3 days to keep fruit wet and release CO₂.  
   • Optionally add staggered nutrient (½ on Day 0, ¼ on Day 1, ¼ on Day 2).  
   • When SG drops to ~1.020 (~Day 5–7), lift out fruit bag, let it drain, then discard or save for jam.  

5) Secondary & bulk conditioning (Days 7–45+)  
   • Rack (siphon) into a sanitised 5 L carboy, leaving lees behind. Attach air-lock.  
   • Fermentation will finish at SG ≈ 1.000 or slightly lower (11–12 % ABV).  
   • After 2 weeks, rack again if a 1 cm lees layer forms.  
   • Leave at 15–18 °C for at least 4 more weeks to clarify. Cold-crash 3 days at 0–4 °C if possible.  

6) Final adjustments (Day 45+)  
   • Taste. If too dry, stabilise with 0.44 g potassium metabisulfite + 2 g potassium sorbate, wait 24 h, then backsweeten with reserved honey (about 50–100 g dissolved in a little mead).  
   • Optionally tweak acidity: dissolve 1 g acid blend in 20 mL water, stir in, taste; repeat up to ~3 g total.  

7) Bottling  
   STILL: Rack to bottling bucket, fill sanitised wine bottles, cork.  
   SPARKLING: Dissolve 20 g table sugar in 100 mL boiling water, cool, add to bottling bucket, rack mead on top. Bottle in pressure-rated bottles; condition 3 weeks at 20 °C.  

8) Maturation  
   • Drinkable at 2–3 months but dramatically better at 6+ months.  
   • Store bottles upright in a cool, dark place.  

EXPECTED PROFILE  

Colour: Deep ruby with violet hues  
Aroma: Fresh strawberry up front, dark berry/cherry mid-note, light floral honey  
Body: Medium, semi-dry (or off-dry if backsweetened)  
Finish: Bright berry acidity, soft tannin, subtle honey warmth  

TIPS & VARIATIONS  

• Oak: Add 5 g French oak chips in secondary for 2 weeks for complexity.  
• Spices: 1 split vanilla bean or 1 cinnamon stick can complement berries—add in secondary.  
• Higher ABV version: Use 1.7 kg honey; OG ≈1.110, final 13–14 %—increase nutrients proportionally.  
• Sorbate is only needed if you plan to backsweeten or leave residual sugars.  

Cleanliness, temperature control, and patience are the three keys to a flavour-packed melomel. Enjoy crafting your 5 L of strawberry-blackberry bliss!
