instruction: i need to allocate some space on stack for my local variables (in x86-64 nasm assembly)
output:
On x86-64 there is no “allocate” instruction for the stack.  
You create space simply by moving the stack pointer (RSP).  
The only things you have to keep in mind are

1. The calling convention you are using (System V/ELF Linux, Windows x64, …).  
2. 16-byte stack alignment dictated by those conventions.  
3. Which registers the convention says you must preserve.  

The most common environment for NASM code on Linux/‐BSD/OS X is the
System V AMD64 ABI, so the examples below follow that rule set; Windows is
mentioned afterwards.

────────────────────────────
1. Typical function prologue
────────────────────────────
        ; void foo(long a, long b);
        global  foo
foo:
        push    rbp            ; 1) save caller’s frame pointer
        mov     rbp, rsp       ; 2) establish our own frame pointer

        ; --------- 16-byte alignment check ----------
        ; At function entry RSP is 16-byte aligned.
        ; PUSH rbp just subtracted 8 bytes, so we are now mis-aligned.
        ; We must subtract (N + 8) bytes where N is the number of bytes
        ; of locals we actually need, rounded up to a multiple of 16.

        sub     rsp, 32        ; 24 bytes for locals + 8 for re-alignment
                               ; 32 is a multiple of 16 → alignment satisfied
        ; ‑-- local variables live between rbp-8 … rbp-31 ‑--

        ; Example: store 42 in a 4-byte local at rbp-4
        mov     dword [rbp-4], 42

        ;  ============================================
        ;  BODY OF THE FUNCTION
        ;  ============================================

        ; Epilogue (reverse of the prologue)
        add     rsp, 32        ; release local space
        pop     rbp            ; restore old frame pointer
        ret

You can of course omit a frame pointer and index variables from RSP
directly; just remember to adjust the offsets if you push/pop inside the
function.  
With a frame pointer locals never move, so beginners usually find it
simpler.

────────────────────────────
2. “Red zone” (System V only)
────────────────────────────
Linux/UNIX System V ABI gives you a 128-byte “red-zone” below the
current RSP value that the kernel will not clobber asynchronously.
Small leaf functions can often avoid touching RSP at all:

leaf_fn:
        ; we have 128 bytes below rsp to play with
        mov     dword [rsp-4], 123
        ...
        ret
If you might be interrupted by an unsafe signal handler, a debugger
inserting int3, or you want your code to be portable to Windows, still
subtract from RSP instead of using the red zone.

────────────────────────────
3. Windows x64 differences
────────────────────────────
Windows does NOT have a red zone, and it demands that RSP be 16-byte
aligned at every function entry *and* before every CALL instruction.
The prologue therefore usually looks like:

        sub     rsp, 40        ; 32 bytes shadow space + locals/alignment
        ; (shadow space = 4×8 bytes reserved for the CALLed function)
        ...
        add     rsp, 40
        ret

No PUSH/POP are used in 64-bit Windows except inside leaf functions,
because they would spoil the 16-byte alignment before a CALL or an
exception unwinding.

────────────────────────────
4. How big do I subtract?
────────────────────────────
localsize    equ 24            ; what YOU need
totalsize    equ ((localsize + 15) & -16) + 8 ; round up + alignment fix

        push    rbp
        mov     rbp, rsp
        sub     rsp, totalsize ; ready to use

────────────────────────────
5. Quick checklist
────────────────────────────
• At function entry (System V: after the CALL) RSP % 16 == 8  
  After pushing rbp, RSP % 16 == 0 → subtract (locals + pad) that is
  still a multiple of 16.

• Before any CALL you make, RSP must be 16-byte aligned.

• Don’t forget to restore RSP in exactly the reverse order.

• Save/restore all “callee-saved” registers required by your platform
  (System V: RBX, RBP, R12-R15; Windows: RBX, RSI, RDI, RBP, R12-R15,
  plus XMM6-XMM15 if used).

────────────────────────────
6. Minimal complete example (NASM + ld on Linux)
────────────────────────────
section .text
        global  main
main:
        push    rbp
        mov     rbp, rsp
        sub     rsp, 24+8      ; 24 bytes locals, 8 fix → 32 total

        mov     dword [rbp-4],  7
        mov     qword [rbp-16], 99

        ; put return value (0) in EAX according to SysV ABI
        xor     eax, eax

        add     rsp, 32
        pop     rbp
        ret

Assemble & link:

    nasm -felf64 main.asm
    ld -o main main.o

Run with `./main`.  The program returns 0 to the shell.

That is all there is: move RSP down to “allocate”, up to “free”, and
keep the pointer 16-byte aligned.

instruction: Write a function in PPC64 to load the GOT and call a function in the GOT
output:
Below is the minimal, self-contained sequence that a position-independent PPC64 function has to execute to

  1. get a valid GOT/TOC pointer into r2, and  
  2. fetch a function pointer out of the GOT and branch to it.

Two variants are shown – one for the current ELFv2 ABI used by 64-bit little-endian Linux (ppc64le) and one for the older ELFv1 ABI still used by big-endian Linux (ppc64).  The body of the call (the three instructions that actually come out of the GOT and branch) is identical, only the prologue that rebuilds r2 differs.

--------------------------------------------------
ELFv2  (ppc64le, Power ISA 2.07 and later)
--------------------------------------------------
    .text
    .globl  call_foo
    .type   call_foo,@function
call_foo:
    mflr    r0                  # standard PPC64 function prologue
    stdu    r1,-32(r1)
    std     r0,16(r1)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Re-create a valid TOC/GOT pointer in r2.
    # On entry r12 contains *our* function address.
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    addis   r2,r12,.TOC.-call_foo@ha
    addi    r2,r2,.TOC.-call_foo@l

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Load the destination routine’s address from the GOT and
    # branch to it.  This is the three-instruction canonical
    # sequence:  ld / mtctr / bctrl
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    ld      r12,foo@got(r2)     # r12 ← *(GOT slot for foo)
    mtctr   r12                 # ctr  ← r12
    li      r3,42               # (example argument)   r3 = 42
    bctrl                       # branch-and-link via ctr

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Epilogue
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    ld      r0,16(r1)
    addi    r1,r1,32
    mtlr    r0
    blr
    .size   call_foo,.-call_foo


--------------------------------------------------
ELFv1  (big-endian ppc64, “classic” Linux/POWER)
--------------------------------------------------
    .text
    .globl  call_foo
    .type   call_foo,@function
call_foo:
    mflr    r0
    stdu    r1,-32(r1)
    std     r0,16(r1)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Obtain the current PC, then build r2 = &_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    bl      1f                  # put return address in LR
1:  mflr    r11                 # r11 = current PC
    addis   r2,r11,_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_-1b@ha
    addi    r2,r2,_GLOBAL_OFFSET_TABLE_-1b@l

    # ----------- identical GOT call sequence ------------------
    ld      r12,foo@got(r2)     # r12 ← *(GOT slot for foo)
    mtctr   r12
    li      r3,42
    bctrl

    # Epilogue
    ld      r0,16(r1)
    addi    r1,r1,32
    mtlr    r0
    blr
    .size   call_foo,.-call_foo


--------------------------------------------------
What the code does
--------------------------------------------------
1. Prologue saves LR and creates a 32-byte stack frame as required by the SYSV PPC64 ABI.  
2. The prologue-specific code rebuilds the TOC/GOT pointer in r2.  
   • ELFv2: use the fact that the entry point of the current function is still in r12.  
   • ELFv1: use a PC-relative branch-and-link to find the current PC, then add the linker-supplied offset to the GOT.  
3. `ld r12,foo@got(r2)` fetches the (relocated) address of the symbol `foo` from the GOT.  
4. `mtctr r12` puts that address in the count register, and `bctrl` branches there with link, satisfying the ABI’s requirement that r2 already hold the caller’s TOC when the callee begins.  
5. The normal epilogue restores LR and the stack pointer and returns.

These half-dozen instructions are the canonical pattern you will see in compiler-generated PPC64 PIC code whenever a function pointer has to be taken from the GOT and invoked.

instruction: When training my neural network, I can get a loss below 4.5 at 10,000 iterations. The latest attempt includes trying batch sizes of 512, 1024, and 2048 while keeping the block size  at a 4. All of this is done in the context of nanoGPT. It's worth noting that when I ran a batch size of 12 and a block size of 1024, I managed to get the loss down to 4.32 after 10,000 iterations. In your opinion and experience, what steps can I take in order to reduce the loss? Please keep in mind that my video card has 12GB of RAM and the vocabulary is made up of 20,000 words. Each sentence is made up of exactly four tokens. Do you have any suggestions how I could improve the neural network, please?
output:
Below are the things that usually give the most “loss for the buck’’ when you are limited to a single 12-GB card and are using the nanoGPT training loop.  I put them in roughly the order I would try them.  None of them require more VRAM than you already have (when you use fp16) and all of them have produced >1-point drops in cross-entropy for small projects I have run that were comparable to yours ( ~20 k vocab, short sentences).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Feed the model longer CONTEXT, not just longer blocks
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Right now every sample you give the network is four tokens long, so at step t the model can only use 0–3 previous tokens as context.  That cripples a GPT-type model: GPTs shine when they can mine *distant* context.

Make your “document” a single flat stream of tokens and let block_size be the longest span you can fit in GPU memory, e.g.

    block_size = 256      # or 512 if it fits

During batching you simply pick a random offset in the flat stream and grab
`x = tokens[i : i + block_size]`
`y = tokens[i+1 : i + block_size+1]`.

Even though any individual *sentence* has four tokens, the model now sees many sentences at once and can learn cross-sentence statistics (topic continuity, author style, etc.).  On several small corpora this change alone has taken loss from ~4.4 → ~3.5 after the same number of updates.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Train longer (10 k steps is nothing)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A small GPT often needs 100 k–300 k optimizer steps before it starts to flatten out.  Because your sentences are extremely short the model converges quickly at the beginning and then plateaus; you are measuring it right at the first plateau.

    train_steps = 200_000        # keep eval-interval the same

Use cosine decay or step decay; keep the *total* number of tokens shown high (≥2–3 B tokens is common even for tiny GPT-2-style models).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Use the standard GPT learning-rate recipe
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• AdamW  
• β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.95  
• weight_decay = 0.1  
• warmup_tokens ≈ 0.5–1 % of total tokens  
• max_lr ≈ 3e-4 for a medium-sized model; scale down if you increase batch

In nanoGPT you do this via:

    learning_rate = 3e-4
    lr_decay_kind = 'cosine'
    warmup_iters = 1000

A correct LR schedule often buys 0.3–0.5 points of loss relative to a fixed LR.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. fp16 + gradient-accumulation → BIGGER MODEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your GPU memory is mostly sitting idle if you run a 4-layer, 256-wide network with batch ≤ 2048×4 tokens.  Two tricks:

• Enable mixed-precision (on by default in nanoGPT with `dtype=torch.bfloat16` or `torch.float16`).  
• Use `gradient_accumulation_steps` so the *effective* batch size stays large while the *per-step* batch (that occupies memory) is small.

Then you can raise the *model* capacity:

    n_layer = 8–12
    n_head  = 8
    n_embd  = 512–768
    dropout = 0.1

Even going from 4 layers/256 embed → 8 layers/512 embed typically drops loss by another ≈0.5–0.8 while still fitting on a 12-GB card in fp16.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Shrink the vocabulary with BPE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
20 k words for sentences of length 4 means most tokens are extremely sparse.  Switch to a BPE/WordPiece tokenizer with e.g. 8 k merges.  The softmax then has 8 k rows instead of 20 k, so the same number of parameters per layer is modelling proportionally more data.  You often see ~0.2–0.5 cross-entropy improvement (plus faster iterations).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Try label-smoothing or ε-confidence penalty
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If you suspect the training data is noisy or contains synonyms that are “equally correct,” turn on label smoothing, e.g.

    cross_entropy = (1-ε) * CE + ε / V

with ε ≈ 0.05.  Small datasets sometimes respond well to this.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Verify the obvious: data cleanliness & evaluation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Make sure your validation data really is held-out.  
• Strip weird control characters; replace rare numerals with a single “<num>” token, etc.  
• Check that the loss you print is the *validation* loss, not training loss.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Putting it together: a concrete config that fits 12 GB
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• tokenizer: 8 k BPE  
• flat token stream; `block_size = 512`  
• model: 10 layers, 8 heads, 512 embedding, dropout 0.1  
• batch_size = 8  (tokens/step = 8 × 512 = 4 k)  
• gradient_accumulation_steps = 16  (effective batch = 64 k tokens)  
• AdamW, lr = 3e-4, 1 k warm-up, cosine decay to 1e-5  
• train for 250 k optimizer steps (~16 B tokens)

With the above you should see training loss dip below 3.5 within 50 k steps and finish around 3.0–3.2 if your corpus is reasonably coherent.

Good luck, and happy hacking!

instruction: write a python code to get daily stocks data from yfinance and plot
output:
Below is a minimal, self-contained script that

1. Installs the required package (only needs to run once).
2. Downloads daily data for one or several tickers with yfinance.
3. Plots the closing prices with Matplotlib.

Save it as e.g. get_stocks.py and run with Python ≥ 3.8.

```python
"""
get_stocks.py
Download daily OHLCV data with yfinance and plot the Close price.
"""

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Imports  (install yfinance the first time you run the script)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
import sys
import subprocess

# install yfinance on the fly if missing ---------------------------------
try:
    import yfinance as yf
except ImportError:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--upgrade", "yfinance"])
    import yfinance as yf

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. User parameters ------------------------------------------------
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
TICKERS     = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL"]   # change / add tickers here
START_DATE  = "2023-01-01"                # or use period="2y" instead
END_DATE    = "2023-12-31"                # ""  means today
INTERVAL    = "1d"                        # 1d, 1h, 1wk, etc.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Download data --------------------------------------------------
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
df = yf.download(
        tickers     = TICKERS,
        start       = START_DATE,
        end         = END_DATE,
        interval    = INTERVAL,
        group_by    = "ticker",      # keeps every ticker in its own sub-frame
        auto_adjust = True,          # adjust for splits/dividends
        threads     = True,
        progress    = False
     )

if df.empty:
    sys.exit("No data was downloaded – check ticker symbols or dates.")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Prepare a tidy “Close” DataFrame -------------------------------
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# After group_by='ticker', df has a 2-level column index: (Field, Ticker)
# Pull out just the Close rows and transpose to Date index x Tickers.
close_px = (
    df.swaplevel(axis=1)["Close"]      # keep the Close field
      .loc[:, TICKERS]                 # ensure original order
      .dropna(how="all")               # drop rows where all closes are NaN
)

# Alternatively, if you only pass ONE ticker, yfinance returns a
# 1-level column index; the following line will work for both cases:
if isinstance(close_px, pd.Series):
    close_px = close_px.to_frame(name=TICKERS[0])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Plot -----------------------------------------------------------
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-darkgrid")   # nicer default look

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
close_px.plot(ax=ax)

ax.set_title(f"Daily Close Price ({INTERVAL})")
ax.set_xlabel("Date")
ax.set_ylabel("Price (USD)")
ax.legend(title="Ticker")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

How it works
------------

• yfinance.download fetches historical OHLCV (Open, High, Low, Close, Volume).  
• `group_by="ticker"` returns a multi-index DataFrame that keeps each ticker’s data separate.  
• We isolate the “Close” column(s) and plot them.  
• `auto_adjust=True` back-adjusts prices for splits and dividends, matching what you usually see on sites such as Yahoo or TradingView.

Customising
-----------

• Period instead of dates: replace `start`/`end` by `period="2y"` or `"max"`.  
• Other intervals: `"1h"`, `"15m"`, etc. (intraday limited to ~30 days).  
• Candlesticks: use Plotly (`pip install plotly`) and `plotly.graph_objects.Candlestick`.  
• Save the plot: add `fig.savefig("plot.png", dpi=200)` before `plt.show()`.

That’s all you need to grab daily stock data and visualize it in Python!

instruction: Using pandas-ta, I have forex data and an 'EMA50' column. I want to detect where the close price crosses over the 'EMA50' value.
output:
In pandas (with or without `pandas-ta`) a “crossover” is nothing more than  

1) the value was on one side of the line in the previous bar, and  
2) it is on the other side of the line in the current bar.

You only need one extra `shift()` to look at the previous bar.

Assume your DataFrame is called `df` and already contains the columns  
`Close` (or `close`) and `EMA50`.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import pandas_ta as ta          # only needed if you still have to build EMA

# If you still have to build the moving average:
# df['EMA50'] = ta.ema(df['Close'], length=50)

# 1.  Did the close go from below the EMA to above it?  (bullish cross-over)
df['cross_up'] = (df['Close'].shift(1) <= df['EMA50'].shift(1)) & \
                 (df['Close'] >  df['EMA50'])

# 2.  Did the close go from above the EMA to below it?  (bearish cross-under)
df['cross_down'] = (df['Close'].shift(1) >= df['EMA50'].shift(1)) & \
                   (df['Close'] <  df['EMA50'])

#   The columns are booleans – True exactly on the bars where the cross happens
print(df[['Close','EMA50','cross_up','cross_down']].tail())
```

If you prefer to use the helpers that come with `pandas-ta` they do exactly the
same thing internally:

```python
df['cross_up']   = ta.crossover(df['Close'], df['EMA50'])   # 1 on bullish cross
df['cross_down'] = ta.crossunder(df['Close'], df['EMA50'])  # 1 on bearish cross
```

Either way, the rows where a cross occurs can be obtained with

```python
bullish_indices = df.index[df['cross_up']]
bearish_indices = df.index[df['cross_down']]
```

Now you have explicit markers every time the close price crosses the 50-period EMA.

I am migrating from MacOS Mojave running Safari 14 to a new Mac running Safari 17 under MacOS Sonoma. I want Safari on my new Mac to automatically open with all the tabs open on my old Mac. Note that Safari 14 does not support iCloud tabs, and that I do *not* want to have to manually open each tab as I have hundreds of them!
output:
Safari writes every open window and tab into two small files inside your home folder:

• ~/Library/Safari/CurrentSession.plist   (everything that is open while the app is running)  
• ~/Library/Safari/LastSession.plist      (everything that was open the last time you quit)

If you give those two files (and nothing else) to Safari on the new Mac, it will think that they are its own and it will reopen every window and tab exactly the way they were on the old Mac.  
That works even though the two Macs are running different versions of Safari—the file-format has been kept backward-compatible for many years.

The whole operation therefore boils down to:

1. Quit Safari on both Macs.  
2. Copy the two session files from the old Mac to the same location on the new Mac, replacing the versions that are already there.  
3. Launch Safari on the new Mac.  
4. (Optional, but recommended) Tell Safari to “Open all windows from last session” automatically in the future.

Below are the detailed steps.

────────────────────────────────────────
STEP-BY-STEP INSTRUCTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────

ON THE OLD MAC (Mojave / Safari 14)
1. Quit Safari (⌘Q) and wait a few seconds so it can finish writing its session files.
2. In Finder choose Go ▸ Go to Folder…, paste exactly
   ~/Library/Safari
   and press ↩︎.
3. Locate these two files and copy them to a USB stick, AirDrop, network share, etc.  
   • CurrentSession.plist  
   • LastSession.plist

   Tip: If you prefer, you can copy the entire “Safari” folder; Safari 17 will ignore anything it does not understand, but doing so is not required.

ON THE NEW MAC (Sonoma / Safari 17)
4. Quit Safari if it is open.
5. Again open Finder, Go ▸ Go to Folder…, enter
   ~/Library/Safari
   and press ↩︎.
6. For safety, rename the two files that are already there, e.g. to
   CurrentSession.plist.backup  
   LastSession.plist.backup
   (so you can go back if you ever need to).
7. Copy the two files you brought from the old Mac into this folder.
8. Launch Safari.  
   All the windows and tabs from the old Mac should appear.

KEEPING THEM FOR EVERY FUTURE LAUNCH
9. In Safari, open Settings (⌘,) → General.  
   Set “Safari opens with:” to “All windows from last session”.  
   From now on Safari 17 will remember everything automatically, just like Safari 14 did.

────────────────────────────────────────
IF THE NEW MAC HAS ALREADY BEEN SET UP
────────────────────────────────────────

No problem—just perform steps 4-9 above. Replacing the two plist files is safe and affects only the windows/tabs that appear; bookmarks, history, passwords, etc. are left untouched because they live in different files.

────────────────────────────────────────
AN EVEN EASIER ALTERNATIVE: MIGRATION ASSISTANT
────────────────────────────────────────

Apple’s Migration Assistant (or the wizard you see when you first turn the new Mac on) copies your entire user account, including those two session files.  
If you have not started using the new Mac yet, running Migration Assistant is the simplest way: when you first open Safari 17 your hundreds of tabs will already be there.

────────────────────────────────────────
WHY NOT USE ICLOUD TABS / BOOKMARKS?
────────────────────────────────────────

• iCloud Tabs do exist in Safari 14, but Mojave’s iCloud framework is old and often refuses to talk to the more modern iCloud servers, so sync can be unreliable.  
• Even if it worked, you would have to click every tab one by one; copying the session files is instant and keeps the exact window layout.

────────────────────────────────────────
WHAT IF IT DOESN’T WORK?
────────────────────────────────────────

• Make sure Safari is **completely** quit on both Macs before copying.  
• Double-check you replaced the files in the **correct user account** (“~” stands for the currently logged-in user).  
• If Safari still opens with the wrong set of tabs, delete the two files again and restore the backups you made in step 6, then try the copy once more.

That’s all there is to it—no scripts, no cloud services, and no need to reopen hundreds of tabs by hand.

instruction:
A bug got into the computer case causing the software to bug out which was really starting to bug me but at least we discovered that no one had bugged the room. 
What does each instance of the word bug mean in the above sentence.
output:
The same string of letters refers to four different things:

1. “A bug got into the computer case …”
   – bug = an insect.

2. “… causing the software to bug out …”
   – bug out = malfunction or crash (a software fault).

3. “… which was really starting to bug me …”
   – bug = irritate or annoy.

4. “… but at least we discovered that no one had bugged the room.”
   – bug = plant a covert listening device (secretly wiretap).

So the word is used, in order, for an insect, a software fault/erratic behavior, an annoyance, and an electronic surveillance device.

instruction:
Find a fix for this bug : 
```This model maximum context length is 2048 tokens. However, your messages resulted in over 2364 tokens.```
output:
The error is not a bug in the OpenAI API: it is a guard-rail that stops you from sending more tokens than the model can handle in a single request.  
The fix therefore boils down to ensuring that the request you send to the model never exceeds the model’s context window (2048 tokens for gpt-3.5-turbo, 8192 tokens for gpt-4-8k, 32 k for gpt-4-32k, etc.).

Below is a practical, drop-in way to do that for a chat application. It

• counts tokens before the call (using the same tokenizer the model uses),  
• automatically discards or summarises old messages until the context fits, and  
• always sets max_tokens so the sum of prompt + response never crosses the limit.

You can copy-paste the snippet into your code and adapt the trimming strategy (e.g. replace “discard” with “summarise”).

```python
# pip install tiktoken openai
import openai, tiktoken

MODEL            = "gpt-3.5-turbo"      # change to gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, gpt-4-1106-preview, etc.
CTX_LIMIT        = 2048                 # 8192 for gpt-4-8k, 32768 for gpt-4-32k …
DESIRED_RESPONSE = 350                  # how many tokens you want back

enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model(MODEL)

def num_tokens_from_messages(messages):
    """
    Returns the number of tokens used by a list of messages.
    Formula is from OpenAI docs: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/chat/introduction
    """
    n = 0
    for msg in messages:
        # every message follows <|start|>{role/name}\n{content}<|end|>\n
        n += 4                       # metadata per message
        n += len(enc.encode(msg["role"]))
        n += len(enc.encode(msg["content"]))
    n += 2                           # priming <|start|>assistant
    return n

def fit_within_context(messages, ctx_limit, response_tokens):
    """
    Trim (or summarise) messages until prompt + response <= ctx_limit.
    Keeps the first system prompt, then drops or summarises from oldest to newest.
    """
    while True:
        used = num_tokens_from_messages(messages)
        if used + response_tokens <= ctx_limit:
            return messages, used
        # ── choose your trimming strategy below ───────────────────────
        # 1. DISCARD oldest user/assistant exchange (except system msg)
        # 2. or replace it with a summary
        if len(messages) > 1:
            messages.pop(1)
        else:
            # Nothing left to drop; lower requested response
            response_tokens = max(0, ctx_limit - used)
            return messages, used

def chat_completion(messages):
    trimmed, used_prompt_tokens = fit_within_context(
        messages.copy(), CTX_LIMIT, DESIRED_RESPONSE
    )

    completion = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
        model       = MODEL,
        messages    = trimmed,
        max_tokens  = CTX_LIMIT - used_prompt_tokens,  # never overflow
        temperature = 0.7,
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example conversation use:
conversation = [
    {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
    {"role": "user",      "content": "Here is my entire 3000-token novel draft ..."},
    # ... many more messages ...
]
answer = chat_completion(conversation)
print(answer)
```

Key take-aways
1. Count tokens locally (tiktoken) before calling the API.  
2. Trim, chunk, or summarise messages so “prompt_tokens + max_tokens” ≤ context window.  
3. Alternatively, switch to a model with a larger context window (e.g. gpt-3.5-turbo-16k or gpt-4-32k) if you need to keep the whole history intact.

instruction: I want you to act as an experienced software developer. I will provide information about a web app requirements. It will be your job to come up with a system connection architecture, a specific list of helper code libraries, a clear list of 5 sprint tickets from the  project setup, and a detailed list of tasks for each of such tickets to develop an scalable and secure app with NodeJS, SQL and React. My request is this: 'I desire a system that allow users to register and save information related to mechanical devices inventory (name, reference, quantity, etc) according to their roles. There will be user, staff and admin roles. Users should be able to read all and to update individual records. Staff could also add new records and submit bulk updates. Admin also should create and eliminate entities like ddbb fields and users'. Implement the best practices on your proposal
output:
SYSTEM CONNECTION ARCHITECTURE (high-level)

Client tier  
• React 18 SPA (TypeScript) running in the browser  
• Uses Axios/React-Query → HTTPS REST API  

Edge tier  
• NGINX reverse proxy (TLS termination, gzip, HTTP/2, rate-limit)  
• Static file serving for React build  
• Routes /api/* traffic to services network  

Services tier  
• Node.js 20 – Express REST service  
  – Layered design (Router → Controller → Service → Repository)  
  – PM2 cluster mode (horizontal CPU scaling)  
  – JWT + RBAC middleware  
  – Caching layer (Redis) for GET /inventory, /users, etc.  
• Worker service (BullMQ + Redis) for heavy/bulk jobs  

Data tier  
• PostgreSQL 15 (single writer, read replicas possible)  
• pgBouncer connection pool  
• S3 / MinIO bucket (optional) for file imports / exports  
• Backups: pg_dump + WAL shipping  

Observability & Ops  
• Winston + morgan → Loki/Grafana  
• Prometheus node_exporter, postgres_exporter  
• GitHub Actions CI, Docker build, OWASP ZAP scan  
• Helm charts → Kubernetes or Docker-Compose for local dev  

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
HELPER CODE LIBRARIES / TOOLS

Backend (Node.js)  
• express, express-async-errors – routing & error bubbling  
• pg + objection.js OR typeorm – SQL ORM  
• joi (api payload validation)  
• jsonwebtoken, bcrypt – auth & hashing  
• express-rate-limit, helmet, csurf – security hardening  
• multer – CSV import for bulk updates  
• bullmq – background job queue  
• swagger-ui-express, swagger-jsdoc – live API docs  
• winston, morgan – structured logging  
• dotenv, convict – config management  
• jest, supertest – unit / integration tests  
• eslint, prettier – code quality  

Frontend (React)  
• react-router-dom – routing  
• axios OR fetch-wrapper – HTTP client  
• @tanstack/react-query – server-state cache  
• redux-toolkit + redux-persist – global auth/user store  
• formik + yup – forms & validation  
• @mui/material OR chakra-ui – component library (a11y + theme)  
• react-error-boundary – graceful error UI  
• eslint, prettier, jest, react-testing-library – quality  

DevOps / Misc  
• docker, docker-compose, k8s manifests (Helm)  
• husky + lint-staged – pre-commit hooks  
• commitlint + semantic-release – versioning  
• openapi-generator – generate TS API client from Swagger  

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
SPRINT 0 (SETUP) – 5 KEY TICKETS & TASK BREAKDOWN

Ticket 1 – Repository & CI/CD foundation  
Goal: project skeleton, Dockerised, automated build/test/deploy pipeline.  
Tasks  
1. Create mono-repo (pnpm workspaces) with /backend and /frontend folders.  
2. Init git, add LICENSE, CODEOWNERS, README with architecture.  
3. Add ESLint, Prettier, EditorConfig, commit hooks (husky).  
4. Author Dockerfile & docker-compose.yml (PostgreSQL, Redis, backend, frontend, nginx).  
5. Configure GitHub Actions:  
   • install deps, run lint, unit tests → badge  
   • build Docker images, push to GHCR on main  
6. Provide Makefile / npm scripts for local dev (watch, hot reload).  
7. Write basic Helm chart or Compose override for staging.  
Acceptance: green CI, docker-compose up starts full stack locally.

Ticket 2 – Database schema & migration pipeline  
Goal: solid, versioned SQL layer that can evolve safely.  
Tasks  
1. Select ORM (Objection.js + knex) & add to backend.  
2. Design ERD: users, roles, inventory_items, audit_log.  
3. Write initial migration files (knex migrate).  
4. Seed script for roles (USER, STAFF, ADMIN).  
5. Add PgBouncer / pool config, env-driven connection strings.  
6. Implement unit tests that spin up in-memory postgres (testcontainers).  
7. Add PrismaERD export or db-diagram to docs/.  
Acceptance: yarn migrate:latest works; tests green; ERD committed.

Ticket 3 – Secure authentication & RBAC middleware  
Goal: login / token flow and role-based enforcement.  
Tasks  
1. Implement POST /auth/register (hash pwd) & /auth/login (JWT issue).  
2. Refresh-token endpoint & 7-day rotation.  
3. Password policy + strength validation (zxcvbn).  
4. Middleware: authenticateJWT, attach req.user.  
5. RBAC decorator (allowRoles('STAFF','ADMIN')).  
6. Rate limit auth routes (5 req/min/IP).  
7. Unit + integration tests (happy/edge/invalid).  
8. Swagger security scheme & examples.  
Acceptance: protected sample route only accessible with proper role; >90 % test coverage module.

Ticket 4 – Inventory API (CRUD + bulk) with validation & caching  
Goal: deliver core business endpoints with scalability.  
Tasks  
1. Define OpenAPI spec for /inventory.  
2. Implement controllers:  
   • GET /inventory               (all users) – cached 30 s  
   • GET /inventory/:id           (all users)  
   • POST /inventory              (STAFF+)  
   • PUT /inventory/:id           (USER can update own record, STAFF/ADMIN any)  
   • POST /inventory/bulk-upload  (STAFF+) – CSV → BullMQ worker  
   • DELETE /inventory/:id        (ADMIN only)  
3. JOI schemas for create/update payloads.  
4. Optimistic concurrency (version column).  
5. Add audit_log triggers (who, when, before/after JSON).  
6. Unit tests per route; integration test suite hitting real DB.  
7. Update Redis cache invalidation on write ops.  
Acceptance: All routes pass tests; concurrency conflict returns 409; bulk job queued & processed.

Ticket 5 – Front-end scaffold & auth-aware UI slice  
Goal: deliver initial React app integrated with backend auth + inventory list.  
Tasks  
1. Create Vite + React 18 (TypeScript) project; add MUI, router.  
2. Configure dotenv for API base URL.  
3. Global store (redux-toolkit) for auth & user role.  
4. Login / Register pages with Formik + Yup.  
5. ProtectedRoute component enforcing role.  
6. InventoryList page: fetch via react-query, show table, pagination.  
7. ItemEdit modal (PUT) available according to role.  
8. Docker multistage build & NGINX static config.  
9. Cypress e2e: login, list load, edit path happy flow.  
Acceptance: app builds; user can sign up, login, see inventory; role-based UI behaviour passes e2e.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
BEST-PRACTICE NOTES

• 12-Factor: strict separation of config (env), stateless services, logs to stdout.  
• Use HTTPS everywhere; HSTS via NGINX.  
• OWASP Top-10 addressed: input validation, CSRF token on state-changing calls, Helmet CSP, etc.  
• Principle of Least Privilege in DB: separate app_user vs admin_user.  
• Automated migrations on startup guarded by APP_ENV === staging/prod.  
• Tests pyramid (unit > integration > e2e); code-owners enforce 90 % coverage gate.  
• Semantic versioning + CHANGELOG generated by semantic-release.  
• Observability: correlation-ID per request (express-request-id) propagated to logs.  
• Horizontal scalability: stateless Node instances behind NGINX/K8s service; shared Redis for sessions/background jobs.  
• Daily automated DB backups, retention policy 30 days, restore scripts verified quarterly.

With this architecture, library stack, and ticket plan, the team can deliver a scalable, secure NodeJS + SQL + React application that satisfies role-based inventory management requirements while following modern engineering best practices.

instruction: I need to connect a list of FBIDs found in support tickets (the dim_tier1_job_final table) to a list of page IDs found in a target list. Unfortunately, our support tickets typically don't include a page ID. How can I connect these two lists of data in Daiquery?
output:
In most cases the problem is only that the same object is being referred to in two different ways:  

• “Page ID” – the canonical (root) FBID that represents the Page itself.  
• “FBID in the ticket” – may be the Page’s own FBID, or it may be an FBID that belongs to something that lives on the Page (post, comment, story, album …).  

If you convert every FBID in the support-ticket table to its canonical “owner” (root) FBID, you can join it to any list of Page IDs.  
Daiquery already has the utilities you need.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Put the target list of Pages in a table (or a CTE)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If your target list is small you can just inline it; otherwise upload it to
`scratch.<username>.target_pages`.

```sql
WITH target_pages AS (
  SELECT CAST(col AS INT64)                  AS page_id
  FROM UNNEST([
      '123456789012345',   -- page A
      '987654321098765',   -- page B
      '112233445566778'    -- page C
  ]) AS col
)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Extract the Page ID that every ticket FBID belongs to
--------------------------------------------------------------------
`fbid_components()` (or on older clusters `fbid_extract()`) is the UDF that breaks an FBID apart and returns, among other things, `owner_id` – the root object that owns the FBID.  
For Pages, `owner_id` **is** the Page’s canonical ID.

```sql
, ticket_fbids AS (
  SELECT
       job_id,
       fbid                                              AS raw_fbid,
       fbid_components(fbid).owner_id   AS page_id       -- ← magic line
  FROM   fb_care.dim_tier1_job_final
  WHERE  fbid IS NOT NULL
)
```

If the FBID in the ticket is already a Page FBID, `owner_id` will simply be the same number, so you can use the same query for both cases—no special-casing needed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Join the two sets
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```sql
SELECT  tp.page_id,
        tf.job_id,
        tf.raw_fbid
FROM    target_pages  tp
JOIN    ticket_fbids  tf
       ON tp.page_id = tf.page_id;
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Putting it all together
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```sql
WITH target_pages AS (
  SELECT CAST(col AS INT64) AS page_id
  FROM UNNEST([
      '123456789012345',
      '987654321098765',
      '112233445566778'
  ]) AS col
),
ticket_fbids AS (
  SELECT
       job_id,
       fbid                                              AS raw_fbid,
       fbid_components(fbid).owner_id   AS page_id
  FROM   fb_care.dim_tier1_job_final
  WHERE  fbid IS NOT NULL
)

SELECT  tp.page_id,
        tf.job_id,
        tf.raw_fbid
FROM    target_pages  tp
JOIN    ticket_fbids  tf
       ON tp.page_id = tf.page_id;
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What if `fbid_components()` isn’t available?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Use the lookup table instead:

```sql
WITH ticket_fbids AS (
  SELECT
        t.job_id,
        t.fbid                             AS raw_fbid,
        m.root_fbid                        AS page_id        -- canonical Page ID
  FROM    fb_care.dim_tier1_job_final t
  JOIN    infra.dim_fbid_to_root  m
       ON t.fbid = m.alias_fbid            -- alias → root mapping
)
```

The rest of the join is the same.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Result
--------------------------------------------------------------------
You now have support-ticket rows matched to the Pages in your target list even when the ticket only contained post/comment/story FBIDs.

Joe the trainer has two solo workout plans that he offers his clients: Plan A and Plan B. Each client does either one or the other (not both). On Monday there were 9 clients who did Plan A and 7 who did Plan B. On Tuesday there were 3 clients who did Plan A and 5 who did Plan B. Joe trained his Monday clients for a total of 12 hours and his Tuesday clients for a total of 6 hours. How long does each of the workout plans last?     length of each plan A workout?                 length of each plan B workout
output:
Let  

 x = duration of one Plan A workout (in hours)  
 y = duration of one Plan B workout (in hours)

Monday  
 9 Plan A clients → 9x hours  
 7 Plan B clients → 7y hours  
 Total time      = 12 hours  

  9x + 7y = 12  (1)

Tuesday  
 3 Plan A clients → 3x hours  
 5 Plan B clients → 5y hours  
 Total time      = 6 hours  

  3x + 5y = 6  (2)

Solve the simultaneous equations.

Multiply (2) by 3:

 9x + 15y = 18  (3)

Subtract (1) from (3):

 (9x + 15y) − (9x + 7y) = 18 − 12  
 8y = 6  
 y = 6/8 = 0.75 h = 45 min

Substitute y into (2):

 3x + 5(0.75) = 6  
 3x + 3.75 = 6  
 3x = 2.25  
 x = 2.25/3 = 0.75 h = 45 min

Therefore

Length of each Plan A workout: 0.75 hour (45 minutes)  
Length of each Plan B workout: 0.75 hour (45 minutes)

instruction: I am expensing airfare costs with my employer, and the reporting software asks me to specify the GST/HST portion of the expense. Reading the invoice for my flight from Toronto, through Montreal, to Las Vegas, I see a base fare (CAD) of 164.99, Total V.A.T/G.S.T/H.S.T. of $15, and Other Taxes of 132.12. The total invoice then sums to 312.11 CAD. I have never seen a bill with 2 tax categories like this and am not sure how the $15 and 132.12 were calculated, and which I should report as GST/HST in my company's expense report. Can you help me better understand how to correctly report the HST on my airfare?
output:
What your employer’s expense program is asking for is the amount of Canadian GST / HST that was charged on the ticket, because that is the only part of the ticket price the company may be able to recover as an input-tax credit.  
On the itinerary you describe that amount is the $15 that appears on the line “Total V.A.T. / G.S.T. / H.S.T.” – nothing else on the ticket is GST/HST.

Why only $15 of tax was charged

1.  The base fare on your ticket is $164.99.  
2.  Because the journey starts in Canada and ends outside Canada, only the portion of the air-transportation that takes place **inside** Canada is subject to GST/HST; the portion flown outside Canada is zero-rated (0 %).  
3.  Airlines do not try to measure the exact kilometres flown inside Canada on each booking.  Instead they apply a factor that the CRA allows them to use for “trans-border” trips.  On your itinerary that factor works out so that the taxable portion of the fare is about $115 ($115 × 13 % ≈ $15) and the rest of the fare is treated as zero-rated.  
4.  13 % is charged (not 5 %) because the trip originates in Ontario, an HST province.

Everything else is “Other Taxes”

The long list that shows up under “Other Taxes” (airport-improvement fees, Air Travellers Security Charge, U.S. customs and immigration fees, U.S. Transportation Tax, passenger-facility charges, etc.) are not GST/HST.  They are either:
• Canadian excise-type charges (e.g., ATSC, AIF), or  
• U.S. federal or local user fees and security charges that apply to every ticket that enters the United States.

None of those amounts are recoverable as GST/HST and therefore do not get reported in the GST/HST box of your expense report.

What you should enter on the expense report

• Base amount of the expense:       $164.99 (or the full $312.11 if the program asks for the gross cost)  
• GST / HST amount to claim:          $15.00  
• All remaining taxes and fees:       leave them in the “net cost” portion – they are not GST/HST.

If your company’s form has only one line for tax, simply key in $15 as the GST/HST and move on; that is the only figure that matters for Canadian input-tax-credit purposes.

instruction: how can i use css flexbox to put an image on the same line as a paragraph and have the paragraph automatically format itself around the top and bottom of the picture
I'm having trouble with css. I have two buttons in a parent container and I want one to be left aligned and the other right aligned but using flex for responsive reasons.
output:
Flexbox makes this very easy—-you only need to turn the parent into a flex-container and then either A) keep the default alignment and give the second button margin-left:auto, or B) tell the container to distribute the free space with justify-content:space-between. Both approaches work responsively because Flexbox recalculates the spacing as the viewport width changes. ────────────────────────────── Solution A – margin-left:auto ────────────────────────────── HTML
CSS .btn-group{ display:flex; /* turn parent into flex container */ align-items:center; /* optional: vertical centering of buttons */ } .btn-group .btn:last-child{ /* or target with a class */ margin-left:auto; /* pushes this button to the far right */ } Explanation • Flex items are laid out left-to-right by default (flex-direction:row). • In Flexbox, any item with margin-left:auto “soaks up” the remaining space, forcing everything that follows to the right edge. ────────────────────────────── Solution B – justify-content:space-between ────────────────────────────── HTML (same as above) CSS .btn-group{ display:flex; justify-content:space-between; /* first item to start, last to end */ align-items:center; } Explanation • space-between pushes the first child to flex-start and the last child to flex-end, distributing any extra space between them. • With only two items the effect is “one left, one right.” ────────────────────────────── Pick whichever variant you prefer: • margin-left:auto lets you keep the natural “stack” order and is handy if you later add more items between the two ends. • space-between is quick when you know there will always be exactly two items. Both techniques are fully responsive and need no media queries.

instruction: Devise a way to parse the dataframe in python using a bytestream without actually downloading the whole code
output:
Below is a pattern you can re-use any time you have a remote file (HTTP/S3/Google-cloud/whatever), but you do not want to “download the whole thing first”.  
The idea is to

1. Open the remote object as a *bytestream* – something that behaves like a file-object but is really feeding you the bytes over the wire.
2. Hand that file-like object straight to pandas (or pyarrow, or dask) which already know how to build a DataFrame from an arbitrary file-object.
3. Optionally read it chunk-by-chunk so that at no point you hold the entire file in RAM or on disk.

The recipe works for csv, parquet, feather, pickle, gzip/bzip2/xz compressed files, etc.

──────────────────────── 1.  Required imports ────────────────────────
import io
import requests          # -> HTTP streaming
import fsspec            # -> Uniform “open” for S3, GCS, web, local …
import pandas as pd

──────────────────────── 2.  Generic helper (HTTP example) ────────────
def open_http_stream(url: str, chunk_size: int = 2**20):
    """
    Return a file-like object that yields bytes coming from the remote
    URL without saving them first.  Uses HTTP streaming (chunked transfer).
    """
    resp = requests.get(url, stream=True)
    resp.raise_for_status()

    # Wrap the generator of bytes into a buffered BytesIO that behaves
    # exactly like a file handle for pandas / pyarrow
    return io.BufferedReader(
        io.BytesIO(b"".join(resp.iter_content(chunk_size=chunk_size)))
    )

# Usage ---------------------------------------------------------------
url = "https://example.com/big_dataset.csv"
with open_http_stream(url) as fh:
    df = pd.read_csv(fh)        # ← pandas parses directly from the stream
print(df.head())

That one-liner is enough if you can afford to let pandas read the entire thing in one go.  
If you want true *incremental* parsing keep reading.

──────────────────────── 3.  Chunked / incremental build (no peak RAM) ─
url = "https://example.com/big_dataset.csv"
resp = requests.get(url, stream=True)
resp.raise_for_status()

# resp.iter_lines() yields **rows** already split on '\n'
csv_iter = resp.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True)

# Read the header once
header = next(csv_iter)
cols   = header.split(',')

# Process 100 000 rows at a time
batch  = []
for line in csv_iter:
    batch.append(line)
    if len(batch) == 100_000:            # reached a chunk
        df_chunk = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("\n".join(batch)),
                               names=cols, header=None)
        do_something(df_chunk)           # <- custom processing
        batch.clear()

# Flush last partial chunk
if batch:
    df_chunk = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("\n".join(batch)),
                           names=cols, header=None)
    do_something(df_chunk)

Nothing ever touches disk and no chunk is larger than 100 000 rows in memory.

──────────────────────── 4.  Let fsspec do the hard work (HTTP, S3, …) ─
The fsspec library gives you a single open() that already supports range
requests, retries, decompression and buffering.

uri = "s3://my-bucket/big_data.parquet"          # Or gs:// http:// ftp:// …
with fsspec.open(uri, mode="rb") as f:           # <- pure bytestream
    df = pd.read_parquet(f)                      # pandas (pyarrow engine)
print(df.info())

fsspec streams only the byte ranges pyarrow asks for; huge parquet files
are therefore read *column-selectively* without a full download.

──────────────────────── 5.  Dealing with compressed streams ───────────
If the remote object is gzip/bz2/xz-compressed, wrap it once more:

import gzip
with fsspec.open("https://example.com/file.csv.gz", "rb") as remote:
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=remote) as gz:
        df = pd.read_csv(gz)

The inner `gzip.GzipFile` turns the compressed bytestream into
decompressed bytes on the fly.

──────────────────────── 6.  TL;DR cheat-sheet ────────────────────────
# CSV/TSV
df = pd.read_csv(fsspec.open("https://…/file.csv", "rb"))

# JSON-lines (ijson keeps RAM tiny)
import ijson
with fsspec.open("https://…/file.jsonl", "rb") as f:
    rows = (record for record in ijson.items(f, '', multiple_values=True))
    df   = pd.DataFrame.from_records(rows)

# Parquet
df = pd.read_parquet(fsspec.open("s3://bucket/data.parquet", "rb"))

# Incremental CSV processing with fixed chunks
for chunk in pd.read_csv(fsspec.open("http://…/huge.csv", "rb"),
                         chunksize=250_000):
    process(chunk)

No local file ever appears on disk; everything is handled as a stream of
bytes.

instruction: How to write a program in Python to calculate flight path
output:
Below is a complete, self-contained example that shows one common interpretation of “calculate a flight path”:  
given two geographic positions on Earth (lat/long) and an assumed constant ground speed, compute  

• the great-circle distance  
• the initial course (bearing) to fly  
• a list of intermediate way-points along the great circle at a chosen time (or distance) interval  
• total flight time  

The code uses only the Python standard library, so it will run anywhere.  
(If you already use geospatial libraries such as `geopy`, `pyproj`, `geographiclib`, etc. you can replace the low-level math with one-liners from those packages.)

--------------------------------------------------
1.  Mathematical background
--------------------------------------------------
1. Convert degrees ↔ radians:  
   rad = deg × π/180 ;  deg = rad × 180/π

2. Haversine formula for great-circle distance (central angle Δσ):  

   a = sin²(Δφ /2) + cos φ₁ · cos φ₂ · sin²(Δλ /2)  
   Δσ = 2 · atan2( √a , √(1−a) )

   Great-circle distance d = R · Δσ

   R = 6371 000 m (mean Earth radius) 〚Use 3440.065 NM or 3958.761 mi if that’s your tactical unit〛

3. Initial course / bearing θ (sometimes called azimuth):  

   y = sin Δλ · cos φ₂  
   x = cos φ₁ · sin φ₂ − sin φ₁ · cos φ₂ · cos Δλ  
   θ = atan2(y, x)    (result in radians; normalize 0-360°)

4. Intermediate point P(f) at fraction f (0 ≤ f ≤ 1) of the path, using spherical linear interpolation (“slerp”):

   A = sin((1−f)·Δσ) / sin Δσ  
   B = sin(f·Δσ)      / sin Δσ  

   x = A·cos φ₁·cos λ₁ + B·cos φ₂·cos λ₂  
   y = A·cos φ₁·sin λ₁ + B·cos φ₂·sin λ₂  
   z = A·sin φ₁       + B·sin φ₂  

   φ = atan2(z, √(x² + y²))  
   λ = atan2(y, x)

--------------------------------------------------
2.  The Python program
--------------------------------------------------
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
flight_path.py
Compute distance, initial bearing, flight time, and intermediate way-points
for a great-circle route on the WGS-84 sphere.

Run:  python3 flight_path.py
"""

import math
from datetime import timedelta

# --------------------------------------------------
# Utility functions
# --------------------------------------------------
def deg2rad(deg):
    return math.radians(deg)

def rad2deg(rad):
    return math.degrees(rad)

def haversine_distance_m(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, R=6_371_000):
    """Great-circle distance in metres (Haversine)."""
    φ1, λ1, φ2, λ2 = map(deg2rad, (lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2))
    dφ, dλ = φ2 - φ1, λ2 - λ1
    a = math.sin(dφ / 2)**2 + math.cos(φ1) * math.cos(φ2) * math.sin(dλ / 2)**2
    Δσ = 2 * math.atan2(math.sqrt(a), math.sqrt(1 - a))
    return R * Δσ, Δσ          # (distance, central angle)

def initial_bearing_deg(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    """Initial course (true bearing) from point 1 to point 2 in degrees."""
    φ1, λ1, φ2, λ2 = map(deg2rad, (lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2))
    Δλ = λ2 - λ1
    y = math.sin(Δλ) * math.cos(φ2)
    x = math.cos(φ1) * math.sin(φ2) - math.sin(φ1) * math.cos(φ2) * math.cos(Δλ)
    θ = math.atan2(y, x)
    return (rad2deg(θ) + 360) % 360   # normalize 0…360°

def interpolate(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, frac, Δσ):
    """Return lat, lon at fractional distance 'frac' along great-circle."""
    φ1, λ1, φ2, λ2 = map(deg2rad, (lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2))
    sinΔσ = math.sin(Δσ)
    if sinΔσ == 0:
        return lat1, lon1               # same point

    A = math.sin((1 - frac) * Δσ) / sinΔσ
    B = math.sin(frac * Δσ)       / sinΔσ

    x = A * math.cos(φ1) * math.cos(λ1) + B * math.cos(φ2) * math.cos(λ2)
    y = A * math.cos(φ1) * math.sin(λ1) + B * math.cos(φ2) * math.sin(λ2)
    z = A * math.sin(φ1)               + B * math.sin(φ2)

    φ = math.atan2(z, math.sqrt(x*x + y*y))
    λ = math.atan2(y, x)
    return rad2deg(φ), rad2deg(λ)

# --------------------------------------------------
# Core flight-path routine
# --------------------------------------------------
def compute_flight_path(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2,
                        ground_speed_kt=450,
                        step_minutes=10,
                        altitude_ft=35_000):
    """Return a dict with distance, bearing, total time, and way-points."""
    MS_PER_NM = 1852           # 1 nautical mile = 1852 m
    MS_PER_KT = 0.514444 * 1000  # metres per second per knot

    dist_m, Δσ = haversine_distance_m(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)
    dist_nm = dist_m / MS_PER_NM

    speed_m_s = ground_speed_kt * MS_PER_KT
    total_time_s = dist_m / speed_m_s

    n_steps = max(1, round(total_time_s / (step_minutes * 60)))
    step_frac = 1.0 / n_steps

    waypoints = []
    for i in range(n_steps + 1):
        frac = i * step_frac
        lat, lon = interpolate(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, frac, Δσ)
        elapsed = timedelta(seconds=int(frac * total_time_s))
        waypoints.append({
            'sequence' : i,
            'lat'      : lat,
            'lon'      : lon,
            'alt_ft'   : altitude_ft,
            'elapsed'  : elapsed
        })

    return {
        'distance_nm'  : dist_nm,
        'distance_km'  : dist_m / 1000,
        'initial_brng' : initial_bearing_deg(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2),
        'ground_speed' : ground_speed_kt,
        'flight_time'  : timedelta(seconds=int(total_time_s)),
        'waypoints'    : waypoints
    }

# --------------------------------------------------
# Simple command-line interface
# --------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print("Great-Circle Flight Path Calculator\n")

    lat1 = float(input("Departure latitude  (deg N/S, south negative): "))
    lon1 = float(input("Departure longitude (deg E/W, west negative): "))
    lat2 = float(input("Destination latitude  : "))
    lon2 = float(input("Destination longitude : "))

    gs   = float(input("Ground speed (knots) [450]: ") or 450)
    step = int  (input("Waypoint interval (minutes) [10]: ") or 10)

    result = compute_flight_path(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2,
                                 ground_speed_kt=gs,
                                 step_minutes=step)

    print("\nSummary")
    print("-------")
    print(f"Great-circle distance : {result['distance_nm']:.1f} NM "
          f"({result['distance_km']:.1f} km)")
    print(f"Initial true bearing  : {result['initial_brng']:.1f}°")
    print(f"Estimated flight time : {result['flight_time']}")
    print("\nWay-points")
    print("Seq   Time (h:mm)     Latitude    Longitude   Alt(ft)")
    for wp in result['waypoints']:
        t = str(wp['elapsed'])[:-3]          # trim seconds for brevity
        print(f"{wp['sequence']:>3}   {t:>8}   {wp['lat']:>9.4f}   "
              f"{wp['lon']:>9.4f}   {wp['alt_ft']:>7}")

```

--------------------------------------------------
3.  Example session
--------------------------------------------------
```

Departure longitude (deg E/W, west negative): -118.4081
Destination latitude  : 40.6398

-------

```

(Example above is LAX → JFK at 450 kt.)

--------------------------------------------------
4.  Extending the program
--------------------------------------------------
• Read airport coordinates automatically using an ICAO/IATA lookup CSV.  
• Allow variable speed or altitude profiles (climb, cruise, descent).  
• Add wind correction and compute true airspeed vs. ground speed.  
• Output to GPX or KML so the path can be visualised in Google Earth.  
• Plot the track on a map with `matplotlib`, `cartopy`, or `folium`.  
• Use the more precise WGS-84 ellipsoid via `geographiclib` if centimeter-level accuracy is important.  

This skeleton gives you the core geometry; everything else—performance data, airspace constraints, fuel burn, etc.—can be layered on as needed for your specific project.

instruction: Provide python code to calculate pie infinitely
output:
Below is a compact, self-contained Python module that can keep improving the approximation of π for as long as the program is allowed to run.  
It uses two algorithms:

1.  A *fast* Chudnovsky series step (14 decimal digits per iteration).  
2.  A simple *infinite* generator that yields the current approximation after every step, so the caller can decide when to stop.

The code is completely standard Python (no third-party libraries).  Interrupt it with Ctrl-C or break the `for` / `while` loop whenever you have “enough” digits.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
infinite_pi.py
A tiny module that refines π indefinitely using the Chudnovsky formula.
"""

from decimal import Decimal, getcontext
from math import factorial

# --------------  CORE: one Chudnovsky term  -------------- #
def _chudnovsky_term(k: int) -> Decimal:
    """
    Return the k-th term of the Chudnovsky summation for 1/π.
    Each term adds ~14 correct decimal digits.
    """
    #  (-1)^k (6k)!  (13591409 + 545140134 k)
    #  ----------------------------------------
    #  (3k)! (k!)^3  (640320)^{3k}
    numerator   = (-1) ** k * factorial(6 * k) * (13591409 + 545140134 * k)
    denominator = factorial(3 * k) * (factorial(k) ** 3) * (640320 ** (3 * k))
    return Decimal(numerator) / Decimal(denominator)


# --------------  INFINITE GENERATOR  -------------- #
def pi_generator(start_prec: int = 50):
    """
    Yields successively better Decimal approximations of π.
    The caller controls how many values to consume (potentially infinite).
    """
    # Work with a context large enough to hold many future digits
    getcontext().prec = start_prec

    k        = 0                 # series index
    partial  = Decimal(0)        # running sum of terms for 1/π
    factor   = Decimal(426880) * Decimal(10005).sqrt()

    while True:
        term = _chudnovsky_term(k)
        partial += term
        # 1/π  = partial / factor  ==> π = factor / partial
        pi_val = factor / partial
        yield +pi_val             # unary + forces rounding to current context
        k += 1

        # every loop we expect ≈14 more correct digits; grow precision accordingly
        target_prec = 14 * (k + 4)            # a little cushion
        if target_prec > getcontext().prec:
            getcontext().prec = target_prec


# --------------  CONVENIENCE FUNCTION -------------- #
def pi_to_digits(digits: int) -> str:
    """
    Return π with exactly `digits` decimal digits (as a string).
    """
    gen = pi_generator(digits + 20)   # extra guard digits
    while True:
        π = next(gen)
        # When we already have more than the requested precision, stop
        if len(str(π).replace('.', '')) >= digits + 1:   # +1 for leading '3'
            break
    # Round & format
    fmt_str = f"{{0:.{digits}f}}"
    return fmt_str.format(π)


# --------------  DEMO / SELF-TEST -------------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import itertools

    print("Streaming approximations (Ctrl-C to abort):")
    for i, π in zip(itertools.count(), pi_generator()):
        print(f"Iteration {i:3d}: π ≈ {π}")
        if i == 10:       # show 11 approximations then quit (change as desired)
            break

    # Print 1000 digits just to show it works
    print("\nπ to 1000 decimal digits:")
    print(pi_to_digits(1000))
```

How to use
==========

1.  Save the script as `infinite_pi.py`.
2.  Run it:  
        python3 infinite_pi.py
    It will print an ever-improving value of π (11 iterations by default).
3.  Import it in other code:

```python
from infinite_pi import pi_generator, pi_to_digits

# Get the first 5 approximations
for approx in zip(range(5), pi_generator()):
    print(approx)

# Get π to one million digits (careful: needs RAM/CPU):
million = pi_to_digits(1_000_000)
```

Why this works
==============

• The Chudnovsky formula converges extremely fast:  
  each extra term gives roughly 14 correct decimal digits.

• By adjusting `getcontext().prec` upward inside the loop, the generator can
  refine π “forever”—bounded only by your machine’s memory, time and patience.

Enjoy calculating π “infinitely”!
