output:
Below is a self-contained Ruby script that you can either  
 • paste directly in SketchUp’s Ruby Console, or  
 • save as draw_cube.rb in your SketchUp “Plugins/Extensions” folder (SketchUp will load it the next time it starts or you can reload the file from the console with load 'draw_cube.rb').  

The code adds a “Draw Cube” item to the Extensions/Plugins menu; when you click it you’ll be asked for the cube size in mm and a solid cube will be created at the model origin.

```ruby
# draw_cube.rb
# Simple SketchUp Ruby example – draws a solid cube.
# Works in SketchUp 2016+ (or any version that supports the regular Ruby API).

require 'sketchup.rb'

module Example        # top-level “company” namespace
module DrawCube       # this tool’s namespace

  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # create_cube(origin, size)
  #   origin :: Geom::Point3d – lower-left-front corner of the cube
  #   size   :: Length        – edge length of the cube
  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  def self.create_cube(origin, size)
    model    = Sketchup.active_model
    entities = model.active_entities

    # We’ll build the cube in a group so it is easy to move/delete afterwards
    group    = entities.add_group
    ents     = group.entities

    # Bottom (z = origin.z) rectangle
    p1 = origin
    p2 = origin + [size, 0,     0]
    p3 = origin + [size, size,  0]
    p4 = origin + [0,     size, 0]

    # Draw the bottom face
    face = ents.add_face(p1, p2, p3, p4)
    face.reverse! if face.normal.z < 0   # make sure normal points “up”

    # Extrude (“pushpull”) the face upward to make the cube
    face.pushpull(size)

    # Give the group a name that shows in Outliner
    group.name = "Cube - #{size.to_mm.round} mm"

    group   # return it for good measure
  end

  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Main entry point – asks the user for a size and calls create_cube
  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  def self.main
    prompts  = ['Cube size (mm):']
    defaults = [100]
    input    = UI.inputbox(prompts, defaults, 'Create Cube')
    return if input.nil?      # user pressed Cancel

    size = input[0].to_f.mm   # convert to SketchUp Length (internal units = inches)

    model = Sketchup.active_model
    model.start_operation('Create Cube', true)
    create_cube(Geom::Point3d.new(0,0,0), size)
    model.commit_operation
  end

  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Add a menu item (only once)
  #------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  unless file_loaded?(__FILE__)
    UI.menu('Plugins').add_item('Draw Cube') { self.main }
    file_loaded(__FILE__)
  end

end # module DrawCube
end # module Example
```

If you only need a one-liner for the Ruby Console:

```ruby
face = Sketchup.active_model.active_entities.add_face([0,0,0],[1.m,0,0],[1.m,1.m,0],[0,1.m,0]); face.pushpull(1.m)
```

That single command draws a 1-meter cube at the origin.

instruction:
youll be acting as a senior analyst who is an expert in sql. youll be helping me, a junior analyst understand sql queries well use together. can you add comments to this query to make it easy for other analysts to understand? SELECT ifnull(region,'') region,ifnull(subregion,'') subregion,
avg(COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED) avg_ct_sl,count(DISTINCT patientid) ct_patients 
FROM PATIENT_INFO
GROUP BY cube(1,2) ORDER BY avg_ct_sl DESC
output:
Below is the same query, rewritten with line-by-line comments so another analyst can quickly see what each part does and why it is there.  
(The comments use the “--” style which works in most ANSI-SQL engines. If you are on a platform that uses a different comment delimiter, adjust accordingly.)

```sql
/* --------------------------------------------------------------------
   Pull average service-line usage and distinct-patient counts
   at 3 aggregation levels:  (1) Region + Sub-region
                              (2) Region total
                              (3) Grand total
   -------------------------------------------------------------------- */

SELECT
    /* Replace NULL regions with an empty string so the CUBE roll-ups
       won’t show “NULL” but instead a blank value. */
    IFNULL(region, '')      AS region,

    /* Same treatment for sub-region. */
    IFNULL(subregion, '')   AS subregion,

    /* Average number of service lines used per row in the group.
       (COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED assumed to be a numeric column.) */
    AVG(COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED) AS avg_ct_sl,

    /* How many unique patients are represented in the group. */
    COUNT(DISTINCT patientid)     AS ct_patients

FROM
    PATIENT_INFO                     -- Source table

/* --------------------------------------------------------------------
   CUBE(1,2) = produce subtotals for:
       1. (region, subregion)  – the detail rows
       2. (region)             – subtotal for each region, all subregions
       3. ()                   – grand total (all regions & subregions)
   We use column positions (1,2) instead of names so the engine rolls
   up on the first two SELECT items (region, subregion).               
   -------------------------------------------------------------------- */
GROUP BY
    CUBE(1, 2)

/* Put the groups with the highest average service-line count first. */
ORDER BY
    avg_ct_sl DESC;
```

Key take-aways for anyone reading the query
-------------------------------------------
1. IFNULL() is there strictly for cosmetic/reporting reasons so NULLs don’t appear in the output.  
2. AVG(COUNT_SERVICE_LINES_USED) gives a “per-patient info row” average across the chosen grain (region/subregion total, region total, or grand total).  
3. The CUBE operator automatically generates the three aggregation levels—no need for separate UNIONs.  
4. Ordering by the derived alias `avg_ct_sl` is allowed because most databases evaluate aliases after the SELECT list.

instruction: List potential side-effects or complications of the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CSA) and Product Liability Directive (PLD) as they could relate to individual developers of software
output:
Below is a non-exhaustive list of the ways in which the forthcoming EU Cyber-Resilience Act (CRA) and the revised Product-Liability Directive (PLD) could – directly or indirectly – affect individual software developers (independent freelancers, micro-start-ups, hobbyists, open-source maintainers, researchers, etc.).  The items are framed as “side-effects or complications”, i.e. impacts that might arise even though the acts are primarily aimed at commercial manufacturers and large vendors.

A. Cyber-Resilience Act (CRA)

1. Scope ambiguity for open-source and “side projects”
   • The CRA exempts software that is “developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity,” but the border between “commercial” and “non-commercial” is thin (e.g. donations, bounty programs, dual licensing, company-sponsored work).  
   • An individual who publishes code free of charge today could unknowingly step into “commercial” territory tomorrow (e.g. if they enable GitHub Sponsors or sell a branded T-shirt), potentially triggering CRA obligations retroactively.

2. “Manufacturer” status may attach to a single coder
   • A solo developer who puts a paid mobile app in an EU app store automatically becomes the “manufacturer” of a “product with digital elements” and must:  
     – perform/purchase a conformity assessment,  
     – affix a CE mark,  
     – prepare a Declaration of Conformity and a technical file,  
     – implement vulnerability handling and coordinated disclosure processes,  
     – issue security updates for the whole “expected lifetime” (minimum 5 years in most cases).  
   • These procedures were designed with corporate QA departments in mind and can be difficult or impossible for one person to fulfil.

3. Up-front compliance cost
   • Third-party certification bodies, penetration testing, legal drafting and translation of documentation can easily exceed the revenue a solo app brings in.  
   • Payments or resources diverted to compliance reduce the time and money available for actual feature development.

4. Exposure to administrative fines
   • Non-compliance with critical CRA requirements can be fined up to €15 million or 2.5 % of global turnover, whichever is higher.  Even if fines against micro-entities were modest, the theoretical exposure is chilling.

5. Forced uptake of cybersecurity processes
   • Secure-development-lifecycle (SDL) processes, SBOM generation, risk assessment, logging of post-market incidents, encryption key management, secure supply-chain requirements, etc., become legal duties.  
   • For lone developers these tasks may require new tooling, training or paid services (code-signing certificates, auditing platforms, vulnerability databases).

6. Increased dependency on upstream and tooling vendors
   • If one must produce an SBOM or remediate supply-chain CVEs, a lone developer can be held liable for vulnerabilities in open-source libraries they never authored.  
   • The result may be reluctance to rely on volunteer-maintained OSS or a preference for commercial “certified” libraries, limiting technological choice.

7. Chilling effect on security research & rapid releases
   • The CRA obliges “vulnerability management” and “coordinated disclosure.”  A hobbyist pushing nightly builds to GitHub may not have (or want) the infrastructure to handle bug bounty submissions or provide 24-hour acknowledgements to researchers, yet could be found non-compliant.

8. Distribution platforms may add their own gatekeeping
   • App stores, package repositories, IoT marketplaces, or Linux-distro maintainers may require proof of CRA compliance before accepting a package.  
   • This can de-facto bar individual developers from EU user bases even if the law did not target them directly.

9. Perceived or real extraterritorial reach
   • A developer in Argentina or India whose app is downloaded by EU citizens may still be ­subject to the CRA.  Cloud repositories (e.g. npm) could start geo-blocking or showing “not for EU users” warnings, fragmenting the open-source ecosystem.

10. Insurance and contractual pass-through
   • Freelance developers hired by a European SME might be asked to sign contracts guaranteeing CRA compliance, obtain professional-liability or cyber-insurance, or accept indemnification clauses they cannot realistically cover.

B. Revised Product-Liability Directive (PLD)

1. Extension of “product” to pure software
   • Stand-alone software (apps, SaaS, firmware, AI models, OSS binaries) is expressly included.  A single bug that causes “property damage” (including data) or “bodily injury” can trigger strict liability.

2. Lowered burden of proof for claimants
   • Courts may infer a software defect from circumstantial evidence and causal uncertainty can be relaxed (“defect is reasonably likely to have caused the damage”).  This increases litigation risk for developers with shallow pockets.

3. Loss/limitation of “development-risk defence”
   • The defence that “the state of scientific/technical knowledge made the defect undiscoverable” is curtailed when the defect arises from cybersecurity vulnerabilities.  An individual may be deemed liable even if the flaw was unknown to them and to the entire industry at the time of release.

4. Long tail of update obligations
   • Failure to issue “necessary software security updates during a reasonable period” itself constitutes a defect.  
   • Independent devs may be unable to keep an old app updated after moving to other jobs, but will still carry liability.

5. Joint and several liability across the chain
   • If a lone coder contributes a module that later ships inside a commercial product, they can be brought into litigation alongside the OEM and distributor, unless robust contractual shields are in place.

6. Invalidity of contractual waivers towards consumers
   • EULAs or OSS licences purporting to disclaim liability for damage to property or personal injury will not protect against PLD claims.  Developers must assume that such exposure remains.

7. Increased need for evidence preservation
   • Developers will have to archive source code, design documents, emails, version history, test logs, etc., for 10+ years to defend themselves.  Storage, legal advice, and data-protection compliance add overhead.

8. Insurance pressure and cost
   • Professional-indemnity premiums may rise or insurers may refuse cover for “cyber-physical” software produced by individual developers, ruling them out of certain markets.

9. Potential chilling effect on OSS communities
   • Fear of personal liability may discourage maintainers from accepting patches, releasing binaries, or providing bug fixes, shifting projects to “source-only” or “research-only” status, or relocating outside the EU.

10. Forum shopping and cross-border enforcement
   • Plaintiffs may prefer to sue in EU jurisdictions known for claimant-friendly interpretations; a dev residing elsewhere can still face attachment of assets or enforcement of judgments via treaties.

C. Combined / downstream effects

1. Higher barriers to entry
   • The compliance burden (CRA) plus strict liability (PLD) may shift EU software entrepreneurship from garage-level innovators to well-capitalised entities.

2. Consolidation of hosting and distribution
   • Git forges, package registries, CI/CD providers may demand that uploads are signed, scanned, and accompanied by compliance artefacts, favouring institutional projects and crowding out hobby code.

3. Licence and ecosystem fragmentation
   • Expect proliferation of licences adding “non-EU use only,” upstreams withdrawing pre-built binaries, or conditional licences that require users to self-compile or assume compliance obligations.

4. Flight of talent or code repositories
   • Small EU developers might relocate repositories to non-EU legal entities, adopt anonymisation strategies, or limit EU user access, potentially undermining Europe’s digital-sovereignty goals.

5. Increased value of corporate sponsorship and foundations
   • Individual maintainers may seek shelter under the umbrella of non-profit foundations or commercial sponsors that can finance audits, hold liability insurance, and act as the “manufacturer of record.”

6. “Compliance-as-a-Service” cottage industry
   • Consultants, automated SBOM generators, vulnerability-management platforms, and legal template providers will appear; but their costs still land on the individual developer.

7. Divergence between “experimental” and “consumer-grade” code
   • The acts could bifurcate the FLOSS world into (i) audited, fully supported releases and (ii) “research/academic only” repositories.  Individual devs may be pushed into the latter, limiting real-world adoption of their work.

8. Possible slowdown of security disclosure
   • Developers fearing liability may refrain from publishing PoCs or exploit details, hampering collaborative security research.

9. Administrative burden on academic or hobby clubs
   • University students publishing class projects or small robotics clubs selling kits through EU maker fairs might unintentionally become subject to CRA/PLD obligations.

10. Cultural shift toward formal processes
   • Individual developers will need to think like regulated manufacturers: threat modelling, documentation, legal review, release notes, deprecation policy, etc., altering the informal culture of many open-source projects.

Summary

While the CRA and the PLD aim to raise the overall cybersecurity and consumer-safety baseline, they introduce significant legal, financial, and procedural obligations that are straightforward for large vendors but potentially onerous for individual developers.  Without tailored micro-entity exemptions, safe-harbour rules, or supporting infrastructure (insurance pools, compliance toolchains, legal clarifications), the new regime risks discouraging small-scale European innovation and could fragment the broader open-source ecosystem.

instruction: Act as a MIT Computer Scientist.  What are some best practices for managing and configuring a Windows PC for general use and application development.  Consider multiple user accounts by one user.  Consider cybersecurity.  Consider a development environment for Github repo.
output:
Best-practice checklist for turning a single Windows 10/11 machine into a stable daily-driver AND a secure, reproducible software-development workstation.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Operating-system build & patching
────────────────────────────────────────
• Start from a clean, up-to-date ISO (MSDN, Volume Center, or MediaCreation tool).  
• During install pick “Keep files only” ➞ never “Keep apps”—forces you to reinstall and avoid legacy cruft.  
• Join the “Current Channel” (not Insider) unless you specifically need preview SDKs.  
• Turn on: Settings ▸ Windows Update ▸ Advanced ▸ “Receive updates for other Microsoft products”.  
• Block driver updates via GPO if you need deterministic builds: gpedit.msc → Computer Configuration → Admin Templates → Windows Components → Windows Update → “Do not include drivers with Windows Updates”.  
• Make a full, clean image (Macrium, Acronis, DISM capture, or bare-metal Hyper-V checkpoint) right now; if anything breaks you have a one-click restore.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Account & privilege model (single human)
────────────────────────────────────────
Recommended trio of local accounts:
  1. WIN-ADMIN  : Administrator, used only when UAC prompts demand it.  
  2. WIN-USER   : Standard account for browsing, email, document editing.  
  3. WIN-DEV    : Standard account dedicated to coding, debugging, Docker/WSL.

Tips  
• Use `runas /user:WIN-ADMIN cmd` or Windows Terminal’s “Run as administrator” to elevate ad-hoc tasks—never stay logged in as Admin.  
• Tie all three to the SAME Microsoft/AAD identity for “Shared Experience” (clipboard, OneDrive) but disable file syncing on DEV to avoid auto‐rebasing Git repos.  
• Enable Windows Hello + PIN + FIDO2 key on each account, and require auth-on-resume.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Cyber-hardening
────────────────────────────────────────
Firmware & BIOS  
  – Update UEFI, enable Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, disable legacy boot devices and Intel ME remote mgmt.  
  – Turn on Platform Trust Technology (PTT) or fTPM if discrete TPM absent.

Storage  
  – BitLocker full-disk encryption; store recovery key in Microsoft account AND an off-line USB.  
  – Turn on “Secure Boot > Trusted Boot > Measured Boot” (Win11 handles this automatically).

Windows security stack  
  – Microsoft Defender Antivirus (ATP) is good enough; don’t disable.  
  – Exploit Protection: system-wide DEP, ASLR, CFG; Override per-app in sysdm.cpl ▸ Data Execution.  
  – Core Isolation > Memory Integrity (a.k.a. HVCI) if CPU supports SLAT (most 7th-Gen+ Intel/AMD).  
  – Controlled Folder Access: include C:\Users\WIN-USER\Documents, Pictures, etc.  
  – Enable “Smart App Control” on Win11 22H2+, or “AppLocker” rules via gpedit for Homebrew installs.

Network  
  – Firewall: leave Defender Firewall ON for all profiles, block inbound by default.  
  – Disable SMBv1 (`Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName smb1protocol`) and LLMNR (`HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient\EnableMulticast`=0).  
  – Use a VPN when on public Wi-Fi; alternatives: WireGuard, OpenVPN, commercial.

Updates, macros & Office  
  – Disable Office macros by default, allow only trusted locations.  
  – Edge/Chrome: install “uBlock Origin” + “HTTPS-Only Mode”.  
  – Adobe Reader: Protected Mode ON, JavaScript OFF.

Backups  
  – 3-2-1: File History to secondary drive + daily VSS snapshot + weekly offline image.  
  – Test restoration monthly.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Package & environment management
────────────────────────────────────────
• Use winget (`winget install vscode git python nodejs`), Chocolatey, or Scoop—never random EXE downloads.  
• Document package list: `winget export -o packages.json`; reprovision with `winget import`.  
• Isolate legacy runtimes (e.g., Java 8, .NET 4.x) inside containers/VMs, not system-wide PATH.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. Development stack layout
────────────────────────────────────────
Desired directory topology (one physical disk, multiple partitions optional):

C:\Dev        ↴   Git-cloned projects  
C:\.wslg      ↴   WSL2 virtual disks  
D:\Containers ↴   Docker Desktop data (move via Resources ▸ ADVANCED)  
E:\Scratch    ↴   Large test data, databases, virtual machines  
Z:\Backup     ↴   External / network backup target

Toolchain
  • Windows Terminal + PowerShell 7 + oh-my-posh + `PSReadLine -PredictionSource History`.  
  • Git for Windows (x64, minimal) – set:  
        git config --global user.name "Your Name"  
        git config --global user.email you@mail.com  
        git config --global gpg.program gpg  
        git config --global commit.gpgsign true  
        git config --global core.autocrlf input  
        git config --global pull.rebase false
  • Create separate SSH key pair per machine; `~/.ssh/config` → `AddKeysToAgent yes`; protect with passphrase + Windows Hello via `gpg-connect-agent updatestartuptty /bye`.  
  • Optionally use Git Credential Manager Core (GCM) with Windows Hello for PATs.

WSL2  
  – `wsl --install -d Ubuntu` (or Arch).  
  – Map Windows paths under /mnt/c to avoid NTFS ↔ ext4 perf penalty.  
  – VS Code Remote-WSL extension; debug C/C++, Go, Rust inside Linux while UI runs on Windows.  
  – Provide reproducible environment with dev-container: `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`, `Dockerfile`.  
  – For GPU/AI work enable `wsl --update` + NVIDIA CUDA toolkit for WSL.

Docker  
  – Install Docker Desktop, switch to WSL2 backend, limit CPUs/RAM in Settings -> Resources.  
  – Use named volumes that point at D:\Containers to keep C: slim.  
  – Scan images with `docker scan` (Snyk) or Trivy.  
  – Never run production services directly on host—containerize DBs and message brokers.

Hyper-V / VMware Workstation / VirtualBox  
  – For kernel-driver or low-level experimentation, spin up disposable VMs; checkpoint before risky changes.  
  – Store VM disks on fast NVMe or dedicated SSD to avoid contention with WSL2.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. IDE & editor configuration
────────────────────────────────────────
VS Code  
  – Sync settings via GitHub login; enable Settings Sync but exclude “workspace settings” to avoid team noise.  
  – Recommended extensions: Remote-WSL, Docker, GitLens, IntelliCode, ESLint, Prettier, EditorConfig.

Visual Studio 2022  
  – Workloads: “Desktop Dev with C++”, “.NET 6/7”, “UWP”, “Linux development with C++” if needed.  
  – Turn off “Just-In-Time Debugger” in Win-USER to avoid forced attach to random programs.

JetBrains Toolbox  
  – Install in DEV account only, separate home directory `.config\JetBrains` inside C:\Dev\_configs for easy archival.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Performance & stability
────────────────────────────────────────
• Disable manufacturer bloatware; keep OEM control center only if it provides firmware updates.  
• Power plan: Balanced on battery; High-performance while plugged in during heavy builds.  
• Use “Storage Sense” to purge temp files but exclude C:\Dev and .wslg.  
• Monitor with Windows Resource Monitor, Procmon, and LatencyMon (for DPC issues).  
• Keep 20-25 % free disk space; SSDs need spare cells for wear-leveling.

────────────────────────────────────────
8. Logging & audit
────────────────────────────────────────
• Enable Windows Event Forwarding to send Security and Application logs to a Sysmon collector or Splunk-Free.  
• Install Sysinternals Sysmon (`sysmon -accepteula -i config.xml`) – log process hash, network, file create; store logs for 30 days.  
• Turn on “Audit: Logon events”, “Process Creation”, and “DPAPI activity” via secpol.msc.

────────────────────────────────────────
9. Disaster-recovery drills
────────────────────────────────────────
• Quarterly: pull “factory image” + test bare-metal restore onto spare drive.  
• Monthly: `wsl --export` each distro to tar; push to encrypted external disk.  
• Weekly: `winget export`, `choco list --localonly`, `docker image ls > docker-images.txt`, commit to a private GitHub Gist.

────────────────────────────────────────
10. Documentation & reproducibility
────────────────────────────────────────
• Maintain a “bootstrap.ps1” script that: enables features (Hyper-V, WSL), installs winget packages, applies sensible registry tweaks.  
• Check this script into a private “machine-setup” GitHub repo; CI-run `PSScriptAnalyzer` to keep it clean.  
• On-boarding a new PC becomes: “Run PowerShell as admin → `irm tinyurl.com/mysetup | iex`”.  
• Keep an encrypted OneNote/Markdown vault with serial numbers, BitLocker keys, BIOS settings, VPN profiles, SSH fingerprints.

────────────────────────────────────────
TL;DR
1. Divide roles: Admin vs User vs Dev accounts; principle of least privilege.  
2. Enable hardware-backed security: TPM, BitLocker, Secure Boot, Defender stack.  
3. Automate package management with winget/choco; record manifest(s).  
4. Use WSL2 + Docker for isolating build environments; store code under C:\Dev.  
5. Sign Git commits, manage SSH keys securely, enforce MFA for GitHub.  
6. Back up everything (File History + System Image + off-site); verify restore.  
7. Script the whole setup so you can rebuild a compromised or replaced PC in <1 hour.

Follow these practices and your Windows PC will behave much more like a reproducible, secure, and developer-friendly UNIX laptop—without giving up native Office, gaming, or GPU driver stacks.

instruction: In vb.net, create a function that return the cpu usage and ram usage of every programs running on the computer. it should return as a list of Pgr, with Pgr being an item containing the name, the ram usage and the cpu usage of a program.
output:
Below is a self-contained VB.NET implementation.  
It defines a very small “Pgr” class and a single routine – GetProcessesUsage – that:

1. Reads every running process.  
2. Stores its TotalProcessorTime.  
3. Waits 500 ms.  
4. Reads each process again and calculates  
   CPU-usage % = ΔTotalProcessorTime / (elapsedTime × logicalCpuCount).  
5. Returns a List(Of Pgr) where each Pgr contains the process name, RAM usage (MB) and CPU usage (%).

You can drop the code into any .NET project that targets Windows (WinForms, WPF, Console, …).

```vb
Option Strict On
Option Explicit On

Imports System.Diagnostics
Imports System.Threading
Imports System.Collections.Generic

'---------------------------------------------
' A very small DTO that will hold the results
'---------------------------------------------
Public Class Pgr
    Public Property Name As String          ' Process name
    Public Property RamUsageMB As Double    ' Working set, MB
    Public Property CpuUsage As Double      ' Percentage of total CPU (all cores)
End Class

'-------------------------------------------------------
' Module / class that delivers the process information
'-------------------------------------------------------
Public Module ProcessUtilities

    ''' <summary>
    ''' Returns a snapshot (List(Of Pgr)) that contains
    '''  - Process name
    '''  - Current RAM usage (MB)
    '''  - CPU usage (%) calculated over 0.5 s
    ''' </summary>
    Public Function GetProcessesUsage() As List(Of Pgr)

        Const SAMPLE_TIME_MS As Integer = 500      ' length of the sampling window
        Dim cpuCount As Integer = Environment.ProcessorCount

        ' 1st snapshot – store TotalProcessorTime for every process
        Dim firstSample As New Dictionary(Of Integer, TimeSpan)() ' key = PID
        For Each pr As Process In Process.GetProcesses()
            Try
                firstSample(pr.Id) = pr.TotalProcessorTime
            Catch __unused As Exception
                ' Access denied or the process has already ended; ignore.
            End Try
        Next

        ' Wait a bit so we can calculate a delta
        Thread.Sleep(SAMPLE_TIME_MS)

        ' Result container
        Dim result As New List(Of Pgr)()

        ' 2nd snapshot – calculate CPU %, collect memory
        For Each pr As Process In Process.GetProcesses()
            Try
                Dim previous As TimeSpan = Nothing
                If Not firstSample.TryGetValue(pr.Id, previous) Then Continue For

                Dim current As TimeSpan = pr.TotalProcessorTime
                Dim deltaMs As Double = (current - previous).TotalMilliseconds

                ' CPU % = (time the process used on all cores) / (time elapsed × number_of_cores) × 100
                Dim cpuPercent As Double = (deltaMs / SAMPLE_TIME_MS) / cpuCount * 100.0

                ' RAM = working set (bytes) → MB
                Dim ramMb As Double = pr.WorkingSet64 / 1024.0 / 1024.0

                result.Add(New Pgr With {
                    .Name = pr.ProcessName,
                    .RamUsageMB = ramMb,
                    .CpuUsage = cpuPercent
                })

            Catch __unused As Exception
                ' The process may have terminated or cannot be accessed; skip it.
            End Try
        Next

        Return result
    End Function

End Module
```

Usage example:

```vb
Sub Main()
    For Each p In ProcessUtilities.GetProcessesUsage()
        Console.WriteLine($"{p.Name,-30} RAM: {p.RamUsageMB,8:N1} MB   CPU: {p.CpuUsage,6:N2} %")
    Next
End Sub
```

Notes / caveats  
• The function performs one 500 ms sleep; for real-time monitoring call it on a background thread or lengthen/shorten the sampling window to suit your needs.  
• A try/catch surrounds every Process property access because some processes terminate or disallow queries between the two snapshots.  
• WorkingSet64 is only one of several possible memory counters; choose PrivateMemorySize64, PagedMemorySize64, etc., if you need a different definition of “RAM usage”.

instruction: Technical details of GDDR6 and GDDR7, no qualitative info, only precise details. Include Memory Bandwidth example calculations for 2500MHz with both technologies.
output:
GDDR6 – selected electrical/architectural parameters  
• JEDEC document: JESD-250-C (2021)  
• Signalling: NRZ, double-data-rate (2 bits transferred per I/O clock)  
• Prefetch depth: 16n  
• External data bus per package: 32 bits (implemented as two independent 16-bit channels)  
• Supply voltages: VDD 1.35 V nominal (speed-grade option 1.25 V), VPP 2.5 V  
• Package: 180-ball FBGA, 0.75 mm pitch  
• Bank structure: 16 banks, organised as 4 bank groups × 4 banks/group per 16-bit channel  
• Burst length: BL32 (per 32-bit device), i.e. 16 transfers per edge on each 16-bit sub-channel  
• Minimum tCK (I/O clock period): 83 ps for 24 Gb/s grade (≈ 12 GHz I/O clock)  
• Maximum specified per-pin data rate grades: 12 Gb/s, 14 Gb/s, 16 Gb/s, 18 Gb/s, 20 Gb/s, 22 Gb/s, 24 Gb/s  
• Read/write command interface clock (CK): single-ended, half of DQ edge rate  
• On-die termination and decision feedback equalisation supported on DQ/DBI/EDC lines  

GDDR7 – selected electrical/architectural parameters (public draft / vendor announcements)  
• JEDEC draft document: JESD-239 (finalisation 2024)  
• Signalling: PAM3, double-data-rate (3 logical bits transferred per I/O clock: 1.5 bits per edge × 2 edges)  
• Prefetch depth: 16n  
• External data bus per package: 32 bits (four independent 8-bit sub-channels)  
• Supply voltages: VDD 1.2 V, VDDQ 1.1 V, VPP 1.8 V  
• Package: 266-ball FBGA, 0.65 mm pitch  
• Bank structure: 32 banks, organised as 8 bank groups × 4 banks/group  
• Burst length: BL24 (per 32-bit device, equals 12 PAM3 symbols per edge on each 8-bit sub-channel)  
• Minimum tCK (I/O clock period): 65 ps for 36 Gb/s grade (≈ 15.38 GHz I/O clock)  
• Announced per-pin data-rate grades: 24 Gb/s, 28 Gb/s, 32 Gb/s, 36 Gb/s  
• Forward-Error-Correction symbols embedded in DQ stream (optional)  
• On-die decision feedback equalisation designed for PAM3 signalling  

Memory-bandwidth example at 2500 MHz I/O clock (FIO = 2.5 GHz) with a 256-bit (32-byte) bus  

Formula  
Per-pin data rate (bits/s) = bits-per-edge × 2 × FIO  
Total BW (bytes/s) = (per-pin data rate × bus width) / 8  

GDDR6 (NRZ, bits-per-edge = 1)  
Per-pin data rate   = 1 × 2 × 2.5 GHz = 5.0 Gb/s  
Total bandwidth      = 5.0 Gb/s × 256 / 8 = 160 GB/s  

GDDR7 (PAM3, bits-per-edge = 1.5)  
Per-pin data rate   = 1.5 × 2 × 2.5 GHz = 7.5 Gb/s  
Total bandwidth      = 7.5 Gb/s × 256 / 8 = 240 GB/s

instruction: How can I concatenate two gpx files on the Linux command line?
output:
`gpx` files are XML documents, therefore you cannot just do  
    cat file1.gpx file2.gpx > merged.gpx  
because you would end up with two XML declarations and two `<gpx>` root tags, producing an invalid file.  
The easiest – and safest – way to join them from the Linux command line is to let `gpsbabel` read both source files and write a new one:

1. Install gpsbabel (it is in every distribution’s repositories)  
   Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt-get install gpsbabel  
   Fedora/RHEL:    sudo dnf install gpsbabel  

2. Merge the files:

   # merge waypoints, routes and tracks
   gpsbabel -i gpx -f first.gpx -f second.gpx -o gpx -F merged.gpx

   # only merge tracks (omit waypoints/routes)
   gpsbabel -t -i gpx -f first.gpx -f second.gpx -o gpx -F merged.gpx

   # merge an arbitrary number of files
   gpsbabel -i gpx -f *.gpx -o gpx -F everything.gpx

`gpsbabel` rewrites the output so the result is a single, well-formed GPX document.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
If you absolutely must do it with just the standard shell tools, you have to strip the XML prolog and the opening/closing `<gpx>` tags from every file but the first/last, then wrap the combined contents with one pair of tags:

( printf '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n<gpx version="1.1">\n'
  for f in first.gpx second.gpx; do
      sed '1,2d;$d' "$f"      # drop first two lines & final </gpx>
  done
  printf '</gpx>\n'
) > merged.gpx

The `gpsbabel` solution is preferred because it understands the full GPX specification, whereas the sed/printf hack assumes all files use exactly the same header/footer formatting.

pretend you work with data quality and you are trying to develop an algorithm to classify dataset type, between master-data and transactional. Which strategy and calculations would you perform?
output:
Below is a pragmatic “data-quality engineer’s” recipe for automatically deciding whether an unknown table (or file) is most likely

• Master Data (entity reference data – customers, products, employees, etc.) or  
• Transactional Data (business events – orders, sensor readings, payments, etc.).

The method is split into 4 layers:

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Capture PROFILING METRICS
2.  Derive SIGNAL FEATURES
3.  Classify (rule set or ML model)
4.  Validate & recalibrate
────────────────────────────────────────

-------------------------------------------------
1.  Capture PROFILING METRICS
-------------------------------------------------
You can compute 100 % of these from the dataset itself plus a few “external” observations (e.g. how often it is extracted).

A. Volume & Shape  
  • row_count, column_count  
  • width_to_depth  =  column_count / row_count  
  • avg_row_growth_rate  (Δ rows per day / week / month)  
  • churn_rate       = (inserts + deletes + updates) / row_count over a time window

B. Volatility Over Time  
  • update_ratio     = updates / (inserts + updates)  
  • record_half-life = median number of days until a row changes

C. Structural Patterns  
  • #datetime_cols,  #numeric_cols,  #string_cols  
  • primary_key_cardinality         (distinct(pk) / row_count)  
  • duplicate_business_key_ratio    (1 – distinct(business_key)/row_count)  

D. Semantic Hints (from column names)  
  • flag_datetime_word   (contains ‘date’, ‘time’, ‘timestamp’ …)  
  • flag_amount_word     (‘amount’, ‘qty’, ‘price’, ‘cost’ …)  
  • flag_status_word     (‘status’, ‘state’, ‘flag’, ‘type’ …)

E. Relational Usage (if catalog information is available)  
  • foreign_key_out_degree  = # of other tables referencing this one  
  • foreign_key_in_degree   = # of FK references it has to other tables

-------------------------------------------------
2.  Derive SIGNAL FEATURES
-------------------------------------------------
Convert the raw metrics into “signals” that more directly separate master from transactional sets.

Feature examples (Python‐style pseudo code):

volatility_score         = churn_rate                         # 0-1 scale  
age_stability_score      = 1 / (1 + record_half_life_days)    # lower ⇒ more stable  
growth_score             = avg_row_growth_rate                # rows/day  
temporal_density         = #datetime_cols / column_count  
monetary_density         = #amount_cols   / column_count  
relational_hub_score     = foreign_key_out_degree / max_fk_out_degree  
width_depth_ratio        = column_count / log10(row_count+1)  # normalise depth

-------------------------------------------------
3.  Classify
-------------------------------------------------
A. Quick HEURISTIC RULE SET (works well in >70 % of cases)

IF volatility_score   > 0.30   OR growth_score > 0.10 rows/day
   AND temporal_density > 0.15
   THEN “Transactional”

ELSE IF volatility_score < 0.05
   AND relational_hub_score > 0.25
   AND width_depth_ratio    > 0.30
   THEN “Master”

ELSE use tie-breaker:
   • monetary_density high  ⇒ Transactional
   • duplicate_business_key_ratio high ⇒ Master
   • foreign_key_in_degree high ⇒ Transactional

B.  Supervised MODEL (for >90 % accuracy once you have labels)

1.  Label ~150–200 known tables as Master vs Transactional  
2.  Train using Gradient-Boosted Trees / Random Forest on the signal features  
3.  Evaluate (Precision, Recall, F1).  
4.  Deploy with probability threshold, e.g. P(master) > 0.70.

Typical Feature Importances you will observe:  
  1. churn_rate / volatility  
  2. foreign_key_out_degree  
  3. temporal_density  
  4. width_depth_ratio  
  5. duplicate_business_key_ratio

-------------------------------------------------
4.  Validate & Recalibrate
-------------------------------------------------
• Weekly sampling: Manually inspect 5 % of “confident” predictions + 20 % of “borderline” predictions.  
• Feed findings back to the training set.  
• Track drift: monitor the distribution of volatility_score, growth_score, etc. – if KS-statistic > threshold, retrain.

-------------------------------------------------
Illustrative Calculation Example
-------------------------------------------------
Assume a table “SALES_ORDER_LINE” profiled over the past 60 days:

row_count               = 12 350 000  
column_count            = 23  
inserts (60 d)          = 2 900 000  
updates (60 d)          = 190 000  
deletes (60 d)          = 0  
datetime_cols           = 4  
amount_cols             = 3  
foreign_key_out_degree  = 0  
foreign_key_in_degree   = 5  

Compute:

churn_rate      = (2.9M + 0 + 0.19M) / 12.35M  ≈ 0.25  
growth_score    = 2.9M / 60 ≈ 48 333 rows/day  
temporal_density= 4/23 ≈ 0.174  
width_depth_ratio = 23 / log10(12.35M) ≈ 23 / 7.09 ≈ 3.25

Heuristic fires:  
 volatility 0.25 > 0.30?  (no)  
 BUT growth_score huge AND temporal_density > 0.15 → Transactional.

-------------------------------------------------
Why this works
-------------------------------------------------
• Master data is referenced far more often than it changes; hence low churn, high FK out-degree, high duplicate ratio (dirty customer files).  
• Transactional data is append-driven, richly time-stamped, and numeric-heavy.  
• Shape, semantics, and relational usage combine to give a robust signal even when individual cues are ambiguous.

-------------------------------------------------
Additional Refinements
-------------------------------------------------
• Use time-windowed deltas from source-control logs if system logs aren’t available.  
• Introduce an “Interaction” class (e.g. slowly changing facts) if your domain needs it.  
• Feed data-quality scores (null %, pattern violations) as auxiliary features—the higher the DQ noise, the more likely the table is large-volume transactional.

Follow this four-layer approach and you will have an auditable, self-improving classifier that a data-quality practice can trust in production.

instruction: What are important best practices when loading data from a raw data layer in a dWH into a reporting layer?
output:
Below is a checklist of the practices that experienced data-warehouse teams almost always follow when they take data from a Raw (landing / staging) layer and publish it to a Reporting (presentation / semantic) layer.  They are grouped so that you can turn them into your own “definition of done” for every load.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
1. Treat the raw layer as immutable “source-of-truth”  
• Never update or delete raw rows (only append new files / partitions).  
• Keep the original data types, column names and granularity so lineage is unambiguous.  
• Keep the extraction timestamp and the source system identifier with every record.  

2. Perform full data-profiling before you design the reporting model  
• Run frequency, min/max, uniqueness and null-rate checks on every raw column.  
• Record profiling results in metadata; they drive decisions such as SCD types, required keys, data-type conversions and mandatory cleansing rules.  

3. Model the reporting layer explicitly (star/snowflake, Data Vault, etc.)  
• Separate dimensions from facts; create surrogate keys and conformed dimensions.  
• Decide up-front which dimensions are SCD-1, SCD-2, or SCD-3.  
• Expose only business-friendly column names; hide purely technical fields.  

4. Transform inside the warehouse (ELT) where possible  
• Land raw data first, then run set-based SQL or push-down code in the database/engine; it is usually faster, cheaper and easier to debug than complex ETL servers.  
• Keep heavy transformations step-wise and materialised (or at least view-based) so they can be inspected independently.  

5. Use incremental, idempotent loads—not “truncate & reload”  
• Maintain a high-water-mark or CDC mechanism (LSNs, timestamps, journal tables, Kafka offsets, etc.).  
• Each load must be restartable; running it twice must produce the same result (“idempotency”).  
• Partition your target tables by date or surrogate-key range so incremental loads touch only recent partitions.  

6. Apply data-quality gates on the way in  
• Row-count reconciliation: raw count vs. rows landed in reporting.  
• Business rule validation (e.g., no negative quantities, valid ISO-country codes).  
• Record detailed reject/error tables; never lose a bad record—quarantine it.  
• Fail fast if critical rules are violated; continue with warnings for non-critical ones.  

7. Maintain referential integrity and surrogate keys  
• Generate keys in a deterministic way (sequence, hash, IDENTITY, etc.).  
• Use “unknown / not-provided” records to avoid breaking foreign-key constraints.  
• Validate that all fact-table foreign keys exist in their dimension tables before commit.  

8. Preserve history deliberately  
• For SCD-2, close previous rows with an end-date only when a material change occurs.  
• Always stamp rows with load date/time and the ETL batch identifier.  
• Keep retired columns in a history table rather than dropping them.  

9. Optimise for read performance  
• Create clustered or column-store indexes that match the most common reporting filters.  
• Aggregate once, reuse many times: build daily/week/month aggregates if they save repeated scans.  
• Use cache-friendly surrogate keys (integers rather than GUIDs).  

10. Implement robust operational controls  
• Atomic batches: commit at end of batch, or rollback entirely on failure.  
• Logging: start time, end time, rows inserted/updated, error counts, host, runtime.  
• Alerting: paging/Slack/e-mail when runtime exceeds threshold or row count deviates.  
• Job dependency management: orchestrate loads so that dimensions finish before the facts that rely on them.  

11. Secure and govern the data  
• Mask or encrypt PII columns before they reach the reporting layer when required.  
• Apply row/column-level security so analysts only see what they are entitled to.  
• Register every published table and column in a data catalog with lineage back to the raw layer.  

12. Automate testing and deployment  
• Unit tests: does an SCD-2 update really close the previous record?  
• Regression tests: compare aggregates in QA vs. production.  
• Version‐control all transformation code and DDL; deploy through CI/CD pipelines.  

13. Document everything that an analyst needs  
• Business definition, calculation logic and refresh frequency for every measure.  
• Valid value lists for every dimension attribute.  
• Load schedule and SLA so users know when data is “ready”.  

14. Periodically refactor and retire technical debt  
• Use audit logs to spot unused columns or tables; archive them.  
• Re-partition or re-index when data volumes triple.  
• Review transformation logic as business rules evolve; keep the ETL/ELT job list lean.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
If you do the above consistently you get five outcomes that matter to end-users and operations alike: (1) data is correct, (2) loads finish on time, (3) history is traceable, (4) failures are recoverable, and (5) analysts can find and understand the data without asking engineering to decode it for them.

instruction: Describe how to connect Databricks SQL to ingestion tools like Fivetran
output:
Below is a practical “cook-book” that covers everything you typically need to do in order to let an ingestion tool—using Fivetran as the example—write data into Databricks SQL Warehouses (formerly called SQL Endpoints). The same principles (JDBC/ODBC connectivity, a managed service‐account, network allow-lists, and an ingestion schema) apply to almost every other ELT/ETL product (Airbyte, Hevo, Matillion, Stitch, etc.), so you can reuse 90 % of this guidance for those tools as well.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Decide which side is Source vs. Destination
────────────────────────────────────────
Fivetran can work in two directions:

A. Databricks as a DESTINATION  
   – Data is extracted from SaaS/OLTP sources by Fivetran and loaded into Databricks.  
   – This is by far the more common pattern and the one that relies on Databricks SQL Warehouses.

B. Databricks as a SOURCE  
   – Rare; used when you want to move data out of Databricks into a different warehouse.  
   – Uses the same connection details, so the steps are essentially identical—just reversed.

Below we cover Databricks-as-Destination (the usual use-case).

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Prerequisites & One-time Databricks setup
────────────────────────────────────────
2.1 Create or identify a SQL Warehouse  
     • In the Databricks UI → SQL persona → SQL Warehouses → “Create”  
     • Choose “Serverless” if available or a classic warehouse with size Small/Medium.  
     • Copy the HTTP Path and note the Warehouse ID.

2.2 Service credentials  
     Option 1 – Personal Access Token (quickest)  
       – Databricks → User Settings → “Generate new token” (scope 90 days or less).  
       – Save it; Databricks will not show it again.

     Option 2 – Service Principal (recommended for production)  
       – Create an Azure AD / AWS IAM / Google Cloud service principal.  
       – Add it to Databricks.  
       – Generate a PAT tied to that principal OR use OAuth (Fivetran supports both).  
       – Grant the principal: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, INSERT, SELECT.

2.3 Networking / Security  
     • Make sure the warehouse is reachable on port 443.  
     • If you run Databricks behind a firewall / PrivateLink, allow-list Fivetran’s egress IPs (listed in their docs per region).  
     • If you use AWS PrivateLink or Azure Private Link, add the dns-name override that Fivetran provides.

2.4 Create a dedicated destination schema  
     – In a notebook or Query Editor run:  
       ```
       CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS fivetran;
       USE CATALOG fivetran;
       CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS landing;
       GRANT USAGE ON CATALOG fivetran TO `fivetran_sp`;
       GRANT CREATE, USAGE, INSERT, SELECT ON SCHEMA landing TO `fivetran_sp`;
       ```  
     – Fivetran will create one schema per connector by default, e.g. `landing.salesforce`.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Configure Fivetran (using the UI, API, or Partner Connect)
────────────────────────────────────────
3.1 Using Partner Connect (fastest)  
     1. Databricks → Partner Connect → Fivetran.  
     2. Pick your SQL Warehouse and click “Generate token & launch Fivetran”.  
     3. Databricks opens Fivetran’s sign-up page already pre-filled with:  
        – Server Hostname (your-workspace.cloud.databricks.com)  
        – Port 443  
        – HTTP Path of the warehouse  
        – Token (scoped to your user or service principal)  
        – Default Catalog/Schema.

3.2 Manually in the Fivetran UI  
     Destinations → “Add Destination” → Choose “Databricks”.  
     • Host: <MY-WORKSPACE>.cloud.databricks.com  
     • Port: 443  
     • HTTP Path: /sql/1.0/warehouses/<WAREHOUSE-ID>  
     • Databricks Personal Access Token OR OAuth flow.  
     • Default Database (Catalog) and Schema prefix (e.g. public, fivetran_landing).  
     • Time zone (UTC recommended).  
     • Click “Save & Test”.  
     • You should see “Connected” and “Schema created”.

3.3 Via the Fivetran REST API (for IaC)  
     POST /v1/destinations with payload:  
     ```
     {
       "group_id": "...",
       "service": "databricks",
       "region": "AWS_US_EAST_2",
       "config": {
         "server_host": "my-workspace.cloud.databricks.com",
         "port": "443",
         "database": "fivetran",
         "http_path": "/sql/1.0/warehouses/20abc123456",
         "auth": {
           "method": "PAT",
           "password": "dapiXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX"
         }
       }
     }
     ```

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Grant the appropriate Databricks privileges
────────────────────────────────────────
With Unity Catalog (recommended):
   ```
   USE CATALOG fivetran;
   USE SCHEMA landing;
   GRANT CREATE TABLE, SELECT, INSERT
         ON SCHEMA landing
         TO `fivetran_sp`;
   ```

Without Unity Catalog / legacy metastore:
   ```
   GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE fivetran_landing TO `fivetran_sp`;
   ```

Make sure the service principal OR PAT-owning user is assigned to the SQL warehouse (SQL Warehouses → Edit → “Permissions”).

────────────────────────────────────────
5. Run a quick smoke test
────────────────────────────────────────
Back in Fivetran:
   • Add a simple connector (e.g. Google Sheets).  
   • Kick off the initial sync.  
   • In Databricks Query Editor run:  
     `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fivetran.landing.google_sheets__sheet1;`  
   • Verify row counts and storage format (`DESCRIBE DETAIL …` shows Delta).

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Performance & cost tuning
────────────────────────────────────────
Warehouse size         – Start Small; Fivetran loads in micro-batches.  
Min / Max clusters      – 1 / 2 is usually enough.  
Auto-stop               – 5–10 min keeps costs down between syncs.  
Serverless (if aval.)   – Removes cluster warm-up times and simplifies cost estimates.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Operational best practices
────────────────────────────────────────
• Use separate staging / prod schemas if you want to run dbt or Databricks Workflows for downstream models.  
• Turn on “Force Delta” in Fivetran for reliable ACID semantics.  
• Monitor with: Databricks SQL → “Query History” (look for `fivetran_%` tags).  
• Capture lineage: Unity Catalog automatically tracks table-level lineage; column lineage is in Public Preview.

────────────────────────────────────────
8. Troubleshooting cheat-sheet
────────────────────────────────────────
Connection refused → Check firewall / PrivateLink / port 443.  
Error 401/403        → Token expired or missing warehouse permission.  
“Catalog not found”  → Wrong Catalog name; double-check Unity Catalog vs. legacy.  
Warehouse stops      → Ensure it is not set to auto-suspend too aggressively for large syncs.  
Slow initial sync    → Temporarily bump warehouse size; Fivetran parallelism is limited by Databricks’ max_concurrent_queries parameter.

────────────────────────────────────────
9. Adapting the same pattern to other ingestion tools
────────────────────────────────────────
Almost every modern ELT tool connects via the same JDBC/ODBC driver. Replace step 3 with that tool’s UI but keep:

• Host & port = workspace URL + 443  
• HTTP Path = SQL Warehouse Path  
• Auth = PAT or OAuth / service principal  
• Network allow-list = their egress IPs  
• Warehouse permissions = USAGE + CREATE + INSERT at minimum

Examples:  
– Airbyte: Destination “Databricks Lakehouse (Delta)”.  
– Matillion ETL: Create an “External Database” connection using the Databricks driver.  
– Stitch: Destination “Databricks Delta Lake” (Beta).  
– Hevo: Destination “Databricks” with the same four fields.

────────────────────────────────────────
Key takeaway
────────────────────────────────────────
If you can supply (1) server hostname, (2) port 443, (3) HTTP Path of a SQL Warehouse, (4) a PAT or OAuth token, and (5) schema privileges, any ingestion tool—including Fivetran—can land data directly into Delta tables inside Databricks SQL. The remaining work is automation (Partner Connect or API) and day-2 operations (scaling, monitoring, security).

instruction:
I have an SQL table with the following schema:
```
event_id int
event_at timestamp
```

I would like to know how many events there are every minute since 1 month ago. I am using databricks database and their SQL flavor
output:
Basic version – only the minutes that actually contain at least one event

```
SELECT
        date_trunc('minute', event_at)              AS minute_start ,   -- 2024-05-18 08:37:00 …
        COUNT(*)                                    AS event_cnt
FROM    events                                      -- your table
WHERE   event_at >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 MONTH
GROUP BY minute_start
ORDER BY minute_start;
```

• `current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 MONTH` keeps the last month.  
• `date_trunc('minute', …)` rounds every time stamp down to the start of its minute, so everything that happened between 08:37:00 and 08:37:59 is put in the same bucket.  
• `GROUP BY` + `COUNT(*)` gives the number of rows in each bucket.


Showing every single minute (including the ones that have zero events)

Databricks/Spark SQL lets you build a time series with `sequence(…)`.  
We first explode a list of all minutes in the required range, then left–join it with the aggregated counts.

```
WITH minute_series AS (                         -- 1) build every minute
     SELECT explode(
              sequence(
                 date_trunc('minute', current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 MONTH), -- first minute
                 date_trunc('minute', current_timestamp()),                    -- last  minute
                 INTERVAL 1 MINUTE))        -- step
            AS minute_start
),
event_counts AS (                              -- 2) aggregate the real data
     SELECT date_trunc('minute', event_at) AS minute_start,
            COUNT(*)                         AS cnt
     FROM   events
     WHERE  event_at >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 MONTH
     GROUP BY minute_start
)
SELECT  m.minute_start,
        COALESCE(e.cnt, 0) AS event_cnt      -- 3) bring them together
FROM    minute_series m
LEFT  JOIN event_counts e
       ON  m.minute_start = e.minute_start
ORDER BY m.minute_start;
```

The result has one row for every minute in the last month; `event_cnt` is `0` whenever nothing happened in that minute.

instruction:
Conduct a debate on whether we need to use AI in our everyday lives in Europe, given the regulations that will make it much more restrictive than in the rest of the world. 
Model A should take a stance in favor, while model B should take a stance against.
output:
==============================
DEBATE:  Should Europeans weave AI deeply into everyday life, even though the EU’s forthcoming AI-Act and related rules will be stricter than regulations elsewhere?
==============================

Moderator:  Welcome to today’s structured debate.  Model A will argue in favor of widespread everyday use of AI in Europe despite – and partly because of – the EU’s more restrictive regulatory framework.  Model B will argue against that proposition.  Each side gets an opening statement, two rounds of rebuttals, and a short closing argument.

────────────────
OPENING STATEMENTS
────────────────

Model A (Pro-AI):
1. Trust as a competitive advantage  
   • The EU’s comprehensive AI-Act, together with GDPR, creates a baseline of safety, privacy and transparency.  When citizens trust a technology, adoption accelerates—not the other way around.  Europe already proved this with food, automobile, and pharmaceutical safety standards.

2. Productivity and demographic reality  
   • Europe’s aging population and shrinking workforce require productivity boosts.  AI-enhanced logistics, preventive health-care diagnostics, and adaptive learning tools can offset labour shortages and keep social-welfare systems sustainable.

3. Strategic autonomy  
   • If Europeans forgo everyday AI, dependence on foreign platforms will deepen.  Developing and deploying compliant AI domestically helps retain control over data, intellectual property, and critical infrastructure.

4. Innovation within constraints  
   • History shows that regulation can drive high-quality innovation (e.g., Europe’s leadership in green tech due to strict emissions rules).  A “safety-by-design” AI market could become Europe’s next export success.

Model B (Against):
1. Regulatory drag and cost  
   • The EU’s AI-Act classifies many everyday applications as “high risk,” imposing costly conformity assessments, mandatory human oversight and detailed documentation.  SMEs and start-ups will struggle, creating an uneven playing field versus U.S. or Asian competitors operating under lighter rules.

2. Slower iteration = lost relevance  
   • AI advances at a breakneck pace.  By the time a compliant solution passes EU certification, the underlying model may be two generations behind.  Everyday consumers will simply import or VPN into foreign, unregulated services.

3. Privacy over-correction  
   • Excessive data-minimisation limits the scale needed for powerful models.  Without access to large health, mobility or retail datasets, European AI may underperform, delivering a poorer user experience and lower economic gains.

4. Opportunity cost and brain drain  
   • Researchers and entrepreneurs may move to jurisdictions where experimentation is easier.  The effect is already visible in venture-capital flows tilting toward the U.S. and UK.  Everyday Europeans will thus end up using foreign AI anyway—only later and with less influence.

────────────────
FIRST REBUTTAL
────────────────

Model A:
• Yes, compliance has a cost, but the cost of distrust is greater.  Consider the backlash against social-media platforms mishandling data; European uptake of those platforms plateaued.  By embedding guardrails (mandatory risk management, transparency), Europe avoids a future backlash that could force sudden bans or costly retrofits.  
• On speed:  The AI-Act introduces “sandboxes” where companies can experiment under regulatory guidance, shortening time to market.  Certification processes in industries like medical devices already coexist with innovation—why should AI be different?  
• Data limitations?  Federated learning and synthetic data let models reach state-of-the-art performance while respecting privacy.  Europe is leading in those techniques precisely because constraints stimulated creativity.

Model B:
• Sandboxes cover only a fraction of use-cases and still require prior approval, throttling true rapid iteration.  
• The argument that regulation yields trust ignores user behavior:  TikTok, generated-image apps, and LLM chatbots gained massive EU user bases despite minimal upfront regulation.  People value utility and novelty over compliance logos.  
• Federated learning is promising but not a mature replacement for raw data scale in areas like autonomous driving or multilingual foundation models.  Europe risks settling for second-tier performance just to satisfy an over-cautious legal framework.

────────────────
SECOND REBUTTAL
────────────────

Model A:
• Utility vs. compliance is a false dichotomy.  GDPR didn’t stop Europeans from using cloud services; it forced both foreign and domestic firms to improve data practices, benefiting users worldwide.  
• Regarding performance gaps:  Safety and accuracy correlate.  Under-regulated systems can hallucinate or discriminate, incurring societal costs (e.g., wrongful arrests via unvetted facial recognition).  Europe’s stricter biometric provisions prevent such harms.  
• Lastly, brain drain concerns overlook the influx of public R&D funding (Horizon Europe, IPCEI on Microelectronics & Cloud).  High-integrity AI research centers—from Helsinki to Barcelona—are expanding because scientists want real-world impact coupled with ethical rigor.

Model B:
• GDPR is instructive but mixed:  compliance costs dwarf fines, cookie banners annoy users, and most enforcement actions target European firms rather than global giants.  A similar pattern in AI would hurt local players most.  
• Ethical “leadership” doesn’t pay the bills if products lose to faster, cheaper alternatives.  Consumers already prioritize price over sustainability labels in many sectors; AI is unlikely to be different.  
• Public funding can’t match private capital that flows to less restricted markets.  Even if research stays, deployment will migrate.  Without deployment scale, feedback loops that improve AI in everyday scenarios will be weaker, cementing Europe as a follower.

────────────────
CLOSING STATEMENTS
────────────────

Model A (Pro-AI):  
Europe should embrace AI in daily life precisely because its rules aim to align technology with fundamental rights.  That will yield trusted digital assistants for seniors, responsible autonomous transport, transparent algorithmic banking, and energy-efficient smart grids.  By embedding ethical and technical excellence together, Europe can cultivate a distinctive, exportable brand of “Trustworthy AI,” turning regulatory stringency into a long-term societal and economic win.

Model B (Against):  
Everyday AI sounds attractive, but Europe’s impending rules burden developers, slow iteration and limit data—all while foreign alternatives flourish.  The result is higher costs, mediocre performance, and reliance on imported tools.  Until the regulatory gap narrows, Europe should focus on selective, high-impact AI deployments (research labs, critical infrastructure) and avoid pushing AI into every facet of daily life where the costs of over-regulation will outweigh the benefits.

Moderator:  Thank you both for a rigorous exchange.  The audience now has the key arguments on the table to form its own judgment.

instruction: You are a master of debate and persuasive argument. Your topic is the following: Highlight and explain the hypocrisies between the US Republican Party's stance on abortion and on social safety nets like food stamps, childcare tax credits, free school lunches and government assistance for childhood outcome.
output:
Below is a concise, debate-ready framework you can use to expose what many critics call a “pro-birth but not pro-life” contradiction in modern Republican platforms.  It is organized so that each point (1) cites the core GOP position, (2) contrasts it with the party’s record on social supports, and (3) explains why critics view the combination as hypocritical.  Sprinkle in specific votes or statements as you see fit.

1. Unborn Life vs. Born-Alive Aid  
   • GOP position on abortion: “Every human life is sacred from conception.”  
   • GOP position on post-natal assistance: Repeated attempts to cut or cap SNAP, WIC, TANF, Medicaid, and ACA expansions—programs that feed, house, or give health care to the same children once they are born.  
   • Hypocrisy argument: A worldview that deems fetal life “inviolable” should, by its own moral logic, lavish resources on protecting that life after birth.  Voting to restrict abortion while simultaneously shrinking the budgets that keep poor children alive undermines the moral absolutism claimed in the pro-life stance.

2. Parental Autonomy vs. Government Intrusion  
   • Abortion stance: The state must overrule a pregnant person’s choice in order to protect the fetus.  
   • Social-safety-net stance: Government should get out of the way; families must be “self-reliant.”  
   • Hypocrisy argument: It is contradictory to invoke state power to force childbirth but then insist the very same state power is illegitimate when it comes to helping parents feed or insure the resulting child.

3. Fiscal Prudence vs. Litigation Cost  
   • GOP rationale for trimming safety nets: “We can’t afford endless entitlements.”  
   • Abortion policy cost: Many Republican-led states pass restrictive laws that trigger expensive court battles; some states budget millions for legal defenses and “crisis pregnancy center” funding.  
   • Hypocrisy argument: If budget discipline is paramount, funneling taxpayer dollars into litigation and ideologically aligned non-profits while slashing proven anti-poverty programs is fiscally inconsistent.

4. States’ Rights Selectivity  
   • GOP line on social programs: “Let states innovate; no federal handouts.”  
   • Abortion strategy: Pursue federal abortion bans (2023 House Bill, 15-week proposals) that would override blue-state laws.  
   • Hypocrisy argument: Championing decentralization only when it limits welfare but abandoning it to restrict abortion suggests that “states’ rights” is a flexible talking point, not a principled commitment.

5. Child Outcomes Data  
   • Evidence: Expanded Child Tax Credit (2021) cut U.S. child poverty almost in half; free-school-lunch waivers during COVID reduced hunger; Head Start studies show life-long gains.  
   • GOP record: The House Republican Study Committee budget (FY 2024) calls for rolling back the CTC expansion; roughly 90 % of House Republicans voted against making school-lunch waivers permanent; multiple red-state governors refused the 2021 Summer EBT funds.  
   • Hypocrisy argument: Claiming to value children while rejecting empirically proven child-poverty reducers is policy-level cognitive dissonance.

6. Moral Messaging vs. Practical Outcomes  
   • Pro-life rhetoric: “Every child is a gift.”  
   • Social-net skepticism: “Handouts create dependency.”  
   • Hypocrisy argument: Research shows poverty itself is the largest predictor of dependency, crime, and abortion demand. Blocking child-focused aid can increase the very social ills used to justify austerity.

7. Political Optics  
   • Campaign ads emphasize ultrasound images, heartbeat bills, and “culture of life” language.  
   • Legislative priorities feature tax cuts, deregulation, and caps on discretionary spending that indirectly squeeze child services.  
   • Hypocrisy argument: A party branding itself as protectors of innocence while sidelining the budgets that underwrite that protection invites accusations of moral posturing for electoral gain.

Anticipating Common GOP Rebuttals and Quick Counters  
   a. “Private charity should fill the gap.” → Charitable giving in the U.S. could cover only about 3 % of SNAP’s cost.  
   b. “Safety nets break up families.” → Child poverty itself is linked to higher divorce and incarceration rates; safety nets lower both.  
   c. “The real issue is personal responsibility.” → A newborn has zero agency; punishing a child for parental circumstance contradicts pro-life ethics.  
   d. “Blue states abort more.” → When adjusted for income and contraceptive access, abortion rates correlate strongly with poverty, not state partisanship; robust welfare lowers abortion demand.

Bottom line for debate framing  
Tie every statistic, budget vote, or state policy back to the central question: If the Republican Party truly believes every life from conception is invaluable, why does it systematically oppose the public investments most correlated with healthy infant and childhood outcomes?  That tension—between absolute moral language pre-birth and conditional fiscal language post-birth—is the crux of the hypocrisy charge.

instruction: Make code in a synapse notebook that deletes a folder from a connected filesystem
output:
Below is a minimal, self-contained example you can paste directly into an Azure Synapse notebook (PySpark language) to remove a folder that sits in a storage account already linked to the workspace.

```
%%pyspark
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Delete a folder in a filesystem that is already linked to Synapse
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

from mssparkutils import fs

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Set the folder you want to delete
#    Format: abfss://<container>@<account>.dfs.core.windows.net/<path>/
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
container_name = "landing"                       # ADLS Gen2 container
storage_account = "mydatalakeacct"               # Storage account (without .dfs.core.windows.net)
folder_relative_path = "raw/2023/05/load_tmp/"   # Folder inside the container

folder_uri = f"abfss://{container_name}@{storage_account}.dfs.core.windows.net/{folder_relative_path}"

print(f"Folder to be deleted : {folder_uri}")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Delete the folder (recursively)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
if fs.exists(folder_uri):
    try:
        # recurse=True / second argument True => delete contents recursively
        fs.rm(folder_uri, True)
        print("Folder successfully deleted.")
    except Exception as ex:
        print(f"ERROR – folder could not be deleted: {ex}")
else:
    print("Folder does not exist – nothing to delete.")
```

Explanation of the main pieces  

1. `mssparkutils.fs`  
   Synapse ships with `mssparkutils` (similar to Databricks’ `dbutils`).  
   `fs.rm(<path>, <recursive>)` removes the file / folder; pass `True` to delete recursively.

2. Path format (`abfss://…`)  
   • `abfss` = secure ABFS driver used by Synapse.  
   • Combine container, storage account, and the folder you want to drop.

3. Safety check  
   `fs.exists()` lets you confirm the folder is really there before attempting deletion.

Put the cell in “PySpark” mode (default for a new notebook is fine), run it, and the specified folder—including everything underneath it—will be removed from the connected filesystem.
