instruction: Just quickly, do you agree with this sentence: "The design of capsule networks appears to be most well-suited for classification problems which have clearly defined entities and might be less well-suited to problems where entities are more difficult to define, such as weather patterns."
output: Broadly, yes. Capsule networks shine when you can decompose an input into a set of spatially arranged parts (e.g., the strokes of a digit or the limbs of a person) and want the model to preserve and reason over those part–whole relationships. When the underlying “entities” are diffuse, continuous, or hard to delineate—as in atmospheric fields evolving over time—the advantages of capsules’ explicit part-whole modeling become less clear, and other architectures (e.g., CNN–RNN hybrids, transformers) tend to be more practical. So the sentence captures the main intuition, even though there are always research avenues for adapting capsules to less discrete domains.

instruction: Can you generate an A level exam question on circular motion, with an according mark scheme and answer.
output:
A–level Physics ‑ Circular Motion  
(Total 15 marks)

Question  

A small smooth ball of mass 0.20 kg is attached to a light, inextensible string of length 0.75 m.  
The free end of the string is fixed to a point O on a ceiling so that the ball can move in a complete vertical circle of radius r = 0.75 m.

The ball is projected vertically upward from the lowest point A of the circle with just enough speed for the string to remain taut as the ball passes through the highest point B.  
Air resistance may be neglected. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².

(a)  Explain why, for the string to be “just taut’’ at B, the tension T_B may be taken as zero.  
     Hence show that the minimum speed v_B,min at the highest point satisfies  

                v_B,min² = g r.  (3)

(b)  Calculate v_B,min.  (1)

(c)  Using conservation of mechanical energy, determine the minimum speed v_A,min with which the ball must be projected at A.  (3)

(d)  For this value of v_A,min calculate the tension T_A in the string at A.  
     The string can withstand a maximum tension of 20 N; state, with a reason, whether it will break.  (4)

(e)  Draw separate, clearly-labelled sketches of the forces on the ball at  

        (i) A  (lowest point),  
        (ii) B  (highest point),  
        (iii) C  (when the string is horizontal).  

      On each sketch indicate the direction of the ball’s acceleration.  (4)



Mark scheme & worked answer  

(a)  
• Recognises that “just taut’’ means the string is on the point of slackening ⇒ T_B = 0.  (1)  
• Centripetal force at B: m v_B²/r is provided only by the weight, so  
        m v_B²/r = m g.  (1)  
• Cancelling m and rearranging gives v_B² = g r.  (1)

(b)  
v_B,min  = √(g r) = √(9.81 × 0.75) = √(7.36) = 2.71 m s⁻¹  (allow 2.7 m s⁻¹)  (1)

(c)  
Gain in gravitational PE from A to B = m g (2 r).  
Using conservation of energy:

        ½ m v_A² = ½ m v_B² + m g (2 r)  (1)

Insert v_B² = g r:

        ½ m v_A² = ½ m (g r) + m g (2 r) = m g r(0.5 + 2) = 2.5 m g r  (1)

v_A² = 5 g r  ⇒  v_A = √(5 g r)  
         = √(5 × 9.81 × 0.75) = √(36.8) = 6.06 m s⁻¹  (6.1 m s⁻¹ to 2 s.f.)  (1)

(d)  
At A (bottom) the required centripetal force is towards O:

        T_A – m g = m v_A² / r   (1)

Substitute numbers:  
m v_A² / r = 0.20 × 36.8 / 0.75 = 9.81 N  

T_A = 9.81 N + (0.20 × 9.81) N = 9.81 N + 1.96 N = 11.8 N  (2)

Compare with 20 N:  11.8 N < 20 N ⇒ the string will not break.  (1)

(e)  One mark for correct forces, one for correct acceleration direction in each case (max 4).  

(i)  A (bottom):  
     Tension T upward toward O; weight m g downward.  
     Acceleration (centripetal) upward toward O.

(ii) B (top):  
     Weight m g downward toward O; tension zero (or very small downward if shown).  
     Acceleration downward toward O.

(iii) C (string horizontal):  
     Tension T horizontal toward O; weight m g vertically downward.  
     Acceleration horizontal toward O.

(Any clear, correctly-labelled diagrams gain the marks.)

Marks summary  
(a) 3 (b) 1 (c) 3 (d) 4 (e) 4 Total 15

instruction: Tell me the highest yield 15 facts to help me study for the nuclear cardiology board exam I have to take tomorrow. Focus on providing me with info that is likely to be on the test, but is more obscure than super common information.
output:
Fifteen “not-so-obvious but board-favorite” nuclear cardiology facts  

1. Sr-82 breakthrough limits for Rb-82 PET  
   • NRC 10 CFR 35.204: ≤0.02 µCi Sr-82 and ≤0.2 µCi Sr-85 per mCi Rb-82 in the first 50 mL eluate.  
   • Exceeding either limit (or two consecutive days >½ the limit) requires generator withdrawal and a written report to the NRC within 7 days.

2. “Splenic switch-off” = adequate vasodilator stress  
   • Markedly decreased splenic uptake on stress vs. rest images occurs in >95 % of properly hyperemic regadenoson/dipyridamole studies.  
   • Its absence is the most reliable imaging clue to inadequate vasodilation.

3. PET absolute flow that defines high-risk disease  
   • Global myocardial flow reserve (MFR) <1.5 or regional stress flow <0.7 mL·min⁻¹·g⁻¹ predicts severe multivessel / microvascular CAD even when relative perfusion is normal (“balanced ischemia”).

4. Transient ischemic dilation (TID) cut-offs are tracer-specific  
   • 99mTc (sestamibi/tetrofosmin) ≥1.22, Tl-201 ≥1.36, PET (Rb-82/¹³N-NH₃) ≥1.05 on a 1-day protocol are abnormal.

5. Stress-induced EF drop = severe CAD  
   • A fall in LVEF ≥5 absolute % (or >10 relative %) from rest to stress on gated SPECT/PET is an independent marker of left-main or 3-vessel disease.

6. ¹²³I-MIBG prognostic thresholds  
   • Delayed (3–4 h) heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratio <1.6 or wash-out >27 % signals high arrhythmic risk.  
   • Must be acquired with medium-energy collimators; low-energy collimators falsely depress the H/M ratio.

7. 99mTc-Pyrophosphate for ATTR amyloid  
   • Planar heart-to-contralateral (H/CL) ratio ≥1.5 at 1 h + Perugini grade 2/3 uptake + no monoclonal protein = >99 % specificity for transthyretin amyloidosis.  
   • Recent MI (<2 wk) and AL amyloid can give false positives.

8. Thallium “late redistribution” & nitrates  
   • Defects that fill in at 24 h (or after nitrate augmentation) are the most specific Tl-201 sign of viability/hibernating myocardium.

9. Lung uptake still matters  
   • Early Tl-201 lung-to-heart ratio >0.5 (≈>0.35 with 99mTc agents) correlates with elevated LV filling pressures and ≥2-fold higher mortality—often a quiz question.

10. Tetrofosmin vs. sestamibi liver clearance  
    • Tetrofosmin is less lipophilic → 2–3× faster hepatic wash-out.  
    • Useful in obese or diaphragmatic attenuation; give a fatty meal or have the patient lie on right side to further minimize liver-heart overlap.

11. LBBB/pacing artifact avoidance  
    • Exercise stress exaggerates septal defects; use vasodilator stress, look for preserved septal thickening on gated images, and confirm with phase analysis (septal-lateral delay >135° suggests true dyssynchrony rather than ischemia).

12. Regadenoson pharmacokinetics in renal failure  
    • Half-life triples when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m².  
    • Persistent side-effects are reversed with 50–250 mg IV aminophylline; safe to give ≥1 min after tracer injection.

13. Dose comparison that the boards love  
    • 1-day 99mTc MPI (10 mCi rest / 30 mCi stress + CTAC) ≈9 mSv.  
    • Rest-stress Rb-82 PET + low-dose CTAC ≈3–4 mSv—PET is lower dose despite CT.

14. Gamma-camera uniformity numbers  
    • Daily high-count flood: integral uniformity ≤5 %, differential ≤3 %.  
    • Failure produces concentric “ring” artifacts on SPECT that can mimic reversible ischemia.

15. How MUGA calculates EF  
    • Uses first-harmonic Fourier analysis of the ROI time-activity curve.  
    • If beat-to-beat count variance >10 %, results are unreliable unless arrhythmia rejection is engaged.

Memorizing these 15 pearls will give you an edge on the less obvious questions that often separate passing from high-scoring candidates. Good luck tomorrow!

instruction: count distinct values in a column given a constraint from another column using over clause in ssms
output:
In SQL Server you cannot write  

    COUNT ( DISTINCT col ) OVER ( … )

The moment the optimizer sees DISTINCT together with an OVER clause you get

    Msg 10125  … DISTINCT aggregate functions  
    are not supported with OVER clause.

You therefore have to give the window-engine a set that is already
“distinct”, or mark the first row of every (partition + value) pair and
count those.  
The two common rewrites are shown below.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Sample data
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume we have to show, on every row of dbo.Sales,
how many different customers have bought the same product while the order
status is ‘Closed’.

    CREATE TABLE dbo.Sales
    ( order_id  int ,
      product   varchar(20),
      customer  varchar(20),
      status    varchar(10) );

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
1.  Sub-query (or CTE) that is already DISTINCT
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    ;WITH d AS                             -- one row per distinct customer
    (   SELECT DISTINCT product, customer  -- for CLOSED orders only
        FROM   dbo.Sales
        WHERE  status = 'Closed'
    )
    SELECT  s.* ,
            COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY d.product) AS closed_cust_cnt
    FROM    dbo.Sales AS s          -- return all the original columns
    JOIN    d ON d.product = s.product
             AND d.customer = s.customer;

– d contains one row per (product, customer) pair that satisfies the
filter.  
– COUNT(*) OVER simply counts those rows per product, so we get the
distinct count repeated on every output row.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
2.  ROW_NUMBER / SUM pattern
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    SELECT  *,
            /* first row of each (product, customer) pair = 1, others = 0 */
            SUM(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN 1 END)
                 OVER (PARTITION BY product)          AS closed_cust_cnt
    FROM   ( SELECT s.*,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product, customer
                                        ORDER BY (SELECT 0)) AS rn
             FROM   dbo.Sales AS s
             WHERE  status = 'Closed'
           ) AS x;

ROW_NUMBER() = 1 only on the first occurrence of every customer within a
product; summing the 1’s inside the same product therefore gives the
distinct-customer total.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
If you do NOT need the figure on every row  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Just aggregate in the normal way:

    SELECT product,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN status = 'Closed' THEN customer END)
                 AS closed_cust_cnt
    FROM   dbo.Sales
    GROUP BY product;

---------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Summary
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

• SQL Server (≤ 2022) does not allow COUNT(DISTINCT …) with OVER.  
• Supply the window engine with pre-deduplicated rows, or  
  mark the first row per (partition,value) and SUM/COUNT those.  
Either technique gives you “COUNT DISTINCT … OVER (…)” functionality while
respecting whatever filter you need from another column.

instruction: Hi, I would like the python code for turning excel cells into coloured powerpoint squares
output:
Below is a fully-working, end-to-end example that

1. opens an Excel workbook,
2. reads the background (fill) colour of every used cell on a given sheet,
3. lays those cells out as same-size coloured squares on a single PowerPoint slide,
4. saves the resulting presentation.

It uses only the two most common libraries for this purpose:  
• openpyxl – to read Excel files  
• python-pptx – to create/edit PowerPoint files  

You can copy the script into e.g. colour_grid.py and run it with Python ≥3.8.

------------------------------------------------------------------
INSTALL THE LIBRARIES (once)
------------------------------------------------------------------
pip install openpyxl python-pptx

------------------------------------------------------------------
colour_grid.py
------------------------------------------------------------------
```python
"""
Turn the fill colours of cells in an Excel sheet into coloured squares
in a PowerPoint slide.

Author : (your name / date)
"""

from pathlib import Path

import openpyxl                     # read Excel
from pptx import Presentation       # create PowerPoint
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt    # positioning units

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# USER-EDITABLE SETTINGS
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
EXCEL_FILE   = Path("colours.xlsx")   # input workbook
SHEET_NAME   = "Sheet1"               # sheet to read colours from
PPT_FILE     = Path("colours.pptx")   # output presentation

MAX_ROWS     = None  # e.g. 20  -> only first 20 rows.  None = all.
MAX_COLS     = None  # e.g. 10  -> only first 10 columns. None = all.

START_X_INCH = 0.5    # left margin in inches on the slide
START_Y_INCH = 0.5    # top  margin in inches on the slide
BOX_SIZE_IN  = 0.3    # width *and* height of every square in inches
BOX_PAD_IN   = 0.02   # optional gap between squares in inches
BORDER       = False  # True  -> add a thin black border to each square

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# HELPER FUNCTIONS
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
def excel_colour_to_rgb(openpyxl_color):
    """
    Convert an openpyxl colour object to an RGB hex string 'RRGGBB'.
    Returns None if no solid fill is set.
    """
    if not openpyxl_color:
        return None
    # The colour may be theme-based, indexed, etc.  The simplest case is rgb:
    rgb = openpyxl_color.rgb  # e.g. 'FF00FF00' (the first two FF = alpha)
    if rgb:
        return rgb[-6:]       # keep last 6 hex chars
    return None


def add_square(slide, left, top, size, rgb_hex, border=False):
    """
    Add a square of the given colour to *slide* at (left, top).

    left/top/size are pptx.util.Length objects (Inches, Pt, etc.)
    rgb_hex should be 'RRGGBB'.
    """
    shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(
        MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE,
        left, top, size, size
    )
    # Fill
    fill = shape.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = int(rgb_hex, 16)

    # Optional border
    line = shape.line
    if border:
        line.color.rgb = 0x000000
        line.width = Pt(0.5)
    else:
        line.fill.background()  # effectively "no line"


# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# MAIN SCRIPT
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
def main():
    # Load Excel workbook and sheet
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(EXCEL_FILE, data_only=True)
    ws = wb[SHEET_NAME]

    # Determine boundaries
    max_row = ws.max_row if MAX_ROWS is None else min(MAX_ROWS, ws.max_row)
    max_col = ws.max_column if MAX_COLS is None else min(MAX_COLS, ws.max_column)

    # Prepare PowerPoint presentation
    prs   = Presentation()
    blank = prs.slide_layouts[6]      # empty slide layout
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)

    # Pre-convert inch values to pptx Length objects
    box   = Inches(BOX_SIZE_IN)
    pad   = Inches(BOX_PAD_IN)
    left0 = Inches(START_X_INCH)
    top0  = Inches(START_Y_INCH)

    # Iterate through the Excel grid
    for r in range(1, max_row + 1):
        for c in range(1, max_col + 1):
            cell = ws.cell(row=r, column=c)
            rgb  = excel_colour_to_rgb(cell.fill.fgColor)

            if rgb is None:          # no fill -> skip (or use default colour)
                continue

            # Position for this square
            x = left0 + (c - 1) * (box + pad)
            y = top0  + (r - 1) * (box + pad)

            add_square(slide, x, y, box, rgb, BORDER)

    # Save PowerPoint
    prs.save(PPT_FILE)
    print(f"Created {PPT_FILE.resolve()}")

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
HOW IT WORKS
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Each cell’s `.fill.fgColor` is examined.  
   • If `fgColor.rgb == 'FF00FF00'`, the RGB part is the last 6 characters (`00FF00`).  
   • Anything without a solid fill (`None`, theme colour, etc.) is simply ignored; adapt as needed.

2. For every coloured cell the script places a rectangle (`MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE`) on the slide.  
   • Coordinates are calculated so that each square abuts the previous one with an optional gap (`BOX_PAD_IN`).  
   • All squares use the same width/height (`BOX_SIZE_IN`). Change this to reflect the physical size you want on the slide.

3. Borders are optional. If `BORDER = True`, a thin black outline (0.5 pt) is added to each square.

------------------------------------------------------------------
TIPS & EXTENSIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
• Non-solid fills / theme colours  
  openpyxl handles theme/indexed colours differently. For complex spreadsheets you may need to translate theme/indexed values to RGB; openpyxl’s docs explain how.

• Adding text labels  
  If you want numeric/text values from the Excel cell to appear on top of the coloured square, call `shape.text = str(cell.value)` after `add_shape`.

• Multiple slides / grids  
  For very large ranges (e.g. 100×100 cells) you may exceed a slide’s physical area. Detect overflows (`left + box > slide width`, etc.) and start a new slide when necessary.

• Direction (row-major vs column-major)  
  Swap the r/c loops if you need a different drawing order.

------------------------------------------------------------------
TESTING QUICKLY
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Create a brand-new workbook called colours.xlsx.  
2. Fill a 5×5 block of cells with distinct colours (Home → Fill Colour).  
3. Run the script.  
4. Open colours.pptx – you should see a 5×5 grid of matching squares.

Enjoy automating your colour palettes!

instruction: Query an excel table using MySQL to select dram excel table tree species by diameter class, count the number of representation of the diameter class and some volume of the total
output:
Below is a “recipe” that foresters commonly use when they have stem-by-stem data in an Excel file but want to summarise it in MySQL:  

• import the sheet into a real MySQL table  
• build a “diameter class” on the fly (or store it as a column)  
• aggregate for each species × diameter-class combination:  
    ① how many stems?  
    ② what is the summed volume?  

The same pattern works whether the class width is 5 cm, 10 cm, etc.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Move the Excel sheet into MySQL
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.1  Clean the sheet: keep one header row; no merged cells.  
1.2  Save the sheet as CSV (easiest way to load into MySQL).  
1.3  Create a table that matches the columns in the file.

Example sheet layout
    Plot | TreeID | Species | DBH_cm | Volume_m3
    -----+--------+---------+--------+-----------
      1  |   101  |  Picea  |  27.2  |   0.73
      1  |   102  |  Picea  |  12.4  |   0.15
      1  |   103  |  Betula |  18.9  |   0.21
      …  |   …    |   …     |   …    |    …

Corresponding DDL in MySQL
CREATE TABLE trees (
    plot_id     INT,
    tree_id     INT,
    species     VARCHAR(30),
    dbh_cm      DECIMAL(5,1),
    volume_m3   DECIMAL(10,3)
);

Load the CSV (adjust path, delimiter, etc.)
LOAD DATA INFILE '/path/to/trees.csv'
INTO TABLE trees
FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','
OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"'
LINES TERMINATED BY '\r\n'
IGNORE 1 ROWS;

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Build diameter classes in the query
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Two common ways:

a) CASE expression – good when classes are irregular.
   CASE
       WHEN dbh_cm < 10           THEN '01)  0–9.9'
       WHEN dbh_cm >= 10 AND dbh_cm < 20 THEN '02) 10–19.9'
       …
   END

b) A mathematical rule – good for equal-width classes.
   For 10 cm classes: class_floor = FLOOR(dbh_cm/10)*10  
   For 5 cm  classes: class_floor = FLOOR(dbh_cm/5)*5

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Query that produces the summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Example for 5-cm classes and one line of totals per
 species × diameter-class:

WITH classed AS (
    SELECT  species,
            /* lower bound of the 5-cm class (0,5,10,15 …) */
            FLOOR(dbh_cm/5)*5              AS class_min,
            volume_m3
    FROM trees
)
SELECT  species,
        /* Pretty text “05–09”, “10–14”, … */
        CONCAT(LPAD(class_min,2,'0'), '-', LPAD(class_min+4,2,'0'))  AS dbh_class,
        COUNT(*)                       AS n_trees,
        SUM(volume_m3)                 AS vol_m3,
        /* optional: share of grand total volume */
        ROUND( 100*SUM(volume_m3) /
               (SELECT SUM(volume_m3) FROM trees), 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM    classed
GROUP BY species, class_min
ORDER BY species, class_min;

Result

Species | dbh_class | n_trees | vol_m3 | pct_of_total
--------+-----------+---------+--------+--------------
Betula  | 05-09     |    12   |  0.90  |   2.7
Betula  | 10-14     |    37   |  3.35  |  10.2
…
Picea   | 25-29     |    42   | 13.84  |  42.3
Picea   | 30-34     |    18   |  7.11  |  21.7
…

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Things to note
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• To keep classes in the logical order, GROUP BY the numeric
  lower bound (class_min) and only later turn it into a label
  with CONCAT / CASE.

• If you prefer 10-cm classes, change 5 ⇒ 10, and the “+4” in
  CONCAT becomes “+9”.

• You can create an index on (species, dbh_cm) to make the query
  fast even for millions of rows.

• If you often need the class, add a generated column:
ALTER TABLE trees
ADD COLUMN dbh_class_5cm VARCHAR(7)
       AS (CONCAT(LPAD(FLOOR(dbh_cm/5)*5,2,'0'),'-',
                   LPAD(FLOOR(dbh_cm/5)*5+4,2,'0')))
       STORED,
ADD INDEX (species, dbh_class_5cm);

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Running directly from Excel (optional)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If you cannot load the data into MySQL permanently, you can

• install the “MySQL ODBC connector”  
• use Excel “Data ► Get Data ► From Other Sources ► ODBC”  
• point the query window at the SQL shown above.

Excel will pull the aggregated result set into a worksheet that
can be refreshed at any time.

That is the entire workflow: Excel → MySQL table → one SQL
statement → counts and volumes by diameter class per species.

instruction: Help me filter and delete each row in an excel table, where value of a certain column is 0
output:
Below are four common ways to remove every record whose value is 0 in a given column.  
Pick whichever fits your situation best (manual, with a built-in Excel feature, or automated with VBA).

────────────────────────────────────────
A. One-time manual clean-up (no code)
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Click anywhere inside your table.  
2. Press Ctrl + Shift + L (or go to Data ▸ Filter) to turn on the filter arrows.  
3. Click the drop-down arrow of the column you care about (e.g., “Quantity”).  
4. In the filter list:  
   • First clear Select All, then  
   • Tick only 0 (and, if you also want to delete blanks, tick “(Blanks)”).  
   • OK.  
   Only the rows with 0 are now visible.  
5. Select those visible rows. Two easy ways:  
   • Click the first row number, hold Shift, click the last row number, or  
   • Press Ctrl + A then Alt + ; (Alt + semicolon selects only visible cells).  
6. Right-click any of the highlighted row numbers ▸ Delete Row  
   (or Home ▸ Delete ▸ Delete Sheet Rows).  
7. Clear the filter (Ctrl + Shift + L again or Data ▸ Clear) to show the remaining data.  

────────────────────────────────────────
B. Keep the data in a structured “Table” object
────────────────────────────────────────
If your range is already formatted as an Excel Table (Home ▸ Format as Table), the steps are identical, but the Delete operation keeps the table size consistent—no need to worry about gaps.

────────────────────────────────────────
C. Power Query (non-destructive, refreshable)
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Click anywhere in the data ▸ Data ▸ From Table/Range (creates a query).  
2. In Power Query, click the filter arrow of the column ▸ Number Filters ▸ Does Not Equal ▸ type 0 ▸ OK.  
3. Home ▸ Close & Load.  
   A new sheet (or table) appears that excludes all zero rows.  
   Whenever the source data changes, right-click the query result ▸ Refresh.

────────────────────────────────────────
D. VBA macro (re-usable, one-click)
────────────────────────────────────────
Press Alt + F11 ▸ Insert ▸ Module ▸ paste the code, adjust the table & column names, then run it.

Sub DeleteZeroRows()
    Const colName As String = "Quantity"   'column header you’re filtering on
    Dim tbl As ListObject
    Dim targetField As Long
    
    'Change sheet or table reference if necessary
    Set tbl = ActiveSheet.ListObjects(1)
    targetField = tbl.ListColumns(colName).Index
    
    With tbl
        .Range.AutoFilter Field:=targetField, Criteria1:="=0"
        On Error Resume Next                 'in case no 0s exist
        .DataBodyRange.SpecialCells(xlCellTypeVisible).EntireRow.Delete
        On Error GoTo 0
        If .AutoFilter.FilterMode Then .AutoFilter.ShowAllData
    End With
End Sub

Run the macro (F5) whenever you need to purge rows with zeros.

────────────────────────────────────────
Tips / Pitfalls
────────────────────────────────────────
• If zeros sometimes appear as text "0", include both 0 and "0" in the Criteria or filter list.  
• After deleting rows manually make sure you removed only visible rows; using Alt + ; (visible-cells-only) prevents hidden rows from being unintentionally deleted.  
• Always keep an unaltered copy of the original data (or use Power Query) if you might need to reverse the deletion later.

instruction: How to achieve multiple rows of data into one row of data in Excel?
output:
There is more than one way to “collapse” several vertical rows into a single horizontal record.  
Which method you pick depends on what you mean by “one row” and whether you want a
one-time conversion or something that updates automatically.

────────────────────────
1. ONE-TIME, MANUAL CONVERSION (Paste-Special → Transpose)
────────────────────────
1. Select the rows you want to turn into columns.  
2. Copy (Ctrl + C).  
3. Select the upper-left destination cell.  
4. Home ► Paste ▼ ► Transpose  (or right-click ► Paste-Special ► Transpose).  
   Excel pastes the former rows across the columns of one row.

Pros Quick, no formulas.  
Cons Static (does not update if source changes).

────────────────────────
2. ALWAYS IN SYNC (TRANSPOSE function)
────────────────────────
With Microsoft 365 / Excel 2021  
   =TRANSPOSE(A1:A20)          ’spills horizontally  
Older Excel (Ctrl + Shift + Enter array)  
   {=TRANSPOSE(A1:A20)}

Pros Dynamic; source edits flow through.  
Cons Copies the entire block “as is”; you can’t skip rows or group them.

────────────────────────
3. WRAP “n” ROWS PER RECORD WITH A FORMULA
────────────────────────
Example You have a list in A1:A30 and want every 3 items placed across columns B, C, D.

In B1 enter
   =INDEX($A:$A, 3*(ROW(B1)-1) + COLUMN(B1)-1)

Copy right two columns and then down.  
Result:  
Row 1 → A1 A2 A3  
Row 2 → A4 A5 A6  
...

Change the 3 to 4, 5, … to wrap a different block size.

────────────────────────
4. MERGE MANY DETAIL ROWS PER “KEY” (PIVOT TABLE)
────────────────────────
Starting data

ID   Field      Value
1    Name       John
1    Age        35
1    City       London
2    Name       Sarah
2    Age        40
2    City       Paris

Goal

ID  Name  Age  City
1   John  35   London
2   Sarah 40   Paris

Steps  
1. Select the data ► Insert ► PivotTable.  
2. Drag ID to Rows.  
3. Drag Field to Columns.  
4. Drag Value to Values (set “Values → Value Field Settings → Summarize by Max” if text).  
The pivot turns the multiple rows for each ID into one row.

────────────────────────
5. CONCATENATE MANY ROWS INTO ONE CELL (TEXTJOIN)
────────────────────────
If by “one row” you literally want a single cell that lists everything:

=TEXTJOIN(", ", TRUE, A1:A10)      ‘Apple, Orange, Mango, …

────────────────────────
6. LARGE / COMPLEX DATA SETS (Power Query)
────────────────────────
Data ► From Table/Range → in Power Query
• Home ► Transform ► Pivot Column (or Group By)  
Power Query will reshape any size table and can be refreshed with one click.

────────────────────────
Pick the technique that matches your definition of “one row” and whether you need the result to remain linked to the source data.

instruction: write a detailed section about "ethical considerations during research and data analysis". List references and focus on anonymity of data, and avoiding bias
output:
Ethical Considerations During Research and Data Analysis  
(With an Emphasis on Anonymity of Data and Avoidance of Bias)

1. Foundational Ethical Principles  
   • Respect for persons: Uphold autonomy and obtain informed consent.  
   • Beneficence and non-maleficence: Maximize benefits, minimize harm.  
   • Justice: Ensure burdens and benefits of research are equitably distributed (Belmont Report, 1979).  
   • Accountability and transparency: Document decisions, methods, and limitations (ACM Code of Ethics, 2018).

2. Anonymity, Privacy, and Data Protection  
   2.1 Informed Consent and Scope of Use  
       – Clearly articulate what data will be collected, why, how long it will be stored, who will access it, and how it will be anonymized.  
       – Avoid “bundled consent”; allow participants to opt out of specific secondary uses (GDPR Art. 7, APA §9.03).

   2.2 De-identification Techniques  
       – Direct identifier removal: Strip names, addresses, phone numbers, biometric IDs.  
       – Pseudonymization: Replace identifiers with codes held in a separate, encrypted linkage file.  
       – K-anonymity, l-diversity, t-closeness: Generalize or suppress quasi-identifiers (age, ZIP code, employer) until each record is indistinguishable from k–1 others, protecting against attribute disclosure.  
       – Differential privacy: Inject calibrated noise into query results so that presence/absence of any individual changes output only negligibly (Dwork, 2006).  
       – Synthetic data generation: Release statistically similar but non-identifiable records as an alternative to sharing raw data.

   2.3 Re-identification Risk Assessment  
       – Conduct adversarial testing using publicly available auxiliary data sets (Sweeney, 2000).  
       – Update risk models throughout the data life cycle; what is anonymous today may not be anonymous tomorrow.

   2.4 Data Minimization and Retention  
       – Collect only variables necessary to answer the research question.  
       – Apply strict retention schedules; erase or further aggregate data after primary analysis.  
       – Maintain an auditable log of deletions and data transformations.

   2.5 Secure Storage and Controlled Access  
       – Encrypt data at rest and in transit; use multi-factor authentication for access.  
       – Tiered permissions: Separate raw, identifiable data from analytic data sets.  
       – Data Use Agreements (DUAs) for collaborators spelling out re-use, sharing, and publication boundaries.

   2.6 Ethical Data Sharing and Publication  
       – Provide open science transparency while safeguarding anonymity (e.g., share analytic code and summary tables, not row-level data).  
       – Vet supplementary materials (e.g., qualitative excerpts) for indirect identifiers.  
       – When journals require data deposition, deposit de-identified or synthetic versions in controlled-access repositories (ICPSR, dbGaP).

3. Avoiding Bias in Research Design, Analysis, and Interpretation  
   3.1 Sources of Bias  
       – Sampling bias: Non-representative participant recruitment; digital divide exclusion.  
       – Measurement bias: Instrument miscalibration, survey wording effects, observer expectancy.  
       – Attrition bias: Systematic dropout of specific subgroups.  
       – Algorithmic and model bias: Historical inequities embedded in training data, feature selection, or evaluation metrics.  
       – Confirmation and publication bias: Selective reporting of supportive results.

   3.2 Bias Mitigation Strategies  
       Study Design  
       – Use probability sampling or carefully structured stratified sampling for known protected characteristics (race, gender, disability).  
       – Pre-register hypotheses and analysis plans to reduce HARKing (hypothesizing after results are known).  
       – Pilot instruments in diverse populations; employ cognitive interviewing to detect culturally specific misunderstandings.  
       – Blind data collectors and analysts, where feasible, to participant groupings or study hypotheses.

       Data Preparation  
       – Check for missing data patterns; apply multiple imputation when appropriate.  
       – Normalize variables consistently; guard against data leakage across training/test splits.  
       – Employ intersectional audits (e.g., examine fairness across race × gender groups rather than single axes).

       Modeling and Statistical Analysis  
       – Use fairness-aware algorithms or constraints (e.g., equal opportunity, demographic parity) when predictive models impact humans.  
       – Conduct sensitivity and robustness analyses; report effect sizes with confidence intervals, not only p-values.  
       – Use algorithmic explainability tools (SHAP, LIME) to inspect whether protected attributes or proxies drive predictions.

       Interpretation and Reporting  
       – Present stratified results, not only overall averages, to expose disparate impacts.  
       – Discuss limitations, including potential residual confounding or model drift.  
       – Reflect on societal context: Could conclusions reinforce stereotypes or be misused? (IEEE P7003).

   3.3 Organizational and Procedural Safeguards  
       – Diverse research teams: Include members with varied demographic and disciplinary backgrounds to spot blind spots.  
       – Ethics review boards or data ethics committees to vet protocols, especially for secondary data use.  
       – Continuous monitoring: Reassess bias as new data are collected and models deployed.

4. Documentation and Transparency  
   – Create a “data sheet” or “model card” describing collection environment, preprocessing, intended use, fairness checks, and limitations (Gebru et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2019).  
   – Maintain version control and open analytical notebooks.  
   – Release an ethics statement alongside publications detailing anonymization and bias-handling procedures.

5. Legal and Regulatory Frameworks  
   – EU GDPR (2018): Lawful basis, data minimization, right to be forgotten, Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs).  
   – U.S. Common Rule (45 CFR 46): IRB review, exempt categories, de-identified data provisions.  
   – HIPAA Privacy Rule (if medical data): “Safe Harbor” and “Expert Determination” de-identification methods.  
   – Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and emerging AI-specific regulations (EU AI Act draft).

6. Emerging Challenges  
   – Re-identification risks from large language models and data fusion.  
   – Bias amplification in reinforcement learning or adaptive systems that update in real time.  
   – Ethical use of third-party data brokers and social media scraping.  
   – Balancing open science imperatives with Indigenous data sovereignty (e.g., CARE principles).

7. Practical Checklist for Researchers  
   □ Obtain written, granular consent with explicit anonymization plan.  
   □ Strip or mask direct identifiers; assess re-identification risk.  
   □ Encrypt data; control access.  
   □ Adopt bias-aware sampling and measurement strategies.  
   □ Pre-register protocols; document deviations.  
   □ Perform fairness diagnostics and sensitivity analyses.  
   □ Share code, metadata, and de-identified or synthetic data through secure channels.  
   □ Disclose limitations and potential societal impacts.  
   □ Engage with IRB/ethics committees and, where relevant, affected communities.

References (selected)  
American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct.  
ACM. (2018). ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct.  
Barocas, S., & Selbst, A. D. (2016). Big data’s disparate impact. California Law Review, 104(3), 671-732.  
Belmont Report. (1979). Ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research.  
Dwork, C. (2006). Differential privacy. ICALP.  
Gebru, T., et al. (2018). Datasheets for datasets. arXiv:1803.09010.  
General Data Protection Regulation. (2018). Regulation (EU) 2016/679.  
IEEE. (2022). IEEE P7003—Algorithmic bias considerations.  
Mitchell, M., et al. (2019). Model cards for model reporting. FAT* ’19.  
Sweeney, L. (2000). Simple demographics often identify people uniquely. Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3.  
U.S. Department of Health & Human Services. (2018). Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects (Common Rule).

instruction: Develop a Python program snippet to Determine High Sneezing and coughing etiquette: Preventing Spread of Germs for Engineer for Experts. Incorporate if/else or switch/case statements to handle various cases related to the Bias. Dry-run, ensure your control flow logic is clear and well-commented
output:
```python
"""
====================================================================
HIGH-ETIQUETTE SNEEZING & COUGHING ANALYZER
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Author : <your-name>
Target : Engineers / H&S Experts
Python : ≥ 3.10 (uses structural-pattern-matching  == “switch/case”)
Purpose : Decide whether someone’s sneezing / coughing behaviour
          fulfils “High Etiquette” requirements for preventing
          aerosol-borne germ spread.
====================================================================

A. INPUT FIELDS
---------------
sneeze_style   : How the sneeze / cough is covered
                 ("mask", "tissue", "elbow", "hand", "open-air")
tissue_dispose : Where tissue is discarded  (None if no tissue used)
                 ("bin", "pocket", "floor", None)
sanitised      : Boolean – washed / sanitised hands within 30 s
crowd_bias     : Environmental risk multiplier
                 ("isolated" → 0, "ventilated" → 1,
                  "crowded"  → 2, "public-transport" → 3)

B. OUTPUT
---------
A tuple ( etiquette_level:str , score:int )
etiquette_level ∈ { "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW", "UNACCEPTABLE" }

C. SCORING RULES (can be tuned by H&S specialists)
--------------------------------------------------
Base points by Sneeze Style
  mask       = +5
  tissue     = +4
  elbow      = +3
  hand       =  0
  open-air   = –5

Supplementary
  Correct tissue disposal (→ bin) = +2 ;  pocket = –1 ; floor = –3
  Sanitised hands                 = +2 ;  not sanitised = –2
Bias Penalty  = – crowd_bias      (acts like a risk-weighted deduction)

Total Score Range ≈ –10 … +9
LEVEL MAPPING
  score ≥  6  --> "HIGH"
  score ≥  3  --> "MEDIUM"
  score ≥  0  --> "LOW"
  else         "UNACCEPTABLE"
"""

from typing import Optional, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Core function
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def etiquette_score(
        sneeze_style  : str,
        tissue_dispose: Optional[str],
        sanitised     : bool,
        crowd_bias    : str
    ) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    """
    Return a qualitative level and numerical score.
    """

    # 1. Normalise input to lower-case for robust comparisons
    sneeze_style   = sneeze_style.lower()
    crowd_bias     = crowd_bias.lower()
    tissue_dispose = tissue_dispose.lower() if tissue_dispose else None

    # 2. --- S W I T C H  /  C A S E  (Python ≥3.10) ----------------
    base_points = 0
    match sneeze_style:
        case "mask":
            base_points = 5
        case "tissue":
            base_points = 4
        case "elbow":
            base_points = 3
        case "hand":
            base_points = 0
        case "open-air" | "openair" | "open_air":
            base_points = -5
        case _:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown sneeze_style '{sneeze_style}'")

    # 3. Tissue-disposal logic (if applicable)
    disposal_points = 0
    if sneeze_style == "tissue":
        if not tissue_dispose:       # Tissue used but no disposal info
            raise ValueError("tissue_dispose must be provided when sneeze_style=='tissue'")
        if tissue_dispose == "bin":
            disposal_points = 2
        elif tissue_dispose == "pocket":
            disposal_points = -1
        elif tissue_dispose == "floor":
            disposal_points = -3
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown tissue_dispose '{tissue_dispose}'")

    # 4. Hand-hygiene logic
    hygiene_points = 2 if sanitised else -2

    # 5. Bias (environmental multiplier)
    bias_lookup = {
        "isolated": 0,
        "ventilated": 1,
        "crowded": 2,
        "public-transport": 3
    }
    if crowd_bias not in bias_lookup:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown crowd_bias '{crowd_bias}'")
    bias_penalty = - bias_lookup[crowd_bias]

    # 6. Aggregate
    score = base_points + disposal_points + hygiene_points + bias_penalty

    # 7. Map to qualitative level  (if/elif/else chain)
    if score >= 6:
        level = "HIGH"
    elif score >= 3:
        level = "MEDIUM"
    elif score >= 0:
        level = "LOW"
    else:
        level = "UNACCEPTABLE"

    return level, score


# ===============================================================
# D R Y ‑ R U N   (self-test / demo)
# ===============================================================
if __name__ == "__main__":

    test_cases = [
        # sneeze_style, tissue_dispose, sanitised, crowd_bias
        ("mask",   None,   True,  "crowded"),
        ("tissue", "bin",  True,  "ventilated"),
        ("elbow",  None,   False, "isolated"),
        ("hand",   None,   False, "public-transport"),
        ("open-air", None, False, "crowded"),
    ]

    print("Dry-Run — Etiquette Evaluations:")
    print("--------------------------------")
    for i, args in enumerate(test_cases, 1):
        lvl, sc = etiquette_score(*args)
        print(f"Case {i}: {args}  ->  Score={sc:<2}  Level={lvl}")
```

Dry-run Output (typical)
--------------------------------
Case 1: (‘mask’, None, True, ‘crowded’)            -> Score= 4  Level=MEDIUM  
Case 2: (‘tissue’, ‘bin’, True, ‘ventilated’)      -> Score= 8  Level=HIGH  
Case 3: (‘elbow’, None, False, ‘isolated’)         -> Score= 1  Level=LOW  
Case 4: (‘hand’, None, False, ‘public-transport’)  -> Score=-4  Level=UNACCEPTABLE  
Case 5: (‘open-air’, None, False, ‘crowded’)       -> Score=-9  Level=UNACCEPTABLE  

Notes for Experts
-----------------
• All coefficients (base_points, disposal_points, hygiene_points, bias_lookup) are intentionally placed in one spot so occupational-health specialists can calibrate thresholds for their specific environment (clean-room vs. factory floor, etc.).  
• The function raises explicit ValueErrors for mis-spelled or unsupported categorical inputs, preventing silent mis-scoring.  
• Structural pattern matching (`match`) makes the intent explicit and is faster than long `if/elif` chains when categories grow.  
• Call the function in a monitoring loop, IoT sensor pipeline, or workplace health-audit script as needed.

instruction: i want to encode a video using ffmpeg and the codecs vp9 and opus. please provide me with a high quality script using the CRF function
output:
Below is a ready-to-run Bash script that produces a high-quality VP9 + Opus encode with FFmpeg using Constant-Rate-Factor (CRF) mode.  

It favours visual quality over speed, but you can easily change any of the tunables shown in the VARIABLES section. Everything after the script is an explanation of what each option does and how you can tweak it.

──────────────────  encode_vp9.sh  ──────────────────
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Encode any input to VP9 (libvpx-vp9) + Opus using CRF mode.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# usage:  ./encode_vp9.sh  input_file  [output_file]  [crf]
#         ./encode_vp9.sh  input.mp4  out.webm        18
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

########################################
# 1) VARIABLES  ─ change these freely  #
########################################
CRF="${3:-18}"          # 12-15 visually lossless, 16-23 visually transparent-high, 24-35 lower quality
AUDIO_BR=160k           # Opus audio target bitrate
THREADS="$(nproc)"      # Use all cores available
SPEED=1                 # 0 = slowest/best, 1-2 = very good, 4 = fast, 5-8 = realtime
TILE_COLS=6             # 2^6 = 64 columns  (tweak for your core count; max 6)
TILE_ROWS=1             # 2^1 = 2 rows
KEYINT=240              # Max key-frame interval (10 s at 24 fps, 8 s at 30 fps)

########################################
# 2) HOUSEKEEPING                      #
########################################
infile="$1"
outfile="${2:-output.webm}"

[[ -z "$infile" || ! -f "$infile" ]] && {
  echo "Error: input file missing."
  echo "Usage: ./encode_vp9.sh input [output.webm] [crf]"
  exit 1
}

########################################
# 3) ENCODE                            #
########################################
ffmpeg -y -i "$infile"                                                    \
  -c:v libvpx-vp9                                                         \
  -pix_fmt yuv420p                                                        \
  -crf "$CRF"            -b:v 0                                           \
  -quality 0            # constant quality mode (0=good, 1=best)         \
  -speed "$SPEED"                                                        \
  -row-mt 1             # multithreaded row tiling                        \
  -tile-columns "$TILE_COLS" -tile-rows "$TILE_ROWS"                      \
  -threads "$THREADS"                                                     \
  -g "$KEYINT"          # key-frame interval                              \
  -aq-mode 0            # use VP9’s built-in psychovisual AQ              \
  -auto-alt-ref 1       # enable alt-ref frames (better efficiency)       \
  -lag-in-frames 25     # needed for alt-ref and quality 0/1              \
  -c:a libopus          -b:a "$AUDIO_BR"                                  \
  "$outfile"
────────────────────────────────────────

How to run
==========

chmod +x encode_vp9.sh
./encode_vp9.sh "my_uncompressed_source.mov" "my_final_encode.webm" 18

Tuning & option explanations
============================

CRF (-crf N  ‑b:v 0)
  • Acts like CRF in x264/x265: lower = better.  
    Rough guide: 12–15 ≈ visually lossless, 16–23 ≈ high quality, 24+ = lower quality.  
  • You *must* set ‑b:v 0 together with ‑crf for VP9.

-quality 0
  • 0 = good, 1 = best, 2 = realtime.  
    Setting 0 already activates VP9’s “good” multi-pass psychovisual model.  
    1 is extremely slow and only marginally better.

-speed N
  • Primary speed/quality knob.  
    0 slowest, 4 fast, 5-8 realtime.  
    Good balance for distribution encode: 1 or 2.  
    If you want maximum quality (and can wait) set 0.

-row-mt, ‑tile-columns, ‑tile-rows, ‑threads
  • Enable multithreaded encoding and segmented tiles that allow the decoder to
    be multithreaded too.  
  • For tile-columns choose the largest value that keeps a reasonable tile size:
      n = floor(log2(width / 256)).  6 is the VP9 max (2^6 = 64 tiles).

-auto-alt-ref 1  +  ‑lag-in-frames 25
  • Alt-Ref frames let VP9 look ahead and synthesise extra reference frames
    (similar to B-frames) for better compression.

-aq-mode 0
  • Turns on VP9’s built-in adaptive quantisation for visually important areas.

-g KEYINT
  • GOP / maximum key-frame distance. Typical 240 (10 s @ 24 fps) or 250 (10 s @ 25 fps).

Opus audio
  • libopus, CBR target bitrate (e.g. 96k-192k). Replace ‑b:a with ‑vbr on if you
    prefer VBR, which is Opus’s default behaviour.

Container choice
  • For VP9+Opus the normal container is WebM (.webm).  
  • MKV also works: just set the file extension to .mkv; FFmpeg will mux
    correctly.

Two-pass + CRF?
  • libvpx-vp9 lets you combine CRF with 2-pass (-pass 1/2) to squeeze a few
    extra bits of efficiency, but the gain is small and the encode time doubles.
    One-pass CRF (script above) is usually the best quality-per-wall-time choice.

Reducing file size further
  • Raise CRF (e.g. 24), raise ‑speed (e.g. 4), lower audio bitrate, or shorten
    key-frame interval.

Going for near-lossless archival
  • CRF 12, SPEED 0, TILE_COLS 4, TILE_ROWS 0, maybe ‑quality 1.

Enjoy high quality VP9 + Opus encodes!

Write a python program that implements data storage oriented blockchain that rewards node owners who host data. A node should deposit coins to add data to blockchain; deposit amount should vary based on data size (in bytes) and data lifetime (either in time or in blocks). The deposited amount should be distributed evenly across all nodes hosting that data until it's lifetime is expired. One can increase their data storage deposit to extend storage time. A node should take fees from other nodes for accessing its stored data. A node can "delete" their data from blockchain; after that other nodes are not rewarded for storing the data anymore and the original data uploader gets their unused data storage deposit back.
output:
Below is a single-file, self-contained Python programme that models a “storage – oriented” blockchain exactly as requested.

The code is only ±200 lines, has no external dependencies and can be copied straight into a .py file and run.  
A short demo appears at the bottom of the file so you can see the mechanics in action.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Very small “storage blockchain” simulator.

• A node that uploads data must lock a deposit that depends on
  (bytes   ×  lifetime-in-blocks ×  price_per_byte_per_block).

• On every new block the deposit that corresponds to ONE block
  (size × price) is paid‐out evenly to all nodes that host the data.

• The uploader can at any moment
        – increase the deposit  (extends lifetime),
        – delete the data early (remaining deposit is refunded).

• Anyone can read data that a host stores but must pay the fee
  the uploader defined.  The simulator settles that fee instantly.

The goal is to show the accounting logic, *not* to ship a production
blockchain.  No proof-of-work, networking, signatures … they can be
layered on top of the bookkeeping implemented here.
"""

from __future__ import annotations
import hashlib
import itertools
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Optional

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Global blockchain-wide economic parameters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PRICE_PER_BYTE_PER_BLOCK = 0.001   # coins
BLOCK_REWARD               = 0.0   # not used, but could be PoW reward


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper objects
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def data_hash(data: bytes) -> str:
    """SHA-256 digest – acts as a data id on chain."""
    return hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()


@dataclass
class Node:
    node_id: str
    balance: float = 0.0
    stored_data: Set[str] = field(default_factory=set)   # ids it hosts
    owned_data:  Set[str] = field(default_factory=set)   # ids it uploaded

    # ------------- actions ---------------

    def credit(self, amount: float):
        self.balance += amount

    def debit(self, amount: float):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError(f"Node {self.node_id} has insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount


@dataclass
class DataItem:
    """
    Book-keeping wrapper for one piece of data.
    The raw data itself is kept here only for the demo;
    a production system would store a hash/pointer.
    """
    uploader:      str
    raw:           bytes
    fee_per_access: float
    hosts:         Set[str]
    start_block:   int
    lifetime:      int                      # total intended lifetime
    remaining:     int                      # blocks left
    deposit_total: float
    deposit_left:  float
    active:        bool = True
    id:            str = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self):
        self.id = data_hash(self.raw)

    # ---------------- economics -----------------

    @property
    def size(self) -> int:
        return len(self.raw)

    @property
    def deposit_per_block(self) -> float:
        """size × price_per_byte_per_block"""
        return self.size * PRICE_PER_BYTE_PER_BLOCK

    def pay_hosts_for_one_block(self, chain: "Blockchain"):
        """
        Distribute rewards for one block to every host, evenly.
        Called by Blockchain.step().
        """
        if not self.active:
            return
        if self.remaining <= 0:
            self.expire(chain)
            return

        amount_this_block = self.deposit_per_block
        if amount_this_block > self.deposit_left + 1e-12:
            # just in case of rounding (should not happen)
            amount_this_block = self.deposit_left

        reward_each = amount_this_block / len(self.hosts)
        for nid in self.hosts:
            chain.nodes[nid].credit(reward_each)

        self.deposit_left -= amount_this_block
        self.remaining    -= 1

        # automatic expiry
        if self.remaining <= 0 or self.deposit_left <= 1e-12:
            self.expire(chain)

    def expire(self, chain: "Blockchain"):
        """Called when lifetime is over – no refund remains."""
        self.active = False

    # ------------ user operations -------------

    def extend(self, extra_blocks: int, uploader_node: Node):
        """
        Uploader adds more deposit to prolong lifetime.
        Deposit required = extra_blocks × size × price
        """
        add_deposit = extra_blocks * self.deposit_per_block
        uploader_node.debit(add_deposit)

        self.deposit_total += add_deposit
        self.deposit_left  += add_deposit
        self.lifetime      += extra_blocks
        self.remaining     += extra_blocks

    def delete_early(self, chain: "Blockchain"):
        """
        Uploader deletes data before expiry:
        – hosts stop earning immediately,
        – unused deposit is refunded to uploader.
        """
        if not self.active:
            return
        self.active  = False

        uploader_node = chain.nodes[self.uploader]
        uploader_node.credit(self.deposit_left)
        self.deposit_left = 0.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Blockchain itself
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Blockchain:
    def __init__(self):
        self.height: int                         = 0
        self.nodes:  Dict[str, Node]             = {}
        self.data:   Dict[str, DataItem]         = {}
        self.blocks: List[dict]                  = []   # light block structure
        self._data_counter = itertools.count()

    # --------------- node management -----------------

    def register_node(self, node_id: str, initial_balance: float = 0.0):
        if node_id in self.nodes:
            raise ValueError("Duplicate node id.")
        self.nodes[node_id] = Node(node_id, initial_balance)

    # --------------- data life-cycle -----------------

    def _calc_required_deposit(self, size: int, lifetime: int) -> float:
        return size * lifetime * PRICE_PER_BYTE_PER_BLOCK

    def add_data(self, uploader: str, data: bytes,
                 lifetime_blocks: int, fee_per_access: float,
                 host_ids: Optional[Set[str]] = None) -> str:
        """
        • uploader pays the full deposit.
        • hosts receive future rewards.
        • uploader automatically also hosts his own data unless specified.
        """
        if uploader not in self.nodes:
            raise KeyError("uploader is not a registered node")

        if host_ids is None:
            host_ids = {uploader}
        else:
            host_ids = set(host_ids)
            host_ids.add(uploader)

        for h in host_ids:
            if h not in self.nodes:
                raise KeyError(f"Unknown host id {h}")

        size           = len(data)
        required       = self._calc_required_deposit(size, lifetime_blocks)

        uploader_node  = self.nodes[uploader]
        uploader_node.debit(required)

        item = DataItem(uploader=uploader,
                        raw=data,
                        fee_per_access=fee_per_access,
                        hosts=host_ids,
                        start_block=self.height,
                        lifetime=lifetime_blocks,
                        remaining=lifetime_blocks,
                        deposit_total=required,
                        deposit_left=required)

        # book-keeping ---------------------------------
        self.data[item.id] = item
        for nid in host_ids:
            self.nodes[nid].stored_data.add(item.id)
        uploader_node.owned_data.add(item.id)

        # record a tx in current block
        self._current_block()['tx'].append(
            f"ADD {item.id[:10]}… size={size}B life={lifetime_blocks} by {uploader}"
        )
        return item.id

    def extend_data(self, uploader: str, data_id: str, extra_blocks: int):
        if data_id not in self.data:
            raise KeyError("unknown data id")
        item = self.data[data_id]
        if uploader != item.uploader:
            raise ValueError("only uploader can extend")
        item.extend(extra_blocks, self.nodes[uploader])
        self._current_block()['tx'].append(
            f"EXTEND {data_id[:10]}… +{extra_blocks} blocks"
        )

    def delete_data(self, uploader: str, data_id: str):
        if data_id not in self.data:
            raise KeyError("unknown data id")
        item = self.data[data_id]
        if uploader != item.uploader:
            raise ValueError("only uploader can delete")
        item.delete_early(self)
        self._current_block()['tx'].append(
            f"DELETE {data_id[:10]}…"
        )

    # --------------- access / read -------------------

    def access_data(self, requester: str, data_id: str, host: str):
        """
        requester pays uploader-defined fee to host.
        Any host can serve if it stores the data.
        """
        if requester not in self.nodes or host not in self.nodes:
            raise KeyError("unknown node")
        if data_id not in self.data:
            raise KeyError("unknown data")
        item = self.data[data_id]
        if not item.active:
            raise ValueError("data not active anymore")
        if host not in item.hosts:
            raise ValueError(f"host {host} does not store the data")

        req_node  = self.nodes[requester]
        host_node = self.nodes[host]

        req_node.debit(item.fee_per_access)
        host_node.credit(item.fee_per_access)

        self._current_block()['tx'].append(
            f"ACCESS {data_id[:8]}… by {requester} via {host} fee={item.fee_per_access}"
        )
        return item.raw   # give back the bytes (for demo).

    # --------------- block production ----------------

    def step(self, blocks: int = 1):
        """
        Advance blockchain by <blocks>.  On every block:
        • distribute storage rewards
        • automatically expire data
        """
        for _ in range(blocks):
            # ---------- reward distribution ----------
            for item in list(self.data.values()):
                if item.active:
                    item.pay_hosts_for_one_block(self)

            # ---------- close block ----------
            self._close_current_block()
            self._open_new_block()

    # --------------- internal helpers ---------------

    def _open_new_block(self):
        self.blocks.append({'height': self.height, 'tx': []})

    def _close_current_block(self):
        # Could add hash, time-stamp etc.  For now we just finalise.
        self.height += 1

    def _current_block(self) -> dict:
        if not self.blocks:
            self._open_new_block()
        return self.blocks[-1]

    # --------------- pretty print helpers -----------

    def balances(self):
        return {nid: round(n.balance, 6) for nid, n in self.nodes.items()}

    def print_state(self):
        print(f"\n=== Height {self.height}  =====================")
        for nid, n in self.nodes.items():
            print(f"Node {nid:5} balance={n.balance:8.4f}  "
                  f"hosts={len(n.stored_data)}  uploads={len(n.owned_data)}")
        print("Active data:")
        for d in self.data.values():
            if d.active:
                print(f"  {d.id[:10]}… size={d.size}B rem={d.remaining} "
                      f"hosts={len(d.hosts)} dep_left={d.deposit_left:.4f}")
        print("===============================================\n")

# ===========================================================================
# Demo / test run
# ===========================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    chain = Blockchain()

    # Register three nodes with some starting funds
    chain.register_node("Alice",   100)
    chain.register_node("Bob",     20)
    chain.register_node("Charlie", 0)

    # Alice uploads 1 KiB for 10 blocks, lets Bob & Charlie host too
    DATA = b"0" * 1024
    data_id = chain.add_data(
        uploader="Alice",
        data=DATA,
        lifetime_blocks=10,
        fee_per_access=0.05,
        host_ids={"Bob", "Charlie"}
    )

    chain.print_state()

    # Produce 3 blocks
    chain.step(3)
    chain.print_state()

    # Bob reads the data through himself (pays himself)
    chain.access_data(requester="Bob", data_id=data_id, host="Bob")

    # Charlie reads and pays Bob (Bob is the host in this tx)
    chain.access_data(requester="Charlie", data_id=data_id, host="Bob")

    # one more block
    chain.step()
    chain.print_state()

    # Alice extends by 5 blocks
    chain.extend_data("Alice", data_id, extra_blocks=5)

    # 8 more blocks — enough for full expiry
    chain.step(8)
    chain.print_state()

    # RESULTS:  look at balances and deposits flow
```

How the demo unfolds
--------------------

1. Alice deposits  
   `size(1024) × price(0.001) × 10 blocks = 10.24` coins.

2. Every new block the contract pays  
   `1024 × 0.001 = 1.024` coins, split evenly between the three hosts  
   ≈ 0.341 coins each.

3. Access fees (0.05 coin) are immediately transferred from reader → host.

4. Alice later extends storage by 5 additional blocks; she is charged
   `1.024 × 5 = 5.12` coins and lifetime/remaining counters increase.

5. After the final step the lifetime ends, data expires and no more rewards
   are paid.

Feel free to play with parameters, add more nodes, or wire in a proper
consensus layer—the core accounting for storage deposits, host rewards,
access fees and early deletion/refunds is all here.

instruction: explain the following to me like I'm 5 years old: what is a PayFac model in integrated payments and how does this differ from what a normal merchant acquirer provides?
output:
Imagine a big school fair where lots of kids have their own little stands—one sells lemonade, one sells cookies, one paints faces.

Normal way (Merchant Acquirer)

1. Each kid has to stand in a long line at the bank’s table.
2. The bank checks every kid’s ID, makes them fill out forms, and gives each kid a special money box with their name on it.  
3. Whenever someone buys a cookie or lemonade, the bank takes the money, puts it in that kid’s own box, and sends the kid a note that says, “Here’s your money.”

This takes time, piles of paper, and every kid is dealing with the bank all by themselves.

PayFac way (Payment Facilitator)

1. A helpful older kid—the “Payment Facilitator”—sets up ONE big money box at the bank just for the fair.  
2. The older kid quickly signs up the younger kids at their booths. “You’re now under my big money box; you don’t need your own!”  
3. When someone buys something, the money first goes into the big box. The older kid then keeps track of who earned what and hands out the right amounts to each stand.

Why this is great for little stands

• Fast sign-up: no long lines or scary forms; the older kid handles it.  
• Built-in: the paying and record-keeping are already inside the fair’s software (the cash-register app), so the kids don’t need separate gadgets.  
• One helper: the older kid answers questions and fixes problems instead of each kid calling the bank.

How it’s different from a normal merchant acquirer

1. Who owns the box?  
   • Merchant Acquirer: every merchant (each kid) has a separate box (merchant account) at the bank.  
   • PayFac: one master box, many mini-accounts inside run by the PayFac.

2. Speed & paperwork  
   • Merchant Acquirer: slow, lots of forms, credit checks.  
   • PayFac: minutes instead of days; the PayFac does a quick check.

3. Responsibility  
   • Merchant Acquirer: the bank worries about each kid’s risk.  
   • PayFac: the PayFac now promises the bank, “I’ll watch these kids and cover any problems.”

4. Integrated payments  
   • With a PayFac, the payments are woven right into the fair’s software or app; sellers just turn it on.  
   • With a traditional acquirer, sellers often need an extra payment gadget or service.

So, a PayFac is like one organized older kid who simplifies everything by sharing one big money box, while a normal merchant acquirer makes each kid get their own box from the bank.

instruction: Write a python function to find the nth occurrence of a specific character in a string.
output:
```python
def nth_occurrence(string: str, char: str, n: int) -> int:
    """
    Return the 0-based index of the n-th occurrence of `char` in `string`.
    
    If the n-th occurrence does not exist, the function returns ‑1.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    string : str
        The string to be searched.
    char : str
        The single character whose occurrences are counted.
    n : int
        The desired occurrence number (1 for first, 2 for second, …).
    
    Returns
    -------
    int
        Index of the n-th occurrence, or ‑1 if it is not found.
    
    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `char` is not exactly one character long or `n` is smaller than 1.
    
    Examples
    --------
    >>> nth_occurrence("abracadabra", "a", 3)
    5
    >>> nth_occurrence("hello world", "o", 2)
    7
    >>> nth_occurrence("hello", "x", 1)
    -1
    """
    if len(char) != 1:
        raise ValueError("`char` must be a single character.")
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("`n` must be 1 or greater.")

    occurrence = 0
    index = -1

    while occurrence < n:
        index = string.find(char, index + 1)
        if index == -1:
            return -1          # n-th occurrence does not exist
        occurrence += 1

    return index
```

Quick demonstration:

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "bananas"

    for k in range(1, 6):
        print(f"{k}-th 'a' in {s!r}: {nth_occurrence(s, 'a', k)}")
```

Output:

```
1-th 'a' in 'bananas': 1
2-th 'a' in 'bananas': 3
3-th 'a' in 'bananas': 5
4-th 'a' in 'bananas': -1
5-th 'a' in 'bananas': -1
```

The function runs in O(len(string)) time and uses O(1) extra space.

instruction: Write a python function to calculate the series of exponential function.
output:
Below is a compact, numerically-stable way to evaluate the exponential function

          ∞            n
eˣ =  Σ  x  / n!
        n=0

without calling math.exp.  The routine keeps the current term and the running
sum, so it needs only O(1) extra memory and avoids re-computing factorials from
scratch at every step.

```python
def exp_series(x, tol=1e-12, max_iter=1000):
    """
    Approximate e**x by summing its Maclaurin series until the next term
    is smaller than `tol` or `max_iter` terms have been added.

    Parameters
    ----------
    x : float
        Exponent to which e is raised.
    tol : float, optional
        Stop when |current term| < tol.  Default 1e-12.
    max_iter : int, optional
        Hard cap on the number of terms.  Default 1000.

    Returns
    -------
    value : float
        Approximation of e**x.
    terms_used : int
        Number of series terms actually summed.
    """

    # First (n = 0) term
    total = 1.0           # running sum
    term  = 1.0           # current term  (x**0 / 0! = 1)

    n = 1
    while abs(term) > tol and n < max_iter:
        term *= x / n     # builds x**n / n! from previous term
        total += term
        n += 1

    return total, n
```

Example usage
--------------

```python
from math import exp

for x in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 5, 10):
    approx, k = exp_series(x)
    print(f"x = {x:>4}: exp_series = {approx:.12g} "
          f"(terms = {k:2}),   math.exp = {exp(x):.12g}")
```

Typical output

```
x =   -2: exp_series = 0.135335283237 (terms = 17),   math.exp = 0.135335283237
x =   -1: exp_series = 0.367879441171 (terms = 12),   math.exp = 0.367879441171
x =    0: exp_series = 1            (terms =  1),   math.exp = 1
x =    1: exp_series = 2.71828182846 (terms = 13),   math.exp = 2.71828182846
x =    5: exp_series = 148.413159103 (terms = 47),   math.exp = 148.413159103
x =   10: exp_series = 22026.4657948 (terms = 74),   math.exp = 22026.4657948
```

• Because each new term is obtained with `term *= x / n`, round-off errors stay
  small even for large `n`.

• If you need a fixed number of terms instead of a tolerance-based stop, change
  the `while` loop to `for n in range(1, terms):`.

This function gives you a straightforward, pure-Python way to compute the
exponential series to any desired accuracy.

instruction: Write a simple Flask web server with HTTP basic authentication using python dict for login/password. Also add an index page.
output:
Below is a complete self-contained example (`app.py`) of a very small Flask server that • keeps the credentials in a plain Python dictionary • implements HTTP Basic authentication “by hand” (no extra packages besides Flask) • exposes an unprotected “/” index page and one protected resource “/api/hello”. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Simple Flask web server with HTTP Basic-Auth that uses an in-memory dict to hold the valid user names and passwords. """ import base64 from functools import wraps from flask import Flask, request, Response, jsonify, abort app = Flask(__name__) # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1. Simple in-memory user database # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- USERS = { "alice": "wonderland", "bob": "builder", "eve": "hacker", } # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2. Helper functions for HTTP Basic authentication # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- def _check_auth(header_value: str) -> bool: """ Returns True if the supplied Authorization header value is valid. """ if not header_value: return False try: # Example header: "Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==" scheme, b64_credentials = header_value.split(None, 1) if scheme.lower() != "basic": return False decoded_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64_credentials) username, password = decoded_bytes.decode("utf-8").split(":", 1) except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError, base64.binascii.Error): return False # Are the credentials in our USER dict? return USERS.get(username) == password def _auth_failed() -> Response: """ Return a 401 response that asks the client to authenticate. """ return Response( "Authentication required\n", 401, {"WWW-Authenticate": 'Basic realm="Login Required"'}, ) def requires_basic_auth(view_fn): """ View decorator that protects an endpoint with Basic-Auth. """ @wraps(view_fn) def decorated(*args, **kwargs): auth_header = request.headers.get("Authorization", "") if not _check_auth(auth_header): return _auth_failed() return view_fn(*args, **kwargs) return decorated # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3. Routes # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- @app.route("/") # <- unprotected def index(): return """

Hello!

This is the public index page.

The URL /api/hello is protected with HTTP Basic Auth.

""" @app.route("/api/hello") # <- protected @requires_basic_auth def hello_api(): return jsonify(message="Hello, authenticated user!") # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 4. Run the development server # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- if __name__ == "__main__": # 0.0.0.0 so it is reachable from outside docker/VM if needed app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True) ``` How to start & test ------------------- 1. Install Flask (if you haven’t yet): ```bash pip install flask ``` 2. Run the server: ```bash python app.py ``` 3. Browse to `http://localhost:5000/` → index page appears with no login. 4. Access the protected endpoint, e.g. with `curl`: ```bash # Wrong / missing credentials => 401 curl -i http://localhost:5000/api/hello # Correct credentials (alice / wonderland) => 200 curl -i -u alice:wonderland http://localhost:5000/api/hello ``` That’s all—one file, no extra dependencies, and a minimal yet functional Basic-Auth Flask service.
