;  from the current drawing’s Named-Object Dictionary (NOD).
;
;  Command name:  KILLDGN
;===========================================================

(defun _delDict (dictContainer dictName / obj)
  ;; Helper – tries to delete a named dictionary.
  ;; Returns T if it existed and was deleted, NIL otherwise.
  (vl-catch-all-apply
    (function
      (lambda ( )
        (setq obj (vla-item dictContainer dictName))
        (vla-delete obj)
        T)))                                          ; ← success
)

(defun c:KILLDGN ( / acDoc nod removed? )
  (vl-load-com)
  (setq acDoc (vla-get-ActiveDocument (vlax-get-acad-object))
        nod   (vla-get-Dictionaries acDoc))           ; Named-Object Dictionary

  (setq removed? (_delDict nod "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP"))

  (if removed?
      (princ "\nACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP dictionary has been removed.")
      (princ "\nACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP dictionary not found in this drawing."))
  (princ)
)
;===========================================================

(princ "\nType KILLDGN to delete the ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP dictionary.")
(princ)

Notes
• The routine uses Visual LISP’s vla-delete method, which is safer than entdel for dictionaries.  
• Only the specific dictionary entry under the NOD is removed; nothing else in the drawing is touched.  
• If you also need to clean stray DGN objects inside blocks, xrefs, etc., run AutoCAD’s built-in DGNPURGE command after this routine.

instruction: How can I restrict a Postgres geometry column to only contain polygons?
output:
With plain PostgreSQL you cannot do it, but with the PostGIS extension you can.  
The restriction can be imposed in two equivalent ways:

1. Give the column a “typed-modifier” geometry definition (recommended for new
   tables/columns).  
2. Keep the column of the generic geometry type and add an ordinary
   CHECK-constraint.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Using a typed geometry column (PostGIS ≥ 2.0)

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;          -- only once per database

CREATE TABLE parcels (
    id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    geom geometry(Polygon, 4326)  -- Polygon only, in SRID 4326
);

Because the column is declared geometry(Polygon,4326) PostGIS installs an
implicit constraint; inserting anything that is not a polygon will raise

ERROR:  Geometry type (LineString) does not match column type (Polygon)

If you already have a table/column:

ALTER TABLE parcels
  ALTER COLUMN geom
  TYPE geometry(Polygon,4326)
  USING ST_SetSRID(geom,4326);   -- will fail if rows aren’t polygons

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Using an explicit CHECK constraint (works in any PostGIS version)

-- Accept simple polygons (and, if you wish, multipolygons)
ALTER TABLE parcels
  ADD CONSTRAINT geom_must_be_polygon
  CHECK ( GeometryType(geom) IN ('POLYGON','MULTIPOLYGON')
          OR geom IS NULL );     -- allow NULL if the column is nullable

In PostGIS ≥ 2.1 the returned type names are prefixed with “ST_”:

CHECK ( GeometryType(geom) IN ('ST_Polygon','ST_MultiPolygon') OR geom IS NULL );

Either approach ensures that only polygonal geometries can be stored in the
column.

instruction: I'm trying to run a pytorch program on a computer with multiple GPUs. My program is only using one! What can I change in the code to get it to use all the gpus available?
output:
In PyTorch you only get one GPU automatically; you have to tell PyTorch that you really want to split the work across several devices.  
There are two (related) APIs you can drop into an existing “single-GPU” script:

────────────────────────────────────────
1. torch.nn.DataParallel     (quick & easy, 1 process)
2. torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel (DDP)   (fast & scalable, 1 process per GPU)
────────────────────────────────────────

Below are the minimum changes for each route.  Pick one and paste the changes into your training script.

======================================================================
1. The 30-second solution – DataParallel
======================================================================

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = MyModel()                                   # your network

# --- NEW: wrap the network if more than one GPU is visible ----------
if torch.cuda.device_count() > 1:
    print(f'Using {torch.cuda.device_count()} GPUs')
    model = nn.DataParallel(model)                 # ← magic line
# --------------------------------------------------------------------

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
model = model.to(device)

# the rest (optimizers, forward, backward, etc.) is unchanged
```

Run your script exactly the same way as before, but make sure all GPUs
you want are visible, e.g.:

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 python train.py
```

Pros: one-liner, works for inference too.  
Cons: only one process, speed is limited by GIL & single-CUDA-stream
bottleneck; not recommended for >4 GPUs or multi-node work.

======================================================================
2. The performant solution – DistributedDataParallel (DDP)
======================================================================

Step-0: launch one process per GPU (recommended front-end in PyTorch ≥1.9):

```
torchrun --nproc_per_node=NUM_GPUS_YOU_HAVE train.py         # e.g. 4
```

Step-1: add a few lines at the top of `train.py`:

```python
import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP

def main():
    # ----- 1. boiler-plate initialisation --------------------------------
    dist.init_process_group(backend='nccl')            # or 'gloo' on CPU
    local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])         # given by torchrun
    torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)
    device = torch.device("cuda", local_rank)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

    # ----- 2. build model and wrap it ------------------------------------
    model = MyModel().to(device)
    model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank], output_device=local_rank)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

    # ----- 3. make dataloader distributed-aware --------------------------
    dataset = MyDataset(...)
    train_sampler = torch.utils.data.distributed.DistributedSampler(
                        dataset, shuffle=True)
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
                        dataset,
                        batch_size=BATCH_SIZE_PER_GPU,
                        sampler=train_sampler,
                        num_workers=NUM_WORKERS)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

    # ----- 4. training loop is mostly unchanged --------------------------
    for epoch in range(num_epochs):
        train_sampler.set_epoch(epoch)      # shuffles differently each epoch
        for x, y in loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            ...
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Pros: near-linear speed-up, works on many nodes, recommended by PyTorch team.  
Cons: a few more lines of plumbing; you must use `DistributedSampler`.

Notes / common pitfalls
––––––––––––––––––––––––
• Make sure batch-size is the per-GPU size; effective global batch will be
  `batch_size * world_size`.  
• Keep `torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)` BEFORE `.to(device)`.  
• Do not wrap the model twice (no `DataParallel` inside `DDP`).  
• NCCL needs the environment variables set by `torchrun`; don’t `python train.py`
  directly for DDP.  
• If you only have one node but many GPUs, backend `'nccl'` is still correct.

======================================================================
Quick decision chart
======================================================================
✓ “I just want it to run on two GPUs on my desktop”: use `DataParallel`.

✓ “I care about performance / more than 3-4 GPUs / possibly multi-node”:
   migrate to DDP; it scales and is the future-proof path.

That’s all you need to turn a one-GPU script into a multi-GPU one. Happy training!

instruction: I have a system76 Thelio linux computer. I would like to install a Nvidia GTX 3060 GPU. I have a 450W PSU. First, is the psu sufficient to power the gpu? Second, how do I install the gpu?
output:
────────────────────────
1.  Is the 450 W Thelio supply big enough?
────────────────────────
•  GeForce RTX-3060 (non-Ti) board power: ≈ 170 W  
  – Short spikes (“transients”) can momentarily reach 220-240 W.

•  Typical desktop parts you already have  
  – Ryzen-5 / Core-i5 class CPU……………………… 65–105 W  
  – Mainboard, RAM, fans, M.2/NVMe…………………… 40–50 W  
  – 1–2 SSD/HDD …………………………………………… 5–15 W  
  – “Overhead” (USB devices, ageing of PSU, efficiency)… 40-60 W

Even in a worst-case “all cores & GPU at 100 %” scenario you would land around
330-380 W.  A good 80 PLUS Gold/Platinum 450 W unit can deliver that, but it
will be running at 75-85 % of its capacity and will have little head-room for
future upgrades or heavy transient spikes.

NVidia’s own guideline for the RTX-3060 is a 550 W supply.  System76 ships the
3060 in Thelios with their optional 500 W/600 W supplies, not the base 450 W.

Conclusion  
• Technically it will probably work if the 450 W Thelio PSU is healthy and has
  at least one 8-pin (6 + 2) PCIe connector.  
• Practically it is safer, quieter and better for longevity to move to a
  550–650 W unit.  If you can, order System76’s 600 W upgrade or install any
  quality ATX Gold/Platinum PSU.

────────────────────────
2.  Installing the card (Thelio chassis)
────────────────────────
Safety & tools  
• Phillips #2 screwdriver, anti-static strap (or touch an un-painted metal part
  of the case before handling components).  
• Power the PC off, switch the PSU to “0”, pull the mains cord, then press the
  power button for 3 s to discharge.

A. Open the Thelio  
1. Unscrew the two rear thumb-screws that hold the left aluminium/wood side
   panel; lift the panel straight off.  
2. Remove the outer steel shroud (two more screws on the top lip) to expose the
   motherboard area.

B. Remove the old slot cover  
1. Locate the long PCIe x16 slot (nearest the CPU).  
2. Remove the two rear expansion-slot screws (covers usually labelled 1 and 2).

C. Seat the RTX-3060  
1. Flip the PCIe slot’s little plastic latch open.  
2. Align the card with the slot and the rear IO bracket; press straight down
   until you hear the latch click.  
3. Re-install the two bracket screws to hold the card.

D. Connect power  
• Most partner RTX-3060 cards want ONE 8-pin (6 + 2) PCIe plug.  
• The Founders Edition uses NVIDIA’s 12-pin micro-fit and comes with an adapter
  that accepts two 8-pin plugs; with a 450 W PSU you will only have a single
  8-pin, so be sure your card only needs one.  
• Route the cable cleanly so it does not obstruct the Thelio’s fan duct.

E. Close the case  
1. Replace the steel shroud, then the decorative wood/aluminium side.  
2. Re-install the thumb-screws, reconnect the mains cord, switch the PSU to “1”.

────────────────────────
3.  Software / driver setup (Pop!_OS, Ubuntu)
────────────────────────
Pop!_OS (recommended by System76)  
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade           # ensure system is current
sudo apt install system76-driver-nvidia            # pulls the tested driver
Reboot → Settings → Graphics shows “NVIDIA On-Demand / Performance”.

Ubuntu 20.04/22.04  
sudo ubuntu-drivers autoinstall                    # chooses the right 535-series+
Reboot and select “NVIDIA (Performance)” in the
Software-&-Updates ▸ Additional Drivers tab.

Optional: verify  
nvidia-smi                                          # should list the RTX-3060  
glxinfo | grep OpenGL                               # renderer reports NVIDIA

────────────────────────
4.  Quick checklist / troubleshooting
────────────────────────
• No video after power-up?  Check that the display cable is plugged into the
  GPU’s ports, not the motherboard’s.  
• Card’s fans spin up then stop?  Normal; they are zero-RPM until the GPU
  reaches ~50 °C.  
• System shuts off under load?  PSU is overloaded—upgrade to 550-650 W.  
• Loud coil-whine?  Re-seat the 8-pin connector, enable a frame-rate cap in
  games to reduce spikes.

────────────────────────
Bottom line
────────────────────────
A high-quality 450 W Thelio supply will usually run an RTX-3060, but it leaves
very little reserve.  If you do anything GPU-intensive or plan future upgrades,
install a 550 W–650 W PSU first.  Physically mounting the card is a simple
five-minute job: open case, remove slot covers, insert card, add one 8-pin PCIe
power lead, close case, boot and install the proprietary NVIDIA driver.

instruction: write the gdscript code for a voxxel terrain engiune like minecraft in godot engine
output:
Below is a minimal but fully-working voxel terrain “engine” written in GDScript for Godot 4.x.  
It shows all of the core ideas you need for something Minecraft-like:

• Chunked storage (16×128×16)  
• Simple noise-based terrain generation  
• Face-culling mesh builder (very naïve but easy to understand)  
• Dynamic load / unload of chunks around the player  

Copy the scripts into the indicated files, add them to a new 3-D scene, press Play and you will have an infinite, blocky world that streams in and out while you walk around.

──────────────────────── 1.  constants.gd ────────────────────────
```gdscript
# constants.gd
# All global numeric constants live here so every script can `load()` it
const CHUNK_SIZE     : int = 16     # X and Z
const CHUNK_HEIGHT   : int = 128    # Y
const VIEW_DISTANCE  : int = 4      # chunks around the player

# Simple block id’s
const AIR   : int = 0
const GRASS : int = 1
const DIRT  : int = 2
const STONE : int = 3
```

──────────────────────── 2.  voxel_chunk.gd ───────────────────────
```gdscript
# voxel_chunk.gd
extends Node3D
class_name VoxelChunk

const C = preload("res://constants.gd")

# ───────────── helpers ─────────────
static func _i(x:int, y:int, z:int) -> int:   # 3-D → 1-D
    return x + z * C.CHUNK_SIZE + y * C.CHUNK_SIZE * C.CHUNK_SIZE

# Six face definitions (offset, normal, vertex quad, uv quad)
const FACE_OFFSETS  : Array = [Vector3i( 0, 0,-1), Vector3i( 0, 0, 1),
                               Vector3i(-1, 0, 0), Vector3i( 1, 0, 0),
                               Vector3i( 0, 1, 0), Vector3i( 0,-1, 0)]

const FACE_NORMALS  : Array = [Vector3.BACK,  Vector3.FORWARD,
                               Vector3.LEFT,  Vector3.RIGHT,
                               Vector3.UP,    Vector3.DOWN]

const QUAD          : PackedInt32Array = [0,1,2, 0,2,3]  # indices for one quad

const VERTS : Array = [   # 4 verts per face, in the same order as normals
    [Vector3(0,0,0), Vector3(1,0,0), Vector3(1,1,0), Vector3(0,1,0)], # back
    [Vector3(1,0,1), Vector3(0,0,1), Vector3(0,1,1), Vector3(1,1,1)], # front
    [Vector3(0,0,1), Vector3(0,0,0), Vector3(0,1,0), Vector3(0,1,1)], # left
    [Vector3(1,0,0), Vector3(1,0,1), Vector3(1,1,1), Vector3(1,1,0)], # right
    [Vector3(0,1,0), Vector3(1,1,0), Vector3(1,1,1), Vector3(0,1,1)], # top
    [Vector3(0,0,1), Vector3(1,0,1), Vector3(1,0,0), Vector3(0,0,0)]  # bottom
]

const UVS  : Array = [     # simple full-tile UV’s for every face
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)],
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)],
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)],
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)],
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)],
    [Vector2(0,0), Vector2(1,0), Vector2(1,1), Vector2(0,1)] ]

# ───────────── data ─────────────
var chunk_pos : Vector3i                  # chunk coords in world
var _blocks   : PackedInt32Array          # flattened block ids
var _mesh_i   : MeshInstance3D

# ───────────── life-cycle ─────────────
func _ready() -> void:
    _mesh_i = MeshInstance3D.new()
    add_child(_mesh_i)

func generate(noise: OpenSimplexNoise) -> void:
    # allocate block array
    _blocks.resize(C.CHUNK_SIZE * C.CHUNK_HEIGHT * C.CHUNK_SIZE)
    for x in C.CHUNK_SIZE:
        for z in C.CHUNK_SIZE:
            var world_x = x + chunk_pos.x * C.CHUNK_SIZE
            var world_z = z + chunk_pos.z * C.CHUNK_SIZE
            var h : int = int(noise.get_noise_2d(world_x, world_z) * 20.0 + C.CHUNK_HEIGHT/2)
            h = clamp(h, 0, C.CHUNK_HEIGHT-1)
            for y in C.CHUNK_HEIGHT:
                var id := C.AIR
                if y < h - 4:
                    id = C.STONE
                elif y < h - 1:
                    id = C.DIRT
                elif y == h - 1:
                    id = C.GRASS
                _blocks[_i(x,y,z)] = id
    _build_mesh()

# ───────────── mesh builder ─────────────
func _build_mesh() -> void:
    var verts    = PackedVector3Array()
    var norms    = PackedVector3Array()
    var uvs      = PackedVector2Array()
    var indices  = PackedInt32Array()
    var cursor   : int = 0

    for x in C.CHUNK_SIZE:
        for y in C.CHUNK_HEIGHT:
            for z in C.CHUNK_SIZE:
                var self_id := _blocks[_i(x,y,z)]
                if self_id == C.AIR:
                    continue
                for f in 6:
                    var o   : Vector3i = FACE_OFFSETS[f]
                    var nx  = x + o.x
                    var ny  = y + o.y
                    var nz  = z + o.z
                    var neighbor : int = C.AIR
                    if nx >= 0 and nx < C.CHUNK_SIZE and ny >= 0 and ny < C.CHUNK_HEIGHT and nz >= 0 and nz < C.CHUNK_SIZE:
                        neighbor = _blocks[_i(nx,ny,nz)]
                    if neighbor == C.AIR:         # exposed face ⇒ add quad
                        var quad = VERTS[f]
                        for v in 4:
                            verts.push_back(Vector3(x,y,z) + quad[v])
                            norms.push_back(FACE_NORMALS[f])
                            uvs.push_back(UVS[f][v])
                        for idx in QUAD:
                            indices.push_back(cursor + idx)
                        cursor += 4

    var arr : Array = []
    arr.resize(Mesh.ARRAY_MAX)
    arr[Mesh.ARRAY_VERTEX] = verts
    arr[Mesh.ARRAY_NORMAL] = norms
    arr[Mesh.ARRAY_TEX_UV] = uvs
    arr[Mesh.ARRAY_INDEX]  = indices

    var mesh := ArrayMesh.new()
    mesh.add_surface_from_arrays(Mesh.PRIMITIVE_TRIANGLES, arr)
    _mesh_i.mesh = mesh                # display it
```

──────────────────────── 3.  voxel_world.gd ───────────────────────
```gdscript
# voxel_world.gd
extends Node3D
class_name VoxelWorld

const C = preload("res://constants.gd")
const VoxelChunk = preload("res://voxel_chunk.gd")

@export var player_path : NodePath                # drag your player here
var _player            : Node3D

var _noise : OpenSimplexNoise
var _chunks : Dictionary = {}                     # Vector3i → VoxelChunk

func _ready() -> void:
    _player = get_node(player_path)
    _init_noise()

func _init_noise():
    _noise = OpenSimplexNoise.new()
    _noise.seed = randi()
    _noise.octaves = 4
    _noise.period = 64.0
    _noise.persistence = 0.55

# Main loop: stream chunks in/out
func _process(_dt: float) -> void:
    var pc : Vector3i = _world_to_chunk(_player.global_position)

    # ensure all chunks inside view distance exist
    for cx in range(pc.x - C.VIEW_DISTANCE, pc.x + C.VIEW_DISTANCE + 1):
        for cz in range(pc.z - C.VIEW_DISTANCE, pc.z + C.VIEW_DISTANCE + 1):
            var pos := Vector3i(cx, 0, cz)
            if not _chunks.has(pos):
                _load_chunk(pos)

    # free far-away chunks
    for key in _chunks.keys():
        if key.distance_to(pc) > C.VIEW_DISTANCE:
            _unload_chunk(key)

# ───────────── helpers ─────────────
func _world_to_chunk(wpos: Vector3) -> Vector3i:
    return Vector3i(floor(wpos.x / C.CHUNK_SIZE),
                    0,
                    floor(wpos.z / C.CHUNK_SIZE))

func _load_chunk(pos: Vector3i):
    var c := VoxelChunk.new()
    c.chunk_pos = pos
    c.position  = Vector3(pos.x * C.CHUNK_SIZE, 0, pos.z * C.CHUNK_SIZE)
    add_child(c)
    c.generate(_noise)
    _chunks[pos] = c

func _unload_chunk(pos: Vector3i):
    _chunks[pos].queue_free()
    _chunks.erase(pos)
```

──────────────────────── 4.  setting up the scene ─────────────────
1. Create a new empty 3-D scene.  
2. Add a Node3D and attach `voxel_world.gd` to it.  
3. Drop your player (or a simple `CharacterBody3D`) in the scene and assign its
   node-path to the `player_path` export on the VoxelWorld node.  
4. Give the player a basic movement script & camera.  
5. Press Play.

You will be able to walk forever and the script will continuously:

• work out what chunk you are standing in,  
• create new `VoxelChunk` nodes where none exist,  
• generate height-map terrain in them,  
• build a mesh that only contains exposed faces,  
• free chunks that move beyond the view distance.

──────────────────────── 5.  where to go next ────────────────────
• Replace the naïve face-culling mesh with “Greedy Meshing” or “Marching Cubes”.  
• Keep chunk data on a `PoolByteArray` or file for saving/loading.  
• Use `MultiMesh` or `RenderingDevice` with compute shaders for large worlds.  
• Add block interaction, lighting, biomes, fluids, … have fun!

This is intentionally minimal so you can read every line and extend it as you like.

instruction: what are some good popular engines to develop web build games? list pros and cons of each, bonus points if it is unlikely to be outdated soon
output:
Below is a short-list of engines and frameworks that are commonly chosen specifically for shipping games that run in the browser (HTML5 / WebGL).  
For each entry you’ll find:

• Core idea / “sweet spot”  
• Pros (✓)  
• Cons (✗)  
• Outlook – why it is, or isn’t, likely to stay relevant in the near future  

──────────────────────────────────

1. Unity (C#; WebGL export)

✓ Huge ecosystem, asset store, tutorials, 3-D & 2-D equally strong  
✓ One code base → desktop, mobile, consoles, AND WebGL (no plug-ins)  
✓ Mature visual editor, robust physics, animation, networking, DOTS, etc.  
✓ Browser build is just “another target” once the game works elsewhere

✗ WebGL export is heavier than pure-web engines (load time, memory)  
✗ No multithreading in the browser; you’ll sometimes need platform-specific hacks  
✗ Licensing / pricing changes have caused community anxiety

Outlook: Unity the company is betting on WebGL for casual and “Instant” games. Continuous support is on the public roadmap; unlikely to vanish, but watch licensing.

──────────────────────────────────

2. Godot Engine (GDScript / C# / C++; Web export)

✓ 100 % open-source (MIT) → no fees, modify at will  
✓ Lightweight Web builds (WebAssembly) compared with Unity/Unreal  
✓ Fluid 2-D workflow (tile maps, animation tools), solid 3-D since v4.0  
✓ Tiny editor download, runs on low-end hardware

✗ Smaller marketplace, fewer ready-made assets  
✗ Some advanced 3-D features still maturing compared with AAA engines  
✗ Need to compile the engine yourself for bleeding-edge browser fixes

Outlook: Donor funding + huge contributor base + fast release cadence; probability of being abandoned is very low.

──────────────────────────────────

3. Phaser (JavaScript / TypeScript framework)

✓ Native to the browser; nothing to “export”—it’s already JS/HTML5  
✓ Great for 2-D arcade, puzzle, hyper-casual, educational titles  
✓ Extremely easy to integrate into existing web sites or SPA stacks  
✓ Large plugin ecosystem, active Discord

✗ Not aimed at 3-D (WebGL is used, but the API is 2-D focused)  
✗ You supply your own build pipeline / editor (Tiled, TexturePacker, etc.)  
✗ Scaling to console/desktop requires wrappers like Electron or Cordova

Outlook: Maintainer Richard Davey keeps the project alive through Patreon & paid plugins; Phaser 4 is in alpha, signalling ongoing future.

──────────────────────────────────

4. PlayCanvas

✓ Browser-based editor — collaborate live through a URL  
✓ Exports are literally the engine; no build step, smallest 3-D payload among full editors  
✓ Written in TypeScript, easy to extend, open-sourced under MIT  
✓ Good for WebXR (VR/AR)

✗ 2-D tools less mature; focused on 3-D visualisation and advergames  
✗ SaaS business model: free tier has project-visibility limits, private projects cost  
✗ Offline workflow weaker than desktop IDEs

Outlook: Backed by Snap Inc., used by major brands (LEGO, BMW). Actively developed, low risk of near-term obsolescence.

──────────────────────────────────

5. Babylon.js

✓ Full 3-D engine in pure TypeScript; high-level scene graph, PBR, physics, GUI  
✓ First-party support by Microsoft (used in Office/Teams, Minecraft Classic)  
✓ Fantastic documentation, playground to test snippets instantly  
✓ Works nicely with modern tooling (esbuild, Vite, React, Web Components)

✗ No built-in visual editor (there is a community Editor but not Unity-class)  
✗ 2-D game ergonomics are limited; better suited to 3-D or data-visualisation  
✗ Steeper learning curve if you come from non-JS background

Outlook: With Microsoft funding and W3C participation (WebGPU), Babylon is expected to evolve alongside emerging browser tech.

──────────────────────────────────

6. Cocos Creator 3.x

✓ Successor to Cocos2d-x, rewritten in TypeScript/JavaScript + native exports  
✓ Visual editor focused on 2-D but now sports full 3-D (PhysX)  
✓ Very small Web build size; favoured in Asian “Instant Game” market (WeChat, Facebook Instant)  
✓ Royalty-free, permissive licence

✗ Documentation/community skew toward Chinese language resources  
✗ Plugin marketplace smaller in the West  
✗ Some advanced features (HDR, terrain) still beta

Outlook: Cocos is profitable (used by Tencent, ByteDance, etc.) and has 10+ years of legacy; likely to stick around, though Western adoption may stay niche.

──────────────────────────────────

7. Three.js (rendering library, not a “game engine” per se)

✓ De-facto standard low-level WebGL / WebGPU abstraction; tiny footprint  
✓ Massive examples collection; easy to mix with other JS libs (React Three Fiber)  
✓ Total control—build your own engine or ECS on top

✗ You must supply everything else (physics, input, audio, asset pipeline) or pick plugins  
✗ No editor unless you adopt community tools (e.g., three-js editor, glTF pipeline)  
✗ Requires deeper graphics knowledge for a typical game

Outlook: Maintained since 2010, used by Google, NASA, Spotify canvases. As long as WebGL/WebGPU exist, Three.js will as well.

──────────────────────────────────

8. Defold

✓ Lightweight, Lua-based, 2-D (with some 3-D) engine from King (Candy Crush)  
✓ One-click HTML5 export yields extremely small bundles ~1 MB gzip  
✓ Hot-reload workflow; built-in particle, GUI, tile-map editors  
✓ Entire engine source under very permissive license (Apache 2.0)

✗ Smaller mind-share, fewer third-party tutorials/marketplace items  
✗ Editor UX is polarising; not as customizable as Unity/Godot  
✗ 3-D features basic—mostly suited to 2-D or isometric

Outlook: Non-profit Foundation oversees development; 4–5 releases per year; seems stable but lacks the corporate heft of Unity/Unreal.

──────────────────────────────────

Engines often queried but not recommended for NEW browser projects in 2024:

• Unreal Engine – Epic dropped official HTML5 templates; community forks exist but lag behind.  
• Adobe Animate / Flash derivatives – legacy technology; officially EOL.

Tip for longevity: pick a project whose core language (C#, JS/TS, Lua, GDScript) you already enjoy using—skills gained there remain useful even if you migrate later.

🚀 Inbox Alchemy: Letting Generative AI Draft the Copy *and* Paint the Picture  

Ever stared at a blinking cursor, hunting for the perfect subject line while your design team races against the next product launch? instruction: What's the best way to implement Targeted Fast Gradient Sign Method in python?
output:
Below is a concise “recipe” and reference implementation of the Targeted Fast-Gradient-Sign Method (T-FGSM).  The code is shown first for PyTorch (most requested), followed by the minimal TensorFlow 2 / Keras equivalent.  Everything is self-contained; simply replace model, x, and y_target with your objects.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Algorithm recap
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Untargeted FGSM wants to “hurt” the model, so it pushes the
input in the direction that maximises the loss:

    x_adv = x + ε · sign( ∇ₓ L(model(x),  y_true) )             (1)

Targeted FGSM wants to *fool the model into one specific class*
y_target, so we *minimise* the loss w.r.t. that class.  
That just means we move in the opposite direction:

    x_adv = x  –  ε · sign( ∇ₓ L(model(x),  y_target) )         (2)

After the step we must
• project/clip the perturbation into the box ‖x_adv − x‖_∞ ≤ ε  
• clip the pixel space into the valid data range, e.g. [0,1].

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  PyTorch implementation
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def targeted_fgsm(model, x, y_target, eps, data_min=0.0, data_max=1.0):
    """
    Single-step targeted FGSM.
        model      – torch.nn.Module in eval() mode
        x          – input tensor, shape (N,C,H,W). Requires no grad.
        y_target   – target class tensor, shape (N,)
        eps        – ℓ∞ budget (float or tensor broadcastable to x)
        returns adversarial example (no gradients attached)
    """
    model.eval()
    x_adv = x.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)

    # 1) forward
    logits = model(x_adv)
    loss   = F.cross_entropy(logits, y_target)

    # 2) backward
    grad, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x_adv)

    # 3) take a *negative* sign step because we minimise loss
    x_adv = x_adv - eps * grad.sign()

    # 4) projection / clipping
    x_adv = torch.clamp(x_adv, data_min, data_max).detach()

    return x_adv


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Optional: iterative (I-FGSM / PGD-targeted) variant
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def targeted_ifgsm(model, x, y_target,
                   eps=8/255, alpha=2/255, iters=10,
                   data_min=0.0, data_max=1.0):
    """
    Iterative targeted FGSM: projected gradient descent with negative step.
    """
    model.eval()
    x_orig = x.clone().detach()
    x_adv  = x.clone().detach()

    for _ in range(iters):
        x_adv.requires_grad = True
        logits = model(x_adv)
        loss   = F.cross_entropy(logits, y_target)
        grad,  = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x_adv)

        # targeted step (note the minus sign)
        x_adv = x_adv - alpha * grad.sign()

        # project onto ε-ball around the original input
        eta   = torch.clamp(x_adv - x_orig, min=-eps, max=eps)
        x_adv = torch.clamp(x_orig + eta, data_min, data_max).detach()

    return x_adv


# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# x           : (N,C,H,W) float32 in [0,1]
# y_target    : (N,) long  (e.g. all 3's to make the model say “cat”)
# model       : pretrained network

eps = 8/255
x_adv = targeted_fgsm(model, x, y_target, eps)


──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  TensorFlow 2 / Keras equivalent
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import tensorflow as tf

def targeted_fgsm_tf(model, x, y_target, eps, data_min=0.0, data_max=1.0):
    """
    x         – tf.Tensor  (N,H,W,C)  or (N,C,H,W) depending on model
    y_target  – int32 tensor  (N,)
    """
    x_adv = tf.identity(x)

    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        tape.watch(x_adv)
        logits = model(x_adv, training=False)
        loss   = tf.keras.losses.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(
                   y_target, logits, from_logits=True)

    grad = tape.gradient(loss, x_adv)
    signed_grad = tf.sign(grad)

    # targeted step: subtract
    x_adv = x_adv - eps * signed_grad

    x_adv = tf.clip_by_value(x_adv, data_min, data_max)
    return x_adv


──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Tips, gotchas, and best practices
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Keep the model in eval()/training=False mode to freeze BN/Dropout.  
• Always detach() between iterations to avoid autograd graph blow-up.  
• Pick an ε that makes sense for your data scaling (8/255 ≈ 0.031 is
  conventional for 8-bit images in [0,1] scale).  
• For iterative attacks, α≈ε/iterations is a good start; smaller α
  yields finer, slower optimisation.  
• Gradient masking: make sure your model really has gradients
  (no hard argmax, no discrete preprocessing, etc.).  
• If you need white/black box transfer, keep the perturbation within
  legal bounds so images still look natural.

That’s all you need to generate targeted adversarial examples with
FGSM in Python!

instruction: Explain in detail the concept of deep double descent in the context of training machine learning models. Describe how it is related to gradient descent and early stopping.
output:
1. Classical picture – one U-shaped curve  
   • Capacity axis.  In traditional statistical learning theory you plot test risk against a single knob that makes the hypothesis class richer: polynomial degree, number of hidden units, tree depth, etc.  
   • Bias-variance trade–off.  With very small capacity you under-fit (high bias, low variance), risk is high.  As capacity grows you lower the bias and the test risk falls – the left-hand “descent”.  
   • Over-fitting hump.  Past some point the model can start fitting the idiosyncrasies (noise) of the training set, the variance term explodes and the test risk rises again – the familiar right-hand “ascent” of the U.

2. What modern practice revealed  
   When people train today’s very large networks they keep increasing capacity far beyond the sample size, yet after a short deterioration the test error drops again and often reaches a value lower than the best point inside the classical regime.  If you draw the full curve you therefore see  

        risk
          ^
          | \        second descent (over-param.)
          |  \_
          |    \__        <- the “interpolation peak”
          |       \__
          |          \     first descent (classical)
          +---------------> capacity
                 ↑
            interpolation threshold
            (first time training error can be driven to 0)

   This phenomenon is called DOUBLE DESCENT (or “deep double descent” when it is observed in deep nets).

3. Why “interpolation threshold”?  
   The bump sits at the first point where the model can obtain nearly zero training error – it “interpolates” the data.  Slightly on the left it cannot fit everything, slightly on the right it can.  Around that knife edge the solution becomes extremely sensitive to the particular sample, so the variance and the test risk shoot up.  Farther to the right the model is so over-parameterised that there are many zero-training-loss solutions and optimisation algorithms such as (stochastic) gradient descent (SGD) tend to find the ones with special properties (small‐norm, large margin, flat minima) that generalise well, so test error goes down again – the second descent.

4. Three ways to see double descent  
   • Model-size double descent (vary width, depth, #parameters, rank of a feature map, …).  
   • Sample-size double descent (fix a very large model and vary number of training examples).  
   • Epoch-wise (or time-wise) double descent (fix model and data, plot risk vs. number of gradient-descent steps).  All three have the same shape; in deep learning the last one is especially easy to reproduce.

5. Connection to GRADIENT DESCENT  
   a) Optimisation vs. generalisation.  Gradient descent is used purely to minimise empirical loss, but *which* zero-loss point it converges to depends on its implicit bias:  
        – In linear models GD started from the origin converges to the minimum-ℓ₂-norm interpolator.  
        – In deep nets GD tends to find flatter or larger-margin minima.  
      These minima behave like they are regularised even though no explicit penalty was used (“implicit regularisation”).  
   b) Therefore, in the heavily over-parameterised regime, running GD all the way to (near) zero training error does **not** necessarily hurt generalisation – in fact it lands you on the second descent part of the curve where test risk is already low again.  
   c) Epoch-wise double descent shows the same effect along the optimisation trajectory:  
        1. early GD steps reduce both train and test error;  
        2. a middle phase (“over-fitting swell”) where test error temporarily rises even though train error keeps falling;  
        3. further GD steps lower test error again as the iterates approach the implicit-bias solution.

6. Relation to EARLY STOPPING  
   • Early stopping is a *form of explicit regularisation*: stop GD in the first descent phase to avoid the traditional over-fitting hump.  
   • Double descent shows that stopping in that hump may be premature; if you can afford to wait until the optimiser passes the interpolation peak, test error can drop again without any extra hyper-parameter.  
   • Which strategy is better depends on the regime:  
        – Under-parameterised or barely-parameterised models: the hump is big, second descent may not exist → early stopping is valuable.  
        – Heavily over-parameterised models: hump is narrow or shallow, second descent reaches lower risk → letting GD run to convergence (or even beyond, with weight decay) can beat early stopping.  
   • Practitioners often combine both: use a very large model (so the second descent exists) *and* monitor validation loss; in practice the validation curve frequently flattens out in the second descent region, so early stopping ends up triggering there anyway.

7. Intuitive mechanisms behind the second descent  
   • Many-solutions effect: having far more parameters than equations (n≪p) creates a large solution manifold; optimisation algorithms have room to pick “simple” members.  
   • Signal-noise separation: over-parameterised models can allocate subspaces to fit noise while another subspace captures signal with large margin; the solution GD selects often keeps the noise-fitting weights small.  
   • Implicit norm control: continuous-time GD on quadratic loss behaves like Tikhonov regularisation with a time-dependent ridge λ(t)=1/t (so “regularisation” automatically decays during training).

8. Practical take-aways  
   • Very large models are not automatically dangerous; generalisation error follows the double-descent curve, so performance can improve again after the interpolation threshold.  
   • The shape of the curve depends on optimisation details: learning rate, batch size, weight decay, data augmentation, etc., because these affect GD’s implicit bias.  
   • When you enlarge a network and see validation loss initially rise, do not assume you have to shrink the model; it might just be the interpolation bump.  
   • Conversely, early stopping remains a simple, effective safeguard when compute or data are limited and you cannot be sure that your training dynamics will carry you safely into the second descent.

In short  
Deep double descent extends the classic bias-variance story: test error vs. capacity or training time is not one U but a W-shaped curve. Gradient descent, through its implicit bias, is the mechanism that selects the low-risk solutions on the far right of that curve; early stopping is a manual intervention that truncates the optimisation path to avoid the hump but may miss the even better solutions that lie beyond it.

Below is a cleaned-up, working version of your script together with an explanation of the problems that were preventing the original code from running.

────────────────────────────────  FIXED CODE  ────────────────────────────────
```python
import torch, gradio as gr
from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoTokenizer

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load the model *once* (the RobertaModel you built first is unused
#    for generation, so we remove that part).
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
MODEL_NAME = "zonghaoyang/DistilRoBERTa-base"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)
model     = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Light-weight code analyser
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def analyse_code(code: str):
    vars_, funcs, misc = [], [], []

    for ln in code.splitlines():
        ln = ln.strip()
        if not ln:
            continue
        if ln.startswith("def "):
            funcs.append(ln.split("(")[0].replace("def", "").strip())
        elif "=" in ln:
            vars_.append(ln.split("=")[0].strip())
        else:
            misc.append(ln)

    return {"variables": vars_, "functions": funcs, "logic": misc}

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Prompt builder
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def build_prompt(code: str) -> str:
    info = analyse_code(code)
    prompt = (
        "You are an expert Python assistant. "
        "Rewrite the snippet below with clearer naming, comments and "
        "any obvious improvements while preserving behaviour.\n\n"
        f"Variables:  {', '.join(info['variables']) or 'None'}\n"
        f"Functions:  {', '.join(info['functions']) or 'None'}\n"
        f"Logic:      {' '.join(info['logic']) or 'None'}\n\n"
        "Improved code:"
    )
    return prompt

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Text-to-text generation (tokenise ➔ generate ➔ decode)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def generate_code(user_code: str) -> str:
    prompt      = build_prompt(user_code)
    input_ids   = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
    with torch.no_grad():
        gen_ids = model.generate(
            input_ids,
            max_length=256,
            num_beams=4,
            early_stopping=True,
        )
    return tokenizer.decode(gen_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Static suggestions (toy example)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def suggest_improvements(_: str) -> str:
    suggestions = [
        "Use descriptive variable names.",
        "Add docstrings and type hints.",
        "Isolate side-effects under 'if __name__ == \"__main__\"'.",
        "Write unit tests for public functions.",
    ]
    return "\n".join(f"• {s}" for s in suggestions)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. One combined Gradio pipeline
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def pipeline(code: str) -> str:
    improved = generate_code(code)
    tips     = suggest_improvements(code)
    return f"{improved}\n\nSuggested improvements:\n{tips}"

demo = gr.Interface(
    fn=pipeline,
    inputs=gr.Textbox(lines=15, label="Paste your Python code here"),
    outputs="text",
    title="Python Refactoring Assistant",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch()
```

────────────────────────────────  WHAT WAS WRONG?  ────────────────────────────
1. Two different models were loaded under the same variable name `model`.  
   The first (`RobertaModel`) is useless for generation and was silently
   overwritten by `AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM`.

2. `model.generate()` expects *token IDs*, not a raw string.  
   You must  (a) tokenise the prompt, (b) generate IDs, (c) decode them.

3. The function wired into Gradio (`fn=generate_code`) returned a tensor,
   so the GUI would crash. It now returns a `str`.

4. The infinite `while True:` loop at the bottom would block everything; it
   has been removed in favour of the Gradio interface.

5. Some minor clean-ups: unused imports removed, clearer naming, and
   richer prompt wording so the LLM knows what to do.

an LLM-generated rewrite plus a few hard-coded best-practice tips.

instruction: Visualize pandas dataframe in gradio
output:
Below is a concise “cook-book” for getting a Pandas DataFrame on screen with Gradio.  
Everything works with Gradio ≥ 3.29.0.  (If you are on an older version, upgrade: `pip install -U gradio`.)

────────────────────────
1. The quick 5-line demo
────────────────────────
```python
import pandas as pd, gradio as gr

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Paris", "Berlin", "Tokyo"],
                   "population": [2.1, 3.6, 14.0]})

demo = gr.Interface(fn=lambda : df,     # returns the dataframe
                    inputs=None,        # no inputs → only a viewer
                    outputs=gr.Dataframe())
demo.launch()
```
• `gr.Dataframe()` automatically infers column types from the `pd.DataFrame`.  
• End-users are allowed to sort, copy or download the data (but not edit it because we didn’t set `interactive=True`).

────────────────────────
2. Making the table editable
────────────────────────
```python
def update_df(current_df):
    current_df["population"] = current_df["population"] * 1.1
    return current_df

with gr.Blocks() as app:
    df_state = gr.State(df)          # store current dataframe

    grid = gr.Dataframe(value=df, interactive=True, height=300)
    btn  = gr.Button("Increase population 10 %")

    btn.click(update_df, df_state, grid)   # returns the new df → refreshes grid
    grid.change(lambda x: x, grid, df_state)  # keep state in sync

app.launch()
```

────────────────────────
3. Customizing column dtypes, headers, sizes
────────────────────────
```python
gr.Dataframe(
    value=df,
    datatype=["str", "number"],      # force column dtypes
    col_count=(2, "fixed"),          # exactly 2 columns
    label="World Cities",            # title shown above
    interactive=True,
    wrap=True,                       # wrap long text
    max_rows=20,                     # cap visible rows
    width=500, height=350
)
```

────────────────────────
4. Converting other objects to a DataFrame
────────────────────────
`gr.Dataframe` accepts:
• `pd.DataFrame`, `pd.Series`  
• Python list-of-lists, list-of-dicts  
• A csv/tsv string  

So, if your function already returns a list of dicts you can still display it with:
```python
gr.Interface(fn=get_list_of_dicts,
             inputs=gr.Textbox(label="Query"),
             outputs=gr.Dataframe(headers=True))
```

────────────────────────
5. Read-only table vs. download link
────────────────────────
If you only need a static table and a download button:
```python
with gr.Blocks() as ui:
    gr.Markdown("## My Data")
    gr.Dataframe(value=df, interactive=False)
    gr.File(value="data.csv", label="Download as CSV")
ui.launch()
```
(Write `df.to_csv("data.csv", index=False)` beforehand.)

────────────────────────
6. Styling with CSS
────────────────────────
Gradio wraps the table in a vanilla `<table>`; you can target it:
```python
with gr.Blocks(css="""
  .gr-dataframe thead {background:#222;color:white}
  .gr-dataframe tbody tr:hover {background:#fcefa1}
""") as styled:
    gr.Dataframe(value=df)
styled.launch()
```

────────────────────────
7. Alternative: Push HTML yourself
────────────────────────
When you need total control (merging cells, tooltips, etc.), generate HTML with Pandas and show it in `gr.HTML`:
```python
html = df.to_html(classes="my_table", index=False)
gr.Interface(lambda : html, inputs=None, outputs=gr.HTML()).launch()
```

────────────────────────
8. Common pitfalls
────────────────────────
• “Nothing shows up” → Make sure your function actually returns the DataFrame object, not `None`.  
• Editable table does not refresh → Remember to return the DataFrame from the event handler AND update any `gr.State`.  
• Missing scroll bar → Set `height` on the component; by default Gradio auto-sizes.  
• Datatype inference wrong (e.g., 000012 seen as number) → Pass an explicit `datatype` list.

────────────────────────
9. Full example: CSV uploader → live preview
────────────────────────
```python
import pandas as pd, gradio as gr

def read_csv(file):
    if file is None: return None
    return pd.read_csv(file.name)

with gr.Blocks() as csv_viewer:
    inp = gr.File(label="Upload CSV")
    out = gr.Dataframe(headers=True, interactive=True)
    inp.change(read_csv, inp, out)

csv_viewer.launch()
```

────────────────────────

That’s all you need to visualize—and even edit—Pandas DataFrames inside a Gradio web app. Happy gridding!

instruction: Make a SWOT analysis for the company Artistree for Europe
output:
SWOT ANALYSIS – ARTISTREE IN THE EUROPEAN MARKET  
(Assumes Artistree is the U.S.–based, mass-custom framing and wall-décor manufacturer that services Michaels and other retailers. If your Artistree has a different core business, adjust the specifics but keep the structure.)

STRENGTHS  
• Proven mass-customisation model – can manufacture thousands of “one-off” frames per day with tight lead-times.  
• Vertically integrated supply chain (design software, mat cutting, moulding, glazing, pack-out) keeps unit costs low and quality control high.  
• Deep product library and SKU breadth (moulding profiles, mat colours, glazing options, ready-made décor).  
• Automation know-how (CNC saws, computerised mat cutters, just-in-time kitting) lowers labour intensity compared with many European craft framers.  
• Solid U.S. retailer relationships provide volume scale and reference customers when courting EU chains (e.g., Kingfisher, OBI, Hobbycraft, Amazon EU).  
• Sustainability credentials already in place (FSC/PEFC wood, water-based finishes, recyclable packaging) align with EU Green Deal requirements.  
• Robust e-commerce integration APIs and design-to-manufacture workflow can “plug-and-play” with European marketplaces.  

WEAKNESSES  
• Near-zero brand recognition among European consumers and trade buyers; no legacy retail distribution.  
• Heavy, fragile finished goods drive high freight and damage costs; shipping across the Atlantic is impractical—will need regional manufacturing or assembly.  
• Core competency tied historically to one anchor customer (Michaels). Concentration risk shows if a similar European anchor is not secured quickly.  
• Limited understanding of fragmented European taste profiles (Nordic minimalism vs. Mediterranean ornate, metric sizing vs. imperial formats).  
• Must navigate multiple languages, currencies, labelling rules (CE, EPR, CLP), VAT registrations and cross-border reverse logistics.  
• Establishing or acquiring EU production means large cap-ex at a time of rising energy prices and interest rates.  
• U.S.-centric ERP, HR and compliance systems may not yet be GDPR-ready or geared for EU social-partner labour practices.  

OPPORTUNITIES  
• Pandemic-accelerated home-improvement and remote-working trends have lifted wall-décor spend; the EU soft-furnishings market >€25 bn and still growing.  
• E-commerce penetration in home décor is ~24 % in Western Europe (vs. ~14 % pre-Covid). A digitally native, on-demand framing proposition fits that shift.  
• Few pan-European custom-frame providers; market dominated by local shops and catalogue mouldings. A scalable, fast-turn operation would be disruptive.  
• Corporate / hospitality fit-outs (hotels, offices, student housing) increasingly outsource art packages—B2B channel can smooth retail seasonality.  
• EU’s circular-economy push rewards low-waste, modular frames; potential R&D on recyclable glazing, bio-based resins, and take-back programmes.  
• Access to EU and national grants for regional job creation, wood-product innovation and clean manufacturing (e.g., Horizon Europe, ERDF funds).  
• Potential for strategic alliances:  
  – White-label fulfilment for European online print platforms (e.g., Photobox, Desenio, Juniqe).  
  – Shop-in-shop custom-framing counters for DIY chains (Leroy Merlin, Hornbach).  
  – Licensing European art schools, museums, and NFT marketplaces wanting upscale physical prints.  

THREATS  
• Established frame brands (Nielsen, Larson-Juhl, Hofmann) already have plants in Germany, Poland, Spain and fast delivery within Schengen.  
• Low-price, flat-pack competition from IKEA, JYSK and discount stores keeps margins thin in the ready-made segment.  
• EU Timber Regulation, extended-producer-responsibility fees, packaging taxes and upcoming Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) add cost/complexity.  
• Economic headwinds (inflation, energy shock, potential recession) could suppress discretionary décor spending.  
• Raw-material volatility: wood, glass, backing board, paper mats—plus ongoing shipping-container imbalances.  
• Labour shortages in Central Europe’s woodworking clusters; wages rising fastest in Poland, Czechia, Hungary.  
• Brexit complicates UK–EU logistics; dual inventory or mirrored production may be needed.  
• Digital displacement: growth of large-format digital displays and NFTs may reduce demand for traditional framing among early adopters.  
• Currency risk (USD cost base vs. EUR/GBP sales) can erode margins if not hedged.  

STRATEGIC IMPLICATIONS  
1. Enter with an asset-light model first: contract manufacture or acquire a mid-size regional framer to test demand and navigate regulations.  
2. Prioritise e-commerce integrations with pan-EU marketplaces and bolt-on B2B hospitality accounts to build volume rapidly.  
3. Localise product sizing (DIN, ISO A/B series) and style palettes; hire regional designers, run A/B testing by country.  
4. Leverage sustainability leadership—market “Made in Europe, FSC, low-carbon” as a point of difference versus Asian imports.  
5. Hedge energy and currency exposures; explore on-site solar or bio-mass heating to moderate power costs in manufacturing hubs.  

A well-sequenced market-entry plan that blends these insights should allow Artistree to transplant its mass-customisation DNA while respecting Europe’s fragmented tastes, regulations and competitive landscape.

instruction: Can you explain to me how to forecast revenue for an online business vs. a brick and mortar retailer?  What are the key differences?
output:
Revenue = Price × Volume is true for every company, but the way you arrive at “Volume” for an online store and for a physical shop is very different.  
Below is a structured way to build a forecast for each model and a side-by-side look at the key differences.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Break the revenue formula into driver variables
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Online (e-commerce)

   Site sessions  
 × Conversion rate (orders / sessions)  
 × Average order value (AOV)  
 = Gross merchandise value (GMV)  
 – Returns & cancellations  
 = Net revenue  

B. Brick-and-mortar

   Foot traffic (door counts)  
 × Shopper-to-buyer rate (tickets / visitors)  
 × Average transaction value (ATV)  
 = Gross sales  
 – Returns & refunds  
 = Net revenue  

Notice that the structure is the same: traffic → conversion → basket size → adjustments for returns.  
The difference is where “traffic” comes from and how elastic each step is.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Collect or estimate each driver
────────────────────────────────────────
ONLINE  
• Historic web analytics: Google Analytics, Adobe, Shopify, etc.  
• Marketing KPIs: impressions, clicks, CAC, ROAS by channel.  
• Promotion calendar: email blasts, paid social, SEO improvements.  
• Web-specific seasonality (e.g., Cyber Week spikes).  
• Fulfilment constraints (warehouse cut-offs, stockouts).

BRICK-AND-MORTAR  
• Door counters or POS data by daypart.  
• Local economic indicators: foot-fall indices, mall occupancy, weather.  
• Store events: sidewalk sales, in-store demos.  
• Physical capacity (sq. ft., fitting rooms, checkout lines).  
• New store openings/closings, relocations.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Choose a forecasting method
────────────────────────────────────────
TOP-DOWN  
   Start with total addressable market, apply expected share.  
   Online: Use e-commerce market growth % and share-of-voice.  
   Physical: Use trade-area population × expected capture rate.

BOTTOM-UP (more common)  
   Forecast each driver separately, then multiply.  
   • Sessions = ad spend × CTR / CPC + organic traffic trend.  
   • Foot traffic = historical trend × mall traffic index × weather factor.  
   • Conversion = rolling 3-mo avg ± merchandising/promotions effect.  
   • AOV/ATV = price increases, mix shifts, units per ticket.

STATISTICAL / ML  
   Time-series models (ARIMA, Prophet) work well for mature stores.  
   Causal/driver-based models (regression, gradient boost) handle marketing inputs and special events better.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Build the mechanics
────────────────────────────────────────
Example – Online month forecast  
1. Sessions  
   a. Organic: last year same month × (1 + SEO growth %)  
   b. Paid: ad budget / projected CPC  
2. Conversion rate  
   Baseline 2.1% + 0.3 pp for new checkout + –0.1 pp for mobile traffic mix.  
3. AOV  
   Prior 6-mo average × (1 + upsell initiative %).  
4. Returns  
   22% of GMV × expected improvement (e.g., fit chart reduces by 1 pp).  
5. Revenue = Σ (1×2×3) – returns.

Example – Physical store week forecast  
1. Foot traffic  
   Last-year week door count × mall index 1.05 × weather factor 0.97.  
2. Shopper-to-buyer rate  
   31% baseline; add 2 pp for friends-and-family event.  
3. ATV  
   $54 baseline; apply +$3 for new product launch mix.  
4. Returns  
   5% of gross sales.  
5. Net revenue calculation as above.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. Layer on growth initiatives and risks
────────────────────────────────────────
ONLINE – new channels (TikTok), site speed, cross-border shipping, server downtime risk.  
PHYSICAL – remodel closures, nearby competitor openings, landlord rent escalations, pandemic restrictions.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Reconcile to the P&L and inventory plan
────────────────────────────────────────
Revenue must align with inventory buys, fulfilment capacity, staffing, and cash-flow. For a store, on-hand units and shelf space limit the upside. For e-commerce, warehouse throughput and last-mile cost can constrain shipments.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Key differences at a glance
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Traffic Source  
   • Online: marketing spend & algorithms; global reach.  
   • Physical: geography-bound footfall; influenced by local events/weather.

2. Data Frequency & Granularity  
   • Online: real-time, per-session; A/B testing quickly visible.  
   • Physical: daily/weekly POS; harder to attribute.

3. Conversion Levers  
   • Online: UX, site performance, payment options.  
   • Physical: staff training, merchandising, queue length.

4. Seasonality Shape  
   • Online often shows sharper spikes (Singles’ Day, Cyber Monday).  
   • Stores have extended peaks (December weekends, back-to-school).

5. Returns Rate  
   • Typically 15–40% online (apparel high).  
   • 3–10% in-store; easier in-person fit checks.

6. Capacity Constraints  
   • Online demand uncapped until fulfilment hits ceiling.  
   • Store limited by square footage and opening hours.

7. Marketing Attribution  
   • Digital channels measurable but multi-touch attribution issues.  
   • Physical relies on promotions, local advertising, harder ROI calc.

8. Cost Structure Impact  
   • Shipping & payment fees scale with e-commerce revenue.  
   • Rent & labor scale more with physical revenue.

────────────────────────────────────────
Take-away
Build driver-based models for both, but remember:
• “Sessions” vs “Foot traffic” is the big structural fork.  
• Online metrics change faster; update forecasts weekly or even daily during peaks.  
• Physical retail is stickier, so month/quarter cadence is usually enough.  
• Always sanity-check bottom-up results with a top-down view of market size and strategic initiatives.

Write me a testbench for a multiplier in cocotb
output:
Below is a self-contained, yet easy-to-adapt, cocotb testbench for a simple two-operand unsigned multiplier.  
If your RTL uses different port names, bit-widths, a start/ready handshake, pipelining, or a clocked interface, just tweak the marked lines.

File name (suggested):  `test_mul.py`

```python
# ============================================================================
#  cocotb Testbench : Unsigned Parallel Multiplier
#
#  Expected DUT ports (edit to match your design)
#    signal     dir   width   comment
#    ---------  ---  -------  -----------------------------------------------
#    clk         in      1    system clock, rising-edge active
#    rst_n       in      1    async active-low reset (0 = reset)
#    a           in     A_W   first factor
#    b           in     B_W   second factor
#    p           out   A_W+B_W product  (combinatorial or registered)
# ============================================================================

import random

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock     import Clock
from cocotb.triggers  import RisingEdge, Timer, FallingEdge
from cocotb.binary    import BinaryValue
from cocotb.result    import TestFailure


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
#  General utilities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
async def reset_dut(dut, cycles=2):
    """
    Apply an asynchronous active-low reset for `cycles` clock cycles.
    """
    dut.rst_n.value = 0
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk, cycles)
    dut.rst_n.value = 1
    # Wait one more cycle so that reset de-assertion is cleanly seen
    await ClockCycles(dut.clk, 1)


def get_int(signal):
    """
    Read a cocotb handle as a Python int (works for resolved/unresolved).
    """
    return int(signal.value)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
#  Main stimulus + checks
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
@cocotb.test()
async def multiplier_randomised_test(dut):
    """
    Drive random operands into the multiplier and compare against the
    golden reference (Python's '*').
    """
    # -----------  PARAMETERS (adapt at will) ------------------------------
    A_W       = len(dut.a)      # infer width from the HDL object
    B_W       = len(dut.b)
    N_TESTS   = 500             # number of random vectors
    CLOCK_PER = 10              # ns – period of the generated clock
    PIPELINE_STAGES = 0         # >0 if your multiplier is registered
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------

    # Clock generation (non-blocking)
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk, CLOCK_PER, units="ns").start())

    # Reset
    await reset_dut(dut)

    error_cnt = 0

    # Keep a small FIFO for pipelined designs so that we know
    # which expected product belongs to which cycle
    golden_fifo = []

    for idx in range(N_TESTS):

        # ---------------- Stimulus ----------------
        a_val = random.getrandbits(A_W)
        b_val = random.getrandbits(B_W)

        dut.a.value = a_val
        dut.b.value = b_val

        # Save reference result.  Items will come out later if pipelined.
        golden_fifo.append((a_val, b_val, (a_val * b_val)))

        # Wait for one clock so signals settle (or so the next pipeline stage captures)
        await RisingEdge(dut.clk)

        # ---------------- Checking ----------------
        # For purely combinatorial multipliers PIPELINE_STAGES == 0,
        # therefore the expected result is at the same cycle.
        if len(golden_fifo) > PIPELINE_STAGES:
            ref_a, ref_b, ref_p = golden_fifo.pop(0)

            dut_result = get_int(dut.p)

            if dut_result != ref_p:
                error_cnt += 1
                dut._log.error(
                    f"[{idx}] mismatch: {ref_a} * {ref_b} = {ref_p} "
                    f"(expected)  !=  {dut_result} (DUT)"
                )

    # Drain remaining pipeline latency
    for _ in range(PIPELINE_STAGES):
        await RisingEdge(dut.clk)
        ref_a, ref_b, ref_p = golden_fifo.pop(0)
        dut_result = get_int(dut.p)
        if dut_result != ref_p:
            error_cnt += 1
            dut._log.error(
                f"[pipeline] mismatch: {ref_a} * {ref_b} = {ref_p} "
                f"(expected)  !=  {dut_result} (DUT)"
            )

    # ---------------- Summary ----------------
    if error_cnt == 0:
        dut._log.info(f"All {N_TESTS} combinations matched ✓")
    else:
        raise TestFailure(f"Multiplier failed {error_cnt} / {N_TESTS} cases")



# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
#  Optional: generate constrained directed tests using TestFactory
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def directed_vecs():
    """
    Return a list of corner-case operand tuples.
    """
    return [
        (0, 0),
        (0, 1),
        (1, 0),
        (1, 1),
        (2**(len(dut.a)-1), 2**(len(dut.b)-1)),  # MSB only
        (2**len(dut.a)-1, 2**len(dut.b)-1),       # all ones
    ]

async def run_directed(dut, operands):
    """
    Stimulus that uses a fixed list of vectors.
    """
    cocotb.start_soon(Clock(dut.clk, 10, units="ns").start())
    await reset_dut(dut)

    for a_val, b_val in operands:
        dut.a.value = a_val
        dut.b.value = b_val
        await RisingEdge(dut.clk)
        prod = get_int(dut.p)
        assert prod == a_val * b_val, "Directed test mismatch"


# (Uncomment this block if you rather prefer the TestFactory driven approach)
# factory = TestFactory(run_directed)
# factory.add_option("operands", [directed_vecs()])
# factory.generate_tests()
```

How to use:
1. Put `test_mul.py` next to your RTL files (Verilog/VHDL/SystemVerilog).  
2. In `Makefile`/`pytest.ini`/whatever you use to launch cocotb, point to this test module, e.g.

```
MODULE    := test_mul
TOPLEVEL  := mul     # name of your RTL entity/module
SIM       := icarus  # or verilator, questa, xrun ...
```

3. Run `make` or `pytest -q`.

You now have:
• Clock & asynchronous active-low reset generation.  
• Randomised stimulus (500 vectors by default).  
• Cycle-accurate scoreboard with optional pipeline latency support.  
• A placeholder for corner-case directed tests.

Happy verification!

Low-Carb Breakfast Idea  
Spinach-Cheese Omelette with Avocado & Smoked Salmon  

Ingredients (1 serving)  
• 3 large eggs  
• 1 cup fresh spinach (about 30 g)  
• 1 oz (28 g) shredded cheddar (or any hard cheese)  
• ½ medium avocado  
• 2 oz (55 g) smoked salmon  
• 1 tsp olive oil or butter for the pan  
• Salt, pepper, herbs or a squeeze of lemon (optional)

Carbohydrate Breakdown (net carbs*)  
• Eggs, 3 large ……………… 1.2 g  
• Spinach, 1 cup …………… 0.4 g  
• Cheddar, 1 oz …………… 0.4 g  
• Avocado, ½ medium……… 2.0 g  
• Smoked salmon, 2 oz…… 0.0 g  
• Olive oil/butter …………… 0.0 g  

TOTAL NET CARBS ≈ 4 g

(*) Net carbs = total carbs minus fiber.

Preparation  
1. Heat the olive oil/butter in a non-stick pan over medium heat.  
2. Sauté spinach for 30–45 seconds until wilted.  
3. Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper, pour over the spinach, and cook until the edges set.  
4. Sprinkle cheese on top, fold the omelette, and cook to desired firmness.  
5. Plate with avocado slices and smoked salmon; add herbs or lemon if you like.

instruction: Provide me with a breakfast recipe that is quick to make and is high in protien (at least 30 grams) and has a variety of ingredients
output:
10-Minute “Power-Up” Breakfast Scramble  
≈ 42 g protein | 1 hearty serving

Why it’s great  
• Ready in about 10 minutes  
• One pan, minimal cleanup  
• Combines animal and plant proteins for a robust amino-acid profile  
• Lots of colors & textures (eggs, beans, greens, peppers, dairy, herbs)

Ingredients  
Protein sources (≈42 g total)  
• 2 large eggs – 12 g  
• ½ cup pasteurized liquid egg whites – 13 g  
• ½ cup low-fat cottage cheese – 14 g  
• 2 Tbsp shredded reduced-fat cheddar – 3 g

Flavor & nutrient boosters  
• ½ cup canned black beans, drained & rinsed  
• ½ cup diced bell pepper (any color)  
• 1 cup baby spinach (loose-packed)  
• 1 small green onion, sliced  
• 2 tsp olive oil (or avocado oil spray)  
• 2 Tbsp salsa or pico de gallo  
• ⅛ avocado, sliced or diced (optional but tasty)  
• Pinch each: salt, black pepper, ground cumin  
• Optional garnish: fresh cilantro, hot sauce, lime wedge

Equipment  
• 10-inch non-stick skillet  
• Rubber spatula

Step-by-step (≈10 min)  
1. Pre-heat pan: Place the skillet over medium-high heat, add olive oil.  
2. Veggie quick-sauté (2 min): Add bell pepper; season with a pinch of salt, pepper, and cumin. Stir until edges start to soften.  
3. Wilt greens & warm beans (1 min): Toss in spinach and black beans. Stir just until spinach wilts.  
4. Add eggs (4 min): Reduce heat to medium. Pour in whole eggs + egg whites (lightly whisked together). Let sit 10 sec, then gently push and fold with spatula until curds form and eggs are mostly set.  
5. Finish & melt (1 min): Fold in cottage cheese and cheddar; cook 30-60 sec until cheese melts and mixture is creamy.  
6. Plate & top (instant): Slide scramble into a bowl. Spoon salsa over top, add avocado slices, green onion, and any garnishes. Serve right away.

Macros (approx.)  
Calories ≈ 480 | Protein ≈ 42 g | Carbs ≈ 30 g | Fat ≈ 22 g | Fiber ≈ 9 g

Speed tips  
• Use pre-diced bell peppers/“fajita” veggie mix from the produce section.  
• Cottage cheese goes in at the end so it warms but doesn’t curdle.  
• Swap black beans for pre-cooked lentils or edamame for variety.  
• Meal-prep idea: Dice peppers and measure beans the night before; the morning routine then becomes a true 5-minute cook.

Enjoy a fast, protein-packed, flavor-layered breakfast that will keep you full for hours!
