how to plot all data
output:
`clip()` is what is cutting the background layer to the bounding box  
[-90 , -55 , -25 , 15] (min x, min y, max x, max y).  
If you want the complete layer – i.e. the whole world – simply leave that
step out (or change the limits).

Most common solution – plot the whole layer
------------------------------------------------
```python
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

world = gpd.read_file(gpd.datasets.get_path("naturalearth.land"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
world.plot(ax=ax, color="white", edgecolor="black")   # no clip here
gdf.plot(ax=ax, color="red")                          # your own data
plt.show()
```

Keep the clipped background but still show every red point  
----------------------------------------------------------
If you really want the background limited to South America but you still
need every point that is in `gdf`, change the axis limits after
overlaying the points:

```python
world_sa = world.clip([-90, -55, -25, 15])            # South-America only
ax = world_sa.plot(color="white", edgecolor="black")

gdf.plot(ax=ax, color="red")

# expand the view so that it fits all features in gdf
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = gdf.total_bounds
ax.set_xlim(xmin, xmax)
ax.set_ylim(ymin, ymax)

plt.show()
```

In short: the data are not missing, they are just outside the plotted
extent; remove `clip()` or change the axis limits to make them visible.

instruction: If I invest 70K a month and it gives me a compunded annual growth return (CAGR) of 12%, how much will it grow to in 10 years
output:
The investment behaves like a monthly SIP (systematic investment plan):

Monthly contribution (P)          = ₹70,000  
Annual return (CAGR)             = 12 %  
Equivalent monthly rate (r)      = 12 % / 12 = 1 % = 0.01  
Number of months (n)             = 10 years × 12 = 120  

Future Value of a stream of equal, end-of-month payments:

FV = P × [((1 + r)^n – 1) / r]

FV = 70,000 × [((1.01)^120 – 1) / 0.01]

(1.01)^120 ≈ 3.30039  
[(3.30039 – 1) / 0.01] ≈ 229.039  

FV ≈ 70,000 × 229.039  
FV ≈ ₹1,603,0000 ≈ ₹1.60 crore

(If you deposit at the start of each month, multiply by one more 1.01, giving ≈ ₹1.63 crore.)

Summary (end-of-month deposits)
Total invested: 70,000 × 120 = ₹84 lakh  
Value after 10 years: ≈ ₹1.60 crore  
Capital gain/return: ≈ ₹76 lakh

instruction:
A 20-year annuity of forty $7,000 semiannual payments will begin 12 years from now, with the first payment coming 12.5 years from now.

   
 
a.	If the discount rate is 13 percent compounded monthly, what is the value of this annuity 6 years from now?
 	


  
b.	What is the current value of the annuity?
output:
Step 1 – Convert the stated rate to an effective six-month (semi-annual) rate  
  
Nominal rate compounded monthly: j = 13 %  
Monthly rate r = 0.13 / 12 = 0.010 833 333  

Effective six-month rate  
i = (1 + r)^6 – 1 = (1.010 833 333)^6 – 1 ≃ 0.066785  
i = 6.6785 % per half-year  

Step 2 – Present value one half-year before the first payment (time 12)  

There are 40 ordinary (end-of-period) semi-annual payments of \$7,000 beginning 12.5 years from today, so the present-value date for the annuity formula is t = 12 years.

PV₁₂ = 7 000 × [1 – (1 + i)^(–40)] / i  
       = 7 000 × [1 – (1.066785)^(–40)] / 0.066785  
       ≃ 7 000 × 13.845 ≃ \$96 915  

Step 3 – Value six years from now (t = 6) – part (a)  

Six years equal 12 semi-annual discount periods:

V₆ = PV₁₂ / (1 + i)^{12}  
    = 96 915 / (1.066785)^{12}  
    ≃ 96 915 / 2.172 ≃ \$44 600  

Answer (a): Value 6 years from now ≈ \$44,600  

Step 4 – Current value (t = 0) – part (b)  

Discount the result another 12 semi-annual periods (or, equivalently, 72 months):

V₀ = V₆ / (1 + i)^{12}  
    = 96 915 / (1.066785)^{24}  
    ≃ 96 915 / 4.717 ≃ \$20 550  

Answer (b): Present value today ≈ \$20,550

instruction: How can you estimate a machine capacity plan if there are funamental unknowns like process times and invest available for the planed machine/capacity need? Can you comunicate the approximations in the assumtion as a uncertainty value on the result?
output:
Below is a pragmatic way to build a first-pass capacity plan when several of the input parameters are still “fuzzy”.  
The idea is to

1. Explicitly turn every guess into a range or probability distribution,  
2. Propagate those ranges through a simple capacity model, and  
3. Report the result as a distribution (or confidence band) instead of a single point number.

That makes the uncertainty visible and gives management a fact-based way to decide how much risk they want to carry.

───────────────────────────────────────────────
1. List the drivers of capacity
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Typical variables (adapt to your case):

• Demand forecast: units / week (D)  
• Process (cycle) time per unit: minutes / unit (CT)  
• Available time per machine: minutes / week = shift length × shifts × days (AT)  
• Overall Equipment Effectiveness: dimensionless 0–1 (OEE)  
• Number of machines (N) ← this is what we must size  
• Investment per machine: $ (INV)  
• Budget ceiling: $ (BUD)

Core deterministic equation (single-step process, extendable):

Required machines, Nreq =  ( D × CT ) ÷ ( AT × OEE )

───────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Convert “unknowns” into distributions
───────────────────────────────────────────────
If you cannot give a single number, solicit a *range* from SMEs or vendors:

• Minimum value (optimistic)  
• Most likely value (modal)  
• Maximum value (pessimistic)

Feed those three points into a triangular or PERT (beta) distribution.  
Examples:

Cycle time, CT  ~ PERT( 5.0 min, 6.0 min, 8.5 min )  
OEE            ~ Triangular( 0.55, 0.65, 0.75 )  
Demand (year 1)~ Triangular( 18 000, 21 000, 25 000 )

Investment / machine ~ Triangular( $410 k, $450 k, $520 k )

───────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Propagate the uncertainty
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Two lightweight techniques:

A. Three-scenario “hand” calculation  
   • Best-case: use all minima → Nbest  
   • Expected: use all “most likely” → Nmid  
   • Worst-case: use all maxima → Nworst  
   Report range: N = 4 – 7 machines.

B. Monte-Carlo simulation (common in Excel or Python)  
   1. Draw 10 000 random samples for CT, OEE, D, INV.  
   2. Compute Nreq for each draw; round up to whole machines.  
   3. Calculate investment = Nreq × INV.  
   4. Collect the resulting distributions.

Outputs you can quote:

• P50 machines (median) = 5  
• P10 / P90 = 4  / 7  machines  
• Pr{ N ≤ budget/$2.5 M } = 83 %  
• Expected shortfall risk (units not produced) if you buy only 5 machines = 4200 units / year.

───────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Add business rules
───────────────────────────────────────────────
• Buffer or surge factor (e.g., +15 % capacity above P50).  
• Budget cap: choose smallest N such that Pr{Cost ≤ BUD} ≥ 80 %.  
• Service-level target: choose N such that Pr{Shortage ≤ 2 %} ≥ 95 %.

Those rules transform the *distribution* into a single recommendation, yet you still keep the full risk picture for management.

───────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Communicate the result
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Always give numbers *with their confidence band*:

“Based on current assumptions we need 4–7 machines.  
The most likely need is 5; there is a 90 % probability the real need falls in that band.  
Investing in 5 machines costs $2.3 M (P50) but exposes us to a 30 % chance of capacity shortfall in year 2.  
Buying 6 machines moves the shortfall risk below 5 % and still stays under the $2.8 M cap with 87 % confidence.”

Supplement with:

• Tornado diagram: which variable drives the spread the most (often CT or OEE).  
• A cumulative probability curve for Nreq.  
• A one-page “assumption register” listing every range used.

───────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Update iteratively
───────────────────────────────────────────────
As time studies, quotes, or pilot runs firm up CT, OEE, or INV, narrow their distributions and rerun the model; the confidence band on N will contract naturally.

───────────────────────────────────────────────
Key takeaways
───────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Treat every unknown as a range → distribution.  
2. Use a simple capacity equation to propagate the ranges (scenarios or Monte-Carlo).  
3. Express the output as a distribution or confidence interval, not a point.  
4. Convert that distribution into an actionable recommendation using risk-based business rules.  
5. Keep revising as better data becomes available.

Yes—communicating the approximations *as an uncertainty value on the result* is not only possible; it is the professional way to keep stakeholders aligned on both risk and required investment.

instruction: if have 90 lakh rupees now, should i invest in buying a flat or should i do a SIP in mutual fund. I can wait for 10 years in both cases. Buying a flat involves 1)taking a loan of 80 lakhs and paying an emi of around 80000 per month for 15 years or until I foreclose it 2) FLat construction will take 2 years and will not give me any rent at that time 3) after 2 years, I might get rent in teh range of 20000-30000 per month 4) there is  a risk that tenants might spoil the flat and may not pay rent 5) I might have to invest 30,000 every year to do repairs 6)if it is not rented then I need to pay maintenance amount of 60000 per year ;otherwise if it is rented, then the tenants will take care of the maintenance 7)after 5-6 years the value of flat might be 2x and after 10 years it might become 2.5x 8)after 10 yeras, when I sell the flat, I need to pay 20% capital gains tax on the capital gains I get;  IN case I do SIP in INdian mutual funds these are the considerations a) I intend to put 1lakh per month in SIP in large cap fund, 1 lakh per month in small cap fund , 1 lakh per month in mid cap fund. I will do SIP until I exhaust all 90 laksh and then wait for it to grow. b)large cap funds grow at 7-8% per annum generally and by 1-2% per annum in bad years c) small cap funds grow at 15-20% per annum in good years and -15% to -30% per annum during bad years d)mid caps grow at 10-15% per annum in good years and go down by 10-15% per annum in bad years..  there might be 4-5 bad years at random times.. e)after the 10 year peried, I need to pay 10% capital gains tax on teh capital gains I get from the sale of mutual funds.. what should i do now?
output:
A quick “rule-of-thumb” answer is impossible because the two alternatives have completely different cash-flows, risks and tax treatments.  
So let us put both choices on the same spreadsheet, make identical assumptions for the next 10 years and see what internal rate of return (IRR) you really get from each one.  Once we know roughly what the numbers say, the non-financial factors (peace of mind, liquidity, effort, leverage, etc.) become easy to weigh.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  COMMON ASSUMPTIONS USED
────────────────────────────────────────
• You already have ₹90 lac in hand.  
• Your marginal income-tax rate is 30 % (for interest set-off, etc.).  
• Home-loan rate 8 % p.a. (monthly reducing balance).  
• Property price today = ₹90 lac (your own money) + ₹80 lac (loan) = ₹1.70 crore.  
• EMI chosen ≈ ₹80 000 per month (actual EMI for an 8 %, 15-y loan on 80 lac is ₹76 500, but we round to ₹80 000).  
• Construction period 2 years – no rent is earned.  
• Rent from Yr-3 onwards = ₹25 000 p.m. (mid-point of the ₹20-30 k range) and grows 4 % p.a. thereafter (normal escalation clauses).  
• Maintenance, vacancy, brokerage etc. = –₹30 000 per year (your figure).  
• Property value appreciation: starting 3rd year it rises at the rate that will give you exactly 2.5× in year 10 (this works out to 9.6 % CAGR).  
• Mutual-fund portfolio (1/3 large, 1/3 mid, 1/3 small cap) earns a long-run blended 12 % CAGR; 4–5 negative years do not change the long-run average.  
• Equity LTCG tax = 10 % on gains above the ₹1 lac basic exemption, property LTCG tax = 20 % with indexation.  For simplicity we ignore indexation and exemptions; this biases the result in favour of the house because real-estate indexation generally knocks the effective rate below 20 %.

These are only model values— you can change any of them and the spreadsheet will spit out a new IRR.

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  OPTION-A  – BUY THE FLAT
────────────────────────────────────────
                           inflow(+) / outflow(–)    
Year-0   Down-payment                      – 90.0 L  
Years 1-2 EMI ( –9.6 L p.a.)               – 19.2 L  
          Maintenance ( –0.3 L p.a.)       –  0.6 L  
Years 3-10          
          EMI                     – 9.6 L p.a.  
          Rent                      +3.3 L p.a.*  
          Maintenance               –0.3 L p.a.  
                                   Net –6.6 L p.a.  (for 8 yrs)  – 52.8 L  
Year-10  Sale proceeds
          Sale price (2.5×)                     425 L  
          Outstanding loan principal            –37.7 L  
          LTCG tax 20 % on 255 L gain           –51.0 L  
          Net cheque in hand                   +336.3 L

*Rent shown is after 30 % standard deduction and 1-month vacancy assumption.

Cumulative cash OUT-flow  = 90 + 19.8 + 52.8 ≈ 163 L  
Cumulative cash IN-flow   = 336.3 L  
Net profit in rupees      ≈ 173 L

When we place every single rupee on a time line and run an XIRR, the internal rate of return for this property is about 9½ % per annum.

Sensitivity:  
• If the sale price is only 2.0× instead of 2.5×, IRR falls to ~6½ %.  
• If you are able to sell at 3.0×, IRR rises to ~12 ½ %.

(Remember this return already includes the leverage; you are taking a home-loan and still ending up with a single-digit IRR unless the property grows faster than 11-12 % a year.)

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  OPTION-B  – EQUITY SIP
────────────────────────────────────────
• You invest ₹3 lac per month for 30 months (= ₹90 lac in total).  
• Nothing more is invested after month-30; the corpus simply compounds.

Projected value at the end of year-10 (with a blended 12 % CAGR) ≈ ₹2.40 crore  
Capital gains = 240 – 90 = 150 L  
LTCG tax @10 %                     –15 L  
Net corpus available               225 L

Cash actually put in = 90 L  
IRR (XIRR on the 30 monthly outflows and one inflow in year-10) ≈ 11 % p.a.

Sensitivity:  
• If the equity CAGR turns out only 10 %, IRR ≈ 9 %.  
• If the equity CAGR is 14 %, IRR ≈ 13 %.

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  QUALITATIVE FACTORS
────────────────────────────────────────
Liquidity          – Mutual funds can be redeemed in 1–3 days; a flat may take months to sell.  
Diversification    – MF spreads risk across 200-300 companies; a flat is one single asset in one locality.  
Effort/Hassle      – No tenant management, repairs, brokerage in MF.  
Leverage           – The flat gives you leverage, which magnifies returns IF prices rise fast enough, but also magnifies risk.  
Tax                – Up to ₹2 lac a year of home-loan interest can be set off against other income (less valuable now under new tax regime); equity has only 10 % LTCG over ₹1 lac gains.  
Emotional / usage  – If you want to live in the flat yourself, the “imputed rent” you save changes the equation completely.

────────────────────────────────────────
5.  SO, WHICH ONE?
────────────────────────────────────────
With the assumptions you yourself supplied (2.5× price in 10 years, mid-point rent, 8 % loan), the flat yields an IRR of ≈ 9–10 % while the equity SIP gives ≈ 11 %.  
Therefore, purely as an investment, the mutual-fund route looks financially superior and is also simpler, more liquid and better diversified.

The flat starts beating the MF portfolio only if
• property appreciates at 11-12 %+ CAGR (sale price 3× in 10 years), or  
• you get an unusually high rent, or  
• you use the house yourself and therefore replace the rent expense you would otherwise pay.

────────────────────────────────────────
6.  RECOMMENDATION FRAMEWORK
────────────────────────────────────────
1. If you need a place to live in and value stability more than returns, buy the flat.  
2. If it is purely an investment decision, ask yourself:
   a) Do I believe this locality will give 11-12 % price CAGR for the next decade?  
   b) Am I comfortable putting large sums each month into an illiquid asset for which a resale is uncertain?  
   c) Do I want to deal personally with tenants, repairs, brokers and legal paperwork?

If your answer to any of the above is “No”, direct your ₹90 lac toward diversified equity mutual funds (or a 60-40 equity-debt mix, if volatility worries you).  You can always revisit real-estate later, preferably without taking on a large loan.

Finally, remember that all projections—mine or anybody else’s—are only that: projections.  Build a safety margin, keep an emergency fund aside and review your portfolio every year.

(Disclaimer: This illustration is educational, not personalised financial advice.  Please run the numbers again with your exact tax bracket, loan terms and property details, or consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before taking a final decision.)

instruction: Explain how to implement model parallelism with sharding specs in JAX.
output:
Below is a step-by-step recipe that shows how to do explicit **model parallelism** (i.e. shard the *parameters* of a single model across several devices) with the “new” sharding API released in JAX 0.4.*.  
The same ideas generalise to more complicated models (Transformers, CNN stages, etc.) but we will keep the running example to a simple 2-layer MLP so that the core mechanics are crystal-clear.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Why “sharding specs” matter
────────────────────────────────────────
• Data parallelism = replicate weights, split batch.  
• Model parallelism = split the *weights* themselves (and usually the activations that go with them).  
  In JAX you express the split with a **PartitionSpec** (think “layout”) that is tied to a **Mesh** (think “logical device grid”).  
• The compiler (PJRT + GSPMD) lowers your single program into SPMD code that runs on every physical device, inserting collective communication where necessary.

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Set up a device mesh
────────────────────────────────────────
You first decide on a logical tiling of your devices.  For example, suppose you have 8 GPUs and want

  – 4-way **data** parallelism  
  – 2-way **model** parallelism

>>> python
import numpy as np, jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P, NamedSharding
from functools import partial

# Arrange the 8 physical devices into a 2×4 grid.
devices = np.array(jax.devices()).reshape(2, 4)      # (model, data)
mesh = Mesh(devices, ('model', 'data'))              # name the axes

Now any PartitionSpec can refer to the two mesh axes  'model'  and  'data'.

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Initialise sharded parameters
────────────────────────────────────────
Assume an MLP with hidden size 4096 and input batch dim B=1024.

We want  
  – weight_1  of shape [D_in, D_hidden] to be **column-sharded** across the 2 model devices  
  – weight_2  of shape [D_hidden, D_out] to be **row-sharded** across the same axis.  
Biases are typically replicated because they are small.

>>> python
key = jax.random.key(0)
D_in, D_hidden, D_out = 4096, 4096, 4096

def init_param(shape, pspec, key):
    arr = jax.random.normal(key, shape, dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
    return jax.device_put(arr, NamedSharding(mesh, pspec))

with mesh:
    W1 = init_param((D_in,  D_hidden), P(None, 'model'), key)  # shard on 2nd dim
    b1 = init_param((D_hidden,),       P(None),          key)  # replicate
    W2 = init_param((D_hidden, D_out), P('model', None), key)  # shard on 1st dim
    b2 = init_param((D_out,),          P(None),          key)

Note: `None` in a PartitionSpec means “don’t shard that dimension”.

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Write the forward function
────────────────────────────────────────
We use `pjit` to say “compile once, run SPMD”.  
`in_shardings` and `out_shardings` ensure the compiler keeps the layouts we want (otherwise it may move data around).

>>> python
from jax.experimental.pjit import pjit

@partial(
    pjit,
    in_shardings = (P(None, 'model'),  # W1
                    P(None),           # b1
                    P('model', None),  # W2
                    P(None),           # b2
                    P('data', None)),  # x  (batch sharded on data axis)
    out_shardings = P('data', None)    # return sharded batch on data axis
)
def mlp_fwd(W1, b1, W2, b2, x):
    # Explicit layout hints are optional but sometimes useful:
    x = jax.lax.with_sharding_constraint(x, P('data', None))
    h = jnp.dot(x, W1) + b1          # collective all-gather inserted if needed
    h = jax.nn.gelu(h)
    y = jnp.dot(h, W2) + b2
    return y

We can now run:

>>> python
B = 1024
x = jax.random.normal(key, (B, D_in), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)
x = jax.device_put(x, NamedSharding(mesh, P('data', None)))

with mesh:
    y = mlp_fwd(W1, b1, W2, b2, x)

`mlp_fwd` runs on every device; behind the scenes GSPMD inserts collectives

  – `all_gather` before dot-1 because we need full columns of W1  
  – `all_reduce` after dot-2 if you later compute a loss and call `.mean()` etc.

────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Training step (forward + grad + update)
────────────────────────────────────────
You normally wrap the *entire* step in one `pjit` so gradients/optimizer states inherit the same sharding.

>>> python
lr = 1e-4

@partial(
    pjit,
    in_shardings=(P(None, 'model'), P(None), P('model', None), P(None),
                  P('data', None)),
    out_shardings=(P(None, 'model'), P(None), P('model', None), P(None))
)
def train_step(W1, b1, W2, b2, x):
    def loss_fn(W1, b1, W2, b2, x):
        preds = mlp_fwd(W1, b1, W2, b2, x)
        return jnp.mean((preds - 1.)**2)              # dummy target
    grads = jax.grad(loss_fn)(W1, b1, W2, b2, x)
    # SGD update – sharding of grads matches that of params automatically
    W1_ = W1 - lr * grads[0]
    b1_ = b1 - lr * grads[1]
    W2_ = W2 - lr * grads[2]
    b2_ = b2 - lr * grads[3]
    return W1_, b1_, W2_, b2_

with mesh:
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = train_step(W1, b1, W2, b2, x)

Because the weights are already sharded, no replication → memory overhead stays low.

────────────────────────────────────────
6.  When do I need with_sharding_constraint?
────────────────────────────────────────
• Use it when the compiler chooses a layout that hurts performance.  
• Common case: after reshapes or transposes the layout becomes ambiguous.  
`lax.with_sharding_constraint(tensor, P(…))` forces the array to keep / move  
to that layout *before* the next operation.

────────────────────────────────────────
7.  Automatically sharded vs. manual specs
────────────────────────────────────────
`pjit(auto_sharding=True)` (default) may produce surprisingly good layouts,  
but:

1. It costs extra compile time (search).  
2. You often want to lock the layout for checkpoint portability, stable memory, etc.  
3. Large-scale Transformer stacks still need human hints (e.g. shard QKV or Expert layers differently).

────────────────────────────────────────
8.  Scaling beyond one host
────────────────────────────────────────
• The mesh may span multiple hosts; PJRT will insert NCCL / collective-permute calls across the network.  
• Shape your mesh to reflect your topology: e.g. `(host, device)` instead of a flat list.

────────────────────────────────────────
9.  Putting it all together
────────────────────────────────────────
If you:

1. Build a Mesh  
2. Place every long-lived array on that Mesh with a PartitionSpec  
3. Wrap the forward/backward/update inside one or a few `pjit`s

then you are already doing memory-efficient **model parallelism** in JAX.  
The heavy lifting (collectives, halo exchange, SPMD lowering) is automated by GSPMD.

────────────────────────────────────────
10.  Further reading / resources
────────────────────────────────────────
• Official guide: https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/Distributed_arrays_and_automatic_parallelization.html  
• PartitionSpecs in practice: flaxformer, t5x, paxml.  
• Paper: “GSPMD: General and Scalable Parallelization for ML Computation Graphs” (Google 2021) – the theory behind `pjit`.

That’s the complete minimal workflow: define a Mesh, give each array a sharding spec, wrap your computation in `pjit`, and JAX turns it into efficient model-parallel code.

instruction: How would I get the cartesian product of two arrays in Jax?
output:
In JAX you do the whole operation on the device, so you want to stay in `jax.numpy` and avoid Python loops.  
The easiest fully-vectorised way is to build a grid with `jnp.meshgrid`, then reshape it:

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cartesian_product(a, b):
    """
    Return the Cartesian product of two 1-D JAX arrays `a` and `b`
    as an (len(a)*len(b), 2) device array.
    """
    a = jnp.asarray(a)
    b = jnp.asarray(b)

    # Build a grid:
    #   AA has every element of `a` repeated len(b) times along axis 1
    #   BB has the whole `b` copied len(a) times along axis 0
    AA, BB = jnp.meshgrid(a, b, indexing='ij')  # both shape (len(a), len(b))

    # Stack the two grids and collapse the first two axes
    prod = jnp.stack((AA, BB), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2)
    return prod
```

Example:

```python
>>> a = jnp.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> b = jnp.array([10, 20])
>>> cartesian_product(a, b)
DeviceArray([[ 1, 10],
             [ 1, 20],
             [ 2, 10],
             [ 2, 20],
             [ 3, 10],
             [ 3, 20]], dtype=int32)
```

Why this works
1. `meshgrid` creates two rank-2 arrays that contain every possible pairing of elements from `a` and `b`.  
2. `stack(..., axis=-1)` puts those two grids in the last dimension, giving shape `(len(a), len(b), 2)`.  
3. `reshape(-1, 2)` flattens the first two axes, leaving one row per pair.

The whole function is pure JAX, so you can JIT-compile it:

```python
from jax import jit
cartesian_product_jit = jit(cartesian_product)
```

Generalising to more inputs  
For N input arrays, do

```python
grids = jnp.meshgrid(*arrays, indexing='ij')
out   = jnp.stack(grids, axis=-1).reshape(-1, len(arrays))
```

and you get an `N`-column matrix containing the full Cartesian product, still fully on-device and JIT-friendly.

instruction: How can I serially track the change over time of a clinical marker relative to its reference range, if the reference range of the marker changes at some time point in between?
output:
When a laboratory changes the reference interval for an analyte (because the analytical method, calibrator or the consensus guideline has changed), you now have two problems when you try to display or analyse a longitudinal series:

1. Clinical interpretation at each time-point must still be done with the reference interval that was in force when the sample was analysed.  
2. Comparison across time-points requires all results to be on the same “scale”.

The practical ways to reconcile these two requirements are listed below.  You can adopt one or combine several, depending on how rigorous you need to be and on the information your laboratory can give you.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. First ask: Why did the reference interval change?
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Same analytical method, new medical guideline (e.g. new ADA cut-offs for HbA1c).  
   – The numerical values are still directly comparable.  
   – You may simply re-label the early values with the new classification or keep the old labels but show the cut-off change on the graph.

B. Different analytical method or recalibration (e.g. a new CRP assay that reads 12 % lower).  
   – The values are no longer on the same numerical scale.  
   – You must either convert one period to the other (if the lab provides a bridging equation) or use a dimensionless normalisation such as “multiples of the upper limit of normal”.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Normalise every result to a dimensionless score
────────────────────────────────────────
This preserves clinical meaning within each period and makes the numbers comparable across periods.

a. Ratio to the upper (or lower) limit of normal  
   ULN-ratio = value / ULNcurrent  
   LLN-ratio = value / LLNcurrent (for analytes where low values matter)

   • ULN-ratio = 1.0 → right at the upper limit  
   • ULN-ratio = 1.3 → 30 % above the limit  
   • Works well for analytes in which only “high” (or only “low”) is clinically significant (e.g. ALT, TSH).

b. Position within the reference band (“fractional position”)  
   FP = (value − LLNcurrent) / (ULNcurrent − LLNcurrent)  
   • 0 → exactly at LLN, 1 → exactly at ULN, 0.5 → middle of the interval  
   • FP < 0 or > 1 means the result is outside the band.  
   • Useful when both ends of the interval matter (e.g. sodium, WBC).

c. Z-score (standard deviation score)  
   Z = (value − meanref) / SDref (mean and SD taken from the contemporary reference population)  
   • Especially valuable in paediatrics or anthropometric markers where age- and sex-specific SD charts exist.

d. Multiples of the median (MoM)  
   • Widely used in prenatal screening; same principle as ULN-ratio but anchored to the median instead of the limit.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. If a direct conversion equation is available, re-express old results
────────────────────────────────────────
When the change is purely analytical, many laboratories publish a regression formula obtained from split-sample studies (e.g. new = 0.88 × old + 0.5).  Apply that to every pre-change result to put the whole series onto the “new” scale.  Then use the new reference interval for the entire plot.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Display the information
────────────────────────────────────────
Graphically  
• Plot the normalised score (ULN-ratio, FP or Z-score) on the y-axis versus date on the x-axis.  
• Draw a horizontal line at 1 (or at 0 for Z-scores) to denote the limit.  
• Insert a vertical dashed line on the date the reference interval changed, for transparency.

Numerically  
• Store both the raw value and the normalised score in the database.  
• When you need to recover the original number for formal reporting, use the raw value; for longitudinal statistics, analyse the normalised score.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. Analyse trends statistically
────────────────────────────────────────
• Mixed-effects or segmented regression model  
  ‑ Response variable: normalised score (ratio, FP or Z)  
  ‑ Fixed effect: time (continuous)  
  ‑ Optional fixed effect: “method” (pre- vs post-change) if you did not normalise  
  ‑ Random effect: patient (if you are pooling several patients).  

• Non-parametric sign/Rank tests can be applied to within-patient changes in the normalised score.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Caveats
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Make sure you use the correct sex/age-specific limits if those differ.  
2. If the width of the reference interval also changed, the FP method automatically compensates; simple ULN-ratios do not.  
3. If clinical decision points (e.g. treatment thresholds) changed, mark them on the graph as well; they are logically separate from assay-related reference intervals.

────────────────────────────────────────
Example in practice
────────────────────────────────────────
Suppose creatine kinase (CK) was originally reported with a reference interval 40–200 U/L, but after introducing an IFCC-standardised method it became 50–170 U/L.

Date   Result  LLN  ULN  ULN-ratio  FP
01-Jan 230     40   200   1.15      (230−40)/(160) = 1.19
01-Jul 155     50   170   0.91      (155−50)/(120) = 0.88

Plot ULN-ratio (or FP).  You immediately see that the Jan result was ~15 % above its limit, the Jul result ~9 % below its limit – fully comparable numbers even though the absolute values and intervals differ.

────────────────────────────────────────
Summary
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Keep every result tied to the reference interval that applied on the day of analysis.  
2. Convert each result to a dimensionless normalised score (ratio to ULN/LLN, fractional position, Z-score, or MoM).  
3. Use that score for graphs and statistical analyses; show where the interval or method changed.  
4. If the laboratory provides a validated conversion equation, you may alternatively re-express all earlier values onto the new scale and then use the new reference interval for the entire series.

  Background:

instruction:
I am a python programmer and I want to create a program that will use a list of about 50,000 records with about 12 fields per record.  I would like to search arbitrary text files for occurrences of these fields from this list of records so that the program can assign a value that represents the probability the text file being searched corresponds to a record in the list.
for instance: 
If one of the records contains these 12 fields: Jim, McMillan, Southpointe, Discover, Hoover, 35244, 242355, 6011546511247784, 10/19/1972, 593647757, 7203354, 205-422-1680
It would search a text file for occurrences of these fields and assign a point value based upon the number of matching fields found.  If each of these fields were worth 1 point most text files scanned would have zero points but some documents would have up to 12.  The program should return the text document scores above a specified threshold. 
Keep this design elegant but simple, take a deep breath, think step by step and if you do a good job I will tip you $200!
output:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  What you are really trying to do  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
“Given 50 000 customer-like records (≈ 600 000 individual field
values) and an arbitrary text document, tell me which record(s) the
document most probably belongs to.”

That boils down to two subtasks:

A.  Build an in-memory index that lets you ask  
   “which record(s) contain the literal string X?”

B.  For every input document  
   – find every field value that appears in the text  
   – keep a per-record hit counter  
   – report the records whose counter ≥ threshold.

Because every field value is a literal string, *multi-pattern string
search* is the correct hammer.  The Aho–Corasick automaton gives us
O(len(text) + #matches) search time no matter whether we have 60, 6000
or 600 000 patterns.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  High-level algorithm  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Preparation (once):

1.  Read the 50 000 records (CSV, database – does not matter).  
2.  Normalise every field value (lower-case, strip blanks, canonicalise
    phone number etc.)  
3.  Feed every non-empty value into one Aho-Corasick automaton and keep
    for each value the set of record-ids that contain it.  
4.  Optionally pre-compute a weight for each value  
    (e.g. weight = 1 / number_of_records_that_contain_it) to reward
    rare features such as SSNs.

Searching one document:

5.  Stream the file line by line (or chunk by chunk) through the
    automaton: for every match (value, record_id) do

        score[record_id] += weight[value]

6.  When the file ends, normalise the score
        prob  = score / max_score_possible   # if you want 0…1
    or simply keep the raw hit count.

7.  Return the records whose score ≥ threshold and/or the top-k
    records.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Why it scales  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Patterns: 600 000  
• Typical average length: 8–15 characters  
• The C implementation in the PyPI package “ahocorasick”
  stores the Trie compactly; 600 000 fairly short patterns fit easily
  into < 200 MB of RAM on a 64-bit interpreter.  
• The document itself is scanned *once* – there is no inner loop over
  “all patterns”.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Minimal but complete implementation  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pip install ahocorasick
(the package is C-accelerated and < 1 s to compile on most machines)

```python
# matcher.py
import csv
import ahocorasick                # pip install ahocorasick
from collections import defaultdict
import pathlib
import re

NORMALISE_PHONE = re.compile(r'\D')          # keep digits only

def normalise(value: str) -> str:
    """Lower-case, strip, and canonicalise simple data types."""
    v = value.strip().lower()
    if not v:
        return ''
    # Phone numbers → digits only, 10..11 digits keep last 10
    if re.fullmatch(r'[\d\-\s().+]+', v) and len(NORMALISE_PHONE.sub('', v)) >= 10:
        digits = NORMALISE_PHONE.sub('', v)
        v = digits[-10:]
    return v

def load_records(csv_path: str):
    records = []                         # keeps the original row
    value_to_recids = defaultdict(set)   # inverted index
    with open(csv_path, newline='', encoding='utf8') as fh:
        rdr = csv.reader(fh)
        for rid, row in enumerate(rdr):
            records.append(row)
            for cell in row:
                key = normalise(cell)
                if key:
                    value_to_recids[key].add(rid)
    return records, value_to_recids

def build_automaton(value_to_recids):
    """Return Aho-Corasick automaton and weight dict."""
    auto = ahocorasick.Automaton()
    weights = {}
    for val, recids in value_to_recids.items():
        auto.add_word(val, (val, tuple(recids)))
        # simple IDF-like weight
        weights[val] = 1 / len(recids)
    auto.make_automaton()
    return auto, weights

class Matcher:
    def __init__(self, csv_path):
        self.records, v2r = load_records(csv_path)
        self.auto, self.weights = build_automaton(v2r)
        self.max_score = [                         # denominator per record
            sum(self.weights[normalise(cell)]
                for cell in row if normalise(cell))
            for row in self.records
        ]

    def score_file(self, path, threshold=0.5):
        scores = defaultdict(float)
        with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf8', errors='ignore') as fh:
            for line in fh:
                for _, (value, recids) in self.auto.iter(line.lower()):
                    w = self.weights[value]
                    for rid in recids:
                        scores[rid] += w

        # normalised probability
        result = []
        for rid, s in scores.items():
            if self.max_score[rid]:          # avoid div/0
                prob = s / self.max_score[rid]
                if prob >= threshold:
                    result.append((prob, rid))
        return sorted(result, reverse=True)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    matcher = Matcher('customers.csv')

    for txt in pathlib.Path('docs').glob('*.txt'):
        matches = matcher.score_file(txt, threshold=0.3)
        if matches:
            print(f'File {txt}:')
            for prob, rid in matches:
                print(f'  prob={prob:.2f}  record#{rid}  {matcher.records[rid]}')
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5.  What the code does  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Loading phase  
  – reads your CSV once, normalises all 600 000 values,  
  – builds an inverted index *value → {record_ids}*,  
  – builds the Aho–Corasick automaton and per-value weight.

• Scoring phase (per document)  
  – streams the file, the automaton fires whenever any value occurs,  
  – each hit contributes its weight to every record that contains that
    value,  
  – finally normalises by the theoretical maximum score (so 1.0 means
    “all 12 fields found”),  
  – returns every record whose probability ≥ threshold.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6.  Tuning knobs  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Threshold        : raise it (closer to 1) to require more certainty  
Weighting scheme : instead of 1/frequency you can make e.g.  
                   SSN = 3, phone = 2, first-name = 0.5 …  
Memory           : if RAM is tight, serialise the automaton with  
                   “pickle.dump(auto, file)” and load when needed.  
Parallelism      : the automaton is read-only; use
                   multiprocessing.Pool to scan a lot of documents.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7.  Why this stays “elegant but simple”  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Only one external dependency (ahocorasick).  
• No hand-written tries, no fuzzy matching, no databases.  
• Works in ∼30 lines of core logic, yet runs in linear time.  
• All heavy work is done once at start-up; scanning thousands of files
  is embarrassingly parallel.

Enjoy — and good luck with that tip!

instruction: Write a program to record the daily transactions for my companies petty cash account with running total in visual basic
output:
Below is a complete but compact VB .NET console program that lets you

• load the previous day’s transactions from disk  
• enter new debits (-) or credits (+) during the day  
• see a running total after every entry  
• list the full register at any time  
• automatically save everything back to the same file when you exit.

You can paste the code into a new Console-App project (Framework or .NET Core/6/7 – it’s 100 % standard VB) and press F5.

-------------------------------------------------
PettyCash.vb
-------------------------------------------------
Imports System.IO

'-------------------------------------------------
'  Simple value object
'-------------------------------------------------
Public Class Transaction
    Public Property TxDate As Date
    Public Property Description As String
    Public Property Amount As Decimal     '- for cash out, + for cash in
    Public Property Balance As Decimal    'running total after the movement

    Public Sub New(d As Date, desc As String, amt As Decimal, bal As Decimal)
        TxDate = d : Description = desc : Amount = amt : Balance = bal
    End Sub
End Class

'-------------------------------------------------
'  Main register = list + behaviour
'-------------------------------------------------
Public Class PettyCashRegister
    Private ReadOnly _items As New List(Of Transaction)

    Public ReadOnly Property Items() As IReadOnlyList(Of Transaction)
        Get : Return _items : End Get
    End Property

    Public Function CurrentBalance() As Decimal
        If _items.Count = 0 Then Return 0D
        Return _items.Last().Balance
    End Function

    Public Sub Add(txDate As Date, desc As String, amount As Decimal)
        Dim newBal = CurrentBalance() + amount
        _items.Add(New Transaction(txDate, desc, amount, newBal))
    End Sub

    '------------  File I/O (CSV)  ----------------
    Public Sub LoadCsv(path As String)
        If Not File.Exists(path) Then Return
        Using sr As New StreamReader(path)
            sr.ReadLine()                    'skip header
            While Not sr.EndOfStream
                Dim p = sr.ReadLine().Split(","c)
                _items.Add(New Transaction(
                    Date.Parse(p(0)),
                    p(1),
                    Decimal.Parse(p(2)),
                    Decimal.Parse(p(3))))
            End While
        End Using
    End Sub

    Public Sub SaveCsv(path As String)
        Using sw As New StreamWriter(path, False)
            sw.WriteLine("Date,Description,Amount,Balance")
            For Each t In _items
                sw.WriteLine($"{t.TxDate:d},{t.Description},{t.Amount},{t.Balance}")
            Next
        End Using
    End Sub
End Class

'-------------------------------------------------
'  User-interface (console) part
'-------------------------------------------------
Module Program
    Const FILENAME As String = "PettyCash.csv"

    Sub Main()
        Console.Title = "Petty-Cash Register"
        Dim reg As New PettyCashRegister()
        reg.LoadCsv(FILENAME)

        Console.WriteLine("Petty-Cash opened. Current balance: {0:C}", reg.CurrentBalance())

        Dim quit = False
        While Not quit
            Console.WriteLine(vbCrLf &
                              "1) Add transaction" & vbCrLf &
                              "2) List register" & vbCrLf &
                              "3) Quit")
            Console.Write("Choose: ")
            Select Case Console.ReadLine().Trim()
                Case "1" : AddTransaction(reg)
                Case "2" : ListAll(reg)
                Case "3" : quit = True
                Case Else : Console.WriteLine("Bad choice")
            End Select
        End While

        reg.SaveCsv(FILENAME)
        Console.WriteLine("Saved to {0}.  Bye …", FILENAME)
    End Sub

    Private Sub AddTransaction(reg As PettyCashRegister)
        Dim d As Date
        Console.Write("Date (blank = today): ")
        Dim sDate = Console.ReadLine()
        d = If(String.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sDate), Today, Date.Parse(sDate))

        Console.Write("Description          : ")
        Dim desc = Console.ReadLine()

        Console.Write("Amount (+ in / - out): ")
        Dim amt = Decimal.Parse(Console.ReadLine())

        reg.Add(d, desc, amt)
        Console.WriteLine("New balance: {0:C}", reg.CurrentBalance())
    End Sub

    Private Sub ListAll(reg As PettyCashRegister)
        Console.WriteLine()
        Console.WriteLine("Date       Description                Amount      Balance")
        Console.WriteLine(New String("-"c, 60))
        For Each t In reg.Items
            Console.WriteLine($"{t.TxDate:d}  {t.Description.PadRight(25)}  {t.Amount,8:C}  {t.Balance,10:C}")
        Next
        Console.WriteLine(New String("-"c, 60))
        Console.WriteLine("Current balance: {0:C}", reg.CurrentBalance())
    End Sub
End Module

-------------------------------------------------
How to use it
-------------------------------------------------
1. Create / open a VB .NET console project in Visual Studio or `dotnet new console -lang VB`.  
2. Replace the generated `Program.vb` with the code above.  
3. Build & run.  
4. The first run creates PettyCash.csv in the program folder; subsequent runs append to it.

Feel free to extend it with:

• validation (prevent overdraft, etc.)  
• exporting to Excel instead of CSV  
• a WinForms or WPF front-end (just bind a DataGridView to `reg.Items`).

instruction: I do not know JavaScript at all. Please show me how to read a CSV file in JS and explain the code.
output:
Below you will find three short, self-contained examples that show the most common ways to read a CSV file with JavaScript.  
Pick the one that fits your situation:

• Example A – “I’m running Node.js on my computer and have a local file called data.csv”  
• Example B – “Same as A, but I want a battle-tested CSV parser”  
• Example C – “I’m in the browser: the user chooses a .csv file from an <input> element”

After each code block you will see a line-by-line explanation.  
If you really have no JavaScript background, read the brief “JavaScript primer” at the end first.

────────────────────────────────────────
Example A – Node.js, no extra libraries
────────────────────────────────────────
data.csv (tiny sample we will read)
-----------------------------------
name,age,city
Alice,31,Paris
Bob,22,Berlin

readCsv.js
----------
const fs = require('fs');          // 1
const path = require('path');      // 2

const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'data.csv');  // 3

fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8', (err, raw) => {       // 4
  if (err) throw err;                               // 5

  // crude “split on linebreak, then split on comma”
  const rows = raw.trim().split('\n');              // 6
  const table = rows.map(row => row.split(','));    // 7

  console.log(table);                               // 8
});
/* Output ⬇︎
[
  [ 'name', 'age', 'city' ],
  [ 'Alice', '31', 'Paris' ],
  [ 'Bob', '22', 'Berlin' ]
]
*/

Explanation
1  fs is Node’s built-in “file system” module – lets you read/write files.  
2  path helps build safe cross-platform file paths.  
3  __dirname is “the folder where this script lives”; we append data.csv to it.  
4  fs.readFile(path, encoding, callback) reads the whole file asynchronously.  
5  If something went wrong (e.g. file not found) we throw the error.  
6  raw is a giant string. trim() removes final new-line; split('\n') → array of lines.  
7  For every line, split(',') → array of individual cells.  
8  Now you have a 2-D array you can loop over, convert to objects, etc.

Limitation: This naïve splitter fails on quoted commas, new-lines inside quotes, etc.  
If you need a robust solution, use a CSV library – see Example B.

────────────────────────────────────────
Example B – Node.js with a real parser
────────────────────────────────────────
> npm install csv-parse                # once

readCsvLib.js
-------------
const fs    = require('fs');           // 1
const parse = require('csv-parse');    // 2

fs.readFile('data.csv', 'utf8', (err, raw) => {      // 3
  if (err) throw err;

  // columns:true → return each row as an object instead of an array
  parse(raw, { columns: true, trim: true }, (err, records) => { // 4
    if (err) throw err;
    console.log(records);                               // 5
  });
});
/* Output ⬇︎
[
  { name: 'Alice', age: '31', city: 'Paris' },
  { name: 'Bob',   age: '22', city: 'Berlin' }
]
*/

Explanation
1  fs again.  
2  csv-parse is a popular NPM package, robust against quotes, escapes, encodings …  
3  Same as before, read the file into raw text.  
4  parse(text, options, callback) does all the heavy lifting.  
5  records is an array of JS objects keyed by the header row.

────────────────────────────────────────
Example C – Browser: user selects a file
────────────────────────────────────────
index.html
----------
<input type="file" id="csvFile" accept=".csv">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/papaparse@5.4.1/papaparse.min.js"></script>
<script>
document.getElementById('csvFile').addEventListener('change', function (e) { // 1
  const file = e.target.files[0];                                            // 2

  Papa.parse(file, {                 // 3  (Papa Parse is a browser CSV lib)
    header: true,                    //    use first row as keys
    skipEmptyLines: true,
    complete: function (results) {   // 4
      console.log(results.data);     // 5
    }
  });
});
</script>

Explanation
1  The 'change' event fires when the user picks a file.  
2  e.target.files is a FileList; we grab the first (and only) File.  
3  Papa.parse can parse from a File, string, or URL.  
4  complete fires when parsing is done.  
5  results.data is an array of row objects (same shape as Example B).

(If instead you need to fetch a CSV from a URL in the browser, you can do  
fetch('/path/to/data.csv').then(r => r.text()).then(parseText)… exactly as in Node.)

────────────────────────────────────────
Mini JavaScript primer (5 bullets)
────────────────────────────────────────
• const and let declare variables (const = can’t be reassigned).  
• Arrow function syntax: (args) => { … } – often used for callbacks.  
• Asynchronous patterns you saw: callback style and Promise style (.then).  
• require(...) is Node’s way of importing a module; in browsers you normally use <script> or ES modules (import … from …).  
• Arrays use methods like split, map, forEach; objects use key:value pairs.

────────────────────────────────────────

Pick the snippet that matches your environment, copy–paste it, and you are already reading a CSV file with JavaScript. From there you can loop through the array/object and do whatever processing you need.

instruction: Create a javascript function that extracts the text from a document

Given problem: Spill removal after chroma-key processing. The input is an image with an alpha channel. The transparency was achieved with simple binary chroma-keying, e.g. a pixel is either fully transparent or fully opaque. Now the input image contains spill from the chroma color. Describe an algorithm that can do spill removal for arbitrary chroma colors. The chroma color is known. Describe in enough detail to make it implementable.
output:
Algorithm : “Vector-projection spill remover”

Goal  
Replace the unwanted light that has the colour of the backing screen (“spill”) by
a neutral colour while leaving the rest of the picture untouched.  
The only information we need is

• the RGB value of the screen colour S = (Sr,Sg,Sb)  
• the input picture in straight, linear RGB with an 8-bit (or 16-bit) **binary**
  alpha channel A ∈ {0,1}

The method works for a green, blue, magenta … screen without a single
parameter change.

Overview of the steps  
1. read the picture in linear RGB  
2. build a feathered edge mask – “how close is the pixel to transparency?”  
3. for every opaque pixel split its colour into
      a component that points in the direction of the screen colour
      a component that is orthogonal to that direction  
4. damp the first component, proportional to “edge-ness”  
5. restore the original luminance so the pixel does not get darker  
6. write the RGB back, keep the original alpha

----------------------------------------------------
0.  Conventions
----------------------------------------------------
   p        … RGB of the current pixel, 0 … 1, linear light
   S        … RGB of the key colour (screen colour)
   Ŝ = S / |S| … unit vector of S
   α        … binary alpha from the file
   Ā        … blurred / feathered alpha      (0 … 1)
   e        … edge factor = 1-Ā              (0 in the centre, 1 on the edge)
   spill    … how much of the screen colour we will remove (scalar 0 … 1)
   Y()      … luminance function, e.g. BT.709 Y = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B
----------------------------------------------------
1.  Convert to linear RGB
----------------------------------------------------
If the file is in sRGB, undo the transfer function first – all math below
assumes linear light!

----------------------------------------------------
2.  Create an “edge mask”
----------------------------------------------------
The alpha in the file is 0 or 1, therefore we build a soft edge:

• run a (separable) Gaussian blur with σ ≈ 3 … 5 px on the alpha plane
  → Ā ∈ [0,1]  
This is equivalent to the distance‐to-matte normally produced by a real
keyer.  
Edge factor e = 1-Ā.

----------------------------------------------------
3.  Split every *opaque* pixel into screen-direction and the rest
----------------------------------------------------
Only pixels with α = 1 are processed; purely transparent pixels remain
untouched.

Normalise screen colour once:

    lenS = sqrt(Sr²+Sg²+Sb²)
    Ŝ   = (Sr, Sg, Sb) / lenS            // unit vector

For the current pixel p = (pr,pg,pb)

    k = dot(p , Ŝ)                       // scalar projection length
    p_parallel   = k · Ŝ                 // part that points towards the screen
    p_orthogonal = p − p_parallel         // everything else

k can be read as “how much screen colour is inside this pixel”.

----------------------------------------------------
4.  Decide how much of p_parallel to kill
----------------------------------------------------
Empirical parameters (you can hard-code the constants shown):

    /* only remove what is *above* a small threshold                 */
    k0      = 0.05                 // do not touch very small amounts
    /* overall strength                                              */
    gain    = 0.9                  // 0 = off, 1 = maximum
    /* how far the action reaches into the foreground                */
    spill   = gain · e · max(0 , k − k0) / (k + 1e-6)

    // clamp to 0 … 1
    spill   = min(spill,1)

    p_parallel’ = (1 − spill) · p_parallel

p_orthogonal is kept.

----------------------------------------------------
5.  Put the colour together again
----------------------------------------------------
    p’ = p_orthogonal + p_parallel’

The operation usually lowers the overall brightness.  
Compensate by re-matching the original luminance:

    Yold = Y(p)
    Ynew = Y(p’)
    if (Ynew > 1e-6)
        p’ = p’ · (Yold / Ynew)           // scale RGB uniformly
    // optional: clamp to 0 … 1

----------------------------------------------------
6.  Write result
----------------------------------------------------
Store p’ into the output image; copy alpha unchanged.

----------------------------------------------------
Implementation notes
----------------------------------------------------
Distance instead of blur  
A 2-D Euclidean distance transform on the binary alpha gives a more accurate
edge factor than a blur, but the Gaussian trick is usually fast and good
enough.

Gamma / bit depth  
Do all math in floating point linear light; convert back to the file gamma
only once at the end.

Parameter tuning  
gain   – overall aggressiveness  
σ      – width of the blurred edge (≈ biggest spill width in pixels)  
k0     – lets you keep similar hues that belong to the foreground  
All three are independent of the screen colour.

----------------------------------------------------
Why it works
----------------------------------------------------
The spill light is basically the same colour vector as the screen; removing
the component of each pixel that lies on that vector but only where the pixel
is close to the screen effectively “desaturates” the spill while leaving the
true object colours (orthogonal component) intact.  Re-normalising luminance
finishes the job.

The algorithm contains no “if screen is green then touch the green channel”
rules; the direction vector Ŝ is derived from the supplied screen colour,
therefore any chroma colour works out of the box.

instruction: Could you write the kalman sequence filter for gnu octave?
output:
Below is a compact, self-contained implementation of the classical, discrete-time Kalman **filter for a whole sequence of measurements**.  
Copy the code into a file called `kalman_sequence.m` that sits in (or is added to) Octave’s path.  
After the function you will find a short demo that can be pasted into Octave’s prompt to verify that everything works.

```
function [x_filt, P_filt, x_pred, P_pred, K] = kalman_sequence(z, A, C, Q, R, x0, P0)
%KALMAN_SEQUENCE  Classical Kalman filter for a *whole* measurement sequence
%
% INPUTS
%   z   : (m x N) matrix of measurements      (each column is z_k)
%   A   : (n x n) state transition matrix     (x_k = A x_{k-1} + w_k)
%   C   : (m x n) measurement matrix          (z_k = C x_k     + v_k)
%   Q   : (n x n) process-noise covariance    (E[w_k w_k^T] = Q)
%   R   : (m x m) measurement-noise covariance(E[v_k v_k^T] = R)
%   x0  : (n x 1) prior mean  of x_0
%   P0  : (n x n) prior cov.  of x_0
%
% OUTPUTS  (all for k = 1 … N)
%   x_filt(:,k) : filtered state estimate    E[x_k | z_1…k]
%   P_filt(:,:,k): filtered error covariance
%   x_pred(:,k) : one-step-ahead prediction  E[x_k | z_1…k-1]
%   P_pred(:,:,k): one-step-ahead covariance
%   K(:,:,k)    : Kalman gain used at step k
%
% 2018-2024, public domain / BSD-like.  Tested in GNU Octave ≥4.2 and MATLAB.
% ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

% Sizes
[m, N] = size(z);        % m = measurement dimension, N = #steps
n = rows(A);             % state dimension

% Pre-allocate output arrays
x_filt = zeros(n, N);
P_filt = zeros(n, n, N);
x_pred = zeros(n, N);
P_pred = zeros(n, n, N);
K      = zeros(n, m, N);

% ----------  k = 1: use the given prior  ----------
x_prev = x0(:);          % ensure column vector
P_prev = P0;

for k = 1:N
    % ------ Prediction step ------
    x_prior = A * x_prev;
    P_prior = A * P_prev * A.' + Q;

    % Save 1-step prediction
    x_pred(:,k)   = x_prior;
    P_pred(:,:,k) = P_prior;

    % ------ Update step ------
    S = C * P_prior * C.' + R;          % innovation covariance
    Kk = P_prior * C.' / S;             % Kalman gain (numerically stable)
    innov = z(:,k) - C * x_prior;       % measurement residual

    x_post = x_prior + Kk * innov;      % filtered estimate
    P_post = (eye(n) - Kk * C) * P_prior;

    % Save results
    x_filt(:,k)   = x_post;
    P_filt(:,:,k) = P_post;
    K(:,:,k)      = Kk;

    % prepare for next iteration
    x_prev = x_post;
    P_prev = P_post;
end
end % ---------------------------------------------------- end function
```

How to use it
--------------

Example: scalar position sensor that observes position while the true state is `[pos; vel]` and we assume a constant-velocity model:

```
% ------- Build the model -------
dt = 1;                         % sample time
A  = [1 dt;                     % [pos_k] = [1 dt] [pos_k-1] + w_k
      0  1];                    % [vel_k]   [0  1] [vel_k-1]
C  = [1 0];                     % we measure position only
Q  = 0.01 * eye(2);             % small process noise
R  = 0.5;                       % measurement noise variance

% ------- Generate a fake trajectory and noisy measurements --------
N  = 60;                              % number of samples
x_true = zeros(2,N);
z      = zeros(1,N);
x_true(:,1) = [0; 1];                 % start at pos=0, vel=1
for k=2:N
    x_true(:,k) = A*x_true(:,k-1) + mvnrnd([0;0], Q).';
end
z = C*x_true + sqrt(R)*randn(1,N);    % position measurements

% ------- Run the filter --------
x0 = [0;0];              % prior mean
P0 = 100*eye(2);         % vague prior covariance
[xf, Pf] = kalman_sequence(z, A, C, Q, R, x0, P0);

% ------- Plot -------
t = 0:dt:dt*(N-1);
subplot(2,1,1)
plot(t, x_true(1,:), 'k-', t, z, 'rx', t, xf(1,:), 'b-')
legend('true pos','meas','est pos'); xlabel('time'); ylabel('position')

subplot(2,1,2)
plot(t, x_true(2,:), 'k-', t, xf(2,:), 'b-')
legend('true vel','est vel'); xlabel('time'); ylabel('velocity')
```

That’s all you need for a basic Kalman filter in GNU Octave.  
If you later want smoothing (RTS or similar) just keep the saved `A, x_pred, P_pred, x_filt, P_filt` and run a backward pass—those few extra lines fit neatly on top of the code above.

instruction: can one discovery what was typed in a mechanical keyboard from the audio captured by the microphone?
output:
Short answer  
Yes—under the right circumstances an eavesdropper can infer a surprising amount of what was typed on a mechanical (and even a laptop) keyboard from nothing more than the sound captured by a nearby microphone.  Several academic groups have demonstrated attacks that recover 60-95 % of the keys, and some malware authors have begun to explore the technique.  It is not magic, but a side-channel analysis problem: keys make slightly different sounds and are pressed in language-dependent patterns that a computer can learn and exploit.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Why it works
────────────────────────────────────────
1.1  Per-key acoustic “fingerprints”  
• Mechanical keys do not all strike the plate at exactly the same angle or with identical travel. The vibration pattern that reaches the microphone therefore depends on the key’s physical position and the typist’s finger.  
• Differences are small (≈0.5–3 dB and a few hundred micro-seconds of timing), but a classifier can pick them out.

1.2  Timing shapes words  
Even if the attacker cannot tell every key acoustically, the time intervals form patterns that a language model can map to probable words (“th”“he” spacing, double-letter pauses, etc.).

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  What has been shown in the lab
────────────────────────────────────────
Asonov & Agrawal (2004) – 80 % accuracy after 20 min of labelled training on the same keyboard.  
Zhuang, Zhou & Tygar (2005) – 90 %+ on a variety of keyboards using an n-gram language model.  
Berger et al. (2016) – “When Malware Listens”: malware on the victim PC used the built-in mic, achieved ≈91 % top-5 accuracy (i.e., correct key in five guesses).  
University of Durham / UK (2023) – using a common Zoom microphone trace, a CNN paired with GPT-like language modelling got 93 % word-level accuracy on a MacBook Pro keyboard.

Typical experimental conditions  
• Distance: 15 cm–5 m (mechanical keyboards are loud)  
• Microphone: laptop mic, smartphone mic, or an external shotgun mic  
• Training: 50–300 labelled keystrokes, sometimes just 10 lines of “the quick brown fox…”

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Practical limitations
────────────────────────────────────────
• Need for training data.  Highest accuracies require at least some recording of the target typing known text on the same keyboard/mic combo.  
• Typist variability.  If two people share a keyboard the model usually needs per-typist retraining.  
• Noise.  Music, speech, or a fan near the mic degrades classification quickly.  
• Cheap rubber-dome or scissor-switch boards are quieter and more uniform than clicky MX Blues; accuracy falls to 40–60 % unless the mic is close.  
• Remote compression.  VoIP codecs (Zoom, Teams, Skype) low-pass and quantise the signal, but attacks have still worked over them when typing is fairly loud.

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Attack workflow
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Record: malware, phone on the desk, smart speaker, Zoom call …  
2. Segment: detect keystroke onsets via energy spike.  
3. Extract features: MFCCs, wavelet packets, or raw waveform to deep net.  
4. Classify each keystroke.  (SVM, random forest, CNN, transformer.)  
5. Language decode: run an n-gram or large-language-model search to turn the noisy key stream into the most likely text.

────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Countermeasures
────────────────────────────────────────
Hardware  
• Use quieter keys or dampers (O-rings, silicone pads, “silent” switches).  
• Type on a desk mat to cut chassis resonance.  
• Move mics away from the keyboard or point cardioid patterns away.

Environmental  
• Add masking noise: music, white noise generator, “keyboard chatter” loop at low volume.  
• During sensitive entry (passwords) switch to an on-screen or touch keyboard.

Software/procedural  
• Randomly reorder or delay password characters (some password managers do this).  
• Disable / cover unused microphones; give conferencing apps only push-to-talk permission.  
• Encrypt the typing event itself (e.g., secure password dialogs) — it does nothing to the acoustic channel, but limits the value of partial recovery.

Defensive research  
• “Keytap” noise-shaping: play a short burst of synthetic key-click for every key to drown out real differences.  
• Real-time noise addition by the audio driver when the keyboard is active.

────────────────────────────────────────
6.  Bottom line
────────────────────────────────────────
Mechanical keyboards are acoustically “loud” and non-uniform enough that machine-learning attackers can, with some training data and a reasonably clear recording, reconstruct most of what was typed.  The attack is not flawless and gets harder in real-world noise or with silent keyboards, but it is practical enough that high-security environments treat keyboard sounds as a side channel to be controlled.

instruction: how do you flash a Corne keyboard that has VIA installed
output:
Below is a “from-scratch” recipe for (re-)flashing a Corne (crkbd) that already runs a VIA-enabled firmware.  
The same procedure works whether you simply want to refresh the stock firmware, build your own layout, or add features and still keep VIA support.

The steps are split into four parts:

0. What you need to know first  
1. Build or download a VIA-enabled firmware file (.hex / .bin / .uf2)  
2. Put each half of the Corne into the bootloader  
3. Flash the file with QMK-Toolbox or the QMK CLI  

────────────────────────────────────────
0.  CONTROLLER & BOOTLOADER CHECKLIST
────────────────────────────────────────
Corne kits are usually built with one of these controllers:

• ATMega32u4 “Pro Micro” compatible boards – bootloader is Caterina (same as Arduino-Leonardo) or sometimes QMK-DFU or BootloaderHID.  
• nice!nano / nRFMicro (nRF52840) – uses a UF2 bootloader.  
• RP2040-based controllers (Elite-Pi, nice!nano v2) – also use UF2.  

Below I describe the common ATMega32u4 route first, then the UF2 route in a short add-on.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  GET A VIA-ENABLED FIRMWARE FILE
────────────────────────────────────────
Option A – use the ready-made default
  1. Go to https://github.com/qmk/qmk_firmware/releases/latest
  2. Download `crkbd_rev1_default_via.hex` (or `crkbd_rev1_legacy_default_via.hex` if you built the “Legacy” PCB that still uses I2C).

Option B – compile your own with the QMK CLI
  1. Install QMK (one-time):
        python3 -m pip install qmk
        qmk setup
  2. Build the VIA keymap:
        qmk compile -kb crkbd/rev1 -km via          # serial (recommended)
        qmk compile -kb crkbd/rev1/legacy -km via   # I2C legacy PCB
     The compiled file will appear in `qmk_firmware/.build/` as something like  
     `crkbd_rev1_via.hex`.

Tip: If you want your own layout but still want VIA support, start from the `via`
keymap (`qmk new-keymap -kb crkbd/rev1 -km mylayout`) and keep  
`VIA_ENABLE = yes` in rules.mk.

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  PUT THE KEYBOARD INTO THE BOOTLOADER
────────────────────────────────────────
You have to flash EACH HALF once, because each half owns its own
microcontroller.

Method 1 – use the on-board reset tact-switch  
• Unplug the USB cable from the half you’re about to flash.  
• Hold the reset button (on the underside near the controller) while plugging the USB cable in.  
• The board appears to the computer as a bootloader device for ~8 s.

Method 2 – Boot-magic key combo (only if it still works in the running firmware)  
• Unplug → hold Esc+Space (-L/h left half, ‑R/h right half) → plug in USB.

If the bootloader is QMK-DFU or Caterina you’ll see something like:

  “Device connected: ATm32U4-DFU”  (QMK-DFU)  
  “Arduino Leonardo bootloader (Caterina)” (Caterina)

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  FLASHING
────────────────────────────────────────
Option A – graphical (QMK-Toolbox, Windows/macOS/Linux app)

1. Install QMK-Toolbox from https://qmk.fm/toolbox  
2. Start it, tick “Auto-flash”, and load the .hex you prepared.  
3. Follow step 2 above to reset one half – Toolbox will detect the bootloader,
   flash automatically, verify and reset the half back to normal firmware.  
4. Repeat for the second half.

Option B – command-line (QMK CLI, already installed in step 1B)

# For Caterina (most Pro Micros)
qmk flash -kb crkbd/rev1 -km via -bl caterina

# For QMK-DFU
qmk flash -kb crkbd/rev1 -km via -bl dfu

When the CLI prints “*** Looking for USB-DFU device … Timeout 30s”,
perform the reset sequence for the half you are flashing.  
Do the same for the second half.

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  TEST IN VIA
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Open the VIA desktop application (or https://usevia.app in Chrome/Edge).  
2. The halves enumerate as “Corne-LEFT” and “Corne-RIGHT”; VIA will merge them
   logically into one keyboard.  
3. Start remapping, create layers, etc. Your changes are saved instantly in the
   EEPROM and survive power-cycles.

────────────────────────────────────────
▌ NOTES & TROUBLESHOOTING ▐
────────────────────────────────────────
• You will not “lose VIA” by reflashing as long as the firmware was built with
  `VIA_ENABLE = yes` (the `via` keymap already has this).  

• If QMK-Toolbox shows a yellow “No device available” message, the board is not
  in bootloader mode. Re-do the reset/plug-in step.

• If flashing fails with “Device or resource busy” on Linux, add your user to
  the `dialout` group or use `sudo`.

• You can safely have different keymaps on the left and right halves (useful
  for mirrored number row, etc.) as long as both were compiled with
  `SPLIT_KEYBOARD = yes` and `VIA_ENABLE = yes`.

────────────────────────────────────────
★  UF2-BASED CONTROLLERS (nice!nano, RP2040) ★
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Build a .uf2 file instead of .hex:
     west build -b nice_nano_v2 -- -DZMK_CONFIG=path/to/config -DVIA_ENABLED=y
2. Double-tap the reset pin; a USB mass-storage drive appears.
3. Copy the `.uf2` onto the drive. The board reboots automatically.
4. Repeat for the second half, then open VIA as usual.

────────────────────────────────────────
That’s it—your Corne is now running the fresh VIA firmware!

how do i get the number of unresponsive pods in a cluster using PromQL
output:
In the Kubernetes metrics that kube-state-metrics exports, a pod is considered “Ready” when  

    kube_pod_status_ready{condition="true"} == 1

For every pod the same metric is exported once more with `condition="false"`.  
Therefore a pod is “un-ready / unresponsive” when  

    kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"} == 1

(keep in mind that a “Succeeded” pod is also not ready, but usually you do not want to alert on those).

A concise PromQL expression that returns **one number: how many pods in the whole cluster are currently un-ready** is:

```
count(
  kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"} == 1
  and ignoring(condition)
      kube_pod_status_phase{phase!~"Succeeded"} == 1
)
```

What the query does  
1. `kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"} == 1` – select the series whose value is 1 (i.e. pod is not ready).  
2. `kube_pod_status_phase{phase!~"Succeeded"} == 1` – keep only the pods that have **not** finished successfully (drops Completed Jobs etc.).  
3. The `and ignoring(condition)` join makes sure we are talking about the same pod/namespace labels.  
4. `count( … )` turns the individual per-pod series into a single number.

Variants / refinements

• If you run several clusters and have a label such as `cluster`, get a per-cluster breakdown:

```
count by (cluster) (
  kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"} == 1
  and ignoring(condition)
      kube_pod_status_phase{phase!~"Succeeded"} == 1
)
```

• Only alert when a pod has been un-ready for at least 5 minutes:

```
count(
  max_over_time(
    (kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"} == 1
     and ignoring(condition)
         kube_pod_status_phase{phase!~"Succeeded"} == 1)[5m]
  )
)
```

• If you want to include pods that are stuck in `Pending` but never reached Ready, replace the phase filter with `phase=~"Pending|Running|Unknown"` accordingly.

Those queries give you the live number of “unresponsive” (not-Ready) pods in your cluster using pure PromQL.

""" bot_message = bot_logic(user_message) chat_history = chat_history + [(user_message, bot_message)] return chat_history, "" # second value clears the input box # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3. Build the UI # ------------------------------------------------------------------ with gr.Blocks(title="Simple Gradio Chatbot") as demo: gr.Markdown( """ # 🗨️ Simple Chatbot Demo Type a message and press **Enter** (or click *Send*). """ ) chatbot = gr.Chatbot(height=300) with gr.Row(): txt = gr.Textbox( show_label=False, placeholder="Ask me anything...", container=False, ) clear_btn = gr.Button("Clear") # Wire everything together txt.submit(respond, [txt, chatbot], [chatbot, txt]) clear_btn.click(lambda: [], None, chatbot, queue=False) gr.Markdown( """ Built with Gradio.
