A monad is not a thing you “use once in a while”, it is a small vocabulary that lets the compiler, the library writer and you agree on how to run a sequence of actions that live in some sort of “context” ( ≈ effect, possibility, environment, …).  
It is nothing more (and nothing less) than

    class Monad m where
      (>>=)  :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b   -- called “bind”
      return :: a -> m a                   -- called “pure” in newer code

plus three laws (identity × 2, associativity). When a type supplies those two functions and obeys the laws the compiler, library code and your own code can all combine those computations in the same uniform way.

Below is an intuition-first tour that avoids category-theory jargon and uses every-day analogies.

---------------------------------------------------
1. The KEYWORDS in English
---------------------------------------------------

• “return” (or “pure”):  
  “I have an ordinary value and I want to put it inside the context.”

• “>>=”  (“bind” or “and-then”):   
  “I already have a value inside the context.  
   Give me a function that makes the next step (possibly producing another context)  
   and I’ll glue the two steps together, keeping the context under control.”

If you know these two verbs you can already read Haskell’s do-notation:

    do  x <- action1     -- run action1, take its plain result as ‘x’
        action2 x        -- next action, may or may not use x
        action3          -- etc.

All ‘actionᵢ’ are *in the same monad*, therefore they combine with (>>=) under the hood.

---------------------------------------------------
2. 5′ real-life analogies
---------------------------------------------------

A) Maybe  :  “The gift-box that might be empty”
-------------------------------------------------
• Context = “might fail / be missing”.
• return  = put your value in a gift-box (“Just x”).
• (>>=)   = open the box; if there is a gift call the next step, if not stop now.

Real life story  
   You’re cooking. First fetch eggs from the fridge; they might be missing.  
   If there are eggs, break them into a bowl; that might fail too.  
   If that worked, whisk them, etc.  
   Each step *may fail*, but you never have to write “if missing then abort” each time—the monad does that.

Haskell:

    safeHead :: [a] -> Maybe a
    safeHead []     = Nothing
    safeHead (x:_)  = Just x

    firstCharOfFirstWord :: String -> Maybe Char
    firstCharOfFirstWord s =
      safeHead (words s)      >>= \w  ->
      safeHead w              >>= \c  ->
      return c

(do-notation version is one line shorter)

B) IO  :  “A to-do list for the outside world”
---------------------------------------------
• Context = “performing side-effects in order”.
• return  = no real effect, just yield a value.
• (>>=)   = sequence two effects so that the second may depend on the first.

Analogy  
  Think of an IO value as a *recipe card*: “If somebody picks me up and runs me, I’ll interact with the keyboard, file system, network, etc., and in the end hand you a pure value.”

    echoTwice :: IO ()
    echoTwice = do
        putStrLn "Type something:"
        line <- getLine
        putStrLn line
        putStrLn line

Recipes stay pure data until main; the runtime is the cook.

C) List  :  “Non-deterministic choice / many possible realities”
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Context = “there may be zero, one or many possible results”.
• return  = create a singleton list.
• (>>=)   = for every earlier possibility, run the next step, gather all possibilities.

Analogy  
  You are designing combinations of clothes: pick one T-shirt, one pair of jeans, one pair of shoes.  
  Each pick is a list; bind does all cross-products.

    outfits = ["red","blue"]   >>= \shirt ->
              ["black","gray"] >>= \pants ->
              return (shirt, pants)
    -- result: [("red","black"),("red","gray"),("blue","black"),("blue","gray")]

D) Either e  :  “A computation that may raise a *typed* error”
--------------------------------------------------------------
Same idea as Maybe but the error carries information; think “printed receipt explaining why”.

E) State s  :  “A notepad you pass around invisibly”
----------------------------------------------------
• Context keeps some internal state.  
• return produces a value while leaving the notepad untouched.  
• bind passes the notepad from one step to the next.

Analogy  
  Filling bureaucratic forms: every clerk receives the folder, scribbles something and forwards it. State monad hides the explicit passing.

---------------------------------------------------
3. How the **laws** match the analogies
---------------------------------------------------

Left identity   return a >>= f  ≡  f a  
  “If you wrap a value then immediately unwrap it to hand to the next step, that’s no different from just doing the next step.”

Right identity  m >>= return  ≡  m  
  “If after some contextual work you do nothing except wrap the result, you haven’t changed the plan.”

Associativity   (m >>= f) >>= g  ≡  m >>= (\x -> f x >>= g)  
  “Ordering of parentheses doesn’t matter; the sequence of steps is the same.”  
  For recipes, gift-boxes, notepads etc. that is exactly how we expect them to behave.

---------------------------------------------------
4. One longer realistic example (Maybe + IO)
---------------------------------------------------

Suppose we read an environment variable that *may* be absent, parse it as an Int, and either keep going or fall back to a default.

    import System.Environment (lookupEnv)
    import Text.Read (readMaybe)

    getPort :: IO Int
    getPort = do
      m <- lookupEnv "PORT"                   -- IO (Maybe String)
      let mPort = m          >>= readMaybe    -- Maybe Int
      return (fromMaybe 8080 mPort)

Here we used (>>=) twice in two different monads: the outer do-block sequences IO, and inside we used (>>=) of Maybe to chain “value present” and “parsable”.

---------------------------------------------------
5. Take-away checklist
---------------------------------------------------

1. A monad is just two operations + 3 laws; no metaphysics.
2. “return” = put a value in the context; “>>=” = and-then using that value.
3. The context could be:
      – missing / error      (Maybe, Either e)  
      – many results         ([ ])  
      – side effects recipe  (IO)  
      – hidden state         (State s)  
      – logging, randomness, continuation, …
4. Because all those share the same interface we get:
      • do-notation  
      • generic libraries (e.g. Monad transformers, concurrency libs, Parsec)  
      • ability to compose exotic effects without ad-hoc plumbing.
5. When you meet an unfamiliar monad, ask:  
      “What is the context?”  
      “What does return mean here?”  
      “What extra rules does bind follow?”

Answer those three questions and the monad is tamed.

instruction: I have heard the phrase, "Programs as data", in speaking about computer science and functional programming in Scheme. Explain this concept using Scheme to a computer science student. You are a senior researcher in computer science at MIT. Take a step by step approach using examples and building on prior examples, until the culmination of the lecture is reached.
output:
──────────────────────────────────────
MIT CS Research Colloquium  
Speaker: Dr. ________ (Computer Science & AI Lab)  
Topic: “Programs as Data: From Atoms to Meta-Circuits in Scheme”  
Audience: Junior/Senior CS majors who have had one semester of Scheme or Racket
──────────────────────────────────────

0. Why this matters  
   • Compilers, optimizers, macro systems, DSLs, theorem provers, and AI planners all treat *programs* as *manipulable information*.  
   • Lisp/Scheme gives us a lab bench where the gap between “the thing that runs” and “the thing we compute on” is only a parenthesis apart.

We will climb seven rungs.  Each rung uses the previous one.

RUNG 1 Pure Data  
–––––––––––––––  
Scheme’s primitive aggregate is the list.  A list is written with parentheses:

    '(+ 3 4)      ; the *data* (list + 3 4), length = 3

The leading apostrophe (quote) prevents evaluation; it tells the reader “treat what follows as data”.

    > (car '(+ 3 4))      ⇒  +          ; first element
    > (cadr '(+ 3 4))     ⇒  3

Observation: The *shape* of Scheme code is itself a list.  
Consequently, *any* expression you could hand‐write, you can also build or tear apart with ordinary list code.

RUNG 2 The Thin Membrane: eval  
––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
If we remove the quote—or explicitly ask for evaluation—we cross the membrane from data to executable program.

    > (eval '(+ 3 4) (interaction-environment))
    7

The second argument records the environment in whose namespace evaluation occurs (needed by R5RS standard).

So, we can slide lists back and forth across the membrane:

    (define (compute n)
      (eval `(,n ,n ,n) (interaction-environment)))

This small example is silly, but it demonstrates the *mechanism*: produce a list, ask the interpreter to run it.

RUNG 3 Building Code at Run Time  
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Let’s generate a polynomial evaluator accessorily.

    ;; Return a procedure that computes ax^2 + bx + c
    (define (make-quad a b c)
      (let ((expr `(lambda (x) (+ (* ,a x x) (* ,b x) ,c))))
        (eval expr (interaction-environment))))

    > (define f (make-quad 2 0 -5))   ; builds lambda, compiles then returns
    > (f 3)
    13

Notes  
  • backquote (`) quasi-quotes a template; commas splice in run-time values.  
  • We purposely *manufactured* code from ordinary numbers and symbols, then *ran* it.

RUNG 4 Reflection inside the Language  
––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Because *code == lists*, we can write a function that prints its own source or modifies itself:

    (define (self-echo)
      (let ((me '(lambda () (display 'self-echo) (newline))))
        (eval me (interaction-environment))))

This is not just theoretical curiosity: reflection supports interactive debugging, persistence, dynamic instrumentation, etc.

RUNG 5 Macros: Compile-Time Code-as-Data  
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Macros let us treat programs as data *before* the evaluator runs—during the read/compile stage.  
Example: a compact “unless” macro.

    (define-syntax unless
      (syntax-rules ()
        ((unless test body ...)
         (if (not test) (begin body ...)))))

Now `unless` exists as a new *syntactic* form, although at run time it is gone—it was *transformed* into `if`/`begin`.

Macro expansion phases  
  1. Program read → lists.  
  2. Macro expander rewrites lists by pattern matching.  
  3. Resulting lists are compiled/evaluated.  

Therefore macros are a disciplined, hygienic interface for the “eval trick” but done ahead of time, so no run-time overhead or security risk.

RUNG 6 Meta-Circular Evaluation (MCE)  
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Let’s stand the whole interpreter inside itself.  We’ll sketch the classic *metacircular evaluator* (SICP §4.1):

    (define (my-eval exp env)
      (cond
        ((symbol? exp)   (lookup exp env))
        ((not (pair? exp)) exp)        ; self-evaluating
        (else
         (case (car exp)
           ((quote)  (cadr exp))
           ((if)     (if (my-eval (cadr exp) env)
                         (my-eval (caddr exp) env)
                         (my-eval (cadddr exp) env)))
           ((lambda) (make-procedure (cadr exp) (cddr exp) env))
           (else     (apply-procedure (my-eval (car exp) env)
                                      (map (lambda (arg) (my-eval arg env))
                                           (cdr exp))
                                      env)))))

Here, `exp` is yesterday’s *data* list, but today we interpret it as a *program* by recursively walking its structure.

Implications  
  • Bootstrapping: you can write most of Scheme in Scheme.  
  • Extensibility: tailor evaluators for static analysis, logging, gradual typing, probabilistic semantics, etc.  
  • Educational: demystifies “language implementation”.

RUNG 7 Whole-Program Synthesis (Putting It All Together)  
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Suppose we want an optimizer that recognizes constant sub-expressions.

    (define (const-fold exp)
      (cond
        ((pair? exp)
         (match exp
           [(+ x y) (let ((x' (const-fold x))
                          (y' (const-fold y)))
                      (if (and (number? x') (number? y'))
                          (+ x' y')
                          `( + ,x' ,y')))]
           [( * x y)  ...] ; similar
           [_           (map const-fold exp)]))
        (else exp)))

    (define (compile-and-run e)
      (eval (const-fold e) (interaction-environment)))

    > (compile-and-run '(* (+ 2 3) (+ 4 5)))
    45
    > (compile-and-run '(* x (+ 2 3)))
    ; if x unbound → error, but we still folded (+ 2 3) to 5

We just wrote, in about 20 lines, the core of a compile-time algebraic optimizer.  No separate parser; no Abstract Syntax Tree class hierarchy; just list munging.

──────────────────────────────────────
Key Take-aways  
1. Homoiconicity: code “looks” like data—specifically Scheme lists.  
2. Quote/unquote (’, `, ,) plus `eval` form the portal between data world and execution world.  
3. Macros move that crossing to an earlier (safer) phase.  
4. Once programs are data, you can analyze, transform, synthesize, or even interpret them with astonishing brevity.  
5. This viewpoint scales—from a single `eval` call, through hygienic macros, up to full interpreters, compilers, and DSL ecosystems.

Recommended Projects  
• Write a macro that adds algebraic pattern matching to Scheme.  
• Implement a partial evaluator for simple arithmetic Scheme.  
• Build a Scheme subset in <100 lines using an MCE, then extend it with lazy evaluation.  

Further Reading  
• Abelson & Sussman, “Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs” (ch. 4).  
• Wand & Friedman, “Essentials of Programming Languages”.  
• Shriram Krishnamurthi, “Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation”.

Thank you.  Questions welcome.

instruction: When I buy groceries, I like to get an odd number of coins for change. For example, when  I get 20 cents, I like 2 coins of 5 cents, and 1 coin of 10 cents. If I buy 3 pears at 25 cents each, and 1 lemon for 10 cents, and I pay with a 1 dollar bill, which coins will I get?
output:
The bill comes to  
3 pears × 25 ¢ = 75 ¢  
1 lemon × 10 ¢ = 10 ¢  
Total = 85 ¢  

You pay with 100 ¢, so the change is 15 ¢.

To receive an odd number of coins you must avoid the 10 ¢ + 5 ¢ combination (2 coins, even).  
The next smallest odd-coin possibility is 5 ¢ + 5 ¢ + 5 ¢ = 15 ¢.

So you will get three 5-cent coins (three nickels) as your change.

instruction: I'd like to design a SQL schema where the whole schema can be versioned without sacrificing referential integrity.
output:
Below is a pattern that lets you keep every row in every table in as many “editions” (versions, revisions, snapshots …) as you like while the database itself continues to enforce every foreign-key rule.

The idea in one sentence:
“Whatever is part of a primary key must start with   revision_id.”

-------------------------------------------------------
1.  A table that enumerates the revisions
-------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE revision
( revision_id     bigint   GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY  PRIMARY KEY
, parent_id       bigint   NULL
, branch_name     text     NOT NULL
, created_at      timestamptz DEFAULT now()
, author          text
, comment         text
, FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES revision(revision_id)
);

•  One row per snapshot (v1, v2, v3 …).  
•  parent_id lets you implement branching or simply say “v3 is a copy of v2”.

-------------------------------------------------------
2.  Version every business table
-------------------------------------------------------
Suppose you normally have

   product
   ( product_id  pk
   , name
   , price )

   order_header
   ( order_id    pk
   , customer_id fk → customer.customer_id
   , …)

   order_line
   ( order_id    fk → order_header.order_id
   , line_no
   , product_id  fk → product.product_id
   , qty
   , PRIMARY KEY(order_id,line_no) )

Turn every one of them into a “revisioned” table:

CREATE TABLE product
( revision_id   bigint   NOT NULL
, product_id    bigint   NOT NULL
, name          text
, price         numeric(12,2)
, PRIMARY KEY (revision_id, product_id)
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id)          REFERENCES revision(revision_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE order_header
( revision_id   bigint   NOT NULL
, order_id      bigint   NOT NULL
, customer_id   bigint   NOT NULL
, …
, PRIMARY KEY (revision_id, order_id)
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id)          REFERENCES revision(revision_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id, customer_id)
                    REFERENCES customer(revision_id, customer_id)
);

CREATE TABLE order_line
( revision_id   bigint   NOT NULL
, order_id      bigint   NOT NULL
, line_no       int      NOT NULL
, product_id    bigint   NOT NULL
, qty           int
, PRIMARY KEY (revision_id, order_id, line_no)
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id)           REFERENCES revision(revision_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id, order_id)
                    REFERENCES order_header(revision_id, order_id)
, FOREIGN KEY (revision_id, product_id)
                    REFERENCES product(revision_id, product_id)
);

Rules:

1. revision_id is the first column of every PK.  
2. Every FK repeats that revision_id as its first column.  
3. Each table also has a FK back to revision so you can cascade-delete a whole snapshot with a single DELETE FROM revision WHERE revision_id = …;

Because the foreign keys include revision_id, the database can never join rows from two different revisions – referential integrity holds inside each snapshot automatically.

-------------------------------------------------------
3.  Working with the data
-------------------------------------------------------
Creating a new snapshot

INSERT INTO revision(branch_name,comment) VALUES
  ('main','start of sprint 17')  RETURNING revision_id;

Assume it returns 42.

Now copy (only) the rows you need into revision 42, change them there, and leave older revisions intact:

INSERT INTO product   (revision_id,product_id,name,price)
SELECT 42, product_id, name, price
FROM   product
WHERE  revision_id = 41;      -- previous snapshot

UPDATE product
SET    price = price*1.05
WHERE  revision_id = 42
AND    product_id = 123;

You can automate that “copy-on-write” with triggers, but a plain-SQL copy works too.

Querying a snapshot

SELECT p.product_id, p.name, p.price
FROM   product  p
JOIN   revision r ON r.revision_id = p.revision_id
WHERE  r.revision_id = 42
ORDER  BY p.product_id;

A convenience view so applications don’t have to add the WHERE clause:

CREATE VIEW current_product AS
SELECT *
FROM   product
WHERE  revision_id = (SELECT max(revision_id) FROM revision);

Just change the view’s definition when you want the app to look at a different snapshot.

-------------------------------------------------------
4.  Optional refinements
-------------------------------------------------------
•  Partitioning by revision_id (PostgreSQL native partitioning, MySQL partitions, etc.) keeps big histories fast and makes dropping an old revision a single ALTER TABLE … DROP PARTITION.  

•  Unique across all revisions: if product_id must stay unique no matter the revision, add a generated “global” id or a partial/filtered unique index. Otherwise the same product_id can appear in many revisions.

•  Branching/merging: parent_id in revision lets you record ancestry; merging is an application-level operation that simply populates a new revision from two parents and resolves conflicts.

•  Readability: create RULEs or INSTEAD-OF triggers on the views so applications that only care about “the current data” can still do INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE without even knowing revision_id exists.

-------------------------------------------------------
5.  Result
-------------------------------------------------------
•  Every single SQL foreign-key constraint the original schema had is still there.  
•  You can insert a brand-new version of the whole database without touching—therefore without endangering—the older ones.  
•  A revision can be dropped, backed up, restored or replicated as one logical unit (simply act on the row in table revision).  

In short, prepend revision_id to every primary and foreign key, keep a master table “revision” and the whole schema is now fully versioned while 100 % of referential integrity is enforced by the RDBMS itself.

instruction: Give me a medical description of an inflamed joint, its presentation, emergency referral criteria, and common causes.
output:
Inflamed joint – medical overview

1. Pathophysiological description  
   • Synovitis: hyperaemia and oedema of the synovial lining, infiltration by neutrophils / lymphocytes, fibrin deposition.  
   • Effusion: inflammatory exudate (cell–rich, protein-rich) distends the capsule.  
   • Secondary changes: peri-articular oedema, capsular stretch, irritation of nociceptors → pain; reflex muscle spasm; loss of articular cartilage with sustained inflammation.  

2. Typical clinical presentation  
   Local findings  
   • Pain – usually constant, worse with movement or weight-bearing, night ache common.  
   • Swelling – fluctuant (effusion) or firm (synovial thickening).  
   • Warmth – detectable with dorsum of hand; may be subtle in deep joints.  
   • Erythema – best seen in superficial joints (knee, ankle, MCP, PIP).  
   • Loss of function – limp, reduced grip, limited ROM, pseudo-locking.  
   Systemic / associated features  
   • Fever, rigors, malaise (sepsis, crystalline flare, reactive arthritis).  
   • Skin lesions (psoriasis, meningococcaemia, gonococcal pustules).  
   • Eye pain (uveitis), diarrhoea/urethritis (reactive).  
   • Tophi or calcific nodules (gout / CPPD).  

3. Red-flag (emergency) referral criteria  
   URGENT SAME-DAY OR ED REFERRAL if any of the following are present  
   • Suspected septic arthritis  
     – Single acutely hot, swollen joint with severe pain ± systemic upset  
     – Fever >38 °C, tachycardia, rigors, hypotension, altered mental state  
     – Immunosuppressed, prosthetic joint, intravenous drug use, recent surgery/injection  
   • Suspected acute haemarthrosis  
     – Large tense effusion after trauma or in anticoagulated patient (INR >3)  
   • Neurovascular compromise / impending compartment syndrome around the joint  
     – Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, paraesthesia, pallor, pulselessness  
   • Unreduced dislocation or grossly unstable fracture around the joint  
   • Rapidly progressive crystal flare not responding to oral therapy and unable to mobilise  
   • Suspicion of necrotising fasciitis or cellulitis spreading beyond the joint area.  

   24–48 H REFERRAL (early specialist review)  
   • New-onset inflammatory arthritis of ≥1 joint ≥6 weeks (possible RA, psoriatic, JIA).  
   • Recurrent mono-arthritis with unclear diagnosis.  
   • Polyarthritis with systemic features (rash, weight loss, anaemia, elevated inflammatory markers).  

4. Common aetiologies of an inflamed joint  
   Infective  
   • Bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus (most common), β-haemolytic streptococci, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Gram-negatives (elderly, IV-drug users), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (sub-acute).  
   • Viral: Parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C, HIV, rubella, mumps, chikungunya, SARS-CoV-2.  
   • Spirochaetal: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme).  
   Crystal-induced  
   • Gout – monosodium urate crystals.  
   • Pseudogout / CPPD – calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate.  
   • Basic calcium phosphate (Milwaukee shoulder).  
   Auto-immune / inflammatory  
   • Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis.  
   • Systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective-tissue disease, vasculitides (eg, polyarteritis nodosa).  
   Reactive / post-infectious  
   • Post-GI (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia) or GU (Chlamydia) infection.  
   Degenerative with secondary inflammation  
   • Osteoarthritis flare (synovitis from cartilage wear debris).  
   Traumatic / mechanical  
   • Acute soft-tissue injury with haemarthrosis, intra-articular fracture, meniscal tear.  
   Metabolic / other  
   • Haemophilia or anticoagulation-related haemarthrosis.  
   • Sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome – ankle peri-arthritis).  
   • Malignancy: leukaemic or metastatic infiltration (rare).  

Key take-home points  
• Any acutely hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise—arrange same-day assessment, joint aspiration and culture.  
• Crystal arthritis, trauma and flare of chronic inflammatory disease are the next most frequent causes.  
• A thorough history, focused examination and basic tests (aspiration, FBC, CRP, blood cultures, X-ray, polarised microscopy) will usually establish the diagnosis or guide urgent referral.

There are two security problems in this contract, both caused by a misunderstanding of how “private” works in Solidity and by a missing-access-control bug.

1. Anyone can change the password  
   setPassword() is declared external and contains no ownership check.  
   ```solidity
   function setPassword(string memory newPassword) external {
       s_password = newPassword;   // ← no “if (msg.sender == s_owner)” test
   }
   ```  
   Any address can therefore overwrite the password, which completely defeats the purpose of keeping an owner-only secret.

2. The “private” keyword does **not** keep the password secret  
   Marking the state variable  
   ```solidity
   string private s_password;
   ```  
   as private only prevents other Solidity contracts from reading it via a public getter.  
   Every value stored on-chain is publicly accessible with `eth_getStorageAt`, a block-explorer, or a simple script. Anybody can read the raw storage slot that contains the string and recover the password.

Combined, these flaws mean:
• An attacker can freely overwrite the password.  
• Even if the owner resets it, the attacker (or anyone else) can still read it directly from the blockchain.

Fix
```
function setPassword(string calldata newPassword) external {
    if (msg.sender != s_owner) revert PasswordStore__NotOwner();
    s_password = newPassword;
}
```
and understand that truly secret data must never be stored on-chain; it should be kept off-chain or encrypted with a key that never appears on-chain.

My situation is this: I’m setting up a server running at home Ubuntu to run an email server and a few other online services. As we all know, for my email to work reliably and not get blocked I need to have an unchanging public IP address. Due to my circumstances I am not able to get a static IP address through my ISP or change ISPs at the moment.

The solution I have found is to buy a 4G SIM card with a static IP (from an ISP that offers that), which I can then use with a USB dongle. However this 4G connection costs me substantially per MB to use.

But. Mail is the only server that needs a static IP address. For everything else using my home network connection and updating my DNS records with DDNS would be fine. I have tested this setup previously for other services and it has worked.

So. I was wondering. Would it in theory be possible to: connect the server to two network interfaces at the same time and route traffic depending on destination port. I.e. all outgoing connections to ports 25, 465, 587, and possibly 993 should be sent through the 4G dongle interface (enx344b50000000) and all other connections sent over eth0. Similarly, the server should listen for incoming connections on the same ports on enx344b50000000 and listen on all other ports (if allowed by ufw) on eth0.

I would then need DNS records from mail.mydomain.tld —> <4g static public IP> and mydomain.tld —> <home public IP> (updated with DDNS, and NAT configured on my home router).

Computers on the internet would then be able to seamlessly connect to these two IP addresses, not “realising” that they are in fact the same machine, as long as requests to mail.mydomain.tld are always on the above mentioned ports.

Question: Is this possible? Could it be a robust solution that works the way I hope? Would someone be able to help me set it up?

So I thought I would ask about my own specific use case
output:
Yes – a single Linux host can sit on two completely different Internet links and decide “this packet must leave through interface A, that packet through interface B”.  
What you need is

• one additional routing table for the 4 G link  
• one or two policy-routing rules that say “packets that are either marked = 1 or whose source address is the 4 G address must be looked-up in that table”  
• a few iptables (or nftables) rules that put mark = 1 on the packets whose TCP destination ports are 25/465/587/993.

Nothing has to be done in the mail server itself except, optionally, telling it to bind its
outgoing SMTP socket to the 4 G address so that the source address always matches the MX
record.

The recipe below is written for a recent Ubuntu (20.04/22.04) that still uses iptables.
With nftables the ideas are identical, only the syntax differs.

Assumptions
===========

eth0               : your “normal” broadband, DHCP, dynamic public address  
enx344b50000000    : the 4 G dongle, static public address 203.0.113.2, gateway 203.0.113.1

(Replace all addresses, interface names and table numbers with your own.)

Step 1 – create an additional routing table
-------------------------------------------

Echo a name/number pair into /etc/iproute2/rt_tables once:

    echo "200 lte" | sudo tee -a /etc/iproute2/rt_tables

Step 2 – populate that table with the routes that belong to the 4 G link
------------------------------------------------------------------------

    sudo ip route add 203.0.113.0/24 dev enx344b50000000  scope link  table lte
    sudo ip route add default via 203.0.113.1 dev enx344b50000000      table lte

(On reboot you can put the two commands into a systemd-unit or into /etc/rc.local, or use
netplan/network-manager “routing-policy”.)

Step 3 – tell the kernel when to look into that table
-----------------------------------------------------

• for packets that already have the 4 G address as their source  
• for packets that the firewall will later mark “1”

    sudo ip rule add from 203.0.113.2/32 table lte
    sudo ip rule add fwmark 1           table lte

(Nodes are checked top-to-bottom, keep both.)

Step 4 – mark the mail traffic
------------------------------

    # outgoing SMTP
    sudo iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 25  -j MARK --set-mark 1
    # submission / SMTPS
    sudo iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 465 -j MARK --set-mark 1
    sudo iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 587 -j MARK --set-mark 1
    # IMAPS (if you fetch your own mail remotely)
    sudo iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 993 -j MARK --set-mark 1

Save your iptables set (e.g. `iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4`).

Step 5 – relax reverse-path filtering
-------------------------------------

Because incoming packets arrive on one interface and replies can leave on the
other, the strict RPF check must be disabled or weakened:

    sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2    # loose mode
    sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter=2
    echo "net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 2"    | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-rpf.conf
    echo "net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 2"      >> /etc/sysctl.d/90-rpf.conf

Step 6 – mail-server niceties (optional)
----------------------------------------

Postfix:  
    smtp_bind_address = 203.0.113.2

Dovecot: nothing special, it listens on * and the rules above make sure that
connections opened on port 993 from the inside go out through 4 G.

Step 7 – DNS
------------

@ (A / AAAA)            → your dynamic address (updated by DDNS)  
mail.<domain> (A / AAAA) → 203.0.113.2  
MX record                → mail.<domain>

How it works
============

1. Your default route (in table “main”) points to eth0, so all ordinary traffic
   uses the cheap residential link.

2. When Postfix opens an SMTP connection to the outside world (dport 25,465,587)
   the firewall puts mark = 1 on the packet, the kernel matches the
   `ip rule ... fwmark 1 table lte`, therefore looks the route up in table “lte”
   and sends it out through enx344b50000000.

3. Incoming mail from the Internet is addressed to 203.0.113.2; it therefore
   enters through the 4 G interface.  The reply packets naturally have the same
   source address, hit rule “from 203.0.113.2/32 table lte” and leave the same
   way they came.  No asymmetry, no trouble.

Robustness / caveats
====================

• Advanced routing is part of the kernel; once configured it is as reliable as any
  ordinary single-WAN setup.

• Make sure that your 4 G provider really gives you a *public* static address, not
  just a “static private address behind CG-NAT”.

• Turn off any “strict NAT” or ALG in the 4 G device if it can do that.

• Remember that IMAP/POP traffic from your laptop/phone will go through the
  metered 4 G link too.  If that may become expensive, do not include port 993 in
  the iptables list – instead reach the server through the dynamic address when
  you are yourself outside.

• Alternatively, instead of operating your own inbound SMTP you could pay a few
  dollars a month for a relay such as Mailgun, Postmark, etc., but if you prefer
  the “do-it-yourself” approach the configuration above works fine.

That’s all: two links, one server, port-based policy routing – and no more worries
about black-listed dynamic addresses.

instruction: Write a Python function that returns a list of email addresses from a string.
output:
```python
import re

def extract_emails(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """
    Return every e-mail address found in *text*.

    The pattern is intentionally a little stricter than the common
    ‘[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+’ shortcut while still being readable.  
    It accepts most everyday addresses (RFC 5322 “dot-atom” form),
    but it deliberately avoids matching things that are clearly
    not e-mail addresses (e.g. a trailing dot or missing TLD).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> extract_emails(
    ...     "Mail jane_doe@example.co.uk or admin@sub.example.com!  "
    ...     "Fallback: foo.bar+baz@my-domain.io"
    ... )
    ['jane_doe@example.co.uk',
     'admin@sub.example.com',
     'foo.bar+baz@my-domain.io']
    """
    email_rx = re.compile(
        r"""
        [a-zA-Z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+      # local part first atom
        (?:\.[a-zA-Z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+)*   # additional dot-atoms
        @
        [a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?   # first domain label
        (?:\.[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?)*  # sub-domains
        \.[a-zA-Z]{2,}                                      # TLD
        """,
        re.VERBOSE,
    )

    # re.findall returns a list with every match of the entire regex
    return email_rx.findall(text)
```

How it works (in brief)
• `re.VERBOSE` lets us split the pattern across lines and add comments.  
• The local part: one or more “atoms” separated by dots, containing the
  characters that RFC 5322 allows without quoting.  
• The domain part: labels of up to 63 characters, separated by dots,
  ending in a 2+ character ASCII TLD.  
• `re.findall` returns every non-overlapping match, already as strings,
  so the function returns a plain list of addresses.

If you need to de-duplicate, just wrap the call in `set()` or use
`dict.fromkeys` to preserve order:

```python
unique_emails = list(dict.fromkeys(extract_emails(text)))
```

How do you add another IP address on a specific VLAN to a network interface in Linux?
output:
With Linux you treat a VLAN as just another (virtual) interface, so adding an ­additional address is exactly the same as adding a “secondary”/“alias” address to any other interface.

────────────────────────
1.  Make sure the VLAN interface exists
────────────────────────
# modprobe 8021q                         # loads 802.1Q support (usually already loaded)
# ip link add link eth0 name eth0.30 type vlan id 30    # create vlan-30 on eth0
# ip link set eth0.30 up                                # bring it up

(If eth0.30 already shows up in ip link, skip the creation step.)

────────────────────────
2.  Add the extra IP address (runtime)
────────────────────────
# ip addr add 192.168.30.22/24 dev eth0.30

That is immediately active until the next reboot or until the address is deleted with
# ip addr del 192.168.30.22/24 dev eth0.30

────────────────────────
3.  Make it persistent (examples for the common distros)
────────────────────────
A. Debian/Ubuntu (/etc/network/interfaces)
------------------------------------------
auto  eth0.30
iface eth0.30 inet static
        address 192.168.30.10
        netmask 255.255.255.0
        vlan-raw-device eth0
        # add a second address
        up   ip addr add 192.168.30.22/24 dev $IFACE
        down ip addr del 192.168.30.22/24 dev $IFACE

B. RHEL/CentOS/Alma/Rocky (/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts)
----------------------------------------------------------
ifcfg-eth0.30
    DEVICE=eth0.30
    ONBOOT=yes
    VLAN=yes
    BOOTPROTO=none
    IPADDR=192.168.30.10
    PREFIX=24

Add a file for the additional address (classic alias style):

ifcfg-eth0.30:0
    DEVICE=eth0.30:0
    ONBOOT=yes
    IPADDR=192.168.30.22
    PREFIX=24

(Or use an ifcfg-eth0.30-range* file if you prefer the “range” syntax.)

C. Systemd-networkd (any modern distribution)
---------------------------------------------
/etc/systemd/network/eth0.30.network
    [Match]
    Name=eth0.30

    [Network]
    Address=192.168.30.10/24
    Address=192.168.30.22/24
    VLAN=30

Then
# systemctl restart systemd-networkd

────────────────────────
Quick ‑ one-liner variant with legacy ifconfig
────────────────────────
# ifconfig eth0.30:1 192.168.30.22 netmask 255.255.255.0 up
(works but iproute2 is preferred; “eth0.30:1” is only an alias name.)

────────────────────────
Summary
────────────────────────
• Create or identify the VLAN interface (ethX.VLANID).  
• Use ip addr add <ip>/<mask> dev <vlan-if> to assign additional addresses.  
• Put the same ip addr add command (or an alias/secondary stanza) in your distro’s
  persistent network configuration files to survive reboots.

instruction: How do I use a package from nixpkgs unstable with nix-shell -p
output:
`nix-shell -p` always takes the package that lives in the
<nixpkgs> that is found through your NIX_PATH.  
So you merely have to make that
symbol <nixpkgs> point at the **unstable** tree for the call you are about to
make.

The two most convenient ways to do that are shown below; both leave the rest of
your system on the stable channel and affect only this single invocation of
nix-shell.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. With a channel you already have (or are willing to add)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# once (as normal user):
$ nix-channel --add https://nixos.org/channels/nixpkgs-unstable nixpkgs-unstable
$ nix-channel --update

# every time you want a package from unstable:
$ nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p <package>

example
$ nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p nodejs

`-I nixpkgs=…` temporarily overrides only the <nixpkgs> path that is looked
up during evaluation, so the rest of your user profile or system is unchanged.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Without adding a channel – hand the tarball/URL directly
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
$ nix-shell \
    -I nixpkgs=https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/archive/nixpkgs-unstable.tar.gz \
    -p <package>

example
$ nix-shell \
    -I nixpkgs=https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/archive/nixpkgs-unstable.tar.gz \
    -p firefox

The tarball will be fetched (and cached) automatically; again the override
applies only to this single command.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
That’s all that is required—`nix-shell -I nixpkgs=… -p` forces evaluation
against the tree you specify, so the package comes from “unstable” while the
rest of your system keeps using the channel it normally follows.

instruction: Is it possible to update the shell.nix to add new packages while I am already inside the shell, without restarting nix-shell?
output:
No – `nix-shell` does all of its work (building the derivations, computing the PATH, setting environment variables, etc.) once, at the moment it starts.  
After the interactive shell has been spawned it is just an ordinary process; it is not connected to the Nix daemon any more and it never re-reads the `shell.nix` file.  
Therefore any change you make to `shell.nix` is invisible to the shell you are already in and the only way to pick those changes up is to start a fresh environment:

  • Leave the shell and run `nix-shell` again, or  
  • From inside the shell do `exec nix-shell` (which replaces the current shell process with a new one, effectively the same thing).

If you want an almost-transparent “reload when the file changes” workflow, use tools that wrap `nix-shell`, e.g. `direnv` (often together with `lorri` or `nix flake nix develop`). These tools detect that `shell.nix` has been modified when you (re)enter the directory and automatically spawn a new environment, but under the hood they still create a brand-new `nix-shell`; the running shell itself can’t be updated in place.

Write a Python function that takes user input as a string, as well as a mapping of variable names to values (both strings) passed as a dict. The function should search the user input string for each variable name specified, and replace them with the variable value. Variables in the input string must be within angle brackets (< and >), and can be no longer than 30 characters. When found, the function should replace the variable name as well as the angle brackets with the variable value. Text that matches a variable name but is not in angle brackets should not be touched. Variables longer than 30 characters in length should not be touched. Function should return the modified string after the variable replacements.
output:
```python
import re
from typing import Dict

def replace_variables(user_input: str, var_map: Dict[str, str]) -> str:
    """
    Replace occurrences of <variable_name> in `user_input` with the
    corresponding value from `var_map`.

    Rules
    -----
    1. A variable must be wrapped in angle brackets, e.g. <name>.
    2. The name between the brackets must be 1–30 characters long.
    3. Only variables present as keys in `var_map` are replaced.
    4. Text that matches a key but is not bracketed is left untouched.
    5. Bracketed text longer than 30 characters is left untouched.

    Parameters
    ----------
    user_input : str
        The original string supplied by the user.
    var_map : Dict[str, str]
        Mapping of variable names to the values that should replace them.

    Returns
    -------
    str
        The modified string with all valid variable occurrences substituted.
    """
    # Regex:  <  then 1–30 chars that are not < or >  then >
    pattern = re.compile(r'<([^<>]{1,30})>')

    def _replacer(match: re.Match) -> str:
        var_name = match.group(1)
        return var_map.get(var_name, match.group(0))

    return pattern.sub(_replacer, user_input)
```

Example usage
-------------
```python
template = "Hello, <first_name> <last_name>! Your order <order_id> is ready."
values = {
    "first_name": "Jane",
    "last_name": "Doe",
    "order_id": "A123"
}

print(replace_variables(template, values))
# Output:  "Hello, Jane Doe! Your order A123 is ready."
```

• The function scans for `<…>` tokens up to 30 characters long.  
• For each match, it looks the token up in `var_map`; if found, it substitutes the value, otherwise the original text (including the angle brackets) is left intact.

TASK  
Read every Markdown file in my Obsidian vault and suggest relevant tags for each note.

instruction: please give a step by step guide of setting up and using quartz, a static site generator for Obsidian to publish my notes
output:
Below is a “from-zero-to-live-site” walkthrough for Quartz v4 (the current version at the time of writing) aimed at Obsidian users who want to turn their vault into a public digital garden.  
All commands shown work on macOS, Linux and Windows (PowerShell); if something is OS-specific it is called out.

────────────────────────────
0.   What you need first
────────────────────────────
• A GitHub account (other git hosts work, but the official docs assume GitHub).  
• Git installed and working from the terminal (git --version).  
• Node 18 or newer (node --version) – use nvm, Volta or the installers from nodejs.org.  
• pnpm (preferred) or npm/yarn.  Install pnpm once with:  
  npm install -g pnpm  
• Obsidian (obviously) with a vault that lives on disk (not iCloud/OneDrive-only).  

Optional but recommended  
• A code editor (VS Code, WebStorm, etc.)  
• The “Obsidian Git” community plug-in if you want to push updates to GitHub from inside Obsidian.  

────────────────────────────
1.   Create the public repo
────────────────────────────
1. Sign in to GitHub → New repository → call it e.g. my-digital-garden.  
2. Choose “Public” (GitHub Pages only works on public repos unless you have a paid plan).  
3. Don’t add any README, licence or .gitignore yet – Quartz will create its own.  
4. Copy the clone URL (HTTPS or SSH).  We’ll push to it later.

────────────────────────────
2.   Scaffold a Quartz site
────────────────────────────
Quartz provides a CLI that bootstraps everything.

Terminal
# 1-time install of the CLI
pnpm add -g quartz-cli        # or  npm install -g quartz-cli

# generate a new site in a folder
quartz create my-quartz-site

What the wizard asks
• “Where do you want to create it?”  
  → Accept default (./my-quartz-site)  
• “Template?” → choose “obsidian” (pre-configured for Zettelkasten-style notes)  
• “Install dependencies?” → Yes  
• “Initialize git and GitHub repo?” → Skip, because we already created the repo.

When it finishes you’ll have a folder that looks like:

my-quartz-site/
  quartz.config.ts     ← site metadata & options
  content/             ← where your notes will live
  public/              ← static assets (images, favicon, etc.)
  scripts/             ← helper scripts
  tsconfig.json
  package.json
  …

────────────────────────────
3.   Wire your Obsidian vault
────────────────────────────
There are three common ways; pick ONE.

A. Simple copy  
   Periodically copy or move notes you want public into my-quartz-site/content.  
   Good for small/curated sets.

B. Git submodule / subtree  
   Keep your main vault as its own repo and add it as a submodule so content stays in sync but histories are separate.

C. Symlink (recommended if local only)  
   On macOS/Linux:  
     ln -s /path/to/your/obsidian/vault my-quartz-site/content  
   On Windows (PowerShell):  
     New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink `
       -Path my-quartz-site\content `
       -Target C:\path\to\vault  

   In Obsidian you can then tag which notes are public by putting them in a “Public” folder or with “published: true” YAML front-matter – Quartz ignores any file that starts with draft: true.

────────────────────────────
4.   Configure your site
────────────────────────────
Open quartz.config.ts in your editor and change at least:

export default {
  siteMetadata: {
    name: "My Digital Garden",
    author: "Your Name",
    description: "Thoughts, notes, and half-baked ideas.",
    // baseUrl is crucial for links to work once deployed
    baseUrl: "https://<your-github-username>.github.io/my-digital-garden",
  },
  // optional tweaks:
  // defaultToDarkMode: true,
  // enableSPA: true,
}

Other common tweaks:  
• Replace public/favicon.svg, logo.png, etc.  
• Edit content/index.md (this is your landing page).  
• Custom CSS → create styles/custom.css and add its path to quartz.config.ts under css.

────────────────────────────
5.   Preview locally
────────────────────────────
Terminal
cd my-quartz-site
pnpm dev                 # or  npm run dev

Quartz compiles the site and starts a local web-server at http://localhost:8080 (default).  
Edit any .md file – the browser reloads instantly.  
Resolve any warnings such as broken links now; they’ll show in the terminal.

────────────────────────────
6.   First commit & push to GitHub
────────────────────────────
Terminal (still inside the project folder)

git init
git branch -m main
git remote add origin https://github.com/<you>/my-digital-garden.git
git add .
git commit -m "Initial garden 🌱"
git push -u origin main

────────────────────────────
7.   Enable GitHub Pages
────────────────────────────
1. On GitHub → Repository → Settings → Pages  
2. Source → “Deploy from a branch”  
3. Branch → gh-pages (Quartz will create this on your first deploy)  
4. Save.  GitHub shows the URL it will serve e.g. https://you.github.io/my-digital-garden

────────────────────────────
8.   Deploy the site
────────────────────────────
Quartz has a one-liner:

Terminal
pnpm deploy              # or  npm run deploy

What happens under the hood  
• `quartz build` → static HTML in .quartz/build  
• It then pushes that folder to the gh-pages branch (keeping main untouched).  

Within a minute or two GitHub Pages goes green and your site is live 🎉

────────────────────────────
9.   Daily workflow (Obsidian → Web)
────────────────────────────
1. Write notes in Obsidian as usual.  
2. Tag private notes with draft: true in the YAML front-matter OR keep them outside the symlinked “content” folder.  
3. From Obsidian’s command palette (if using Obsidian Git) → “Push”.  
   Otherwise run in the project folder:

   git add .
   git commit -m "update $(date)"
   git push

4. Optionally preview locally: pnpm dev  
5. Deploy: pnpm deploy  

GitHub Actions alternative  
Add the supplied .github/workflows/deploy.yml to have GH automatically build & push every time you push main.  Then you only `git push` from Obsidian; the action runs `quartz build && quartz upload`.

────────────────────────────
10.  Optional: custom domain
────────────────────────────
1. Buy / use an existing domain (example.com).  
2. In your DNS manager add a CNAME record:  
   Type CNAME  |  host: www  |  value: <you>.github.io  
3. In the GitHub Pages settings set “Custom domain” → www.example.com → Save → Enable “Enforce HTTPS”.  
4. Add or update public/CNAME (just the domain name inside).  
5. Commit and deploy again.

────────────────────────────
11.  Adding extra features
────────────────────────────
• Analytics: drop e.g. plausible script tag in quartz.config.ts under head.  
• Comments: add giscus or utterances embed in the same place.  
• Mermaid: Quartz bundles mermaid.js – include ```mermaid code fences in notes.  
• MathJax/KaTeX: enableMath: true in config then write $…$ or $$…$$.  
• Dark theme only: defaultToDarkMode: true and remove light theme variables in styles/custom.css.  
• Custom sidebar order: create _sidebar.md in /content and list wikilinks.  

────────────────────────────
12.  Keeping things tidy
────────────────────────────
Broken links  
pnpm lint links          # lists any unresolved wikilinks

Large assets  
Keep images < 1 MB where possible; Quartz copies them into /assets automatically.  
Videos → put on YouTube/Vimeo and embed, or host separately.

Backups  
Because everything is already in GitHub you get version history + off-site backup automatically.  
For heavy users also enable GitHub “branch protection” so you don’t force-push over gh-pages by accident.

────────────────────────────
13.  Troubleshooting quick list
────────────────────────────
• “pnpm: command not found” → install pnpm globally (see step 0) or use npm.  
• Local preview works, GitHub shows 404 → baseUrl is wrong or Pages source branch not set.  
• Styles not loading on sub-path (my-digital-garden) → again baseUrl must include the repo name.  
• Note shows but images broken → make sure image paths are relative (./img.png) or put them in /public.  
• Custom domain stuck on “Certificate in progress” → remove any A-records; leave only the CNAME.

────────────────────────────
14.  TL;DR cheat-sheet
────────────────────────────
quartz create my-quartz-site            # scaffold
cd my-quartz-site && pnpm dev           # live preview
git push                                 # publish code
pnpm deploy                              # upload built site
# or let GitHub Action do the last step

That’s everything you need to get a Quartz-powered digital garden online from an Obsidian vault. Happy gardening! 🌱

TypeError: not a function


How to fix this error?
I need to access  the last manytomany filed id in odoo
output:
In Odoo a Many2many field is just a record-set (like every relational field).  
So to “get the last one” you treat it exactly as you would any other record-set:

Python (server side)
────────────────────
```python
# ❶ – single record
last_rec  = record.my_m2m_field[-1]          # the last record
last_id   = last_rec.id                      # its id

# ❷ – if you only need the id and you know the set is not empty
last_id = record.my_m2m_field.ids[-1]

# ❸ – in a compute or onchange
@api.depends('my_m2m_field')
def _compute_last_id(self):
    for rec in self:
        rec.last_line_id = rec.my_m2m_field.ids[-1] if rec.my_m2m_field else False
```

QWeb / templates
────────────────
```xml
<t t-esc="o.my_m2m_field[-1].id"/>
```

With domains (if you do not have the record yet)
───────────────────────────────────────────────
```python
# last related partner of a sale.order for example
last_id = self.env['res.partner']._search(
            [('id', 'in', order.partner_ids.ids)],
            order='id desc', limit=1)
```

Important notes
───────────────
1. A Many2many set has no intrinsic ordering in SQL, but the Odoo ORM **always
   returns it ordered by the `id` column ascending**, so “last” really means
   “the one with the greatest id”.  If you defined `order=` on the target
   model that will be used instead; in that case you may want

   ```python
   last_rec = record.my_m2m_field.sorted(key=lambda r: r.id)[-1]
   ```

2. If the field can be empty make sure to guard against it:

   ```python
   last_id = record.my_m2m_field and record.my_m2m_field[-1].id or False
   ```

That’s all you need—index or slice the record-set, then read `.id`.
