instruction: What does the title of pharaoh comes from and mean. Be explicit on the linguistic evolutions and its uses during Antiquity and modern usage, all of this accross geographies.
output:
ORIGIN IN EGYPTIAN

Old- and Middle-Kingdom writing  
Hieroglyphs: 𓉐 pr ‘house’ + 𓂝 Ꜥꜣ ‘great, big’ → pr-Ꜥꜣ “Great House”.  
Pronunciation (approx.)  
• Old Egyptian: */par-ʕaʔ/  
• Late Egyptian: */pʰarɔʕ/  
• Coptic (c. 3rd C. CE): /pʰrəʔ/ > ⲡⲣⲁⲟ, then ⲫⲣⲁⲟ “pharao”.

Original sense = the royal palace as a building or as a courtly institution (“Great House” = “court” or “White House”).  
Earliest secure occurrence: reign of king Nynetjer, 3rd Dynasty (c. 2 800 BCE) – always the palace, never the person.

FROM PALACE TO KING INSIDE EGYPT

• Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 BCE) – still architectural/administrative.  
• 18th Dynasty, Thutmose III → Amenhotep III (15th–14th cent. BCE): formula “the Great House—life, prosperity, health!” is used in letters where the writer clearly means the living monarch; the metonymy is born.  
• Ramesses II (13th cent. BCE): royal names may be preceded by pr-Ꜥꜣ in monumental texts, but the king can still be styled simply “His Majesty (nsw)”.  
• 22nd–25th Dynasties (10th–7th cent. BCE): mixed practice—either “Pharaoh” alone or “Pharaoh NN”.  
• 26th Dynasty onward (7th cent. BCE) it becomes normal to add the birth name: “Pharaoh Necho”, “Pharaoh Apries”, etc.  
• In Ptolemaic temple inscriptions the Egyptian text still uses pr-Ꜥꜣ, but Greek documents prefer basileus; after the 1st cent. CE the Egyptian word disappears from everyday use.

SPREAD INTO NEAR-EASTERN LANGUAGES

Akkadian of the Amarna Letters (14th cent. BCE): pir’u (logographically written with a house determinative), used by Canaanite vassal-kings addressing the Egyptian court.

Ugaritic (13th cent. BCE): pʿrʿ, same value.

Biblical Hebrew: פרעה parʿōh /parˈʕoːh/ (Late Biblical Hebrew /parˈʕoː/). Always definite (“the Pharaoh”), occasionally with a name in the later books (“Pharaoh-nechoh”).

Biblical/Imperial Aramaic: פרעה parʿō(ˀ).

Classical Syriac: ܦܪܥܘܢ P(a)rʿawn.

Arabic (Qurʾān and Classical Arabic): فِرْعَوْن firʿawn. The shift p > f is regular (Arabic lacks /p/); the final –n is an Aramaic/Syriac augment that entered very late.

Geʕez (Ethiopic liturgy): ፍርዒዐውን firʿawn, borrowed from Arabic.

GREEK, LATIN AND THE MEDITERRANEAN

Greek: φαραώ pharaō.  
• First appears in the 3rd-cent. BCE Greek Pentateuch (Septuagint), transliterating the Hebrew.  
• Classical writers who knew Egypt (Herodotus, Diodorus) normally say βασιλεύς “king” and give the man’s name; φαραώ is confined to Biblicising or priestly contexts.

Latin: Pharao (nom.), Pharaōnis or Pharaōnis (gen.). Entry by way of the 2nd-cent. BCE Greek Bible and early Christian writings. Remains an indeclinable proper name in Vulgate prose.

Coptic (Egypt’s last native phase): ⲫⲣⲁⲟ or ⲡⲣⲁⲟ “the Pharaoh”, used only when quoting Scripture; indigenous rulers of the Christian period are styled ⲟⲩⲣⲟ “king”.

MEDIEVAL AND EARLY-MODERN EUROPEAN LANGUAGES

French pharaon, Spanish faraón, Italian faraone, German Pharao, English Pharaoh, Russian фараон etc. All continue the Latin/Greek form and are used loosely for every ancient Egyptian monarch from Narmer to Cleopatra. Figurative extension (“domineering or oppressive ruler”) is first recorded in English in the 16th cent.

The word has also generated secondary compounds:  
• Pharaoh ant (Monomorium pharaonis) 18th cent. taxonomic name.  
• Pharaoh hound (Maltese dog breed).  
• Titles of operas, oratorios (Rossini’s Mosè, Handel’s Israel in Egypt), films (The Ten Commandments) etc.

WHEN AND WHERE THE TITLE WAS ACTUALLY BORNE

Time-line (inside Egypt):  
3000–1550 BCE: pr-Ꜥꜣ = palace only.  
1550–1300 BCE: honorary epithet for the unnamed living king.  
1300–700 BCE: may stand alone or precede the king’s birth name.  
700–330 BCE: always with the name; one of several royal titles.  
330 BCE–1st cent. CE: in hieroglyphic formulae only.  
after c. 100 CE: gone from native usage; survives solely in Jewish, Christian and later Muslim scripture.

Geographical spread of the loan word:  
• Levant and northern Arabia (Hebrew, Phoenician, Aramaic, Arabic).  
• Mesopotamia (Akkadian imperial chancery).  
• Anatolia (Neo-Hittite Hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions have BORNE-GREAT-HOUSE logogram for Egyptian monarch).  
• Greek-speaking Mediterranean (Septuagint, Patristic texts).  
• Entire Christian and Muslim ecumene through Bible and Qurʾān.  
• Modern Europe, the Americas, Asia—via the European colonial languages.

SEMANTIC PATH IN ONE SENTENCE

“Great house” (the palace) → “the court” → “His/Her Majesty” (living monarch without naming) → “King NN” (full royal title) → Scriptural stereotype of the king of Egypt → generic label for any ancient Egyptian ruler → figurative ‘despotic head of state’.

WHY EGYPTOLOGISTS OFTEN PREFER “KING”

Because in Egyptian itself the commonest formal title for the monarch is nsw-bjt (“King of Upper and Lower Egypt”) or ḥm nṯr “the Divine Majesty”, while pr-Ꜥꜣ is chronologically restricted. When absolute accuracy is required, Egyptologists write:

pr-Ꜥꜣ  (r. c. 1279–1213 BCE) Rʿ-ms-sw “Ramesses II, Pharaoh”.

SUMMARY TABLE OF THE FORM

Egyptian   pr-Ꜥꜣ  
Akkadian   pir’u  
Hebrew     parʿōh  
Aramaic    parʿō(ʾ)  
Arabic     firʿawn  
Greek      φαραώ  
Latin      Pharao  
Coptic     ⲫⲣⲁⲟ  
Modern     Pharaoh / Pharaon / Faraón / Pharao / Фараон …

Thus “Pharaoh” is ultimately a metonymic Egyptian phrase “the Great House” that travelled, phonologically reshaped, through the chancelleries and scriptures of the Near East into Greek and Latin, and from there into the modern languages of the world, where it now serves as the default word for any ruler of ancient Egypt and, by extension, for any over-mighty or tyrannical authority.

instruction: Build me econometric model.  To forecast the price of oj with independent variables of carryover , crop size, Brazilian imports
output:
Below is a complete “cook-book” for building and using an econometric model that forecasts the (real) monthly price of frozen concentrated orange juice (OJ).  
The same logic works for weekly/quarterly data—just adjust the lags and seasonal dummies.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. ECONOMIC LOGIC & PRIORS
────────────────────────────────────────
Price ↓ when (i) carry-over stocks rise, (ii) the new Florida crop is large, or (iii) cheap Brazilian imports surge.

Expected signs (in logs):  
βcarryover < 0 ; βcrop < 0 ; βimports < 0

────────────────────────────────────────
2. DATA
────────────────────────────────────────
Frequency       : Monthly (m) – balances timeliness vs. noise  
Span            : ≥ 15 y (≈ 180 obs) to support lags & diagnostics

Variables
 P_t            : Spot or nearby futures price, deflated by CPI (real $/lb).  
 CAR_t          : Carry-over stocks at start of month (mil. lbs solid).  
 CROP_t         : Florida crop size expectation released that month (mil. boxes or solids).  
 IMPBR_t        : Brazilian imports of FCOJ during month (mil. lbs solid).  
 Z_t (optional) : Weather shocks, energy prices, exchange rate, etc.  
 S_k            : 11 seasonal dummies if monthly.

Suggested sources – USDA Citrus Outlook, FAS, ICE futures, CEPEA, BLS CPI.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. PRE-MODELING CHECKS
────────────────────────────────────────
a. Plot levels & logs; confirm plausible correlations.  
b. Unit-root tests (ADF, KPSS) → expect non-stationary levels, stationary first-diff. logs.  
c. If all series I(1) and cointegrated → ECM. If not cointegrated → difference model.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. PREFERRED SPECIFICATION: ARDL / ECM
────────────────────────────────────────
Let p_t = ln P_t, c_t = ln CAR_t, f_t = ln CROP_t, b_t = ln IMPBR_t.

Step 1: Long-run cointegration regression (static OLS)  
p_t = α₀ + α₁ c_t + α₂ f_t + α₃ b_t + seasonals + ε_t

Step 2: Error-correction (short-run dynamics)  

Δp_t = γ₀ + λ̂ EC_{t-1}                       (error-correction term)  
       + Σ_{i=1}^{p} φ_i Δp_{t-i}            (own lags)  
       + Σ_{j=0}^{q1} θ_j Δc_{t-j}  
       + Σ_{k=0}^{q2} ψ_k Δf_{t-k}  
       + Σ_{m=0}^{q3} ω_m Δb_{t-m}  
       + seasonals + η_t

where EC_{t-1}=p_{t-1}−α̂₀−α̂₁ c_{t-1}−α̂₂ f_{t-1}−α̂₃ b_{t-1}.  
λ̂ should be negative and 0 > λ̂ > –1 (speed of adjustment).

Lag orders p,q1,q2,q3 picked by AIC/BIC or general-to-specific testing.

If cointegration rejected, drop Step 1 and use a plain ARDL in first differences (Δ logs) or an ARIMAX.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. ESTIMATION STEPS (Python / statsmodels)
────────────────────────────────────────
# 0. Imports
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
from linearmodels.tsa import DynamicOLS

# 1. Load & take logs
df = pd.read_csv('oj_data.csv', parse_dates=['date']).set_index('date')
for v in ['P','CAR','CROP','IMPBR']: df[f'ln_{v}'] = np.log(df[v])

# 2. Cointegration test (Johansen or Engle-Granger)
y = df[['ln_P','ln_CAR','ln_CROP','ln_IMPBR']].dropna()
coint_res = sm.tsa.stattools.coint(y['ln_P'], y[['ln_CAR','ln_CROP','ln_IMPBR']])

# 3a. If cointegrated → DynamicOLS for long run
dols = DynamicOLS(y['ln_P'], sm.add_constant(y[['ln_CAR','ln_CROP','ln_IMPBR']]),
                  leads=1, lags=1).fit()

# 3b. Build EC term
df['EC'] = y['ln_P'] - (dols.params[0] +
                        dols.params[1]*y['ln_CAR'] +
                        dols.params[2]*y['ln_CROP'] +
                        dols.params[3]*y['ln_IMPBR'])

# 4. Estimate ECM
exog_diff = sm.add_constant(pd.concat([
        df['EC'].shift(1),
        df['ln_CAR'].diff(),
        df['ln_CROP'].diff(),
        df['ln_IMPBR'].diff(),
        pd.get_dummies(df.index.month, drop_first=True)], axis=1))

ecm = sm.OLS(df['ln_P'].diff(), exog_diff, missing='drop').fit(cov_type='HAC', cov_kwds={'maxlags':12})
print(ecm.summary())

# 5. Forecast k-steps-ahead
def forecast_ecm(df, k=6):
    preds = []
    last_row = df.iloc[-1].copy()
    for step in range(k):
        ec_term = last_row['ln_P'] - (dols.params[0] +
                                      dols.params[1]*last_row['ln_CAR'] +
                                      dols.params[2]*last_row['ln_CROP'] +
                                      dols.params[3]*last_row['ln_IMPBR'])
        Δp = (ecm.params['EC']*ec_term +
              ecm.params['const'] +
              ecm.params[[col for col in ecm.params.index if 'month' in col]].dot(
                  pd.get_dummies([(last_row.name.month%12)+1])[0]) )
        p_new = last_row['ln_P'] + Δp
        preds.append(np.exp(p_new))      # back-transform to $/lb
        # Set up next step (assume future CAR, CROP, IMPBR are provided or scenario)
        last_row['ln_P'] = p_new
        # … update exogenous scenarios here …
    return preds

────────────────────────────────────────
6. DIAGNOSTIC CHECKS
────────────────────────────────────────
• Serial correlation: Breusch-Godfrey, Ljung-Box on ECM residuals.  
• Heteroskedasticity: White or Breusch-Pagan; if present → HAC or Newey-West SEs.  
• Stability: Recursive coefficients / CUSUM.  
• Normality: Jarque-Bera (for predictive intervals).  
• Multicollinearity: VIF; if high between crop & carry-over, consider principal-components or dropping one.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. FORECAST EVALUATION
────────────────────────────────────────
Split last 3 years as hold-out; compute RMSE, MAE, MAPE vs. naive (random-walk) and vs. futures quotes.  
Look for bias (mean error ≈ 0).  
If directional accuracy < 60 % consider adding demand-side or macro variables.

────────────────────────────────────────
8. PRACTICAL ENHANCEMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────
• Include FCOJ #11 nearby futures as an expectation variable (but beware endogeneity).  
• Non-linearities: Add dummies for major freezes, hurricanes; test interaction between crop size and imports.  
• Regime-switching (Markov-switch): captures weather shock vs. normal years.  
• Bayesian shrinkage (BVAR) if many covariates.  
• Ensemble final forecast: average ECM with a machine-learning model (e.g., Gradient Boosted Trees fed with the same regressors and lags).

────────────────────────────────────────
9. INTERPRETATION OF COEFFICIENTS
────────────────────────────────────────
In the long run (cointegration regression):  
α₁ ≈ –0.30 → a 10 % rise in carry-over pushes real OJ price down ≈ 3 %.  
α₂ ≈ –0.25 → a 10 % larger crop lowers price ≈ 2.5 %.  
α₃ ≈ –0.15 → a 10 % rise in Brazilian imports lowers price ≈ 1.5 %.

Short-run (ECM) λ̂ ≈ –0.4 means 40 % of any deviation from long-run equilibrium is closed each month.

────────────────────────────────────────
10. DELIVERABLES TO MANAGEMENT
────────────────────────────────────────
• Dashboard: next 12-month price path with 80 % & 95 % confidence bands, scenario toggles for crop forecast and Brazilian import assumptions.  
• Elasticity table as above.  
• Model diagnostics slides.  
• Code + documentation for replication.

That constitutes an end-to-end econometric model that links carry-over stocks, crop size, and Brazilian imports to orange juice prices, ready for estimation, validation, and ongoing forecasting.

instruction: As a experienced data scientist,  you have been asked to work on pricing project . Main objective to identify profit parabola and build a model to predict effect of pricing on sales.
output:
Below is a compact “play-book” I normally follow when asked to find the profit-maximising price (“profit parabola”) and to build a model that predicts the impact of price changes on sales.  
Feel free to lift sections of it into your project charter, SOW, or technical design doc.

────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Business Framing
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Profit parabola = profit(p)= (p–c)·D(p), where  
  p = price, c = unit cost, D(p) = demand function.  
  For most products D(p) is monotonically decreasing → profit is concave (parabola-shaped).  
• Key questions:  
  – Where is p* = argmax(p) profit(p)?  
  – How sensitive is demand to Δp (own-price elasticity ε)?  
  – What is the impact of cross-prices, promotions, seasonality, distribution, marketing, etc.?

Deliverables
  (i) Reusable demand/price-elasticity model.  
  (ii) Optimisation routine that returns p* by segment/SKU/market.  
  (iii) Scenario simulator (including confidence intervals).  
  (iv) Executive dashboard and playbook for price tests.

Success KPIs
  – Out-of-sample MAPE / RMSE on unit sales.  
  – Correct sign and plausible magnitude of elasticity (–0.5 ≥ ε ≥ –5 is typical for FMCG).  
  – Lift in profit in A/B or hold-out stores ≥ X %.

────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Data Blueprint
────────────────────────────────────────────
Level 0 (mandatory)  
  • Transaction or daily/weekly POS units & net prices  
  • SKU cost (standard or actual)  
  • Calendar & seasonality flags  

Level 1 (highly recommended)  
  • Competitor prices or price indices  
  • Promotion flags (display, feature, coupon)  
  • Distribution (% ACV)  
  • Advertising GRPs / digital impressions  
  • Weather, macroecon (CPI, income)  

Level 2 (nice to have)  
  • Web-scraped price crawls (esp. for e-com)  
  • Loyalty/CRM ID → permits mixed-logit or panel models

Data layout  
  – Granularity: (SKU, store/region, week) gives enough variation.  
  – Minimum history: 104 weeks to capture seasonality and year-over-year comps.

────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Exploratory Analysis
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Plot scatter(price, log(sales)) and LOWESS to eyeball curvature.  
• Compute rolling elasticity ε_t = Δlog(Q)/Δlog(P) over windows.  
• Look for price sparsity (many unchanged weeks) → may need IV or lift-test data.  
• Check for price-promotion collinearity (common in CPG).  
• Winsorise extreme promo weeks or holiday spikes.

────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Feature Engineering
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Price gap to main competitor, own regular vs promo price, price tiers.  
• Lagged price & promo vars to capture post-promotion dip or pantry loading.  
• Interaction: price × season, price × advertising, price × store-income-band.  
• Calendar: week-of-year sin/cos pairs, black-friday flag, Easter shift.  
• Hierarchical keys: SKU-brand-category to enable partial pooling later.

────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Modelling Stack
────────────────────────────────────────────
(We usually fit multiple models, pick the simplest that passes business “sniff test”.)

5.1 Parametric/Econometric Baselines  
  a) Constant-elasticity log-log  
      log(Q) = α + β·log(P) + γX + ε  
      Elasticity ε = β.  
  b) Linear demand / quadratic profit  
      Q = a – b·P  ⇒  Profit = (P–c)(a–bP) = –bP² + (a+bc)P – ac  
      Closed-form optimum P* = (a + bc)/(2b).  

5.2 Semi-parametric / ML  
  – Gradient Boosting (XGBoost / LightGBM) with monotonic constraint (↓ with price).  
  – Random Forests + partial dependence to visualise D(p).  
  – CatBoost handles high-card categorical hierarchy.  
  – GAMs (e.g., pygam) with s(Price) smooth & tensor interactions (Price, Season).  

5.3 Causal & Experiment-aware options  
  – Difference-in-Differences on staggered price tests.  
  – Synthetic control for national price moves.  
  – Bayesian structural time-series (CausalImpact) when you have a clean control group.  

Hierarchical / multi-level trick  
  Fit price coefficient as random effect by SKU or region → borrows strength, stabilises rare SKUs.

Evaluation  
  • Time-series CV: rolling OR expanding window.  
  • Out-of-time hold-out (e.g., last 3 months).  
  • Simulated “what-if” back-test: re-price historical weeks with model and compare realised vs predicted profit.

────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Finding the Profit Parabola
────────────────────────────────────────────
Step 1: For each candidate price grid p ∈ [P_min,P_max]  
         predict demand Ŷ(p).  
Step 2: Profit(p) = (p – c) · Ŷ(p).  
Step 3: Choose argmaxᵖ Profit(p).  
   – For parametric quadratic you can solve analytically.  
   – For ML models, do discrete grid search or use Bayesian optimisation.

Confidence band  
  – Draw bootstraps of model, compute p* per draw → 95 % CI on p*.  
  – Present as “green band” of safe prices.

──────────
Example Snippet (Python/LightGBM)
──────────
prices = np.linspace(df.Price.min()*0.7, df.Price.max()*1.3, 50)
demand_pred = gbm.predict(df_test.assign(Price=prices.reshape(-1,1)))
profit = (prices - unit_cost) * demand_pred
opt_idx = np.argmax(profit)
p_star = prices[opt_idx]

────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Scenario Simulator & Dashboard
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Build a small Flask/Shiny/Streamlit app:  
    Inputs: SKU, region, new price, promo flag, ad spend.  
    Outputs: predicted volume, revenue, gross profit, cannibalisation alerts.  
• Monte-Carlo slider for uncertainty.  
• “Elasticity waterfall” chart: shows factor contributions.

────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Productionisation & Governance
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Model retrain frequency: monthly (FMCG) or daily (e-com).  
• Interrupt if cost changes ≥ threshold.  
• Promote only models whose elasticity sign = –ve in >95 % of bootstrap draws.  
• A/B guard-railed roll-out: 10 % stores → 30 % → 100 %.  
• Version tracking in MLFlow; surfaced via Git tags for reproducibility.

────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Common Pitfalls & Mitigations
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Price endogeneity: higher prices often set in high-demand periods → use IV (e.g., cost shock) or randomised tests.  
• Multi-collinearity with promo discount: treat promo price separately, or include “discount depth” feature.  
• Sparse price moves: inject synthetic variation in controlled pilots.  
• Cannibalisation / halo: include same-category competitors’ prices in X.  
• Edge extrapolation: never propose price outside historical ±30 % without stress-testing own assumptions.

────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Project Timeline (typical 6-week sprint)
────────────────────────────────────────────
WK 1: Kick-off, data extraction spec, cost alignment.  
WK 2: EDA & feature engineering prototype.  
WK 3: Baseline econometric model + first elasticity read-out.  
WK 4: ML model, cross-validation, profit curves, p* drafts.  
WK 5: Optimiser wrapper, scenario tool, stakeholder review.  
WK 6: Pilot test design, dashboard hand-over, exec buy-in.

────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Recommended Tooling
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Python: pandas, statsmodels, sklearn, lightgbm, causalml, mlflow.  
• R: data.table, lme4, mgcv, prophet, CausalImpact, Plumber API.  
• Visualisation: seaborn/plotly or ggplotly.  
• Optimisation: scipy.optimize or pulp if multi-SKU inventory constraints.  

────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Next Actions
────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Confirm data availability (esp. costs & competitive prices).  
2. Agree KPI targets and guard-rails with Finance/Revenue Management.  
3. Pick 1-2 SKUs for quick POC to demonstrate profit parabola visibly.  
4. Lock the pilot design for causal validation of model recommendations.

Once these pieces are in place we can iterate quickly toward an automated, self-tuning pricing engine that finds the peak of the profit parabola—and defends it over time as market conditions shift.

instruction:
Acceptance/rejection method:
to sample from a random variable X with p.d.f fX, consider another random
variable Y with pdf fY , such that there exists a constant c > 0 with
fX(x)
fY (x)
≤ c , ∀x with fX(x) > 0 .
• Generate y from the distribution with density function fY .
• Generate u from a uniform (0, 1) distribution.
• If u ≤ fX(y)/(cfY (y)), then take y as the desired realization; otherwise,
return to step 1.
Y should be “easy” to generate and c should be made as small as possible.
output:
Acceptance–Rejection (A–R) Sampling  
Goal: generate independent observations from a target density fX(x) that is either difficult to sample from directly or known only up to a multiplicative constant.

Algorithm  
1. Choose an “envelope” (or proposal) density fY (x) that  
   a) is easy to sample, and  
   b) dominates the target density: fX(x) ≤ c fY (x) for all x, for some finite constant c ≥ 1.  
2. Draw Y ∼ fY .  
3. Draw U ∼ Unif(0,1), independent of Y.  
4. Accept Y as an observation from fX if U ≤ fX(Y)/(c fY (Y)); otherwise reject and return to step 2.

Why it works  
For any measurable set A,

P(accepted ∩ Y∈A)  
      = ∫A fY (y) [ fX(y) / (c fY (y)) ] dy  
      = (1/c)∫A fX(y) dy.

Similarly, P(accepted) = (1/c)∫ fX(y) dy = 1/c.  
Conditional on acceptance, the density is therefore

[ (1/c)fX(y) ] / (1/c) = fX(y),

so the accepted Y’s follow the target distribution.  
The expected number of proposals per acceptance is c; thus c should be as small as possible.

Choosing fY and c in practice  

1. Analytic domination  
   • Find a tractable fY whose shape resembles fX.  
   • Solve c = sup_x fX(x)/fY (x).

2. Piecewise envelopes (staircase or hat functions)  
   • Split the support of X into intervals where simple envelopes can be constructed.  
   • Can drastically reduce c.

3. Adaptive or squeezing methods  
   • Update or tighten the envelope locally as the algorithm proceeds (e.g., Adaptive Rejection Sampling for log-concave densities).

Examples  

A. Sampling a Gamma(α, 1) with α > 1 (shape-scale form)  
   • Let fX(x) = x^{α−1} e^{−x} / Γ(α), x>0.  
   • Choose fY (x) = Exp(λ) with λ = α−1.  
   • Then c = ( (α−1)^{α−1} e^{−(α−1)} / Γ(α) ) max_x x^{α−1} e^{−x+λx}.  
   • The maximum occurs at x=α−1, giving c = Γ(α)^{−1}(α−1)^{α−1}e^{−(α−1)} e^{α−1}/(α−1)^{α−1} = Γ(α)^{−1}e.  
   • Acceptance rate ≈ 1/e for large α; acceptable but improvable via shape-augmentation methods (e.g., Marsaglia & Tsang “Gamma method”).

B. Normal with Cauchy envelope (toy)  
   • Target fX(x) = ϕ(x) = (2π)^{−1/2} e^{−x²/2}.  
   • Proposal fY (x) = Cauchy(0,1): fY (x)=1/[π(1+x²)].  
   • Compute c = sup_x ϕ(x) / fY (x). Derivative gives maximum at x=±1/√3, yielding c ≈ 1.253.  
   • Acceptance rate ≈ 0.80; but in practice one would choose a Normal envelope or Box-Muller instead.

C. Truncated/unnormalised targets  
   • Suppose fX(x) is known only up to a constant: g(x) ∝ fX(x).  
   • Still valid because the unknown constant cancels in the acceptance ratio:  
     U ≤ g(Y) / [c′ fY (Y)], with c′ chosen so that g(x) ≤ c′ fY (x).

Efficiency tips  

• Match tails: The envelope tail should be similar or heavier than the target tail; otherwise c explodes.  
• Break up support: Piecewise linear or exponential “hat” often yields near-optimal c.  
• Vectorisation/parallelism: Propose many Y’s in batches; accept those meeting the criterion.  
• Record rejection proportion to monitor if c was underestimated (should not exceed 1).

Connections  

• Metropolis–Hastings: Accept–reject step with a state-dependent envelope; always accept one value, possibly the current state.  
• Importance sampling: Same ratio fX/fY appears as weight; here it acts as acceptance probability.

Summary  

Acceptance–Rejection is a general, exact method that transforms draws from an easier distribution into draws from a harder one by filtering through an acceptance test. The method is correct if fX ≤ c fY , and its efficiency is 1/c. Choosing fY that closely tracks fX and computing a tight c are the keys to practical performance.

instruction: How do I calculate gibbs free energy of fibril formation from a solubility value?
output:
The solubility (or “critical concentration”) of a fibril-forming peptide/protein is nothing more than the equilibrium concentration of monomer that co-exists with an indefinitely large amount of fibril.  
At equilibrium

Fibril (solid phase)  ⇌  Monomer (aqueous)

the chemical potentials of the two phases are equal:

µfibril = µmonomer  
µ°fibril (activity = 1) = µ°monomer + RT ln Ceq

Re-arranging gives the standard-state Gibbs free-energy difference between a monomer in the fibril and a monomer in dilute solution:

ΔG° (monomer → fibril) = µ°monomer – µ°fibril = RT ln Ceq

Because the activity of the condensed fibril phase is taken as unity, the equilibrium constant for the dissolution reaction is simply Ceq (in mol L⁻¹).  Thus

For dissolution (fibril → monomer):  ΔG°diss = –RT ln Ceq  
For formation   (monomer → fibril):   ΔG°form =  RT ln Ceq      (1)

Step-by-step procedure

1. Convert the experimentally measured solubility to molarity (mol L⁻¹).  
   • If the reported value is x mg mL⁻¹, first divide by the molecular weight (g mol⁻¹) and then by 1000 to obtain mol L⁻¹.

2. Choose the temperature in kelvin (T).  If no temperature is specified, 298 K (25 °C) is usually assumed.

3. Insert the numbers into Eq. (1).  
   R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 0.008314 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

4. Report ΔG°form in kJ mol⁻¹ (or kcal mol⁻¹ if preferred).

A convenient single-step shortcut at 25 °C

RT = (8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)(298 K) ≈ 2.478 kJ mol⁻¹  
Therefore

ΔG°form (kJ mol⁻¹) ≈ 2.48 × ln Ceq                          (2)

Examples

A. Solubility = 10 µM = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M:  
ΔG°form = 2.478 kJ mol⁻¹ × ln(1.0 × 10⁻⁵)  
          = 2.478 kJ mol⁻¹ × (-11.5129)  
          = –28.5 kJ mol⁻¹  
(The negative sign shows fibril formation is favorable.)

B. Solubility = 1 mM = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M:  
ΔG°form = 2.478 kJ mol⁻¹ × ln(1.0 × 10⁻³)  
          = –17.1 kJ mol⁻¹

What exactly does the number mean?

• ΔG°form is the free-energy change for adding one monomer from a 1 M reference solution to an infinitely long fibril under the specified conditions.  
• If you need the free energy per cross-β layer, per protofilament, etc., divide or multiply accordingly.

Common pitfalls and remarks

• Be sure the solubility really is the equilibrium monomer concentration; kinetic measurements taken before equilibrium is reached will overestimate ΔG°.  
• The calculation assumes an ideal, activity-coefficient-unity solution at low concentration.  At higher ionic strength corrections may be necessary.  
• Pressure dependence is negligible for aqueous systems at ambient conditions; temperature dependence follows directly from RT ln Ceq.

In summary, once you have Ceq in mol L⁻¹, ΔG°form is obtained directly from RT ln Ceq.

instruction: Make a scope and limitation for a research about investigating and defining the tool's effectiveness in promoting accurate and consistent drilling centers across many repeated trials. This includes examining the alignment guides' functionality and assessing its performance in maintaining precision across a range of workpiece dimensions and different materials. The study seeks to establish the tool's limitations and capabilities, providing valuable insights into its practical utility in various drilling scenarios.
output:
Scope

1. Objective  
   • Quantitatively determine the tool’s ability to locate and maintain true-center drilling positions over multiple, consecutive holes.  
   • Examine how the tool’s built-in alignment guides contribute to positional accuracy and repeatability.

2. Experimental envelope  
   • Work-piece materials: mild steel (A36), aluminum 6061-T6, maple hardwood, and acetal plastic (Delrin).  
   • Work-piece sizes: square or round blanks ranging from 20 mm × 20 mm × 3 mm up to 100 mm × 100 mm × 12 mm (or nearest imperial equivalents).  
   • Drill diameters: 3 mm, 6 mm, and 10 mm HSS twist drills.  
   • Equipment: a bench-top, belt-driven drill press operated at recommended surface speeds; the test tool is mounted per manufacturer instructions.  
   • Repetition: 100 holes per material/size combination, giving >2,000 individual data points.  
   • Accuracy metrics: radial deviation (µm) from the intended center measured with a vision CMM; repeatability (σ) across trials.  
   • Operator categories: one novice and one experienced machinist to capture user-dependency.  
   • Ambient laboratory conditions: 20 – 25 °C, 40 – 60 % RH; dry drilling without coolant.

3. Data outputs  
   • Mean positional error and standard deviation for every material/size pair.  
   • Statistical comparison (ANOVA) of error contributions from material, thickness, operator, and drill diameter.  
   • Qualitative assessment of alignment-guide ergonomics, set-up time, and ease of adjustment.  
   • Recommended operating window (material hardness, thickness, bit size) where the tool delivers ≤±0.10 mm centering error at 95 % confidence.

Limitations

1. Equipment and process  
   • Only a single bench-top drill press is used; results may differ on handheld drills, radial arm drills, or CNC machining centers.  
   • Rotational speeds and feeds follow standard charts but are not optimized per material; no evaluation under flood coolant, mist, or lubricated conditions.  
   • Vibration, spindle run-out, and drill-bit wear are not independently varied or isolated.

2. Material spectrum  
   • Testing excludes high-hardness alloys (>40 HRC), composites (CFRP, GFRP), ceramics, or sheet metal thinner than 3 mm or thicker than 12 mm.

3. Durability and service life  
   • The study covers up to 2,000 total holes—adequate for short-term precision analysis but insufficient for long-term wear, corrosion, or fatigue effects on the alignment guides.

4. Performance metrics  
   • Only hole-center accuracy and repeatability are measured; hole geometry (roundness, surface finish, burr formation), tool life, and drilling torque are out of scope.  
   • Cost–benefit, productivity gains, and detailed ergonomic or safety evaluations are not quantified.

5. Comparative breadth  
   • The tool is benchmarked against a simple center-punch baseline, not against a wide range of competing commercial guides or jigs.

6. Environmental context  
   • Tests are at room temperature and controlled humidity; high-temperature, outdoor, or contaminated shop environments are not simulated.

Because of these deliberate boundaries, the findings are most applicable to small-to-medium shop settings that use bench-top drill presses on mild steels, non-ferrous alloys, and common engineering plastics or hardwoods, and where centering accuracy within ±0.10 mm is critical.

It is crucial to conclude your feedback with specific examples and relevant suggestions for improvement when necessary. Additionally, please make sure to identify and correct any spelling errors and highlight weaknesses or inconsistencies in the statements that follow these instructions, which begin with "Arguments = ". Point out any logical fallacies, contradictory statements, or gaps in reasoning. By addressing these issues, you can offer a more robust and reliable analysis.

Be sure to elaborate on why you perceive certain aspects as strengths or weaknesses. Arguments = "Autoregressive models, which generate each solution token by token, have no mechanism to correct their own errors. We address this problem by generating 100 candidate solutions and then select the solution that is ranked highest by the verifier which are trained to evaluate the correctness of model-generated solutions. the verifier decides which ones, if any, are correct. Verifiers benefit from this inherent optionality, as well as from the fact that verification is often a simpler task than generation."
output:
Critique of the passage beginning with “Arguments = …”

1. Spelling, punctuation and grammar
•  “the verifier” should start with a capital “T” because it begins a new sentence.  
•  “…select the solution that is ranked highest by the verifier which are trained…” mixes singular and plural.  Possible corrections:  
   – “…select the solution that is ranked highest by the verifier, which is trained …” (singular)  
   – “…select the solution that is ranked highest by the verifiers, which are trained …” (plural)  
•  The final sentence is grammatically acceptable but would read more smoothly as: “Verifiers benefit from this optionality and from the fact that verification is often simpler than generation.”  
•  A comma after “token by token” would improve readability.

2. Strengths
•  The passage concisely highlights a known weakness of standard, single-pass autoregressive generation (lack of post-hoc self-correction).  
•  It sketches a practical remedy (sampling many candidate solutions and scoring them with a verifier).  
•  It hints at a useful design principle: separating generation and verification can exploit the relative ease of judging correctness compared with creating a correct answer from scratch.

3. Weaknesses & logical gaps
a) Over-generalisation  
   “Autoregressive models … have no mechanism to correct their own errors.”  
   – Many autoregressive systems already employ beam-search re-ranking, self-consistent sampling, or iterative-refinement loops, all of which partially address error correction. Saying “no mechanism” is too absolute.  

b) Unexplained assertions  
   •  “Verifiers benefit from this inherent optionality …” The text never explains why more options necessarily help the verifier, or how optionality is quantified.  
   •  “Verification is often a simpler task than generation.”  In formal mathematics or program synthesis, verifying correctness can be undecidable or at least as hard as generation. The claim needs scope restrictions (e.g., “for many short-answer tasks with deterministic evaluation criteria”).  

c) Cost and feasibility  
   Generating “100 candidate solutions” may be computationally expensive.  The argument would be stronger if it justified the choice of 100, discussed possible diminishing returns, or mentioned resource-aware variants (e.g., adaptive sampling until confidence ≥ τ).  

d) Redundancy and flow  
   The second and third sentences partly repeat the same idea (the verifier selects correct outputs). This space could be used to clarify new information instead.  

4. Revised version (one possible improvement)
“Autoregressive models generate a solution token by token and, during a single forward pass, lack an explicit mechanism for self-correction.  To mitigate this, we sample up to 100 candidate solutions and rank them with a separately trained verifier.  The verifier, designed to assess correctness, then selects the highest-scoring answer (or rejects all if none meet a confidence threshold).  Because the verifier judges complete solutions rather than constructing them, it can often operate with lower complexity than the generator.”

5. Concrete examples and suggestions
Example 1 – Code generation  
   •  Task: write a Python function that returns the nth Fibonacci number.  
   •  Generator: sample 100 implementations.  
   •  Verifier: run unit tests; discard outputs that raise exceptions or fail tests; select the shortest passing implementation.  

Suggestion: provide empirical evidence that 100 samples yield a statistically significant accuracy boost (e.g., “accuracy rises from 58 % with k=1 to 79 % with k=100”).  

Example 2 – Natural-language question answering  
   •  Use a fact-checking verifier that scores candidate answers against retrieved documents.  
   •  Improvement: incorporate a confidence-calibrated threshold so the system can abstain when no answer passes verification.

Optimization ideas  
•  Adaptive sampling: stop generating new candidates once the verifier finds an answer above confidence 0.95.  
•  Ensemble verifiers: combine a unit-test-based checker with a language-model-based entailment scorer to cover both functional and semantic correctness.  

By tempering absolute claims, tightening grammar, and supplying empirical or procedural justification, the argument becomes clearer, more accurate and more persuasive.

instruction:
I have to come up for below ML task with the solution:


 Objective:	Increase Revenue for a vertical (Security)	
Databases Required:	Revenue data,	Sales Pipeline data,Budget data	
Pipeline:	Deals Lost (products not working),	Negotiated Deals
	
	
Revenue	Understand Revenue of different products
	whether we want to concentrate on high revenue product or less revenue product
	
	Which deals to prioritize ?
	
	
Budget (target)	Consider products which are far away form the target
	
	
	
Product Life Cycle	
1	Planning
2	Identify
3	Development reports
4	Negotiate
5	Won
6	Lost
output:
Below is a compact end-to-end blueprint that you can take to a data-science backlog meeting tomorrow and start turning into user-stories or JIRA tickets.

──────────────── 1. BUSINESS QUESTIONS → ML OBJECTIVES ────────────────
A. “Which products should we double-down on?”   
   ➔ ML Objective-1: 90-day revenue forecast for every product in the Security
      portfolio and a ranking of “incremental-revenue potential”.

B. “Which open deals should sales touch first?”  
   ➔ ML Objective-2: Win-probability & expected-value scoring for every live
      opportunity in stages 3-4 (Development / Negotiation).

C. “Where are we under-performing vs. target?”  
   ➔ ML Objective-3: Budget-gap early-warning system that flags any product
      trending 10 %+ below plan.

──────────────── 2. DATA MART ────────────────
Join once, reuse everywhere:

Key tables (grain in parentheses)
• revenue_fact  (product_id, month)  
  – booked_revenue, units, discount, channel, region, customer_segment, …  

• pipeline_fact (opportunity_id)  
  – stage, product_id, opportunity_value, close_date, age_in_stage, number_of_calls,
    competitor, reason_lost (free-text), rep_id, …  

• budget_dim   (product_id, month)  
  – budget_target  

• product_dim  – life-cycle flag (planning/identify/…/lost), launch_date, EOL_date, …  

• customer_dim – firmographics, install-base size, security-spend, …  

ETL hints
• Deduplicate opportunities that were split or merged.  
• Convert free-text “reason_lost” with an NLP step (key word tags: “product issue”,
  “price”, “incumbent”).  

──────────────── 3. FEATURE ENGINEERING ────────────────
Product-level features (Objective-1 / 3)
• trailing_12m_revenue, QoQ_growth, seasonality_index  
• avg_deal_size, win_rate_last_12m  
• budget_gap = (budget_target ‑ actual_revenue)/budget_target  
• life_cycle_phase_onehot, months_since_launch  

Deal-level features (Objective-2)
• monetary: opportunity_value, discount_percent  
• urgency: days_to_quarter_end, deal_age, stage_duration  
• engagement: #meetings, #security_architect_calls, last_demo_score  
• product attractiveness: product_win_rate, product_budget_gap flag  
• customer attributes: previous_spend_with_us, competitor_presence  
• NLP topics from “reason_lost” for resurrected deals  

──────────────── 4. MODELS & METRICS ────────────────
4.1 Revenue-Forecasting (per product)  
    – Gradient Boosting Regression or Prophet/LSTM hybrid  
    – Horizon: 3 months; evaluate with MAPE & direction-al accuracy (>80 %).  
    – Output: expected_revenue and confidence band.  
    – Rank products by “forecasted_revenue – budget_target” (positive & negative).  

4.2 Deal-Win Scoring  
    – Binary classifier (XGBoost / LightGBM) → P(win)  
    – Calibration check with Brier score (<0.18).  
    – Business metric: Precision@Top-N (N = capacity of security sales team).  
    – Expected Value = P(win) × opportunity_value.  

4.3 Budget-Gap Early Warning  
    – Simple rules on the forecast output: flag product if  
      forecasted_revenue < 0.9 × budget_target for two consecutive months.  
    – Push Slack / email alert.  

Advanced add-on (optional)  
• Uplift model (treatment = “extra technical pre-sales engagement”)
  to show which deals would most benefit from attention, not just highest EV.  

──────────────── 5. PRIORITISATION LOGIC ────────────────
Sales dashboard column “PRIORITY_SCORE” per deal:
    PRIORITY_SCORE = Expected Value × (1 + budget_gap_weight) × (1 + product_lifecycle_weight)

Where  
    budget_gap_weight  = +0.3 if product is >10 % under target, else 0  
    product_lifecycle_weight = +0.2 if product in “Identify/Development” (strategic)  
                               –0.1 if product in “End of Life”  

Sort descending; slice top 50 for weekly call list.

──────────────── 6. MLOPS / DEPLOYMENT ────────────────
• Offline retrain every Sunday night; feature store (e.g., Tecton/Feast).  
• Real-time scoring service called from CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot, etc.).  
• Power BI / Tableau revenue-gap dashboard fed from same feature store to avoid drift.  
• Experiment tracking with MLflow.  
• A/B test: hold-out 20 % of reps, measure lift in closed-won revenue after 1 quarter.  

──────────────── 7. INTERPRETABILITY & ACTIONABILITY ────────────────
• SHAP summary plot to show reps the top drivers of win probability
  (e.g., “discount <15 %”, “≥3 technical workshops”).  
• For each flagged product, surface the three largest customers with open deals
  that could close the gap (rank by Expected Value).  

──────────────── 8. ROADMAP / SPRINT 0 CHECKLIST ────────────────
☐ Data inventory & governance sign-off (GDPR, SOC-2).  
☐ Agreement on “win” definition and stage mapping.  
☐ Build the conformed data mart (2-3 weeks).  
☐ Baseline logistic regression model to prove value quickly.  
☐ Stand-up revenue-gap Tableau dashboard.  
☐ Iterate with advanced models & uplift in later sprints.  

──────────────── 9. ANTICIPATED BUSINESS IMPACT ────────────────
• 5–8 % incremental quarterly revenue from higher close-rates on
  priority deals (based on pilot uplift studies in similar SaaS firms).  
• Earlier visibility on at-risk products → marketing funds re-allocated
  ~6 weeks sooner than before.  
• Data-driven coaching for reps; fewer “surprises” at quarter close.  

Use this blueprint as the living document; refine feature lists and weights with domain SMEs and sales leadership while you back-test.

Channel & Alliances (Year 2+)

• Cloud providers (AWS Health, Azure) – Marketplace listings, co-selling credits

────────────────────────────────────────
6. DEMAND GENERATION PLAN
────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────
7. SALES PLAYBOOK
────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────

• Begin paid pilots with 5 net-new pharma/CRO logos

• Channel agreements with 2 scanner OEMs  
• Release Analytics Add-on v1 (multiplex IF quant)  
• EMEA sales hub opened in Basel

Sales

High Cloud Costs → Tiered image-tier storage (S3+Glacier), spot-compute autoscaling

11. TEAM & RESOURCING
────────────────────────────────────────
• VP GTM (life-sci software veteran)

instruction:
I am trying to prompt an LLM model to extract two dates from a long message. I need help coming up with a prompt that will make the task clear to the model.  Here is what I have so far, I'd like you to suggest ways to improve it please:

    prompt = f"""Determine the rollout date and completion date of the event described in the given message below. 
Most of the time the dates will be under a header that looks something like: '[when will this happen:]'. 
Your answer should be formatted as JSON. ONLY RETURN THIS JSON. It must be in this format:

{json.dumps(date_json)}

Dates should always be formatted in MM/DD/YYYY format, unless you cannot determine one, in which case use 'Unknown'.

If there is no specific day given, as in 'we will begin rolling out in october 2023', just use the first day of the month for the day, so your 
answer would be 10/01/2023.
If you cannot determine a value for 'rollout_date' or 'completion_date', use the value 'Unknown'.
    
Message (delimited by triple quotes):\n\n\"\"\"\n{msg}\n\"\"\" 
"""
output:
Below are several ideas for tightening-up the instructions, followed by a rewritten prompt that incorporates them.

────────────────────────
Suggestions
────────────────────────
1. Separate “system” and “user” instructions  
   Put formatting-only rules (e.g., “return JSON only”) in a system message. This prevents the model from “chatting” outside the required format.

2. Define the two dates precisely  
   Tell the model what qualifies as a “roll-out” date versus a “completion” date (first date mentioned vs. last date mentioned, or headings to look for, etc.). Ambiguity here is a common source of errors.

3. Provide a JSON schema up front  
   Showing the exact keys, order, and example values helps the model stick to it.

4. Give 1–2 shot examples  
   A short example block with a miniature message and its correct JSON output boosts accuracy a lot.

5. Guardrails for missing or ambiguous dates  
   Make it explicit that if a range is given (“October 2023 – December 2023”) the start of the range is rollout and the end is completion.

6. Reinforce that no commentary should appear  
   Use wording such as “Output only the JSON object. Do not wrap it in markdown, back-ticks, or text.”

────────────────────────
Improved prompt (single message version)
────────────────────────
System:
You are a date-extraction assistant. Your ONLY output must be a valid JSON object that matches this schema exactly:
{
  "rollout_date": "MM/DD/YYYY or Unknown",
  "completion_date": "MM/DD/YYYY or Unknown"
}

User:
Task  
Extract two dates from the message below:

• rollout_date  = the earliest date at which the event or feature begins rolling out, launching, or starting.  
• completion_date = the date when the rollout is finished, fully deployed, or otherwise completed.

Formatting rules  
1. Use MM/DD/YYYY.  
2. If only a month+year is given, use the first day of that month (e.g., “October 2023” → “10/01/2023”).  
3. If a range is given (“March 1–15, 2024”), the earlier date is rollout_date and the later date is completion_date.  
4. If the date cannot be determined, put "Unknown".  
5. Output ONLY the JSON object with the two keys in the order shown—no extra keys, no comments, no markdown.

Few-shot examples  
Example 1 – single date  
Message: We will begin rolling this out on February 7, 2024. The rollout will be completed by March 2024.  
Output:
{"rollout_date":"02/07/2024","completion_date":"03/01/2024"}

Example 2 – date range  
Message: Rollout schedule: April 10 – April 30, 2024  
Output:
{"rollout_date":"04/10/2024","completion_date":"04/30/2024"}

Example 3 – not enough info  
Message: We’re planning the change, timing TBD.  
Output:
{"rollout_date":"Unknown","completion_date":"Unknown"}

Actual message (delimited by triple quotes)  
"""
{msg}
"""

(Remember: Output ONLY the JSON object.)

`Flask-Sock` hands you a `WebSocket` object that behaves very much like a file-like object:  
`ws.receive()` blocks (or awaits, if you declared the function `async`) until the next message arrives, and it returns `None` if the peer closed the connection.  
So, all you have to do is read (and optionally validate) that first message before you call your update routine.

Synchronous version
-------------------
```python
from flask import Flask
from flask_sock import Sock
import uuid, json               # only needed for validation / parsing

app  = Flask(__name__)
sock = Sock(app)

@sock.route('/reader_flasher')
def updater(ws):
    # 1. Wait for the first message ------------------------------
    raw_msg = ws.receive()          # blocks until client sends something
    if raw_msg is None:             # client disconnected immediately
        return

    # 2. Extract / validate the UUID ------------------------------
    # If you know the client just sends the UUID as plain text:
    uuid_str = raw_msg.strip()

    # optional – make sure it really *is* a UUID
    try:
        device_id = uuid.UUID(uuid_str)
    except ValueError:
        ws.send('Invalid UUID')
        return

    # 3. Call your long-running logic -----------------------------
    update_firmware_full(ws, device_id)
```

Asynchronous version (if you are running Flask with `asyncio`)
--------------------------------------------------------------
```python
import uuid, json
from flask_sock import Sock

@sock.route('/reader_flasher')
async def updater(ws):            # <- note the async keyword
    raw_msg = await ws.receive()  # await instead of block

    uuid_str = raw_msg.strip()
    try:
        device_id = uuid.UUID(uuid_str)
    except ValueError:
        await ws.send('Invalid UUID')
        return

    await update_firmware_full(ws, device_id)
```

Notes
• `ws.receive()` can return either text (string) or binary (bytes).  
• If your front-end sends JSON (`{"uuid": "…"}`) just do:
```python
device_id = uuid.UUID(json.loads(raw_msg)['uuid'])
```
• `update_firmware_full` must be written in the same “style” (sync vs async) as the route.  
• You pass the same `WebSocket` object (`ws`) to `update_firmware_full`, so that function can keep sending progress messages to the client while it flashes the firmware.

instruction: I would like my MATLAB script to wait until the user closes all open figures, in any order, before continuing.  Can you write lines of MATLAB code that will do this?
output:
```matlab
% Block execution until every figure window has been closed
if ~isempty(findall(0,'Type','figure'))   % only bother if a figure exists
    waitfor(0,'CurrentFigure',[]);        % root’s CurrentFigure becomes [] 
end                                       % only when the last figure closes
``` 

`waitfor(0,'CurrentFigure',[])` tells MATLAB to suspend execution until the root object’s `CurrentFigure` property is empty—which happens precisely when the user has closed the last open figure (they may be closed in any order). The script then resumes with the next line of code.
