Example ACL that only allows two Gmail users and blocks everyone else:

{
  "ACLs": [
    { "Action":"accept", "Users":["me@gmail.com","friend@gmail.com"], "Ports":["<jellyfin-hostname>:443"] }
  ]
}

Section 6 – Verify transcoding and bitrate limits
-------------------------------------------------
Because you may have WAN bandwidth constraints, set remote streaming limits in
Jellyfin ⇒ Dashboard ⇒ Playback ⇒ Streaming to avoid saturating your uplink.

Section 7 – Routine maintenance
-------------------------------
• Tailscale auto-renews TLS certs; nothing to do.  
• Keep the package up to date (`sudo tailscale update`) to benefit from new Serve/Funnel features.  
• Check `tailscale funnel status` or the admin console if things stop working (e.g., 90-day cert renewal failures).

Alternative architecture (if you prefer not to rely on Funnel)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Deploy a $5/month VPS (e.g., Hetzner/DO/Linode) as a Tailscale node.  
• Run Nginx + Certbot on the VPS, proxying requests over the tailnet to Jellyfin.  
• Open only 80/443 on the VPS; nothing on your home router.  
This gives you full control over the edge but requires manual TLS and Nginx config.

Recap
─────
1. Install & log into Tailscale on the Jellyfin host.  
2. tailscale serve https 443 http://localhost:8096  
3. tailscale funnel 443 on  
4. (Optional) add custom domain, ACLs, or exit via VPS.  

You now have a secure, TLS-terminated, globally reachable Jellyfin instance with no inbound ports on your LAN and WireGuard encryption for all traffic until it hits Tailscale’s edge.

instruction:
Find root cause for this error:
sshd[54785]: error: kex_exchange_identification: Connection closed by remote host
output:
What the message means  
------------------------------------------------  
When sshd logs

  sshd[54785]: error: kex_exchange_identification: Connection closed by remote host

it has already:

1. accepted a TCP connection on port 22;  
2. started the SSH protocol handshake (waiting for the client to send its
   SSH-2.0 banner);  
3. noticed that the peer closed the socket before any key-exchange (kex) data
   were exchanged.

So, strictly speaking, nothing “failed” inside the server: the socket was
simply closed from the other side before the key-exchange was able to start.
sshd logs the event at the point where it expected to perform
kex_exchange_identification and found the peer gone.

Typical root causes  
------------------------------------------------  
1. Port scans / Internet background noise  
   Mass scanners (nmap, zmap, shodan, etc.) open port 22, learn that it is an
   SSH service and immediately close the connection.  This produces the exact
   line you see.

2. Server-side rate limiting (MaxStartups)  
   If the number of simultaneous unauthenticated connections to sshd exceeds
   the MaxStartups threshold (default 10), sshd intentionally drops the new
   connection.  In this case the “remote host” is actually the server itself
   closing the connection it just accepted.

   auth.log with LogLevel VERBOSE or DEBUG will show lines like  
   “drop connection #<n> from <ip> [preauth]”.

3. Network equipment or security software resetting the session  
   Middleboxes, IDS/IPS, or host-based firewalls sometimes send an RST for
   “unknown” or “disallowed” traffic, again leaving sshd with a half-open
   handshake.

4. The client program crashed, was killed, or times out while waiting in a
   ProxyJump/SSH-config chain.

Diagnosing which case is yours  
------------------------------------------------  
• Look at the source addresses.  Many random IPs ⇒ scanners.  
• Capture traffic (tcpdump -n host <suspect-ip> and port 22).  
  A three-way handshake immediately followed by a RST from the client IP means
  the client really closed it; a RST from the server IP means MaxStartups or
  a local firewall rule.  
• Raise LogLevel to VERBOSE or DEBUG3 in sshd_config and watch /var/log/auth.log
  for “drop connection” or “Too many connections”.

Fix / Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------  
Nothing has to be “fixed” on the server if the lines are caused by external
scans—just ignore them.

If legitimate users are occasionally affected:

1. Increase MaxStartups, e.g.  
     MaxStartups 30:50:100
2. Make sure fail2ban/sshguard rules are not over-triggering.  
3. Check intermediate firewalls or load balancers for aggressive idle-timeout
   or RST behaviour.

Bottom line  
------------------------------------------------  
The message tells you only that the peer broke the TCP connection before the
SSH key-exchange could begin.  The most common root cause is automated
port-scanning on the Internet; the second most common is sshd itself rejecting
excess unauthenticated sessions (MaxStartups).  Unless real users are unable
to log in, the message can usually be ignored.

instruction: Create an "impossible triangle" with an SVG. Make it 3d

Two nonhorizontal, non vertical lines in the $xy$-coordinate plane intersect to form a $45^{\circ}$ angle. One line has slope equal to $6$ times the slope of the other line. What is the greatest possible value of the product of the slopes of the two lines?
output:
Let the slopes of the two lines be m₁ and m₂, with  
m₂ = 6 m₁  (without loss of generality, since one slope is six times the other).

For two non-vertical lines, the (acute) angle θ between them satisfies  

tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.

Here θ = 45°, so tan θ = 1:

|(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| = 1.

Substitute m₂ = 6 m₁:

|5 m₁| / (1 + 6 m₁²) = 1.

Since the denominator is positive, this reduces to

5|m₁| = 1 + 6 m₁².

Let x = |m₁| ≥ 0. Then

6x² − 5x + 1 = 0.

The discriminant is 25 − 24 = 1, giving

x = [5 ± 1]/12 → x = 1/2 or x = 1/3.

Thus |m₁| is either 1/2 or 1/3.  
The product of the slopes is

m₁m₂ = 6m₁² = 6x².

For x = 1/2: 6(1/2)² = 6·1/4 = 3/2.  
For x = 1/3: 6(1/3)² = 6·1/9 = 2/3.

The greatest possible product is therefore 3/2.

instruction: Allow me to use a virtual dataset called Dior. From the Dior dataset, I would like to calculate the total number of female adult customers in the time period 6-7pm in the Orchard outlet, and the average number of male adult customers across 3 time periods (10-11am, 1-2pm, 5-6pm) in the  MBS outlet.  I want these results in a separate table. Save these results into a CSV file called 'dior_seg.csv'. Do this in a single postgreSQL query.
output:
Below is a single PostgreSQL statement that

1. Builds the two requested results in-memory with CTEs  
2. Returns them as a two-row table (column “metric”, column “value”)  
3. Writes that table straight out to a CSV file called dior_seg.csv

Feel free to change the table / column names or the absolute path if they differ in your schema or server setup.

```sql
COPY (
    WITH 
    
    /* 1. Total female adult customers, 6-7 pm, Orchard outlet ---------------*/
    female_tot AS (
        SELECT COUNT(*)::numeric AS tot_female
        FROM   dior           -- <-- main traffic table
        WHERE  outlet      = 'Orchard'
          AND  gender      = 'Female'
          AND  age_group   = 'Adult'
          AND  visit_time::time >= '18:00:00'
          AND  visit_time::time <  '19:00:00'
    ),

    /* 2. Average male adult customers over three slots, MBS outlet ----------*/
    male_avg AS (
        SELECT AVG(slot_cnt)::numeric AS avg_male
        FROM  (
               /* 10-11 am */
               SELECT COUNT(*) AS slot_cnt
               FROM   dior
               WHERE  outlet      = 'MBS'
                 AND  gender      = 'Male'
                 AND  age_group   = 'Adult'
                 AND  visit_time::time >= '10:00:00'
                 AND  visit_time::time <  '11:00:00'
               UNION ALL
               /* 1-2 pm  */
               SELECT COUNT(*)
               FROM   dior
               WHERE  outlet      = 'MBS'
                 AND  gender      = 'Male'
                 AND  age_group   = 'Adult'
                 AND  visit_time::time >= '13:00:00'
                 AND  visit_time::time <  '14:00:00'
               UNION ALL
               /* 5-6 pm  */
               SELECT COUNT(*)
               FROM   dior
               WHERE  outlet      = 'MBS'
                 AND  gender      = 'Male'
                 AND  age_group   = 'Adult'
                 AND  visit_time::time >= '17:00:00'
                 AND  visit_time::time <  '18:00:00'
        ) s
    )

    /* 3. Build the two-row result table ------------------------------------*/
    SELECT 'total_female_adults_orchard_6_7pm'            AS metric,
           tot_female                                     AS value
    FROM   female_tot
    
    UNION ALL
    
    SELECT 'avg_male_adults_mbs_10_11am_1_2pm_5_6pm',
           avg_male
    FROM   male_avg
) 
TO '/var/lib/postgresql/dior_seg.csv'          -- <-- adjust path if needed
WITH CSV HEADER;
```

Execute the statement in `psql` (or any PostgreSQL client that allows server-side writes) and the file `dior_seg.csv` will be created on the database server containing the two metrics you asked for.

instruction: You have a sales table with the following columns: customer_id, week, date, basket_key, sales, units. Write some SQL code that can, for every product in every week, classify customers as "new" or "existing" depending on whether they had purchased that product in the previous 6 weeks.
output:
-- ------------------------------------------------------
-- Example assumes the table is called  SALES
-- and that it also contains a column PRODUCT_ID
-- (change names to match your real schema).
--
-- The query does two things:
--   1. Keeps only one line per
--      (customer , product , week)  – multiple baskets in
--      the same week are collapsed with DISTINCT.
--   2. Looks six weeks back to see if the customer bought
--      that SAME product before.  
--      If he did   ->  ‘existing’
--      If he didn’t -> ‘new’
--
-- The code uses nothing fancier than EXISTS, so it will
-- run as-is in Postgres, Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery,
-- SQL Server, Oracle, etc.
-- ------------------------------------------------------

WITH cust_prod_week AS (         -- 1. normalise to one record per week
    SELECT DISTINCT
           customer_id,
           product_id,           -- ← replace with the real product column
           week
    FROM   sales
),

flagged AS (                     -- 2. look back 6 weeks and flag
    SELECT  cpw.* ,
            CASE
                WHEN EXISTS ( SELECT 1
                              FROM   cust_prod_week  prev
                              WHERE  prev.customer_id = cpw.customer_id
                              AND    prev.product_id  = cpw.product_id
                              AND    prev.week BETWEEN cpw.week - 6    -- previous 6 wks
                                               AND     cpw.week - 1 )
                THEN 'existing'
                ELSE 'new'
            END  AS customer_status
    FROM   cust_prod_week cpw
)

-- ------------------------------------------------------
-- Row-level result: one record per customer/product/week
-- with the NEW / EXISTING flag
-- ------------------------------------------------------
SELECT *
FROM   flagged
ORDER  BY product_id , week , customer_id;



/* -----------------------------------------------------
   If what you actually need is
   “How many NEW vs EXISTING customers did each product
    have this week?”, aggregate the CTE above:

SELECT  week,
        product_id,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_status = 'new')      AS new_customers,
        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_status = 'existing') AS existing_customers
FROM    flagged
GROUP BY week, product_id
ORDER BY product_id , week;
-------------------------------------------------------- */

instruction: write a technical requirements specification for a diagnostic system (reader and consumable) which uses a blood sample to detect sepsis in a european hospital setting
output:
Technical Requirements Specification (TRS)  
Diagnostic System for Rapid Detection of Sepsis in Whole-Blood Samples  
(Comprising an Instrument “Reader” and Single-Use Cartridge “Consumable”)  
Target Use Environment: European hospital wards, emergency departments, and intensive-care units

────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Scope
1.1 This TRS defines mandatory and desirable requirements for design, verification, validation, manufacture, labeling, installation, servicing and end-of-life of a near-patient in-vitro diagnostic (IVD) system that provides a quantitative or qualitative sepsis result from a fresh whole-blood sample.  
1.2 The TRS supports conformity assessment under Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in-vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDR) and is written to serve as the primary input to the system, subsystem and design-input specifications.

2. Normative & Informative References (latest revisions)
• Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)  
• ISO 13485, ISO 14971, ISO 10993-1, ISO 18113-1/2, ISO 23640  
• IEC 62304, IEC 62366-1, IEC 61010-1, IEC 61010-2-101, IEC 61326-2-6, IEC 60601-1-2  
• CLSI EP05, EP07, EP12, EP17, POCT1-A; IHE LIVD/LAB-TF, HL7 v2.8 ORU^R01  
• GDPR 2016/679, ISO/IEC 27001  
• RoHS 3, REACH, WEEE, IEC 62430 (Eco-design)

3. Definitions & Abbreviations
• TAT – Turn-around time  
• LOD – Limit of Detection  
• CV – Coefficient of Variation  
• Reader – Powered analytical instrument (hardware + embedded software)  
• Cartridge – Single-patient disposable containing reagents and microfluidics  

4. Intended Use
The system is intended for the rapid identification of patients with, or at risk of developing, sepsis by quantifying host-response biomarkers (e.g., Procalcitonin, IL-6, CRP and a proprietary sepsis score) in anticoagulated whole blood. Results support clinical decision-making on antimicrobial therapy and escalation of care. For professional use only.

5. User Profiles
• Primary: Registered nurses, biomedical scientists, junior doctors  
• Secondary: Clinical laboratory specialists (for QC oversight)  
No specialised laboratory skills or manual pipetting may be required.

6. Use Environment
• Point-of-care benches, bedside trolleys or satellite labs inside EU hospitals  
• Ambient 15–30 °C; 15–85 % RH non-condensing; altitude ≤2 000 m  
• Mains supply 100–240 VAC, 50–60 Hz with TN-S or TT earthing systems

7. Overall System Description
Blood (0.5 mL) is transferred via supplied capillary or syringe into a bar-coded cartridge. The user inserts the cartridge into the reader; automated mixing, incubation, optical/electrochemical detection, and onboard result-interpretation are performed. Results, QC records and audit logs are stored, displayed and transmitted to LIS/EHR.

8. Functional Requirements
F-01  The reader shall automatically detect cartridge type, lot, expiry, and calibration constants via 2-D DataMatrix.  
F-02  From sample insertion to result display shall not exceed 30 min (95th percentile).  
F-03  The GUI shall provide step-by-step animations in at least EN, DE, FR, ES, IT, PL, NL.  
F-04  The system shall generate three result fields: (a) numeric biomarker concentrations, (b) computed Sepsis Risk Score (0-10), (c) flag (“Sepsis likely/possible/unlikely”) based on validated clinical algorithm.  
F-05  Internal positive and negative process controls shall be run with every test; test is auto-invalidated if controls fall outside limits and an explicit error code is displayed.  
F-06  The reader shall store ≥50 000 patient results, QC and operator IDs with date-time stamp in non-volatile memory ≥10 years data retention.  
F-07  Connectivity options:  
 • 1× RJ-45 Ethernet 10/100/1000-BASE-T with HL7 v2.8 ORU, POCT1-A, IHE LAW profiles  
 • 2× USB-A (host) for barcode reader, firmware update  
 • Optional Wi-Fi 802.11 a/b/g/n via medical-grade dongle, WPA2-Enterprise  
F-08  Reader shall print results via USB or networked printer (optional).

9. Performance Requirements
Clinical
P-01  Sensitivity ≥90 % (95 %CI lower bound ≥85 %) for confirmed sepsis according to Sepsis-3 criteria.  
P-02  Specificity ≥85 % (95 %CI lower bound ≥80 %).  
P-03  Negative Predictive Value ≥95 % in prevalence range 10–25 %.  
Analytical
P-04  LOD for Procalcitonin ≤0.05 ng/mL; LoQ CV ≤20 % at 0.08 ng/mL.  
P-05  Within-run precision ≤10 % CV at medical decision points; between-site reproducibility ≤12 % CV (3 sites, 5 operators, 20 days).  
P-06  Reagent lot-to-lot bias ≤±7 %.  
P-07  No significant interference (bias >10 %) from haemolysis up to 500 mg/dL Hb, lipaemia ≤1500 mg/dL triglycerides, bilirubin ≤30 mg/dL, or common medications per CLSI EP07.

10. Physical & Interface Requirements
• Footprint ≤300 mm (W)×200 mm (H)×300 mm (D); weight ≤8 kg (reader).  
• 10-inch capacitive colour touch display ≥1280×800 px, glove-operable.  
• Acoustic level ≤45 dB(A) in operation.  
• Battery back-up ≥15 min for safe result completion/eject in power loss.  
• Cartridge dimensions ≤110 mm×70 mm×15 mm; material cyclic olefin polymer, medical-grade; leakproof per IEC 61010-2-101.  

11. Safety & Risk-Management Requirements
S-01  Comply with IEC 61010-1 & ‑2-101 (biological risk, sharp protection, splash containment).  
S-02  Single-use cartridge to remain sealed after insertion; no liquid contact possible for operator.  
S-03  Biohazard labelling according to ISO 15223 and ADR UN3291 for disposal.  
S-04  Reader surfaces to withstand ≥5 000 cycles of hospital disinfectants (70 % IPA, quaternary ammonium).  
S-05  System shall perform self-test at power-on and block use if critical failure detected.  

12. Software, Cybersecurity & Data Protection
SW-01  Software lifecycle per IEC 62304; safety classification B.  
SW-02  On-instrument OS shall be a hardened Linux distribution with secure boot, signed updates and partition encryption (AES-256).  
SW-03  Role-based access control: Operator, QC supervisor, Admin.  
SW-04  All PHI stored or transmitted shall be encrypted (TLS 1.2/1.3).  
SW-05  Audit trail immutable; minimum events: log-in/out, test run, QC, calibration, settings change.  
SW-06  System shall support anonymisation mode for training/demo.  
SW-07  Design and documentation shall meet GDPR Articles 25 & 32 (privacy by design, security of processing).

13. Usability & Human-Factors
U-01  Usability engineering file per IEC 62366-1; validation with ≥15 representative users across ≥2 EU languages demonstrating ≤3 use errors/100 runs and no critical use error.  
U-02  Minimum training time target ≤1 h, supported by e-learning modules.  
U-03  Cartridge insertion shall be keyed; force ≤25 N; feedback via audible “click”.  

14. Reliability, Service & Maintainability
R-01  Mean cycles between failure (MCBF) ≥10 000 tests or 12 months.  
R-02  Preventive maintenance limited to annual change of HEPA filter, optical cleanliness check (<30 min by biomed technician).  
R-03  Firmware field-upgradeable in <10 min via USB or network; failsafe rollback available.  

15. Quality-Control & Calibration
QC-01  Built-in electronic self-calibration on every start-up (temperature, optics).  
QC-02  Cartridge contains lyophilised internal calibrators traceable to NIBSC standard 10/286 (PCT).  
QC-03  External (liquid) trilevel controls provided; recommended frequency: daily until 30 consecutive in-control runs, then weekly.  
QC-04  QC lockout: system precludes patient testing if external QC overdue >24 h.  

16. Consumable (Cartridge) Requirements
C-01  Shelf life ≥15 months at 2–8 °C; stable 2 h at 15–30 °C once removed.  
C-02  On-board reader storage capacity for loaded but unstarted cartridge ≤30 min.  
C-03  Free from materials classified SVHC under REACH Annex XIV.  
C-04  UDI-DI and UDI-PI barcodes per IVDR Annex VI.  

17. Packaging, Labelling & IFU
PK-01  Transport pack survivability per ISTA 2A; no cold-chain break >72 h at 40 °C allowed.  
PK-02  Cartridge primary pouch sterile-barrier integrity tested to ISO 11607 (simulate drop 1 m).  
LB-01  Labels in line with ISO 15223-1, IVDR Annex I §23; multi-lingual.  
LB-02  Hazard statements for sodium azide (<0.1 %) included (H- & P-codes).  
IFU   Shall be available printed and PDF; readable at 10-point font on A4; QR-code on device links to e-IFU repository.

18. Environmental & Sustainability
E-01  Reader RoHS 3 compliant; consumable exempt as medical device but heavy-metal concentrations <50 ppm total.  
E-02  Reader to meet IEC 62430 eco-design: standby power <3 W, auto-sleep after 15 min idle.  
E-03  End-of-life recycling instructions provided; plastic parts marked ISO 11469.  
E-04  WEEE symbol moulded on housing; manufacturer offers take-back program in EU.

19. Verification & Validation Plan (high-level)
• Design verification: FMEA, DF-MEA, RQ-traceability matrix, EMC, electrical, environmental stress, drop, ingress (IP22).  
• Analytical validation: Precision (EP05), LOQ/LOD (EP17), interference (EP07), linearity (EP06), lot-to-lot, carry-over (≤0.1 %).  
• Clinical validation: Prospective multi-centre study ≥500 patients, ≥3 EU hospitals, comparing to sepsis diagnosis by blinded expert panel.  
• Usability validation: Summative HF at 2 sites, 15 users/site.  

20. Service & Support Requirements
SVC-01  24 h on-site response in EU27; remote diagnostics via encrypted VPN.  
SVC-02  Spare-part availability ≥7 years post-last-sale.  
SVC-03  Mean time to repair (MTTR) ≤2 h for 90 % of service events (module swap).  

21. End-of-Life & Decommissioning
EOL-01  Reader firmware shall permit secure wipe (DoD-5220.22-M) of patient data.  
EOL-02  Consumable considered clinical waste UN3291; fits into standard 5 L sharps containers.

────────────────────────────────────────────
Revision History
v0.9 – Initial draft for cross-functional review (Regulatory, Design, Marketing).  
v1.0 – Baseline approved by Design Control Board (signature log in DHF).

instruction:
There is a pandas DataFrame with the following columns:
Place, Company, month, year, earnings

I want to know the best month with the most average earnings for each place and company. Give me sample code to do that. Include sample data in your code sample.
output:
```python
import pandas as pd
import calendar

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Sample data
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
data = {
    'Place'   : ['New York']*6 + ['London']*6,
    'Company' : ['A','A','A','B','B','B',
                 'A','A','B','B','B','B'],
    'month'   : [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3,
                 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1],
    'year'    : [2021,2021,2021,2021,2021,2021,
                 2022,2022,2022,2022,2022,2023],
    'earnings': [100, 150, 120,  80,  90, 110,
                 130, 160, 200, 180, 220, 210]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Average earnings per (Place, Company, month)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
g = (df
     .groupby(['Place', 'Company', 'month'], as_index=False)['earnings']
     .mean()
     .rename(columns={'earnings': 'avg_earnings'}))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Pick the month with the highest average for every Place/Company
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
idx = g.groupby(['Place', 'Company'])['avg_earnings'].idxmax()
best_months = g.loc[idx].reset_index(drop=True)

# Optional: add month name for readability
best_months['month_name'] = best_months['month'].apply(lambda m: calendar.month_abbr[m])

print(best_months)
```

Output

```
      Place Company  month  avg_earnings month_name
0  London       A      2        160.0         Feb
1  London       B      3        220.0         Mar
2  New York     A      2        150.0         Feb
3  New York     B      3        110.0         Mar
```

`best_months` now tells you, for every Place/Company pair, which month has the highest average earnings across all years and what that average is.

instruction: behaving like an expert, I want  you to help me design a radar that can detect a 155mm artillery shell. the radar is to be integrated in a vehicle
output:
Below is a complete, engineering-level (“Level-1”) design study for a vehicle-mounted radar able to detect and track a single 155 mm artillery shell in flight and to hand off a sufficiently accurate trajectory for counter-battery or sense-and-warn roles.  Numbers are representative and can be scaled to meet a particular customer specification or vehicle class.

────────────────────────────────────────
1  MISSION & SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────
• Threat: NATO-standard 155 mm HE shell (length ≈ 800 mm, max Ø ≈ 155 mm). 
  – Typical monostatic RCS: 0.01 – 0.1 m² (broadside),  < 0.005 m² (nose-on).  
  – Flight velocity: 280–950 m s⁻¹ depending on zone charge / range.  

• Required detection range (Rd): 18 km (objective 22 km) for 0.9 Pd / 10⁻⁶ Pfa.  
• Track life: ≥ 6 s or ≥ 60° of arc, whichever is smaller.  
• Origin estimation error (miss distance at launch point): ≤ 50 m (threshold), ≤ 25 m (objective) at 20 km.  
• Coverage: 360° in azimuth, −5° to +75° in elevation (high-angle mortar inclusivity).  
• Latency: first detection ≤ 1.0 s after shot-start; origin solution ≤ 4 s.  
• Vehicle class: 4×4 (≈ 7 t curb).  Electrical power export: 6 kW @ 28 Vdc available.  
• SWaP budget for radar (inc. mounts & cooling): ≤ 220 kg, ≤ 0.45 m³, ≤ 4.5 kW.  
• Environmental: MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461G, CIP altitude + EMC, −40 °C to +55 °C ops.  

────────────────────────────────────────
2  ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW
────────────────────────────────────────
• Radar type: Solid-state, software-defined, pulse-Doppler, active electronically-scanned array (AESA).  
• Band: S-band (2.9–3.4 GHz).  
  – Rationale: reasonable shell RCS, minimal rain attenuation, relaxed machining tolerances, allows 1 m aperture within vehicle envelope.  
• Array concept: 1.0 m × 0.6 m planar AESA, 680 T/R modules (∆≈16 mm element pitch = 0.16λ).  
• Scan concept: 120° electronic sector; whole radar mechanically slews in azimuth through three 120° “stares” for 360° every 3 s (like AN/TPQ-53).  
• Waveform set: burst-staggered, LFM chirp pulses, 100 MHz instantaneous BW (1.5 m range resolution) with PRI agility.  
• Signal processing: digital beam-forming (element-level), pulse compression, coherent MTI, multi-hypothesis track-before-detect (TBD), EKF ballistic fitter, and impact / launch point solver.  

────────────────────────────────────────
3  LINK BUDGET & RANGE ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────
Constant-False-Alarm radar equation (monostatic):

SNR = (Pt G² λ² σ) / [ (4π)³ k T₀ F L R⁴ Bn ]  
  
Take:
  – Required post-compression SNRmin = 13 dB (Pd 0.9, Pfa 10⁻⁶ with CFAR).  
  – σ = 0.04 m² (design point; pessimistic vs. broadside).  
  – λ = 0.1 m (3 GHz).  
  – G = 35 dBi ≙ lin(3162).  (1.0 m × 0.6 m aperture, ηap ≈ 0.55).  
  – Pt = 4 kW peak, 10% duty → 400 W avg (solid-state GaN, 6 dB crest).  
  – kT₀ = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W/Hz (290 K).  
  – F = 3 dB (low-noise GaAs LNA).  
  – Losses L (radome, feed, quantisation, scan, etc.) = 6 dB.  
  – Integrated processing gain (pulse compression + coherent integration over 20 pulses) = 37 dB.  
  – Noise bandwidth Bn  = matched to 100 MHz chirp / 20 pulses → ~5 MHz equiv.  

Solving, Rmax ≈ 23 km.  With 6 dB scan loss at 60° off-boresight, 2 km margin remains on the 18 km requirement.  

────────────────────────────────────────
4  MAJOR SUBSYSTEMS
────────────────────────────────────────
4.1  Antenna / AESA Front-End  
• Aperture: 1000 mm × 600 mm × 110 mm.  
• Radiating element: dual-polarised stacked patch with corporate feed network (so each TRM drives one dual-pol element).  
• 680 TRMs (340 dual-pol cells).  
  – TRM spec: 6 W avg, 60 W peak, 45 % PA efficiency, 6 dB gain, phase ± 180°/step, 6-bit amplitude.  
• Radome: RF transparent, bullet splash proof, NBC-decon compatible, < 1 dB insertion.  
• Cooling: cold-plate to liquid loop (propylene glycol) tied to vehicle chilled water / condenser.  

4.2  Exciter / Receiver  
• Direct-digital synthesis (DDS) chirp generator, 0–500 MHz IF, up-convert to 3 GHz.  
• Digital drop receivers (super-heterodyne or direct-sampling at 1.2 GSps, 12-bit).  
• Channelisation in FPGA for element-level DBF.  

4.3  Timing & Control  
• GPS-disciplined OCXO (Allan deviation < 5 × 10⁻¹² 1 s) for phase coherency.  
• Built-in test (BIT) loops: injected CW tone, dummy load, and T/R module loopback.  

4.4  Processing & Algorithms  
• COTS VPX chassis with dual FPGA + dual GPU cards (ex: Xilinx Versal + NVIDIA Orin).  
• Software chain:  
  1. Adaptive DBF weight calc + side-lobe blanking.  
  2. Range compression, STAP-like clutter cancellation.  
  3. Doppler filtering, ordered-statistic CFAR.  
  4. Track-Before-Detect (sequential DP) to boost Pd on low-RCS nose-on portions.  
  5. Multi-sensor fusion hooks (acoustic, EO) [option].  
  6. EKF ballistic fit using 6-DOF shell model, local met data, JBMOU tables.  
  7. Impact / launch point intersection with digital terrain data.  

• Latency from last coherent dwell to track confirmation: ≤ 450 ms.  

4.5  Power & Thermal  
• 4.5 kW @ 28 Vdc DC-DC converter shelf.  
• ~1.9 kW dissipated in TRMs, 0.9 kW in processors, 0.4 kW miscellaneous.  
• Liquid loop removes 3.2 kW; forced air handles remainder.  

4.6  Human-Machine Interface  
• Stand-alone 12.1″ ruggedised touch display or integration with vehicle BMS via Ethernet/UART.  
• Tactical messages:  
  – ASTERIX CAT-210 for tracks, VMF K09 for C-B points, STANAG-4607 for surveillance, J-Series J3.6, J3.7, J15.0 as required.  

4.7  Mount & Vehicle Integration  
• Roof-mount pedestal with azimuth rotary joint (≥ 400 °/s² accel, 180 °/s max).  
• Vibration isolation < 5 g RMS, ballistic steel shield to TRMs.  
• “Lay flat” stow position at 3.3 m clearance.  
• EMI filters + surge arresters to vehicle harness per DEF-STAN 59-411.  

────────────────────────────────────────
5  WAVEFORM & SCHEDULING DETAIL
────────────────────────────────────────
• Sector dwell: 110 µs coherent burst (N = 20 pulses, 100 MHz chirps, 40 kHz PRF stagger).  
• Dwell revisit: 25 ms → gives > 10 revisits per shell in flight (at Rd=18 km shell transits 20° every ~300 ms).  
• Search-track interleaving: phased mission schedule; resources freed immediately after confirmation for other sectors.  
• Adaptive power: TRMs step back 6 dB in clear weather or high Pd margin to reduce thermal load.  

────────────────────────────────────────
6  SWAP & MASS PROPERTIES
────────────────────────────────────────
Component  | Mass (kg) | Vol (L)
Antenna + TRMs       | 85 | 90
Pedestal & Drive     | 28 | 20
RF / Power Shelf     | 42 | 35
Processing Chassis   | 24 | 25
Cabling & Radome     | 11 | 10
Cooling Hardware     | 22 | 25
TOTAL                | 212 | 205

Centre of gravity: 1.0 m above vehicle roof, directly over rear axle → verify roll stability > 30°.  

────────────────────────────────────────
7  TECHNOLOGY RISKS & MITIGATIONS
────────────────────────────────────────
Risk                         | Mitigation
GaN TRM cost / yield         | Multi-foundry sourcing, derate PAE requirements
High PRF range ambiguity     | Multi-PRF stagger, M/N de-alias
TBD computation load         | Use GPU CUDA kernels; hardware-in-loop early
EMC with SDR comms on vehicle| Guard bands + time blanker during Tx windows
Thermal headroom (desert)    | Reserve 25 % coolant flow margin, paint radome IR-reflective

────────────────────────────────────────
8  COMPLIANCE & SAFETY
────────────────────────────────────────
• Radhaz: keep-out zone 3.0 m at boresight when transmitting full power (NAVSEA OP-3565).  
• EMP / lightning arrest: MIL-STD-188-125 zone 1 filter on DC input.  
• Functional safety: IEC 61508 SIL-2 for pedestal motion interlocks.  

────────────────────────────────────────
9  DEVELOPMENT & TEST PROGRAMME (ABBREV.)
────────────────────────────────────────
Phase 0  (3 mo)  – Requirements freeze, high-level arch., ROM costing  
Phase 1  (9 mo)  – AESA sub-array brassboard, digital beam-forming demo  
Phase 2A (6 mo)  – Full array build, indoor anechoic calibration  
Phase 2B (5 mo)  – Vehicle integration, EMI/EMC & road test  
Phase 3  (4 mo)  – Ballistic live-fire & met data coupling (Yuma / Vidsel)  
Phase 4  (2 mo)  – Qualification, docs, transition to LRIP  

────────────────────────────────────────
10  GROWTH & OPTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────
• Dual-band S + X option for fuse detection or UAV surveillance.  
• Passive coherent mode (PCL) exploiting DVB-T for emission control.  
• M-UAS cued-track mode (fast micro-Doppler extract).  
• Interface to effector (C-RAM) with micro-sec time-gates.  

────────────────────────────────────────
CONCLUSION
────────────────────────────────────────
The design outlined above meets the stated requirement to detect and track a 155 mm shell at ≥ 18 km with a vehicle-compatible, solid-state AESA radar.  Key performance drivers—TRM power, aperture size, processing gain, and scan strategy—have been balanced against the 4.5 kW / 220 kg SWaP ceiling.  All components employ commercially available GaN, FPGA, and GPU technologies, putting this radar within a 3- to 4-year engineering programme and suitable for integration on an 8-tonne-class vehicle.

instruction:
on the basis of this information provided write a background section of a copmplete sepcification of a patent, the invention relates to a system for detecting undercurrent faults in the heated grip application for a two wheeled vehicle without the need for a current sensor. "Existing hardware is not having provision to sense the current to trigger under current fault.
The Master ECU sends a command to the Slave ECU to initiate heating of the coil. Upon receiving this command, the Slave ECU starts generating a Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signal to heat the coil and begins reading the temperature sensor. The coil, while heating the element, consumes a significant amount of current. Ideally, there should be a direct provision from the hardware to sense the actual current consumption and provide this information to the microcontroller. Based on this information, the microcontroller can decide whether to set an undercurrent fault or not. However, in the existing hardware setup, there is no provision to sense the current. And adding this current sensing hardware into the existing product, will attract additional costs and complexities in further component arrangements of the product.

The existing solutions may use a current sensor or a shunt resistor to measure the actual current consumption of the coil and compare it with a threshold value. Based on these parameters, the undercurrent detection can be easily done. However, this solution would require additional hardware components, which would increase the cost and complexity of the system. Moreover, the current sensor or the shunt resistor could introduce noise or interference in the PWM signal, affecting the heating performance of the coil."
output:
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION  

Field of the Invention  
The present invention relates to electrical fault-detection systems for accessory heaters on motor-cycles and similar two-wheeled vehicles. More particularly, the invention addresses the detection of under-current (open-circuit or high-resistance) faults in electrically-heated handle-bar grips without employing a discrete current sensor or shunt resistor.

Description of Related Art  
Electrically-heated handle-bar grips (hereinafter “heated grips”) are increasingly fitted to two-wheeled vehicles to enhance rider comfort. A typical architecture employs:  
• a master electronic control unit (ECU) that interprets rider inputs and overall vehicle status;  
• a slave ECU located near the handle-bar that drives the heating element;  
• a resistive heating coil embedded in or bonded to the grip; and  
• a temperature sensor (e.g., an NTC thermistor) mounted on or near the coil.  

During operation the master ECU transmits a heat-request command to the slave ECU. The slave ECU responds by generating a pulse-width-modulated (PWM) drive signal that switches battery voltage across the heating coil. While the coil is energised it should draw a characteristic current—typically several amperes depending on supply voltage, coil resistance and commanded duty cycle.  

It is desirable to monitor the coil current so that under-current conditions can be detected and reported. Such conditions arise when:  
• the coil becomes partially or completely open-circuited;  
• a connector becomes loose or corroded, raising series resistance;  
• a wiring harness sustains damage; or  
• an internal battery-voltage drop or blown fuse limits available current.  

Without timely detection, the rider may receive no heat, yet remain unaware of the fault; furthermore, persistent open-circuit states can mask other electrical faults or create diagnostic ambiguity for service personnel.

Conventional Approach  
Known systems perform under-current detection by inserting either:  
(a) a Hall-effect current sensor in series with the coil lead, or  
(b) a precision shunt resistor through which coil current flows and across which the slave ECU measures voltage drop.  

Both methods allow the microcontroller to compare the measured current (or inferred current in the shunt method) to a calibrated threshold and declare a fault when the measured value falls below the threshold for a defined interval.

Limitations of the Conventional Approach  
Although technically straightforward, the above solutions present several drawbacks when applied to small-form-factor, cost-sensitive vehicle accessories:

1. Additional Hardware Cost and Complexity  
   • A Hall-effect sensor adds a discrete IC, ferromagnetic concentrator, calibrated packaging, PCB real estate and connector pins.  
   • A shunt resistor requires low-thermal-coefficient precision components, differential amplification circuitry and careful layout to avoid Kelvin-sense errors.  
   • Both variants necessitate extra high-current tracks and mechanical fasteners, raising bill-of-materials (BOM) cost and assembly complexity.

2. Packaging and Thermal Management  
   • The heated-grip slave ECU is usually confined to the handle-bar end cap, where space is extremely limited and ambient temperatures can exceed 80 °C.  
   • Accommodating additional power components compromises enclosure size, ingress-protection ratings, and thermal dissipation margins.

3. Signal Integrity Concerns  
   • PWM switching edges can couple into Hall-sensor or shunt-sense traces, giving rise to measurement noise and false fault indications.  
   • Differential amplifiers required for shunt sensing are susceptible to common-mode voltage transients, necessitating further filtering that can slow response time.

4. Reliability and Serviceability  
   • Introducing more solder joints, connectors and discrete parts statistically reduces system reliability.  
   • Field diagnostics must account for possible sensor failures in addition to heater faults, complicating troubleshooting.

Because of these limitations, many commercial heated-grip controllers omit dedicated current sensing altogether, leaving the system blind to under-current faults. Consequently there exists a need for an under-current detection technique that:  
• operates with the existing electrical hardware (master ECU, slave ECU, PWM driver and temperature sensor) without adding current-measurement components;  
• maintains immunity to PWM-induced noise;  
• preserves the form factor and environmental robustness of the grip assembly; and  
• minimises incremental cost while meeting safety and regulatory requirements.

The present invention satisfies this need.

instruction: We run a peer support mobile application with 24 by 7 group chats open. We have a team of peer moderators that monitor and engage with members on the app. I want to create a project document to track the epic - Use NLP/Smarter Alerts to improve peer efficiency with the idea that we can use AI to raise alerts for things like here's a message that is very negative in sentiment or here's a new user posting for the first time or here's an unanswered question. I also want to define tangible metrics that we can use to track project success
output:
Epic Document  
Title: “Smarter Alerts” – Using NLP to Increase Peer-Moderator Efficiency  
Date: _____   Version: _____   Owner: _____  

1. Why are we doing this? (Problem Statement)  
• Live peer-support rooms run 24 × 7, yet ~35 % of high-need messages currently wait ≥10 min for a response.  
• Human moderators cannot read every line; “alert fatigue” and uneven coverage lead to missed crises and missed opportunities to welcome newcomers.  
• We want an automated, privacy-compliant, real-time alert layer that surfaces only the messages that truly need moderator attention, thereby improving user safety, user retention, and moderator well-being.

2. Epic Goal  
Deploy AI/NLP services that detect priority events (e.g., negative sentiment, self-harm language, first-time posters, unanswered questions) and route actionable alerts to moderators, so that:  
a) response times are cut in half,  
b) moderators can cover more rooms with the same (or lower) effort, and  
c) members report a better support experience.

3. Key Outcomes & Success Metrics  

Operational-Service KPIs (measured monthly, compared to 3-month baseline)  
• Median time from “critical message” to first moderator response → ↓ 50 % (from 8 min → ≤4 min).  
• % of critical messages answered within 5 min → ↑ from 55 % → ≥90 %.  
• Unanswered question rate after 10 min → ↓ from 12 % → ≤2 %.  
• New user first-message response within 3 min → ↑ from 60 % → ≥95 %.  
• Moderator coverage ratio (rooms per active moderator) → ↑ by 25 % without loss in quality.  

User-Level Outcomes  
• 7-day retention of first-time members → +10 %.  
• “Felt heard within 5 min” survey item → +15 %.  
• App Store/NPS → +5 points.

Model / Alert Quality  
• Negative-sentiment classifier: F1 ≥ 0.85, recall ≥ 0.90 for “high risk”.  
• Self-harm detector: recall ≥ 0.95, precision ≥ 0.80.  
• Overall alert precision ≥ 80 % (≤1 false positive in 5).  
• Mean end-to-end alert latency ≤ 3 sec.

Moderator Experience  
• Moderator CSAT (“alerts are useful & actionable”) ≥ 4.3 / 5.0.  
• Self-reported burnout score ↓ 10 %.

4. Scope – Event Types in v1/v2  

v1 (MVP – 8 w)  
1. High-negative / self-harm sentiment (suicidal ideation, crisis).  
2. New user first message.  
3. Unanswered question >X min.  

v2 (Continuous – +12 w)  
4. Escalating anger / harassment.  
5. Message surge (room heating up).  
6. Conversation stall (no posts for Y min) for proactive engagement.  

Out of Scope (for now)  
• Automated replies to users.  
• One-to-one DMs (group only).  
• Any location-based or personally identifiable data mining.

5. Functional Requirements  
FR-1  Real-time stream of chat messages sent to NLP pipeline (<1 s ingestion).  
FR-2  Classifier scores and rule engine decide if alert threshold met.  
FR-3  Alert delivered to moderator toolset (mobile push + web dashboard + Slack fallback) with: message excerpt, user alias, room, alert type, time, quick-action buttons (Jump / Acknowledge / Escalate).  
FR-4  Alert auto-expires after configurable period if already addressed.  
FR-5  Audit log and analytics for every alert: timestamps, responder, outcome, false-positive flag.  
FR-6  Role-based access; only peer moderators and staff see user content.  
FR-7  Admin panel to tune thresholds, add rules, or pause alerts.  

6. Non-Functional Requirements  
• P99 end-to-end latency <5 s.  
• 99.9 % alerting uptime.  
• Scales to 50 msg/s (10× current peak).  
• GDPR & HIPAA-adjacent data handling; encryption at rest/in transit.  
• Model re-training pipeline every 4 weeks with human-labelled data.  

7. High-Level Architecture  

Mobile Apps  →  Message Broker (Kafka)  →  NLP Service (transformers + rule layer)  
                                                ↘ Metadata DB  
                                                ↘ Alert Service (gRPC/REST)  →  Moderator Client / Push   
                                                ↘ Analytics Warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery)  

8. Implementation Road-map & Milestones  

Phase 0 (2 w)   Baseline & Data Labelling  
• Instrument current response-time metrics.  
• Sample & label 10 k messages for sentiment & self-harm.  

Phase 1 (4 w)   MVP Pipeline (Rule + Off-the-Shelf Models)  
• Spin up message broker & streaming service.  
• Integrate open-source sentiment model + keyword rules.  
• Deliver alerts to Slack as proof of concept.  
• Pilot in 1 low-traffic room.  

Phase 2 (6 w)   Custom Model & Dashboard  
• Fine-tune transformer on in-domain data ( ≥ 0.85 F1).  
• Build web/mobile moderator alert dashboard.  
• A/B test vs control rooms for 4 weeks.  

Phase 3 (4 w)   Unanswered-Question & New-User Logic  
• Add timer-based detectors.  
• Live experiment; tune thresholds.  

Phase 4 (3 w)   Quality, Alert Fatigue & Auto-Throttle  
• Feedback loop (acknowledge / false-positive button).  
• Automatic suppression if FP > 30 % for any alert type.  

Phase 5 (4 w)   Full Roll-out & Success Review  
• Roll to 100 % of rooms.  
• Compare KPIs vs baseline → decide on graduation.  

Total est. duration: 23 weeks.

9. Team & Responsibilities  
• Product Manager (0.5 FTE) – vision, backlog, A/B test design.  
• Data Scientist (1 FTE) – model development, evaluation.  
• ML Engineer (1 FTE) – streaming infra, deployment, MLOps.  
• Backend Engineer (1 FTE) – broker, alert service, integrations.  
• Mobile Engineer (0.5 FTE) – in-app alerts.  
• QA/Automation (0.5 FTE).  
• Moderator Lead (0.25 FTE) – domain labelling, UAT, training.  

10. Risks & Mitigations  
R-1 High false positives → fatigue.   Mit: human-in-the-loop, auto-throttle, agile tuning.  
R-2 Missing critical self-harm post.   Mit: separate high-recall self-harm model + redundant keyword filter.  
R-3 Privacy/regulatory breach.   Mit: data minimisation, encryption, DPIA completed, legal review.  
R-4 Model drift due to language evolution.   Mit: continuous labelling & retraining cadence.  
R-5 Moderator resistance to new workflow.   Mit: co-design sessions, phased rollout, CSAT survey.  

11. Definitions / Measurement Details  
• “Critical message” = any message tagged by model score ≥0.8 in self-harm or negative-sentiment category.  
• “Response” = first moderator post that @mentions or replies directly to the member.  
• Time-to-response measured server-side using UTC timestamps.

12. Budget Estimate (CapEx + OpEx)  
• Cloud infra (GPU instances, broker, DB) ≈ $1.5 k/mo after full roll-out.  
• One-off annotation cost: ~10 k messages × $0.04 = $400.  
• Optional external security audit: $8 k.

13. Go / No-Go Criteria for Graduation  
Must hit BOTH:  
a) Model precision ≥ 80 % & recall ≥ 90 % for self-harm.  
b) Median critical-message response time ≤ 4 min for two consecutive months.

14. Post-Launch Continuous Improvement  
• Quarterly model benchmarking.  
• Add multilingual support (Q4).  
• Investigate auto-draft “supportive response” suggestions (2025).

15. Approvals  
Product _____   Engineering _____   Data _____  
Compliance _____   Moderator Lead _____  

— End of Epic Document —

instruction: make a python script to sentiment analysis
output:
Below is a fully-working, self-contained Python script (sentiment_analysis.py) that lets you analyse sentiment from the command line, from a text file, or interactively.  
It relies on Hugging Face’s 🤗 transformers library and the lightweight, open-source model distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (≈256 MB).  
The script prints, for each sentence, the predicted label (POSITIVE / NEGATIVE) and the confidence score (0-1).

Dependencies
‒ Python ≥ 3.8  
‒ pip install transformers torch (CPU-only installation of PyTorch is fine)

File: sentiment_analysis.py
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
sentiment_analysis.py
A tiny command-line utility for sentiment analysis using HuggingFace Transformers.

USAGE EXAMPLES
  # Single sentence
  python sentiment_analysis.py --text "I absolutely love this phone!"

  # Sentences stored line-by-line in a file
  python sentiment_analysis.py --file reviews.txt

  # Interactive mode (hit ENTER on an empty line to finish)
  python sentiment_analysis.py
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse
import sys

try:
    from transformers import pipeline
except ImportError:          # Nice error if the user forgot to pip-install
    sys.exit(
        "ERROR  »  Missing dependency 'transformers'.\n"
        "        »  Install with:  pip install transformers torch"
    )


def load_pipeline(model_name: str = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"):
    """
    Load (or download on first run) the sentiment-analysis pipeline.
    """
    print("Loading model … (first run may take ~1 min) ", end="", flush=True)
    nlp = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model=model_name)
    print("✓")
    return nlp


def analyse(texts: list[str], nlp):
    """
    Run inference and prettify results.
    """
    output = []
    for text in texts:
        if not text.strip():
            continue
        prediction = nlp(text, truncation=True)[0]       # [{'label':'POSITIVE','score':0.997}]
        output.append(
            {
                "text": text,
                "label": prediction["label"],
                "score": round(prediction["score"], 4),
            }
        )
    return output


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Sentiment analysis powered by HuggingFace Transformers"
    )
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    group.add_argument(
        "-t",
        "--text",
        help="Analyse a single text string (wrap it in quotes)",
    )
    group.add_argument(
        "-f",
        "--file",
        help="Path to a text file containing ONE sentence (or paragraph) per line",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    # 1. Gather sentences -----------------------------------------------------
    if args.text:
        sentences = [args.text]
    elif args.file:
        try:
            with open(args.file, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
                sentences = [line.rstrip("\n") for line in fh if line.strip()]
        except OSError as exc:
            sys.exit(f"Could not open '{args.file}': {exc}")
    else:  # Interactive fallback
        print("Interactive mode – type sentences; blank line to stop:")
        sentences = []
        while True:
            line = input("> ")
            if not line.strip():
                break
            sentences.append(line)

    if not sentences:
        sys.exit("No sentences supplied – nothing to do!")

    # 2. Load model and run inference ----------------------------------------
    nlp = load_pipeline()
    results = analyse(sentences, nlp)

    # 3. Pretty print ---------------------------------------------------------
    print("\nRESULTS")
    for r in results:
        print(f'  "{r["text"]}"  →  {r["label"]:>8}   (confidence = {r["score"]})')


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

How to run
1. Save the code above as sentiment_analysis.py  
2. Install the dependencies if you have not already:

   ```bash
   python -m pip install --upgrade pip
   pip install transformers torch
   ```

3. Examples

   • Single sentence  
   `python sentiment_analysis.py --text "I can’t stand noisy neighbours."`

   • Analyse a file (one line per sentence)  
   `python sentiment_analysis.py --file my_reviews.txt`

   • Interactive mode  
   ```
   python sentiment_analysis.py
   Interactive mode – type sentences; blank line to stop:
   > The food was fantastic!
   > This service is terrible.
   >
   ```

What you see
```
Loading model … (first run may take ~1 min) ✓

RESULTS
  "The food was fantastic!"  →  POSITIVE   (confidence = 0.9998)
  "This service is terrible."  →  NEGATIVE   (confidence = 0.9991)
```

That’s it—you now have an easy-to-extend sentiment-analysis tool in Python. Feel free to switch to a multilingual model, store results as JSON/CSV, or embed the pipeline in a Web API.

instruction: Admetting that i have word2vec model bunch of words , and that i want a program python using gensim to create vector , can you help me with creating one ?
output:
Below is a complete, minimal example that shows the most typical tasks you may want to do with Gensim’s Word2Vec:

1. Install and import what you need.  
2. Read / pre-process a text corpus.  
3. Train a new Word2Vec model (or load an existing one).  
4. Obtain vectors for individual words, for a whole sentence, etc.  
5. Save / load the model later on.  

You can copy-paste the code into a single Python file or a notebook and adapt the paths / parameters to your needs.

```python
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 1) INSTALL AND IMPORT
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# pip install --upgrade gensim  (run once on your machine)

import logging
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

from gensim.utils import simple_preprocess        # light-weight tokenizer
from gensim.models import Word2Vec, KeyedVectors  # main Word2Vec classes

logging.basicConfig(format="%(asctime)s : %(levelname)s : %(message)s",
                    level=logging.INFO)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 2) READ + TOKENISE A CORPUS
# -----------------------------------------------------------
def iterate_corpus(txt_path):
    """
    Yields tokenised sentences (lists of unicode tokens) line-by-line.
    """
    for line in Path(txt_path).open(encoding="utf-8"):
        # simple_preprocess: lower-cases, strips accent marks, keeps alphabetic tokens
        yield simple_preprocess(line)

# Example: one plain-text file with one sentence per line
corpus_path = "corpus.txt"
sentences = list(iterate_corpus(corpus_path))
print("Number of sentences in corpus:", len(sentences))

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3A) TRAIN A NEW WORD2VEC MODEL FROM SCRATCH
# -----------------------------------------------------------
model = Word2Vec(
    sentences=sentences,      # input sentences
    vector_size=200,          # embedding dimensionality
    window=5,                 # context window size
    min_count=2,              # ignore rare words
    workers=4,                # no. of threads
    sg=1,                     # 1 = skip-gram; 0 = CBOW
    epochs=10                 # training iterations
)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3B) OR: LOAD AN EXISTING / PRE-TRAINED MODEL
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# If you already possess a `.model`, `.kv`, or GoogleNews `.bin` file:
# model = Word2Vec.load("my_word2vec.model")                # model trained w/ gensim
# model = KeyedVectors.load("my_vectors.kv")                # key-vectors only
# model = KeyedVectors.load_word2vec_format(
#          "GoogleNews-vectors-negative300.bin", binary=True)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 4) USING THE MODEL
# -----------------------------------------------------------

word = "science"

# 4.1) Vector for a single word
if word in model.wv:
    vec = model.wv[word]          # ndarray of shape (vector_size,)
    print(f"Vector for '{word}' (len={len(vec)}):\n", vec)

# 4.2) Most similar words
print(model.wv.most_similar(word, topn=5))

# 4.3) Sentences or documents: average (or sum) the word vectors
test_sentence = "science is organized knowledge"
tokens = simple_preprocess(test_sentence)
# keep only words that actually exist in the vocabulary
valid_vecs = [model.wv[t] for t in tokens if t in model.wv]
if valid_vecs:                             # avoid empty list!
    sentence_vec = np.mean(valid_vecs, axis=0)
    print("Sentence vector shape:", sentence_vec.shape)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 5) SAVE + LOAD FOR LATER USE
# -----------------------------------------------------------
model.save("my_word2vec.model")         # whole model (incl. training state)
model.wv.save("my_vectors.kv")          # only word->vector mapping
# Later:
# model = Word2Vec.load("my_word2vec.model")
# keyed_vecs = KeyedVectors.load("my_vectors.kv")

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 6) OPTIONAL: EXTENDING / UPDATING THE VOCAB WITH NEW DATA
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Suppose we have a list of new sentences `new_sents`
# new_sents = [...]
# model.build_vocab(new_sents, update=True)
# model.train(new_sents,
#             total_examples=len(new_sents),
#             epochs=model.epochs)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# NOTES / FAQs
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# • Word2Vec only produces vectors for words seen during training.
#   For true out-of-vocabulary (OOV) handling consider FastText
#   (gensim.models.FastText) which uses sub-word information.
#
# • vector_size, window, min_count, sg, epochs heavily influence quality.
#   Feel free to tune depending on how large and clean your corpus is.
#
# • If your corpus is big, DO NOT turn it into a list in memory
#   (replace `list(iterate_corpus(..))` with a plain generator in model).
#
# • Averaging word vectors is just one simple way to represent sentences.
#   For more sophisticated sentence embeddings look into Doc2Vec,
#   transformers (Sentence-BERT) or similar models.
```

That’s all you need to start generating and using word vectors with Gensim. Adapt the paths, hyper-parameters, and downstream logic to fit your own project. Good luck!

Below is a compact “play-book” you can reuse every time you get a new batch of model outputs. It contains

1. The two visualisations that communicate the story most clearly.
2. Optional “nice-to-have” charts.
3. Typical business / product inferences you can pull from the numbers.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. TWO CORE CHARTS
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Sentiment-over-time “Lollipop” (or Scatter) plot
   • X-axis: Date  
   • Y-axis: Signed score  (score · +1 for POSITIVE, score · –1 for NEGATIVE)  
   • Marker colour: green = POSITIVE, red = NEGATIVE  
   • Marker size: model’s confidence (the absolute score)  

   Why it works  
   ✔ Combines direction (pos/neg), magnitude (score), frequency (multiple points per day) in one glance.  
   ✔ Easy to spot spikes, clusters, or trend drift.

   Example in Python (Plotly)  
   ```python
   df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
   df['signed_score'] = df['score'] * df['label'].map({'POSITIVE': 1, 'NEGATIVE': -1})

   fig = px.scatter(df, x="date", y="signed_score",
                    color="label", size="score",
                    color_discrete_map={'POSITIVE':'#2ecc71',
                                        'NEGATIVE':'#e74c3c'},
                    title="Sentiment over Time")
   fig.add_hline(y=0, line_color='grey')
   fig.show()
   ```

B. Daily sentiment bar (or 100 % stacked bar)
   • Aggregate to day (or week) and calculate  
        – % POSITIVE  
        – % NEGATIVE  
        – Average sentiment score  
   • Plot either two-colour bars or a diverging bar around zero.

   Why it works  
   ✔ Gives a quick “dashboard KPI” view (How good was Monday? How bad was Tuesday?).  
   ✔ Hides the noise of individual posts/tweets/emails if volume is high.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. OPTIONAL CHARTS
────────────────────────────────────────
• Rolling average line (e.g., 3-day mean of signed_score) → shows trend direction.  
• Histogram / density plot of positive vs. negative scores → shows confidence distribution.  
• Calendar heat-map (“GitHub style”) of average sentiment per day → intuitive for long ranges.  
• Pie / Donut of overall share of labels → good for execs who only want “80 % positive”.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY INFERENCES FROM THE SAMPLE DATA
────────────────────────────────────────
Data set: 10 records, 8 POSITIVE, 2 NEGATIVE.

1. Overall sentiment is strongly positive (80 % of instances; mean signed score ≈ +0.83).  
2. POSITIVE scores are extremely confident (median ≈ 0.996).  
3. Two negative spikes occur on consecutive days (9 & 10 Oct) with moderate confidence (~0.82–0.83) – worth examining the underlying text for emerging pain points.  
4. No sustained negative trend: the rolling average never drops below +0.5.  
5. Variability is low for positives (tight cluster near +1) but higher for negatives (only two points → larger uncertainty).

────────────────────────────────────────
4. COMMUNICATION TEMPLATE
────────────────────────────────────────
“Over the last two weeks sentiment remained overwhelmingly positive. The model is highly confident (>0.96) in 80 % of cases. Two negative instances surfaced on 9-10 Oct; they are isolated, but we should review their contents to ensure no latent issue is brewing.”

Using the two main charts you can walk stakeholders through the story in <3 minutes.

tan I copy run_profvis.R to the rootID/temp (root@d47207e50eba:/tmp#) directory of the container by the following command in bash in powershell:
