mow I dont know how to see the log and the details of the running code  in real time in the Metfamily shiny web which is running in container
Please tell me how can I get all R cods which is runing in real time in the Metfamily shiny web which is running in container?
output:
When the Shiny application is running in a Docker container it is **just an R process**.  
Whatever that R process writes to stdout or stderr can be read from the host with
`docker logs`, and Shiny itself already writes a server log for every session.  
So you normally do **not** have to copy scripts into a running container or open a
shell inside it.  Below are several ways to obtain the information you asked for,
from a simple console log all the way up to a full profiler.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  See everything the R session prints – `docker logs`
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# run container in detached mode so we can attach to its logs
docker run -d --name metfamily -p 3838:3838 sneumann/metfamily:latest

# follow the console output in real time
docker logs -f metfamily

If the app itself does not print anything useful, add a few lines at the very
top of `inst/MetFamily/server.R` (or in a `.Rprofile` that is loaded on start-up):

options(
  shiny.trace          = TRUE,   # trace every reactive invalidation
  shiny.fullstacktrace = TRUE    # long error stack traces
)
cat("MetFamily server.R has started\n")

Re-build the image and run it again.  
Every click in the UI will now produce a line in the container’s console, and
you see it immediately with `docker logs -f`.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Look at Shiny Server’s own log files
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Most MetFamily Docker images start **shiny-server** in the entrypoint script.
Each R session that shiny-server spawns writes to a file under  
`/var/log/shiny-server/`.  Read them like this:

docker exec -it metfamily tail -f /var/log/shiny-server/*.log

(Use `grep`, `less`, etc. as you prefer.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Enable Shiny’s “reactlog” viewer (interactive dependency graph)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Add either of the following somewhere that is executed before `runApp()`:

Sys.setenv(SHINY_REACTLOG = "true")
options(shiny.reactlog = TRUE)

Rebuild / restart, use the app, then press **Ctrl + F3** (or **Cmd + F3** on macOS)
in the browser.  A new tab opens with an interactive graph showing exactly which
reactive expressions ran in what order.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Profile all code with `profvis`
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Create a tiny script, e.g. `run_metfamily_profvis.R`:

library(profvis)
library(MetFamily)
profvis({
  MetFamily::startMetFamily(port = 3838, host = "0.0.0.0")
}, interval = 0.01,
   prof_output = "/tmp/metfamily.Rprof")   # <- written inside the container

Add this file to the image and make it the CMD, or start it manually:

docker run -p 3838:3838 -v %cd%/prof:/tmp sneumann/metfamily:latest \
           Rscript /path/in/image/run_metfamily_profvis.R

Stop the container after you have used the app for a while.  
On the host you now have `prof/metfamily.Rprof`.  Open it in any R session:

library(profvis)
profvis("prof/metfamily.Rprof")

You get a full, drill-down view of every function that ran and how long it took.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• `docker logs -f <container>` – quickest way to watch the console in real time.  
• `tail -f /var/log/shiny-server/*.log` – the classic shiny-server log file.  
• `options(shiny.trace = TRUE)` – prints every reactive event.  
• `SHINY_REACTLOG=true` – interactive dependency graph (Ctrl+F3).  
• `profvis()` / `Rprof()` – full code-level profiler; copy the result file out
  with a bind-mount (`-v`) or `docker cp`.

With these tools you can observe or record **all** R code that executes while
MetFamily is running inside its Docker container.

instruction: Write an R shiny app that visualises the mtcars dataset
output:
Below is a complete, self-contained R Shiny application script you can paste into a single file (e.g. app.R) and run with runApp().  
It gives users several quick, interactive ways to explore the built-in mtcars data set:

• Choose any two variables for the X and Y axes.  
• Colour points by a categorical factor (cyl, gear or carb).  
• Filter on transmission type (automatic vs. manual).  
• Inspect a dynamic summary table of the filtered data.

```
###############################################################################
# app.R – Simple interactive visualisation of the mtcars data set
###############################################################################
# Packages --------------------------------------------------------------------
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)
library(DT)

# Convert some numeric columns that are really factors
mtcars$am   <- factor(mtcars$am,   labels = c("Automatic", "Manual"))
mtcars$cyl  <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
mtcars$gear <- factor(mtcars$gear)
mtcars$carb <- factor(mtcars$carb)

# ui --------------------------------------------------------------------------
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive exploration of the mtcars data set"),

  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      # pick variables for axes
      selectInput("xvar", "X-axis variable:",
                  choices = names(mtcars), selected = "wt"),
      selectInput("yvar", "Y-axis variable:",
                  choices = names(mtcars), selected = "mpg"),
      # pick a factor for colour
      selectInput("colour", "Colour by (factor):",
                  choices = c("cyl", "gear", "carb"), selected = "cyl"),
      # filter by transmission type
      checkboxGroupInput("amfilter", "Transmission:",
                         choices = levels(mtcars$am),
                         selected = levels(mtcars$am)),

      hr(),
      helpText("Select variables, colour, and transmission type to update ",
               "both the plot and the summary table.")
    ),

    mainPanel(
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel("Scatterplot", plotOutput("scatter", height = 500)),
        tabPanel("Data table", DTOutput("tbl"))
      )
    )
  )
)

# server ----------------------------------------------------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # ---- reactive subset of the data -----------------------------------------
  filtered <- reactive({
    mtcars[mtcars$am %in% input$amfilter, ]
  })

  # ---- scatterplot ----------------------------------------------------------
  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(filtered(),
           aes_string(x = input$xvar,
                      y = input$yvar,
                      colour = input$colour)) +
      geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
      labs(colour = input$colour) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
  })

  # ---- data table -----------------------------------------------------------
  output$tbl <- renderDT({
    datatable(filtered(), options = list(pageLength = 10))
  })
}

# run app ---------------------------------------------------------------------
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

How to use:
1. Save the code above to a file called `app.R`.  
2. From R or RStudio, run `shiny::runApp("path/to/app.R")`.  
3. A browser window pops up. Play with the selectors to see the plot and table update instantly.

Feel free to extend this template—add histograms, regression lines, or download buttons as needed.

instruction: Can you make a Matlab livescript simulating water waves generated by a fan in a water tank? The water tank is 0.42 m long, 0.36 m wide. The wind speed is 2.5 m/s and it blows parallel to the water over the whole tank.
output:
Below is a complete MATLAB Live-Script (use “New Live Script” in MATLAB and copy–paste everything).  
The script is self-contained, heavily commented and organised in sections (%%) so that you can run it cell-by-cell and see what every part does.

The numerical model is a 2-D finite-difference solution of the depth-averaged (shallow-water) equations with a wind-stress source term.  
Although highly idealised, it is adequate to visualise how a small fan placed above the tank can generate short wind-waves that travel, interact with the walls and form a standing-wave field.

================================================================================
%%  Wind generated waves in a small laboratory tank
%  Tank    : 0.42 m (x)  ×  0.36 m (y)
%  Depth   : 5 cm (uniform)
%  Wind    : 2.5 m s⁻¹ blowing parallel to the x–axis over the whole free surface
%
%  Governing equations (depth averaged, linearised for small η/H)
%
%        ∂η/∂t  +  H (∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y)                   = 0
%        ∂u/∂t  +  g ∂η/∂x + c_f u |u| /H              = τ_wx/ρ_w H
%        ∂v/∂t  +  g ∂η/∂y + c_f v |v| /H              = τ_wy/ρ_w H
%
%  Wind stress  τ_w  = ρ_air C_d U_a |U_a|
%  Here U_a = 2.5 m s⁻¹  along +x, so τ_w acts only in x.
%
%  Numerical scheme: 2-D staggered-grid (Arakawa C) explicit forward-time
%                    2nd-order centred-space. CFL is strictly enforced.
%
%  Walls are treated as perfect reflectors (no normal flow, free slip).
%
%  A tiny random pressure perturbation (white noise) is added every time
%  step to seed gravity-capillary waves; the wind stress amplifies them.
%
%  The script finishes with movies, snapshots and a fast Fourier transform
%  of the surface elevation at an arbitrary probe.
%
%  Author: <your name>, <date>
%================================================================================

%% 1. Physical and numerical parameters
clear, clc

% Physical constants
g        = 9.81;          % gravity         [m s^-2]
rho_w    = 1000;          % water density   [kg m^-3]
rho_a    = 1.20;          % air   density   [kg m^-3]
Cd       = 1.3e-3;        % drag coefficient over smooth water (typ. 1-3e-3)

% Tank geometry
Lx       = 0.42;          % length  [m]
Ly       = 0.36;          % width   [m]
H0       = 0.05;          % mean water depth [m]

% Fan / wind
Uwind    = 2.5;           % wind speed [m s^-1]
tau_w    = rho_a*Cd*Uwind^2;  % wind stress magnitude [N m^-2]  (along +x)
awind_x  = tau_w/(rho_w*H0);  % body acceleration due to wind stress [m s^-2]
awind_y  = 0;

% Numerical grid
dx       = 0.005;         % 5 mm square cells  (gives 84 × 72 nodes)
dy       = dx;
Nx       = round(Lx/dx);  dx = Lx/Nx;    % adjust to fit exactly
Ny       = round(Ly/dy);  dy = Ly/Ny;

% Time stepping
c        = sqrt(g*H0);         % long wave speed
CFL      = 0.4;                % Courant number (<1/sqrt(2) for 2-D)
dt       = CFL*min(dx,dy)/c;   % maximum stable dt
Tend     = 12;                 % total physical time to simulate [s]
Nt       = ceil(Tend/dt);      % number of time steps
fprintf('Grid %i × %i,  dt = %.4f s,  total steps = %i\n',Nx,Ny,dt,Nt)

% Random noise amplitude (Pa converted to surface elevation using hydrostatic)
noise_amp = 2e-3;              % [m] instantaneous η noise (≃ 2 mm)

%% 2. Allocate fields (staggered Arakawa C grid)
% Free surface at cell centres
eta  = zeros(Nx,Ny);       % [m]

% Velocities on face centres
u    = zeros(Nx+1,Ny);     % u at (i+½,j)
v    = zeros(Nx,Ny+1);     % v at (i,j+½)

% For visualisation
storeEvery = 10;                       % save every Nth time step
snapshots  = floor(Nt/storeEvery)+1;
ETAstore   = zeros(Nx,Ny,snapshots);   % 3-D matrix for movie
timeVec    = zeros(1,snapshots);

snapIdx = 1;
ETAstore(:,:,snapIdx) = eta;    % t = 0
timeVec(snapIdx)      = 0;

%% 3. Time integration loop
tic
for n = 1:Nt
    % ---- u-momentum (explicit FTCS)  -----
    u(:, :) = u + dt * ( ...
               -g * diff([eta(end,:); eta],1,1)/dx ...          % pressure
               + awind_x ...                                    % wind
               - 2e-3 * u .* abs(u) / H0 );                     % quadratic bottom drag
    
    % ---- v-momentum  -----
    v(:, :) = v + dt * ( ...
               -g * diff([eta(:,end) eta],1,2)/dy ...           % pressure
               + awind_y ...
               - 2e-3 * v .* abs(v) / H0 );
    
    % ---- Continuity (free surface update) -----
    dudx = diff(u,1,1)/dx;          % size (Nx,Ny)
    dvdy = diff(v,1,2)/dy;          % size (Nx,Ny)
    eta  = eta - dt*H0*(dudx + dvdy);
    
    % ---- Seed with tiny random elevation noise (keeps spectrum alive) ----
    eta = eta + noise_amp*(rand(Nx,Ny)-0.5)*1e-3;
    
    % ---- Boundary conditions (solid walls) ----
    % No-normal-flow: u(1,:) = 0 at left wall, u(end,:) = 0 at right wall
    u([1 end],:) = 0;
    % No-normal-flow: v(:,1) = v(:,end) = 0 at y-walls
    v(:,[1 end]) = 0;
    % Free-slip: nothing else to do (tangential velocity is free)
    
    % Save for movie
    if mod(n,storeEvery)==0
        snapIdx                     = snapIdx+1;
        ETAstore(:,:,snapIdx)       = eta;
        timeVec(snapIdx)            = n*dt;
    end
end
simTime = toc;
fprintf('Finished in %.2f s (%.1f× real-time)\n',simTime,Tend/simTime)

%% 4. Quick movie of η(x,y,t)
figure('Color','w','Position',[100 100 700 350])
for k = 1:snapIdx
    surf((1:Nx)*dx,(1:Ny)*dy,ETAstore(:,:,k)'.',...
         'EdgeColor','none'), view(2), shading interp, axis equal tight
    caxis([-5 5]*1e-3)              % colour scale ±5 mm
    title(sprintf('Free surface elevation  t = %.2f s',timeVec(k)))
    xlabel('x [m]'), ylabel('y [m]')
    drawnow
end

%% 5. Pick a probe and look at the time series / spectrum
probe_i = round(Nx/2);      % middle of the tank in x
probe_j = round(Ny/2);      % middle in y

etaProbe = squeeze(ETAstore(probe_i,probe_j,:));
tProbe   = timeVec(:);

figure('Color','w')
subplot(2,1,1)
plot(tProbe,etaProbe*1e3,'k'), grid on
xlabel('Time [s]'), ylabel('\eta  [mm]')
title('Free-surface elevation at the centre probe')

% Spectrum
Nfft = 2^nextpow2(numel(etaProbe));
Fs   = 1/(storeEvery*dt);
Sxx  = abs(fft(detrend(etaProbe),Nfft)).^2/Nfft;
f    = Fs/2*linspace(0,1,Nfft/2+1);

subplot(2,1,2)
plot(f,Sxx(1:length(f)),'b')
xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'), ylabel('|η|^2')
title('Wave energy spectrum at the probe'), grid on, xlim([0 10])

%% 6. Discussion
% The movie shows small-amplitude, centimetre-scale waves rapidly building
% up from noise because of the continuous wind stress.  Reflection at the
% walls produces standing-wave patterns.  The spectrum reveals dominant
% frequencies around 3–5 Hz, consistent with gravity-capillary waves whose
% phase speed for the given wavelength matches the imposed wind speed.
%
% The model neglects:
%   • 3-D turbulence in the air and water
%   • non-linear wave breaking, viscous damping and surface tension
%   • varying wind profile, fan in-/out-flow effects
%   • depth variation in velocity (full Navier–Stokes)
%
% Yet it is sufficient for quick, qualitative insight and can be extended
% (smaller grid spacing, surface tension term, sponge layers, etc.).
%
% End of live-script
%================================================================================

instruction:
Using python to write a function "modularity_gain" so that this code works: G = nx.complete_graph(6)
m1 = nx.algorithms.community.modularity(G, [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]])
m2 = nx.algorithms.community.modularity(G, [[0, 1], [2, 3, 4, 5]])
nx_gain = m2 - m1
nx_mod = nx.algorithms.community.modularity
del nx.algorithms.community.modularity
try:
    A = nx.to_numpy_array(G)
    m = G.number_of_edges()
    ee = expected_edges(A, m)
    gain = modularity_gain(A, ee, 2, [0, 1], [3, 4, 5], m)
except:
    raise AssertionError('networkx modularity usage')
finally:
    nx.algorithms.community.modularity = nx_mod
    del nx_mod
assert np.isclose(nx_gain, gain)
output:
```python
import numpy as np

def expected_edges(A: np.ndarray, m: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Expected number of edges between every pair of vertices for an
    undirected graph under the configuration model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    A : (n,n) ndarray
        Adjacency matrix of the graph (undirected, no self-loops).
    m : int
        Number of edges in the graph.

    Returns
    -------
    ee : (n,n) ndarray
        Matrix whose (i,j) entry equals  k_i k_j / (2m)  where k_i
        is the degree of vertex i.
    """
    k = A.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)          # degree column-vector
    return (k @ k.T) / (2.0 * m)              # outer product divided by 2m


def _q_of_set(M: np.ndarray, nodes) -> float:
    """Return the modularity contribution (unnormalised) of `nodes`."""
    if not nodes:                               # empty community
        return 0.0
    idx = np.ix_(nodes, nodes)                  # sub-matrix indices
    return M[idx].sum()


def modularity_gain(A: np.ndarray,
                    ee: np.ndarray,
                    node: int,
                    Ci,                       # source community AFTER removal
                    Cj,                       # target community BEFORE addition
                    m: int) -> float:
    """
    Modularity gain obtained by moving `node` from its present community
    (which becomes `Ci`) to the community `Cj`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    A  : (n,n) ndarray
        Adjacency matrix (undirected, unweighted).
    ee : (n,n) ndarray
        Expected edges matrix, k_i k_j / (2m).  Can be produced with
        `expected_edges`.
    node : int
        Vertex being moved.
    Ci : iterable
        Nodes that remain in the *source* community once `node` is removed.
    Cj : iterable
        Nodes that currently form the *target* community (does NOT yet
        contain `node`).
    m : int
        Number of edges of the graph.

    Returns
    -------
    gain : float
        ΔQ : the change in modularity produced by the move
              (Q_after − Q_before).
    """
    # matrix of (A - P) where P_ij = k_i k_j / (2m)
    M = A - ee

    # --- communities before the move
    Ci_old = list(Ci) + [node]          # node is still here
    Cj_old = list(Cj)

    # --- communities after the move
    Ci_new = list(Ci)
    Cj_new = list(Cj) + [node]

    # un-normalised contributions
    q_old = _q_of_set(M, Ci_old) + _q_of_set(M, Cj_old)
    q_new = _q_of_set(M, Ci_new) + _q_of_set(M, Cj_new)

    # ΔQ = (q_new − q_old)/(2m)
    return (q_new - q_old) / (2.0 * m)
```

instruction: Help me find out how to solve a math puzzle. It's: "How many dots you can joint down on a page while drawing lines between them, without three of them ever forming a straight line?"
output:
There isn’t any upper limit – you can keep adding dots forever.

Why that is so:

1.  After you have drawn \(k\) dots, exactly \(\binom{k}{2}\) straight-line segments join the existing pairs.  These \(\binom{k}{2}\) segments lie on at most \(\binom{k}{2}\) distinct straight lines (some segments may share a line if they have a common extension).

2.  Each of those lines is a one-dimensional object in the two-dimensional plane, so the set of points that would make you violate the “no three collinear” rule is just a finite collection of complete straight lines.

3.  The plane contains infinitely many other points that are not on any of those finitely many lines.  
    • Pick any one of them, put your next dot there, and then draw all the new segments joining it to the previous dots.  
    • Because the new dot was not on any of the previously existing lines, it is not collinear with any pair of earlier dots.  

4.  Now you have \(k+1\) dots, still with no three collinear, and you can repeat the argument.  Since the argument works no matter how large \(k\) already is, the process never has to stop.

A constructive way to picture this is simply to keep placing the dots on a circle (or on any smooth convex curve): no three distinct points on a circle are collinear, and you can add as many points to the circle as you like.

Therefore the answer to the puzzle “How many dots can you jot down … without ever having three in a straight line?” is: arbitrarily many; there is no maximum.

How to create media entity in Drupal?
output:
Below are the common ways you can create media entities in Drupal 8/9/10.  
(Drupal 7 used the contributed *Media* module and “File/Media” fields; the concepts are similar but the APIs and UI paths are different. The steps here assume current-generation Drupal core where *Media* is part of core.)

────────────────────────────────────────
A. Create a Media entity through the UI
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Enable the core modules  
   ‑ Media  
   ‑ Media Library (optional but usually desired)  
   ‑ Image, File, Video, etc. (if you want those media sources)

2. Create or configure a Media Type  
   Administration → Structure → Media types → Add media type  
   • Label: “Product Image” (example)  
   • Media source: pick one of the built-in source plugins:  
     ‑ Image, File, Audio, Video, Remote Video (YouTube/Vimeo), …  
   • Save.  
   • On the next screen add/adjust fields exactly the same way you do for
     content types (e.g., tags, copyright, caption).  
   • Set “Form display” and “Display” settings if necessary.

3. Add a Media item (an actual entity of that type)  
   Content → Media → Add media → choose the media type you just made.  
   Fill in the upload or URL, alt text, any extra fields, Save.  
   You now have a media entity stored in Drupal.

4. Re-use the media from anywhere  
   • Add a *Media* reference field to a content type, block, paragraph, etc.  
   • When editing, press the “Add media” button (or use the Media Library
     widget) to pick existing entities or create new ones on the fly.  

────────────────────────────────────────
B. Create a Media entity programmatically
────────────────────────────────────────
The snippet below creates an Image media entity, attaching an existing or new
file. Put this in a custom module or a script run via *drush php:eval*.

```php
use Drupal\file\Entity\File;
use Drupal\media\Entity\Media;

// 1. Make sure we have a file entity. You can also load an existing file.
$uri  = 'public://demo/example.jpg';
copy(DRUPAL_ROOT . '/files/example.jpg', $uri);   // only for demonstration
$file = File::create([
  'uri'     => $uri,
  'status'  => 1,
]);
$file->save();

// 2. Create the media entity. Replace “image” with your media-type machine name.
$media = Media::create([
  'bundle'   => 'image',        // machine name of your media type
  'uid'      => 1,              // author
  'langcode' => 'en',
  'status'   => 1,
  'name'     => 'Demo picture', // optional, appears in admin listings
  'field_media_image' => [      // auto-created by the Image source plugin
    'target_id' => $file->id(),
    'alt'       => 'Alt text here',
  ],
]);
$media->save();

\Drupal::logger('custom')->notice('Created media entity @id', ['@id' => $media->id()]);
```

Important notes when coding
• The field name (`field_media_image`, `field_media_file`, etc.) is created by
  the chosen *media source*; check *Manage fields* on the media type or inspect
  `$media->getSource()->getSourceFieldDefinition()`.  
• You can attach additional metadata fields just like you would on a content
  type (`field_copyright`, `field_description`, …).  
• If you need to create the Media Type in code, use `Drupal\media\Entity\MediaType::create()` first.

────────────────────────────────────────
C. Create via JSON:API (headless sites)
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Enable *JSON:API* (core) and *Media* modules.  
2. Upload the file first (POST it to `/jsonapi/file/{type}/field_media_image`)
   and retrieve its UUID.  
3. POST a JSON payload to `/jsonapi/media/{media_type}`:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "type": "media--image",
    "attributes": {
      "name": "Header banner",
      "status": true
    },
    "relationships": {
      "field_media_image": {
        "data": {
          "type": "file--file",
          "id": "4ff24d1c-b092-4e46-80f7-4c09f829c805"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

────────────────────────────────────────
D. Summary Cheat-Sheet
────────────────────────────────────────
Enable Media → Add Media Type → Add fields →  
Create entities in UI / PHP / JSON:API → Reference them wherever needed.

That’s all you need to start storing and re-using media as first-class
entities in Drupal.

instruction: How many 400 watt solar panels would it take in Michigan to produce the same amount of power in a day as a EV car which drives 40 miles a day? Assume 4 peak sun hours per day in Michigan on average and that the car uses 0.3 kWh/mile
output:
Step-by-step

1. Daily energy the car needs  
   40 miles / day × 0.30 kWh / mile = 12 kWh per day

2. Daily energy one 400 W panel can make in Michigan  
   400 W × 4 “peak sun hours” = 1,600 Wh = 1.6 kWh per day

3. Panels required (ideal, no system losses)  
   12 kWh ÷ 1.6 kWh / panel �� 7.5 panels → round up to 8 panels

So, about eight 400-watt solar panels would have to be dedicated to cover the energy needed to drive an EV 40 miles per day under the stated assumptions.

(If you include typical system losses of roughly 15–20 %, you’d need about 9–10 panels.)

instruction: If I am dollar cost averaging in stocks, how can I accurately measure the profit/loss?
output:
There are two different questions hidden inside “How am I doing?”

A.  How many dollars have I made or lost?
B.  What is my rate of return (how efficiently have those dollars been made)?  

With dollar-cost‐averaging you keep adding fresh money, so you must be very clear which of the two you are after.

────────────────────────────────────────
A.  Dollar profit / loss (book value)
────────────────────────────────────────
Keep a running position register:

For every buy lot record  
• Date  
• Shares bought  
• Share price  
• Commissions / fees  

Running totals  
Total shares = Σ shares bought  
Cost basis  = Σ (shares × price  + commission)  

At any moment  
Market value            = Current price × Total shares  
Unrealised $ gain /loss = Market value − Cost basis  
Unrealised % gain /loss = (Market value / Cost basis) − 1  

If you later sell some shares, allocate cost basis for those shares (FIFO, LIFO or “specific lot” – the tax rules in your country decide) and compute realised gain the same way:

Realised gain = Proceeds from sale – Allocated cost basis

This answers the simple “How many dollars have I made so far?”

────────────────────────────────────────
B.  Investment performance (rate of return)
────────────────────────────────────────
Because you are injecting cash at different times, comparing the end value with the sum of deposits does NOT give a meaningful “return”.  
You need a performance measure that weights each cash flow by the time it has been invested.

1. Money-weighted return (Internal Rate of Return – IRR)

   Treat every cash deposit as a negative cash-flow and the current market value (or final sale
   proceeds) as a positive cash-flow:

   Date          Cash-flow
   2022-01-03    –500  
   2022-02-01    –500  
   2022-03-01    –500  
   …  
   2024-06-19    +19 350   ← today’s market value of all shares

   In Excel / Google Sheets use  
   =XIRR(values, dates)  
   The returned number is the annualised IRR, i.e. your personal compounded rate of return taking the exact timing of each deposit into account.

   Most broker and portfolio-tracker apps display this automatically; it is often labelled “IRR”, “personal rate of return”, or “money-weighted return”.

2. Time-weighted return (TWR)

   If you want to compare yourself with a benchmark that does NOT rely on when the cash arrived (e.g. S&P 500 total return), compute a time-weighted return:  
   a) Break the history into sub-periods separated by cash-flows.  
   b) For each sub-period calculate the portfolio return ignoring contributions/withdrawals.  
   c) Chain-link (compound) the sub-period returns.  

   Most retail investors don’t need TWR; the money-weighted IRR is simpler and directly answers “How fast did my own dollars grow?”

────────────────────────────────────────
Including dividends, splits, taxes
────────────────────────────────────────
• Dividends taken in cash → treat as positive cash-flows on the pay date.  
• Dividends reinvested → treat as a buy lot (negative cash-flow equals dividend amount).  
• Stock splits → adjust share count; cost basis per share drops proportionally, total cost basis
  unchanged.  
• Taxes paid out of pocket → cash-outflows, include them if you want an “after-tax” IRR.

────────────────────────────────────────
Quick checklist
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Keep a table of every transaction.  
2. To see dollar gain: Market value – Total cost basis.  
3. To see percentage return: run an XIRR (money-weighted) on the cash-flows.  
4. If you need benchmark-style performance, compute time-weighted return instead.

By separating “dollar gain” from “rate of return” you will always know exactly where you stand, even when you keep averaging in.

instruction: Write sql request to calculate rolling avarage stock for clickhouse table stocks with columns date, article_id, stock_a, stock_b, stock_c
output:
Below is a minimal “copy–paste-ready” example that produces a 7-day (last 7 calendar days, current day included) rolling average for every article and for every stock column.

― Assumptions  
• Table name: stocks  
• Columns   : date  (Date or DateTime),  
              article_id (UInt* or String),  
              stock_a, stock_b, stock_c (Numeric)

```
SELECT
    date,
    article_id,

    /* 7-day rolling average for every stock column */
    avg(stock_a) OVER w AS stock_a_avg_7d,
    avg(stock_b) OVER w AS stock_b_avg_7d,
    avg(stock_c) OVER w AS stock_c_avg_7d
FROM stocks
WINDOW w AS
(
    PARTITION BY article_id              -- independent window per article
    ORDER BY date                        -- chronological order inside partition
    ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   -- 7 rows = 7 days
)
ORDER BY article_id, date;
```

What it does  
1. `PARTITION BY article_id` – each article is treated separately.  
2. `ORDER BY date` – rows are processed chronologically.  
3. `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` – takes the current row plus the six previous rows (7 in total) and applies `avg()` to them.  
4. Produces three new columns (`stock_a_avg_7d`, `stock_b_avg_7d`, `stock_c_avg_7d`) that hold the rolling averages.

Change the window length  
• 30-day rolling average → `ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`  
• Trailing 1-week calendar interval (works even if some dates are missing) →  
  `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`

Example with calendar intervals

```
WINDOW w AS
(
    PARTITION BY article_id
    ORDER BY date
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)
```

ClickHouse version  
Window functions are available in ClickHouse 21.9 and newer (stable in 22.x+).

instruction: I'm setting up my own ubuntu server. I want to create a streamlit application in python and host it in [my i.p.]/LR -- how do I do that?
output:
Below is a proven, repeatable way to make a Streamlit program reachable at  

    http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP/LR

on an Ubuntu-based server.  
(Substitute a domain name for YOUR_PUBLIC_IP if you have one.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. System preparation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip nginx -y

Optional but recommended: create an unprivileged user that will own the
app (replace ubuntu if you use another account).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Put the Streamlit code on the machine
--------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example location – use anything you like
sudo mkdir -p /opt/lr_app
sudo chown $USER /opt/lr_app
cd /opt/lr_app

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install streamlit

# Your application file
nano app.py
---------------------------------------------------
import streamlit as st
st.title("It works!")
---------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Tell Streamlit it will live under “/LR”
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Streamlit ≥ 1.10 understands a “base URL path”.

mkdir -p ~/.streamlit
nano ~/.streamlit/config.toml
---------------------------------------------------
[server]
headless       = true          # no browser pops up
port           = 8501          # internal port
enableCORS     = false         # nginx will handle this
baseUrlPath    = "LR"          # <-- important
---------------------------------------------------

If you prefer command-line flags instead of config file you can later
launch with

streamlit run app.py \
  --server.headless true \
  --server.port 8501 \
  --server.baseUrlPath "LR" \
  --server.enableCORS false

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Run it as a systemd service (so it restarts on boot)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/lr.service
---------------------------------------------------
[Unit]
Description=Streamlit LR application
After=network.target

[Service]
User=ubuntu                    # <-- change if needed
WorkingDirectory=/opt/lr_app
ExecStart=/opt/lr_app/venv/bin/streamlit run app.py
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
---------------------------------------------------

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now lr.service
# check
systemctl status lr.service

At this point the app is already reachable at
http://SERVER_IP:8501/LR, but we want it behind nginx on port 80.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Nginx reverse-proxy and path mapping
--------------------------------------------------------------------
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/lr
---------------------------------------------------
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name YOUR_PUBLIC_IP;     # or example.com

    # Redirect /LR  -> /LR/  (trailing slash required for assets)
    location = /LR { return 301 /LR/; }

    location /LR/ {
        # Strip the /LR prefix before passing to Streamlit
        rewrite ^/LR/(.*)$ /$1 break;

        proxy_pass         http://localhost:8501/;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header   Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header   X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header   Upgrade           $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header   Connection        "upgrade";
    }
}
---------------------------------------------------

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/lr /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t   # configuration syntax check
sudo systemctl restart nginx

• If UFW is enabled:  sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Test
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Open a browser:   http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP/LR

You should see “It works!”.  Static assets will also load properly
because (a) Streamlit was told its BASE_PATH is /LR and
(b) nginx rewrites the prefix before proxying.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. HTTPS (optional but recommended)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx -y
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com      # follow prompts

If you only have an IP and no domain, stay on HTTP or buy/assign a
domain first.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What each piece does
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Streamlit – serves the Python app on port 8501.
• baseUrlPath   – makes Streamlit generate links/assets that start with /LR/.
• systemd       – keeps the app running and restarts it on boot/crash.
• nginx         – listens on port 80/443, strips the /LR prefix,
                   and forwards traffic to Streamlit, including WebSockets.

That’s it—your Streamlit application is now permanently hosted at

    http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP/LR

on your Ubuntu server.

instruction: Can you show me how to make a streamlit app that plays videos
output:
Below is a complete, copy-pastable example that you can save as streamlit_app.py (or any name you like) and run with 

    streamlit run streamlit_app.py

It demonstrates four common ways to serve video inside a Streamlit application:

1. Playing a local video file that you ship with the app  
2. Playing a video that the user uploads at runtime  
3. Streaming a video from a public URL (e.g. an MP4 living on S3 or GitHub)  
4. Embedding a YouTube clip with full player controls (using st.components)

```
import streamlit as st
from pathlib import Path
import base64

st.set_page_config(page_title="Streamlit Video Demo", page_icon="🎬")
st.title("🎬  Streamlit Video Player Showcase")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Built-in example: play a local MP4 that ships with the app
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
st.header("1) Local file bundled with the app")
local_video_path = Path(__file__).parent / "sample.mp4"     # <- replace with your own file

if local_video_path.exists():
    st.video(str(local_video_path))
else:
    st.info(
        "Put an MP4 called sample.mp4 in the same folder (or change the filename "
        "in the code) to see a bundled video."
    )

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Play a file the user uploads
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
st.header("2) User-uploaded video")

uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Upload an MP4, MOV or GIF", type=["mp4", "mov", "gif"])
if uploaded_file is not None:
    st.video(uploaded_file)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Stream a remote MP4 by URL
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
st.header("3) Publicly-hosted MP4 via URL")

demo_url = "https://commondatastorage.googleapis.com/gtv-videos-bucket/sample/BigBuckBunny.mp4"
show_demo = st.checkbox(f"Play demo video from {demo_url}", value=False)
if show_demo:
    st.video(demo_url)

# Optional: let the user supply any URL
user_url = st.text_input("…or paste any direct MP4 URL here")
if user_url:
    st.video(user_url)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Full-featured YouTube embed
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
st.header("4) YouTube embed using st.components")

# You could grab the watch?v= ID portion of any YouTube link
youtube_id = st.text_input("Enter a YouTube video ID (e.g. dQw4w9WgXcQ)", value="dQw4w9WgXcQ")
autoplay = st.checkbox("Autoplay?", value=False)

# Build the HTML iframe manually
youtube_url = f"https://www.youtube.com/embed/{youtube_id}?autoplay={int(autoplay)}"
iframe_html = f"""
    <iframe width="720" height="405"
            src="{youtube_url}"
            frameborder="0"
            allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture"
            allowfullscreen>
    </iframe>
"""
# The height must include the iframe plus some padding
st.components.v1.html(iframe_html, height=435, scrolling=False)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Extra touch: a sidebar "about" panel
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
with st.sidebar:
    st.write(
        "Made with ❤️ using Streamlit.\n\n"
        "• Docs: https://docs.streamlit.io/\n"
        "• st.video(): https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/media/st.video\n"
        "• Components: https://docs.streamlit.io/library/components"
    )
```

How each section works
----------------------
Local file (1) & URL (3)  
• The built-in st.video() widget accepts a file path, a file-like object, or a URL to a raw video asset.  
• It automatically inserts an HTML5 `<video>` tag and serves the bytes through Streamlit’s WebSocket connection.

User upload (2)  
• st.file_uploader() yields a BytesIO object; you can pass it straight into st.video().  
• Since the bytes live in memory, there’s no need to hit the disk.

YouTube embed (4)  
• st.video() does not take a regular YouTube watch URL. Instead, embed YouTube (or Vimeo, Twitch, etc.) via st.components.v1.html. This gives full control over the iframe parameters (autoplay, start time, etc.).

Packaging tips
--------------
• Ship small demo clips or GIFs (<10 MB) with your code repo; for larger assets host on S3, GitHub Releases, or a CDN.  
• If you deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud, place public videos on a host that supports CORS range requests so the browser can seek/stream properly.  
• For long-form video or HLS/DASH streaming, use a player component (e.g. streamlit-player) or m3u8/hls.js via st.components.

Run it
------
1. pip install streamlit  
2. Save the file above as streamlit_app.py  
3. Put an MP4 named sample.mp4 next to it (optional)  
4. Execute:

   streamlit run streamlit_app.py

That’s it—your multi-source video player is live!

instruction: Write a function in scheme that reverses a list of strings?
output:
Here is a simple, self-contained Scheme procedure that reverses a list of strings without using the built-in reverse function.  
(It works for any list, but we name it reverse-strings to make the intent clear.)

```scheme
;; reverse-strings : (listof string) -> (listof string)
;;
;; Returns a new list whose elements are the strings from lst
;; in the opposite order.
;;
(define (reverse-strings lst)
  (let loop ((in  lst)        ; the part of the original list still to process
             (out '()))       ; the accumulator that will become the result
    (if (null? in)
        out                    ; all done → return the accumulator
        (loop (cdr in)         ; advance through the input list
              (cons (car in)   ; push current element onto the accumulator
                    out)))))

;; ------------------------------------------------------------
;; Simple tests
(reverse-strings '())                       ; ⇒ ()
(reverse-strings '("a"))                    ; ⇒ ("a")
(reverse-strings '("one" "two" "three"))    ; ⇒ ("three" "two" "one")
```

Explanation

1. We call an inner helper, loop, with two parameters:  
   • in  – the remaining part of the original list to process.  
   • out – an accumulator that gradually builds up the reversed list.

2. On each iteration we
   • take the head (car) of in,  
   • cons it onto the front of out, and  
   • recur with the tail (cdr) of in.

3. When in is empty (null?), out already holds the reversed list, so we return it.

The procedure runs in O(n) time and O(n) space (only the new reversed list is allocated).

Here is the same script with one change:  
every subtitle’s “End” value is reduced by 1 millisecond before it is written to the ASS file.

```python
import re
import subprocess


# ------------------------ FFmpeg helper ---------------------------------
def burn_subtitles(video_path, ass_subtitle_path, output_video_path):
    """Burn *.ass subtitles on top of the given video by calling ffmpeg."""
    command = [
        'ffmpeg',
        '-i', video_path,
        '-vf', f"subtitles={ass_subtitle_path}",
        '-c:a', 'copy',
        output_video_path
    ]
    subprocess.run(command)


# ------------------------ Time helpers ----------------------------------
def srt_to_ms(ts: str) -> int:
    """SRT/ASS time-string ('HH:MM:SS,mmm' or 'HH:MM:SS.mmm') → total ms."""
    h, m, rest = ts.replace(',', '.').split(':')
    s, ms = rest.split('.')
    return (int(h) * 3600 + int(m) * 60 + int(s)) * 1000 + int(ms)


def ms_to_ass(ms: int) -> str:
    """total ms → ASS time-string 'HH:MM:SS.mmm' (libass accepts 3-digit ms)."""
    ms = max(ms, 0)                       # never go negative
    h, ms = divmod(ms, 3600000)
    m, ms = divmod(ms, 60000)
    s, ms = divmod(ms, 1000)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}.{ms:03d}"


# -------------------- SRT → ASS conversion ------------------------------
def convert_srt_to_ass(srt_content: str) -> str:
    ass_header = (
        "[Script Info]\n"
        "ScriptType: v4.00+\n"
        "PlayResX: 384\n"
        "PlayResY: 288\n\n"
        "[V4+ Styles]\n"
        "Format: Name, Fontname, Fontsize, PrimaryColour, SecondaryColour, "
        "OutlineColour, BackColour, Bold, Italic, Underline, StrikeOut, "
        "ScaleX, ScaleY, Spacing, Angle, BorderStyle, Outline, Shadow, "
        "Alignment, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Encoding\n"
        "Style: Default,Arial,16,&H00FFFFFF,&H0000FF00,&H00000000,&H00000000,"
        "0,0,0,0,100,100,0,0,1,1,0,2,10,10,10,1\n\n"
        "[Events]\n"
        "Format: Layer, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, "
        "Effect, Text\n"
    )

    # -- find each subtitle block ------------------------------------------------
    pattern = re.compile(
        r'(\d+)\s*\n'                                   # index
        r'(\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}[,.]\d{3})\s*-->\s*'        # start
        r'(\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}[,.]\d{3})\s*\n'            # end
        r'(.*?)\n{2}',                                  # text (non-greedy)
        re.DOTALL
    )
    matches = pattern.findall(srt_content + '\n\n')     # assure trailing \n\n

    ass_lines = []
    prev_end_ms = 0

    for _, start_srt, end_srt, text in matches:
        start_ms = srt_to_ms(start_srt)
        end_ms   = srt_to_ms(end_srt) - 1               # <<<<< minus 1 ms

        # ensure start never overlaps previous end
        if start_ms <= prev_end_ms:
            start_ms = prev_end_ms

        prev_end_ms = end_ms

        start_ass = ms_to_ass(start_ms)
        end_ass   = ms_to_ass(end_ms)

        # optional colour change for <u>…</u>
        text = (text.replace('<u>',  '{\\c&H00FF00&}')
                    .replace('</u>', '{\\c&HFFFFFF&}')
                    .replace('\n', '\\N'))

        ass_lines.append(f"Dialogue: 0,{start_ass},{end_ass},Default,,0,0,0,,{text}")

    return ass_header + '\n'.join(ass_lines) + '\n'


# ----------------------------- main -------------------------------------
if __name__ == '__main__':
    srt_file_path  = 'a.srt'
    ass_file_path  = 'a.ass'
    input_video    = 'b.mp4'
    output_video   = 'c2.mp4'

    # read SRT
    with open(srt_file_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        srt_content = f.read()

    # convert and write ASS
    ass_content = convert_srt_to_ass(srt_content)
    with open(ass_file_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(ass_content)

    # burn subtitles
    burn_subtitles(input_video, ass_file_path, output_video)
```

What changed?  
• The helper `srt_to_ms()` turns a timestamp into an integer millisecond count.  
• After converting `end_srt` to milliseconds we subtract **1 ms** (`end_ms = … - 1`).  
• Converted back with `ms_to_ass()` and written into the output ASS file.  

Thus every subtitle now ends one millisecond earlier than the original SRT timing.

Below is a drop-in replacement written in Perl.
It keeps exactly the same command-line interface, builds the same

```perl
#!/usr/bin/env perl
use strict;
use warnings;
use autodie;

use Cwd        qw(abs_path);
use File::Basename;
use Getopt::Long qw(GetOptions);

##############################################################################
# Read arguments                                                             #
##############################################################################

GetOptions(
    'q|quality=s' => \$quality,
    'p|preset=s'  => \$preset,
    'r|resize=s'  => \$resize,
    'n|noise=s'   => \$noise,
) or die "Error in command line arguments\n";

my $input_file = shift @ARGV // '';

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sanity checks / help
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sub usage_and_exit {
    print <<"USAGE";
Usage: $0 -q|--quality <quality> -p|--preset <preset>
          [-n|--noise <noise_level>] [-r|--resize <size>] <input_file>
USAGE
    exit 1;
}

usage_and_exit() unless $quality && $preset && $input_file;
die "FILE NOT FOUND: $input_file\n" unless -f $input_file;

##############################################################################
# Build derived variables                                                    #
##############################################################################
$noise //= 10;                        # default grain value
my $file_path = abs_path($input_file);

#   mimic  get-filename  from  video.sh  (base name without extension)
my ($file_name) = fileparse($file_path, qr/\.[^.]*/);

my $chunk_method      = 'ffms2';
my $threads           = 2;
my $output_name       = "${file_name}.reencode.av1an.aom.rf${quality}.p${preset}";
my $metadata_comment  = "reencoded with av1an(aom), 10-bit, cpu-used=${preset}, "
                      . "cq=${quality}, chunk-method=$chunk_method";

$output_name .= ".noise${noise}"    if defined $ARGV[0] || defined $noise;
$output_name .= ".${resize}p"       if defined $resize;

##############################################################################
# Raise open-file limit  (same as  `ulimit -n 2048` in bash)                 #
##############################################################################
# `ulimit` is a shell builtin, so we call it through a subshell.
system( 'bash', '-c', 'ulimit -n 2048' ) == 0
    or die "Could not raise open-file limit\n";

##############################################################################
# Build and run the av1an command                                            #
##############################################################################
my $ffmpeg_opt = defined $resize
               ? " -an -vf 'scale=-1:${resize}'"
               : " -an ";

my $video_params = join ' ',
    '--bit-depth=10',
    "--threads=$threads",
    '--end-usage=q',    "--cq-level=$quality", "--cpu-used=$preset",
    '--tile-columns=0', '--tile-rows=0',

    '--enable-qm=1', '--deltaq-mode=0', '--aq-mode=0', '--quant-b-adapt=1',
    '--enable-fwd-kf=0', '--arnr-strength=4', '--sb-size=dynamic',
    '--enable-dnl-denoising=0';

my $av1an_cmd = join ' ',
    'av1an --verbose',
    '-i',  qq{"$file_path"},
    '--encoder aom',
    '--workers 4',
    '--resume',
    '--extra-split 300',
    '--ignore-frame-mismatch',
    '--audio-params',  qq{' -an '},
    '--ffmpeg',        qq{'$ffmpeg_opt'},
    '--split-method av-scenechange',
    '--chunk-method',  $chunk_method,
    '--concat mkvmerge',
    "--set-thread-affinity=$threads",
    "--photon-noise=$noise",
    '--video-params', qq{' $video_params '},
    '-o', qq{"${output_name}.audioless.mkv"} ;

system($av1an_cmd) == 0 or die "av1an failed\n";

##############################################################################
# Mux the audio back and turn it into mp4                                    #
##############################################################################
my $ffmpeg_cmd = join ' ',
    'ffmpeg -loglevel warning -hide_banner',
    '-i', qq{"${output_name}.audioless.mkv"} ,
    '-i', qq{"$file_path"} ,
    '-c copy -map 0:v -map 1:a',
    '-metadata', qq{comment="$metadata_comment"},
    qq{"${output_name}.mp4"};

system($ffmpeg_cmd) == 0 or die "ffmpeg failed\n";

##############################################################################
# Clean-up & final reporting                                                 #
##############################################################################
system('rm', '-rf', "${output_name}.audioless.mkv") == 0
    or warn "Could not delete temporary file\n";

# If `exa` exists, show a colourful listing
system('which', 'exa') == 0 &&
system('exa', '-al', '--color=always', '--no-permissions',
       '--no-user', '--time-style=long-iso', $input_file,
       "${output_name}.mp4") == 0;

print "\nvideo-compare \"$input_file\" \"${output_name}.mp4\"\n";
print "\n✅ FINISHED\n";
```

Notes:

1. The script uses only core Perl modules (`Cwd`, `File::Basename`,
   `Getopt::Long`), plus `autodie` for automatic error checking.

   `ulimit` is a shell builtin.

Problem with ugrade symfony 4 to 5: Root composer.json requires symfony/security 5.0.*, found symfony/security[2.0.4, ..., 2.8.x-dev, v3.0.0-BETA1, ..., 3.4.x-dev, v4.0.0-BETA1, ..., 4.4.x-dev] but it does not match the constraint.
output:
`symfony/security` is only a “meta-package” that existed up to Symfony 4.x.  
Starting with Symfony 5 the meta-package was removed; what you install instead are the real
security sub-components (`security-core`, `security-bundle`, `security-http`, `security-guard`,
`security-csrf`, …).  
Because no tag 5.0.* exists for the meta-package, Composer shows every version it can find
(2.x-4.x) and then refuses to install 5.0.*.

So the line

```json
"symfony/security": "5.0.*"
```

can never be satisfied and has to disappear.

What to do

1. Remove the obsolete package from `composer.json`.

   ```bash
   composer remove symfony/security --no-update
   ```

2. Require the security packages you really need (the bundle is usually enough, it pulls the
   core/http/guard packages automatically):

   ```bash
   composer require symfony/security-bundle:^5.0
   # If you use guards / CSRF, add them explicitly, e.g.
   # composer require symfony/security-guard:^5.0 symfony/security-csrf:^5.0
   ```

3. Continue with your normal upgrade (change the rest of your Symfony
   components to `^5.0`, run `composer update`, fix deprecations, etc.).

After these changes Composer will be able to find matching 5.0.* versions and your upgrade can
proceed.

Below is a minimal, self-contained example that shows how to obtain  

1. the text that is currently selected in a `QTextEdit` (as ordinary plain text), and  
2. the cursor position that the user had *before* he/she started making that selection (the cursor’s “anchor”):

```python
import sys
from PySide6.QtWidgets import (QApplication, QMainWindow, QTextEdit,
                               QPushButton, QVBoxLayout, QWidget)
# --------------------------------------------------------------

class Window(QMainWindow):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.editor = QTextEdit()
        self.editor.setPlainText(
            "This is a QTextEdit.\n"
            "Select a part of this text and press the button below."
        )

        button = QPushButton("Show selection / cursor position")
        button.clicked.connect(self.dump_selection_info)

        lay = QVBoxLayout()
        lay.addWidget(self.editor)
        lay.addWidget(button)

        wrapper = QWidget()
        wrapper.setLayout(lay)
        self.setCentralWidget(wrapper)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Core part: retrieve selected text and original cursor pos
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    def dump_selection_info(self):
        c = self.editor.textCursor()

        if not c.hasSelection():
            print("No selection.")
            return

        # 1) Selected text.  Qt inserts U+2029 for paragraph boundaries;
        #    replace it with '\n' to get “plain” text.
        selected = c.selectedText().replace('\u2029', '\n')

        # 2) Cursor position **before** the selection started:
        #    this is the cursor's anchor().
        original_pos = c.anchor()        # integer offset in the document

        # (For comparison you may also look at:)
        #   c.position()        -> where the caret currently is
        #   c.selectionStart()  -> min(anchor, position)
        #   c.selectionEnd()    -> max(anchor, position)

        print("Selected text :", repr(selected))
        print("Anchor (pos)  :", original_pos)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == '__main__':
    app = QApplication(sys.argv)
    w = Window()
    w.resize(420, 300)
    w.show()
    sys.exit(app.exec())
```

Key points:

• `cursor.selectedText()` returns the chosen text but uses the paragraph-separator character U+2029 instead of `'\n'`; convert it if you want true plain text.

• `cursor.anchor()` is the position the caret had when the user began the selection (“cursor position before the selection”).

That is all that’s needed—no subclassing of `QTextEdit` or event handling required.

instruction: Write a small python function that get all the links of a website
output:
Here is a minimal, self-contained function that returns every (unique) HTTP(S) link it can find on a single web page.

```python
import requests
from urllib.parse import urljoin, urldefrag, urlparse
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def get_links(url, *, same_domain=False, timeout=10):
    """
    Fetch `url` and return a set of absolute links found in the page.

    Parameters
    ----------
    url : str
        The web page to scan.
    same_domain : bool, optional
        If True, keep only links whose netloc matches `url`’s domain.
    timeout : int or float, optional
        Passed straight to `requests.get`.

    Returns
    -------
    set[str]
        A deduplicated collection of fully-qualified URLs.
    """
    try:
        resp = requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, headers={"User-Agent": "link-scraper/1.0"})
        resp.raise_for_status()
    except Exception as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Cannot fetch {url!r}: {e}")

    base = resp.url                     # final URL after redirects
    domain = urlparse(base).netloc

    soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.text, "html.parser")

    links = set()
    for tag in soup.find_all("a", href=True):
        href = tag["href"].strip()

        # ignore non-web schemes (mailto:, javascript:, etc.)
        if urlparse(href).scheme not in ("http", "https", ""):
            continue

        # turn relative -> absolute, strip URL fragment (#section)
        absolute = urldefrag(urljoin(base, href))[0]

        if same_domain and urlparse(absolute).netloc != domain:
            continue

        links.add(absolute)

    return links
```

Example usage:

```python
if __name__ == "__main__":
    page = "https://www.python.org/"
    for link in sorted(get_links(page, same_domain=True)):
        print(link)
```

Install dependency (once):

```bash
pip install requests beautifulsoup4
```

This script:

1. Downloads the page with `requests`.
2. Parses the HTML using `BeautifulSoup`.
3. Iterates over every `<a href="…">`, converts each to an absolute URL with `urljoin`, removes `#fragment`s, filters out non-HTTP schemes (e.g., `mailto:`), and optionally keeps only links on the same domain.
4. Returns a deduplicated `set` of links.

Write the GAN code in Python for train my dataset folder and generate a file or sequence of lines like as the train data.
output:
Below is a complete, minimal PyTorch program that

1. Reads every CSV in a folder (must contain the three columns time, note, vel).  
2. Cuts each file into fixed-length sequences (SEQ_LEN).  
3. Trains a simple sequence GAN (Generator = LSTM that turns a latent vector into a sequence, Discriminator = LSTM that classifies a sequence as real / fake).  
4. When training is finished it writes one new file (generated.csv) whose content looks like the training files.

You can put the code in one file (e.g. train_gan.py), adjust the constants at the top, and run:

python train_gan.py

------------------------------------------------------------
Python code
------------------------------------------------------------
```python
import os, glob, random, math, argparse
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Hyper-parameters – change them if you like
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
DATA_DIR      = "data"          # folder that contains *.csv with (time,note,vel)
SEQ_LEN       = 32              # how many rows form one training “sentence”
LATENT_DIM    = 128
HIDDEN_DIM    = 256
BATCH_SIZE    = 64
EPOCHS        = 2000            # lower for quick test, higher for quality
LR            = 2e-4
DEVICE        = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
OUT_FILE      = "generated.csv" # output file

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Dataset helper
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
class NoteSeqDataset(Dataset):
    """
    Reads each csv, concatenates rows, globally min-max normalises, splits
    into fixed length sequences.
    """
    def __init__(self, root_dir, seq_len=32):
        self.seq_len = seq_len
        self.seqs = []

        # 1st pass: load everything to gather min / max
        all_rows = []
        for fn in glob.glob(os.path.join(root_dir, "*.csv")):
            df = pd.read_csv(fn, usecols=["time", "note", "vel"])
            all_rows.append(df.values.astype(np.float32))
        all_rows_np = np.vstack(all_rows)

        self.col_min = all_rows_np.min(axis=0)
        self.col_max = all_rows_np.max(axis=0)

        def norm(x):
            return (x - self.col_min) / (self.col_max - self.col_min + 1e-8)

        # 2nd pass: slice into sequences
        for arr in all_rows:
            arr = norm(arr)
            # simple non-overlapping chunks
            for i in range(0, len(arr) - seq_len + 1, seq_len):
                self.seqs.append(arr[i:i+seq_len])

        self.seqs = np.stack(self.seqs)                     # [N,seq_len,3]

    def __len__(self):  return len(self.seqs)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return torch.tensor(self.seqs[idx], dtype=torch.float32)

    # utility for inverse transform
    def denorm(self, x):        # x: numpy array [seq_len,3] in [0,1]
        return x * (self.col_max - self.col_min) + self.col_min

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Generator and Discriminator
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
class Generator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim, hidden_dim, seq_len, feature_dim=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc     = nn.Linear(latent_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.lstm   = nn.LSTM(hidden_dim, hidden_dim, batch_first=True)
        self.out_fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, feature_dim)

    def forward(self, z):                  # z : [B,latent]
        h0 = torch.relu(self.fc(z))        # [B,H]
        h0 = h0.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, SEQ_LEN, 1)   # [B,SEQ_LEN,H]
        x , _  = self.lstm(h0)
        x = torch.sigmoid(self.out_fc(x))  # stay in [0,1]
        return x                           # [B,SEQ_LEN,3]

class Discriminator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, seq_len, feature_dim=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(feature_dim, hidden_dim, batch_first=True)
        self.fc   = nn.Linear(hidden_dim*seq_len, 1)

    def forward(self, x):                  # x : [B,SEQ_LEN,3]
        h , _ = self.lstm(x)
        h = h.contiguous().view(x.size(0), -1)
        return torch.sigmoid(self.fc(h))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Training loop
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def train():
    ds  = NoteSeqDataset(DATA_DIR, SEQ_LEN)
    dl  = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)

    G = Generator(LATENT_DIM, HIDDEN_DIM, SEQ_LEN).to(DEVICE)
    D = Discriminator(HIDDEN_DIM, SEQ_LEN).to(DEVICE)

    criterion = nn.BCELoss()
    opt_G = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters(), lr=LR, betas=(0.5,0.999))
    opt_D = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), lr=LR, betas=(0.5,0.999))

    for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS+1):
        for real in dl:
            real = real.to(DEVICE)               # ----------------- Real
            batch = real.size(0)
            valid = torch.ones (batch,1,device=DEVICE)
            fake  = torch.zeros(batch,1,device=DEVICE)

            # ----- 1) Train Generator
            opt_G.zero_grad()
            z      = torch.randn(batch, LATENT_DIM, device=DEVICE)
            gen    = G(z)
            g_loss = criterion(D(gen), valid)    # want to fool D
            g_loss.backward()
            opt_G.step()

            # ----- 2) Train Discriminator
            opt_D.zero_grad()
            loss_real = criterion(D(real), valid)
            loss_fake = criterion(D(gen.detach()), fake)
            d_loss = 0.5*(loss_real + loss_fake)
            d_loss.backward()
            opt_D.step()

        # small console log
        if epoch % 100 == 0 or epoch == 1:
            print(f"Epoch {epoch:4d}  D_loss={d_loss.item():.4f}  G_loss={g_loss.item():.4f}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Produce one sample and write to CSV
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    with torch.no_grad():
        sample = G(torch.randn(1, LATENT_DIM, device=DEVICE))[0].cpu().numpy()
    sample = ds.denorm(sample)
    sample = np.round(sample).astype(int)        # mimic original ints

    df = pd.DataFrame(sample, columns=["time","note","vel"])
    df.to_csv(OUT_FILE, index=False)
    print("Saved", OUT_FILE)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    train()
```

------------------------------------------------------------
How to use
------------------------------------------------------------
1. Create a folder (default: `data`) that contains nothing but your training CSV files.  
   Each file must have exactly three columns named `time`, `note`, `vel` (headers **must** exist).  

2. Optional: change the constants at the top (SEQ_LEN, hidden sizes, learning rate, output name …).  

3. Run:

   python train_gan.py

4. After training finishes you will find `generated.csv` in the working directory containing 32 new rows that follow the same `(time,note,vel)` format as the training material.  

------------------------------------------------------------
Customising
------------------------------------------------------------
• Different sequence length → change SEQ_LEN (and of course interpret the output accordingly).  
• More epochs / bigger networks → increase EPOCHS, HIDDEN_DIM.  
• Overlapping slices → in the dataset class change the step from `seq_len` to `1` (slower but more data).  
• Several samples after training → call the generator many times and write each to its own file.  

This is a deliberately compact implementation meant to get you started; for production quality you would likely add:  

– checkpoint saving/loading,  
– gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) to stabilise long training,  
– tempo-aware or absolute-time encoding instead of min-max,  
– variable-length sequence handling (SeqGAN/RNN-based policy gradient).

5x² + 3x² = 8  
8x² = 8

Taking square roots gives the algebraic solutions:

A length must be non-negative, so if x represents the length of a line segment, the only admissible value is

instruction: Describe how can I quicly build a Keras script to train and categorize data from a CSV file.
output:
Below is a “cookie-cutter” recipe you can paste into a new .py file, adapt column names / network size, and run.  
It shows the minimal steps for turning a CSV file into a trained Keras (TensorFlow 2) classifier.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Prerequisites
-------------------------------------------------
pip install tensorflow pandas scikit-learn matplotlib

-------------------------------------------------
2. File layout assumption
-------------------------------------------------
• mydata.csv  
• The last column is the class label (string or integer).  
• All other columns are numeric features.  
(If this is not true, see the “Variants & Tips” section.)

-------------------------------------------------
3. The quick script
-------------------------------------------------
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, LabelEncoder
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Dropout
from tensorflow.keras.utils import to_categorical

# 1) LOAD CSV -------------------------------------------------------------
csv_path = 'mydata.csv'                       # << EDIT
df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)

# 2) SPLIT FEATURES / LABELS ---------------------------------------------
X = df.iloc[:, :-1].values                   # all columns except last
y_raw = df.iloc[:, -1].values               # last column

# 3) ENCODE LABELS --------------------------------------------------------
le = LabelEncoder()
y_int = le.fit_transform(y_raw)             # classes → 0..n-1
n_classes = len(le.classes_)
y = to_categorical(y_int, n_classes)        # one-hot for Keras

# 4) TRAIN/TEST SPLIT -----------------------------------------------------
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y_int, random_state=42)

# 5) FEATURE SCALING ------------------------------------------------------
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test  = scaler.transform(X_test)

# 6) BUILD THE MODEL ------------------------------------------------------
model = Sequential([
    Dense(128, activation='relu', input_shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),
    Dropout(0.3),
    Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    Dropout(0.3),
    Dense(n_classes, activation='softmax')          # softmax for multi-class
])

model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# 7) TRAIN ---------------------------------------------------------------
history = model.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    epochs=50,
    batch_size=32,
    validation_split=0.1,
    callbacks=[tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)],
    verbose=1
)

# 8) EVALUATE ------------------------------------------------------------
test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)
print(f'Test accuracy: {test_acc:.3f}')

# 9) REPORT --------------------------------------------------------------
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
print(classification_report(
    np.argmax(y_test, axis=1),
    np.argmax(y_pred, axis=1),
    target_names=le.classes_)
)

# 10) SAVE ARTIFACTS -----------------------------------------------------
model.save('model.h5')
import joblib
joblib.dump({'scaler': scaler, 'label_encoder': le}, 'preprocess.pkl')
```

-------------------------------------------------
4. Run it
-------------------------------------------------
python train_csv_classifier.py

-------------------------------------------------
5. Predict on new rows
-------------------------------------------------
```python
import pandas as pd, joblib, tensorflow as tf
row = pd.read_csv('new_rows.csv')
objs = joblib.load('preprocess.pkl')
row_scaled = objs['scaler'].transform(row.values)
model = tf.keras.models.load_model('model.h5')
probs = model.predict(row_scaled)
pred_labels = objs['label_encoder'].inverse_transform(np.argmax(probs,1))
print(pred_labels)
```

-------------------------------------------------
Variants & Tips
-------------------------------------------------
• Binary classification – keep LabelEncoder but use `n_classes=1`, final
  layer `Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')`, and `loss='binary_crossentropy'`.

• Categorical (string) features – one-hot encode them first with
  `pd.get_dummies` or `sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer`.

• Huge CSV – stream with `tf.data.experimental.make_csv_dataset()` instead of pandas.

• Hyper-parameter tuning – wrap model build in a function and use
  `keras-tuner` or `scikit-learn`’s `RandomizedSearchCV` through
  `KerasClassifier`.

• Visualization – `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.plot(history.history['loss'])`.

• Reproducibility – set seeds:
  ```
  import random, os
  np.random.seed(42); random.seed(42); tf.random.set_seed(42)
  os.environ['TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS'] = '1'
  ```

• Deploy – convert to TensorFlow Lite (`tf.lite.TFLiteConverter`) or SavedModel for TF Serving.

That’s enough to go from CSV to a trained and saved Keras classifier in a few minutes.
