I live in Germany and I am a german tax resident. If I trade shares, I'm subject to german income tax. I want to move my trading to a company and let the profits be taxed as for companies. Whattype of a company should I create, and in which country?
output:
Short answer  
If you stay tax-resident in Germany there is virtually no legal way to have the profits from ordinary share trading taxed more cheaply through a company – whether that company is German or foreign. A German GmbH/UG would actually raise the tax burden and an “off-shore” company would, under the German CFC (“AStG-Zwischengesellschaft”) and management-location rules, be treated as tax-resident in Germany anyway.  

Below is the long version so you understand why.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. What you pay today as a private investor
• Capital-gains / dividend tax (Abgeltungsteuer)           25 %  
• Solidarity surcharge (5.5 % of 25 %)                       1.375 %  
• (+ church tax, if applicable)                             ≈  0–2 %  
Effective rate (no church tax):                            26.375 %

That 26 % is final; the money is yours afterwards.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. A German capital company (GmbH, UG, AG)

2.1 Taxes while profits remain in the company  
• Corporation tax (KSt)                              15 %  
• Soli on corporation tax                            0.825 %  
• Trade tax (Gewerbesteuer)                       ≈ 13–17 %  
Typical total                                           29 – 33 %

Result: you already pay more than 26 % while the cash is still locked in the company.  

2.2 When you distribute the profits to yourself  
Dividends are taxed again:  
a) Flat rate (25 % + Soli) or  
b) 60 %-inclusion option (§ 32d (2) Nr.3 EStG) if you hold ≥ 25 % in the GmbH.  
Either way the combined burden ends up around 48–50 %.  

Only if you never distribute, or if you need the money for another corporate activity, could deferral occasionally outweigh the higher rate – but for a pure trading vehicle you usually want the cash at some point.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. A German partnership (vermögens­verwaltende KG, GbR, o. ä.)

• Trade tax can be avoided if the partnership is strictly “asset managing”,  
  BUT the partnership is transparent: the trading income is taxed directly in your hands at the
  same 25 % Abgeltungsteuer you already pay today.  
So no tax saving, just more paperwork.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. A foreign company

4.1 Place-of-management rule (§ 10 AO)  
If you direct the company from your desk in Germany, the company is regarded as tax-resident in Germany irrespective of where it is incorporated. Result: German corporation tax + trade tax again.

4.2 Controlled-Foreign-Company rules (§§ 7–14 AStG)  
Even if you manage to keep the place of management abroad, a company that is  
• low-taxed (< 25 %) AND  
• earns predominantly “passive” income (securities trading is passive)  
is a “Zwischengesellschaft”. 100 % of its profits are deemed distributed to you every year
and subjected to German tax (still 26 %). In other words, Germany collapses the structure.

4.3 Treaty/holding structures  
Using a normal-taxed EU company (e.g., Dutch BV, Estonian OÜ) does not trigger CFC attribution, but if you manage it from Germany § 10 AO pulls it back into German residence. If you really kept the management abroad (board, day-to-day decisions, documented board meetings, etc.) the company would pay foreign corporate tax first and you’d pay 25 % withholding on dividends when they are transferred to you. You are unlikely to beat the 26 % you already have.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. When does a company make sense for an investor?

• You hold share stakes of ≥ 10 % and sell them after one year – in a corporation 95 % of the gain is tax-exempt (participation exemption). That is a private-equity style strategy, not ordinary trading.  
• You actually need an operating company for another business and the trading profits can remain inside the firm to finance that business.  
• You plan to emigrate and will control the company from your new country of residence; then German CFC rules no longer apply.

If none of those applies, a company does not help.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Recommendation

1. If you remain resident in Germany and only trade listed shares, keep doing it in your own name; you are already at the lowest possible German tax rate for that type of income.  
2. If you want limited liability or succession planning, consider a vermögensverwaltende GmbH & Co. KG – it does not save tax but can bundle family assets.  
3. If you are determined to use a corporation despite higher taxes, a German GmbH in a municipality with the lowest Gewerbesteuer multiplier (e.g., Grünwald, Poing, etc.) is the simplest compliant vehicle.  
4. Speak to a German Steuerberater before you sign anything; the fines for an incorrectly structured foreign company can exceed any imagined tax saving.

(And, of course, this is information, not individual tax advice.)

instruction: Assume the role of a tax advisor or accountant familiar with US federal taxes.  If I forgot to withdraw the RMD (required minimum distribution) from my inherited IRA account during one particular year, how do I minimize the penalties I would have to pay the following year?
output:
Below is the standard “damage-control” checklist professionals use when a client forgets to take a required minimum distribution (RMD) from an inherited IRA.  The same procedure applies whether you are a spouse-beneficiary, a non-spouse individual, or a beneficiary of an inherited Roth that is subject to the old 5-year or the new 10-year rules (because an annual RMD was still required for 2020-2023 if the decedent died before his/her required beginning date).  Follow the steps in order; most taxpayers who act promptly and provide a credible explanation get the 50 % penalty waived entirely.

1. Take the missed distribution immediately  
   • Withdraw the exact amount that should have come out for the missed year.  
   • If you are already in the next calendar year, also take that year’s RMD while you are at it so you do not risk a second failure.  
   • Code the brokerage check or EFT as a normal “beneficiary distribution” (it will be reported on next January’s Form 1099-R and carried onto your Form 1040 as taxable income).

2. Prepare Form 5329 for the YEAR that was missed  
   • Form 5329 is the only place where the 50 % “additional tax on excess accumulations” is computed or waived (IRC §4974).  
   • If you already filed last year’s Form 1040 without Form 5329, file a stand-alone Form 5329 or file Form 1040-X with Form 5329 attached.  Either way is acceptable; most preparers mail a stand-alone 5329 because no other numbers on the 1040 change.  
   • Complete Part IX.  Enter the amount that should have been distributed on line 52 and the amount actually distributed (usually zero) on line 53.  The difference is the “shortfall.”

3. Ask for a waiver instead of paying the penalty  
   • On line 54 write the letters “RC” (reasonable cause) and enter “0” for the tax.  
   • Attach a signed statement (one page is plenty).  The statement must:  
       – explain why the RMD was missed,  
       – confirm that the entire shortfall has now been distributed, and  
       – describe steps you have taken to be sure it does not happen again (e.g., written instructions to the custodian, calendar reminders, automatic distribution set-up, hiring an adviser, etc.).  
   • Common, generally accepted reasons: misunderstanding the inherited-IRA rules, death or illness of the beneficiary or close relative, advisor/custodian error, mail or address issues, or reliance on wrong RMD tables.  The IRS does not require perfection—only a credible explanation and prompt correction.

4. Mail Form 5329 (and the statement) to the IRS service center where you would file a paper Form 1040 for that year.  Keep proof of mailing.  There is no electronic-filing option for a stand-alone 5329.

5. Do NOT pay the 50 % tax unless you plan to concede the penalty  
   • Historically the IRS grants almost all waiver requests when the taxpayer has already made up the missed distribution and supplies a coherent explanation.  If the Service disagrees, they will send a bill; you can then pay or pursue an appeal.  Paying up front and then requesting a refund is slower and rarely necessary.

6. Record-keeping for multiple missed years  
   • If you skipped more than one year, prepare a separate Form 5329 (and statement) for EACH year, stapling them in chronological order.  
   • You do NOT amend the 1040 for each year unless some other number changes.  Only the 5329 travels back in time.

7. Prevent a repeat  
   • Put the RMD on auto-withdraw with the custodian.  
   • Ask the broker to process beneficiary RMDs in November so you have time to fix any hiccup before December 31.  
   • Review inherited IRA RMD rules annually—especially important with the SECURE Act 10-year rule, where an annual RMD may or may not be required depending on the decedent’s status at death.

Key references  
   • IRC §4974 (50 % penalty)  
   • Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-1 through ‑5 (RMD mechanics)  
   • IRS Form 5329 & Instructions (see “Waiver of tax” in Part IX instructions)  
   • IRS Publication 590-B, Chapter 1 (“Missed RMDs”)  
   • Notice 2003-49 (still cited for the waiver process)

Bottom line  
Withdraw the missed amount now; file Form 5329 for the missed year; attach a reasonable-cause statement; and ask for a waiver.  In practice, this almost always eliminates the 50 % penalty, leaving you with only the ordinary income tax you would have owed if you had taken the distribution on time.

instruction: Use the greenshields model for traffic flow, the develop a python problem teaching the students how to use if-condition. In the problem the student will estimate the travel time from home to work when there is no rainfall and when there is a rainfall
output:
Python Programming Exercise – Using if-statements with the Greenshields Traffic-Flow Model
==========================================================================================

Context  
Greenshields (1935) proposed a simple *linear* relation between the space mean speed u (km/h) and the traffic density k (veh/km):

        u = u_f · ( 1 – k / k_j )

    u_f : free-flow speed  (speed when the road is “empty”)  
    k_j : jam density      (density at which speed becomes 0)

Once u is known, the travel time t to cover a distance d is

        t = d / u      [hours]

Purpose of the exercise  
You are going to write a short Python program that chooses *different* traffic parameters when it is raining, so you will need an if-statement.  The program finally prints the estimated home-to-work travel time.

Problem statement
-----------------
1. Ask the user for  
   • distance from home to work in km (float)  
   • measured traffic density in veh/km (float)  
   • weather condition (‘y’ if it is raining, ‘n’ otherwise).

2. Use the following baseline values for a **dry** road  

        free-flow speed, u_f_clear = 90  km/h  
        jam density,   k_j_clear  = 150 veh/km

3. When it is **raining** adjust the parameters:  
      u_f_rain  = u_f_clear × 0.80       (-20 %)  
      k_j_rain  = k_j_clear × 0.90       (-10 %)

4. Write an if-statement that  
   • selects the proper u_f and k_j according to the weather,  
   • checks whether the entered density k ≥ k_j.  
     – If it is, print “Road completely jammed – travel time is infinite.” and stop.  
   • otherwise computes  
         u = u_f · (1 – k / k_j)  
         travel time in minutes = d / u × 60

5. Display the average speed (2 decimals) and the travel time (1 decimal).

6. Test the program with at least the two scenarios below:

   a) d = 25 km, k = 40 veh/km, no rain  
      expected speed ≈ 75.0 km/h, time ≈ 20.0 min  
   b) d = 25 km, k = 40 veh/km, rain  
      expected speed ≈ 60.0 km/h, time ≈ 25.0 min

Hints  
• Remember that input() returns a string – convert to float if necessary.  
• You can chain the two if-tests or put one inside the other.  
• Use f-strings for neat output.

Sample run (user input in bold)

    Enter distance home-to-work (km): **25**
    Enter current density (veh/km): **40**
    Is it raining? (y/n): **y**
    Average speed under current conditions : 60.00 km/h
    Estimated travel time                  : 25.0 minutes

Reference solution
------------------

```python
# greenshields_travel_time.py

# 1. get user input
d = float(input("Enter distance home-to-work (km): "))
k = float(input("Enter current density (veh/km): "))
rain = input("Is it raining? (y/n): ").strip().lower()

# 2. choose parameters with an if-statement
if rain == 'y':                         # raining case
    uf = 90 * 0.80                      # km/h
    kj = 150 * 0.90                     # veh/km
else:                                   # dry case
    uf = 90
    kj = 150

# 3. second if-statement: is the road already jammed?
if k >= kj:
    print("Road completely jammed – travel time is infinite.")
else:
    # 4. Greenshields speed
    u = uf * (1 - k / kj)               # km/h
    # 5. travel time
    t_min = d / u * 60                  # minutes

    # 6. nicely formatted output
    print(f"Average speed under current conditions : {u:.2f} km/h")
    print(f"Estimated travel time                  : {t_min:.1f} minutes")
```

How students learn from this exercise
• They must build a *decision* tree (if-condition) for two different environments (dry vs. wet).  
• They practice nested or sequential if-blocks (weather check + jam check).  
• They see a real-world engineering model (Greenshields) translated into code.

instruction:
Apply your critical and analytical thinking and provide well-reasoned insights in response to each of the following four essay questions!
Please click the following link to answer the question no. 1: https://www.theclassroom.com/structuralist-approach-teaching-english-8716712.html 

Drawing upon the principles of structuralism, critically analyze and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the structuralist approach to teaching English. Provide well-reasoned arguments and examples to support your assessment. Consider the implications of this methodology for different age groups and educational levels. Additionally, discuss the balance between the emphasis on proper language mechanics and the potential limitations on creativity in language expression. Ensure that your response reflects a deep understanding of the structural view of language and its implications for English language teaching.
In a critical analysis, compare and contrast the Direct Method and the Grammar-Translation Method. Identify and discuss the key principles that differentiate these two language teaching methods. Additionally, evaluate the effectiveness of the teaching techniques associated with each method. Support your analysis with examples and consider the implications of these methods on language acquisition and proficiency.
In light of the historical context and critiques discussed in the Audio Lingual Method, evaluate critically the reasons behind the decline in popularity of the Audio-lingual Method. Provide specific examples of criticisms and discuss how the method's theoretical foundations contributed to its diminished use in language teaching. 
Considering the evolution of language teaching methods discussed in the course of Communicative Language Teaching (CLT), analyze critically the central concept of "communicative competence" in CLT. Discuss how CLT addresses the limitations of previous methods and evaluate the role of learners and teachers in the CLT approach.
output:
QUESTION 1.  The Structuralist Approach to Teaching English  
—————————————————————————————————————  
1. A concise statement of the structural view  
•  Language is a rule-governed system whose smallest meaningful units (phonemes, morphemes, sentence patterns) combine according to a fixed hierarchy.  
•  In the classroom this translates into teaching syllabi organised “from parts to whole”: sounds → words → patterns → larger discourse.  
•  Accuracy, habit-formation and teacher-controlled practice are privileged; meaning and creativity are normally treated as by-products to be postponed until the structure is mastered.  

2. Strengths  
a) Clear, cumulative sequencing   
   – The “building-block” logic gives teachers an explicit path (e.g., teach /p/ vs /b/ contrasts, add inflectional endings, practise S-V-O order).  
   – Particularly helpful for younger learners and beginners who benefit from concrete, bite-sized objectives and frequent recycling.  

b) Diagnostic precision and error correction  
   – When every exercise is tied to a well-defined structure, errors are easy to locate (e.g., “She *go* yesterday” → past-tense morphology missing).  
   – Corrective feedback is immediate and linked to a specific structural rule, which can raise grammatical awareness at secondary/tertiary levels.  

c) Standardisation and testability  
   – Structural objectives align comfortably with discrete-point tests (gap-fills, transformations), facilitating large-scale assessment and syllabus coordination.  
   – Suits educational systems that demand uniformity (national exams, textbook series).  

d) Suitability for limited-exposure contexts  
   – Where learners get very little authentic input (rural schools, EFL settings), explicit structural drills may provide the only systematic exposure to key patterns.  

3. Weaknesses  
a) Reduced communicative payoff  
   – Mastery of isolated structures does not automatically transfer to spontaneous interaction; learners often fail at discourse management or sociolinguistic appropriacy despite scoring high on structural tests.  

b) Potential suppression of creativity  
   – Over-controlled pattern drills can lead to formulaic output and learner passivity.  
   – Writing tasks may be restricted to “fill-in” exercises, leaving little room for stylistic experimentation or personal voice, which is demotivating for adolescents and adults.  

c) Neglect of meaning and context  
   – A sentence such as “Colourless green ideas sleep furiously” would be judged “correct” structurally yet is pragmatically odd; cultural pragmatics, genre conventions, and strategic competence are under-represented.  

d) Age-group mismatches  
   • Very young learners: Naturalistic, play-based approaches often outperform structure-first teaching because children acquire patterns implicitly through stories and games.  
   • University/ESP learners: Need task-based, content-focused activities that integrate lexis, genre and critical thinking rather than rehearsing already-familiar structures.  

e) Inflexibility with irregularities  
   – English contains many idioms, phrasal verbs and discourse markers that do not conform neatly to the “slot-and-filler” model, forcing teachers either to skip them or to treat them as exceptions.  

4. Balancing mechanics and creativity  
Good practice today mines the organisational clarity of structuralism but grafts it onto meaning-centred tasks.  For example:  
•  Pre-task: brief, inductive focus on the past-perfect.  
•  Task: groups reconstruct an accident story from picture strips, forcing genuine communicative need for the target structure.  
Thus mechanical accuracy becomes the servant—not the master—of expression.  

—————————————————————————————————————  
QUESTION 2.  Direct Method (DM) vs. Grammar-Translation Method (GTM)  
—————————————————————————————————————  
1. Philosophical roots  
• GTM: Humanist/classical tradition; language = written literature; learning = conscious rule learning + L1-L2 comparison.  
• DM: 19th-c. reform movement; language = oral phenomenon; learning = naturalistic L1-like acquisition.  

2. Core principles  
                 Grammar-Translation                     |               Direct Method  
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  
Main goal     Read canonical texts; mental discipline      |  Speak & understand everyday L2  
Medium        L1 is indispensable (translation, rules)     |  L2 only; no mother-tongue use  
Grammar       Explicit explanation, deductive              |  Implicit, inductive; “show not tell”  
Vocabulary    Word lists ordered semantically               |  Concrete lexis taught through objects, actions  
Skills focus  Reading, writing, literary appreciation       |  Listening & speaking (reading/writing later)  
Accuracy vs   Accuracy in form; stylistic fidelity          |  Fluency and correct pronunciation  
fluency  

3. Teaching techniques  
GTM: bilingual word lists, paradigm charts, prose translation (“I gave the letters to the messenger → L2”), reading comprehension questions, deductive rule presentation.  
DM: “real-life” classroom situations, question-answer chains (T: “Where is the book?” Ss: “The book is on the desk.”), demonstration with pictures/realia, dictation, limited phonetic annotation.  

4. Effectiveness evaluation  
Advantages of GTM  
• Efficient for large classes with few resources.  
• Develops metalinguistic knowledge valuable for academic purposes (e.g., future translators, linguists).  
• Facilitates rapid vocabulary build-up in cognate-rich language pairs (Spanish–Italian).  

Drawbacks of GTM  
• Oral/aural proficiency remains minimal; fossilised pronunciation errors.  
• Low motivational appeal; cognitive overload for younger learners.  

Advantages of DM  
• Rapid improvement in listening-speaking, especially with small motivated groups.  
• Contextualised vocabulary retention (objects/actions anchor meaning).  
• Naturalistic rhythm aids pronunciation and intonation.  

Drawbacks of DM  
• Requires highly proficient, energetic teachers and small classes; difficult in state-school realities.  
• Neglect of explicit grammar can result in plateau and fossilisation of errors in writing.  
• Abstract or academic vocabulary hard to teach without L1 mediation.  

Implications for acquisition  
Research (e.g., Pica 1988) shows that comprehensible input and pushed output foster L2 competence; thus DM aligns better with psycholinguistic findings on interaction, but GTM’s focus on form may bolster explicit knowledge that, according to skill-building theories (DeKeyser 2007), later feeds proceduralisation. Blended models (e.g., present rule in L1 briefly, practise orally in L2) tap both systems.  

—————————————————————————————————————  
QUESTION 3.  Decline of the Audio-Lingual Method (ALM)  
—————————————————————————————————————  
1. Theoretical foundations  
• Behaviourism (Skinner): language learning = habit formation through stimulus-response-reinforcement.  
• Structural linguistics: language = finite set of patterns; teach them via dialogue memorisation and pattern drills.  

2. Key criticisms leading to decline  
a) Psychological challenge: Chomsky’s 1959 review of Skinner’s Verbal Behavior argued that language is rule-governed creativity, not chain association. This undercut the habit-formation premise of ALM.  

b) Empirical classroom results  
   – After years of drill, many learners could not transfer “automatic” patterns to real conversation. Savignon’s (1972) experiment showed that groups with communicative practice outperformed purely audio-lingual ones on spontaneous speaking tests.  

c) Artificiality of input  
   – Dialogues (“Is this a book? – No, it isn’t. It’s a pencil.”) lacked semantic and cultural authenticity, producing learner boredom and ridicule, especially in tertiary settings.  

d) Teacher/technology dependence  
   – Method presupposed language labs, tapes, and native-like teacher models. In many schools machines broke, tapes bored students, teachers reverted to L1 explanations.  

e) Neglect of meaning and affect  
   – Krashen’s (1982) Input Hypothesis and Affective Filter notions favoured meaningful input over rote drills, making ALM appear outdated.  

3. Curricular incompatibilities  
   – Growing demand for communicative competence (study abroad, business English) exposed ALM’s limitation: little pragmatic or sociolinguistic training.  
   – National syllabi in the 1970-80s (e.g., Council of Europe’s Threshold Level) shifted toward functional-notional descriptors, marginalising pattern-drill lists.  

Result: By the late 1980s ALM survived mainly in military/aviation phraseology and some ESL pronunciation labs, replaced in mainstream education by Communicative Language Teaching and later Task-Based Learning.  

—————————————————————————————————————  
QUESTION 4.  Communicative Competence in Communicative Language Teaching (CLT)  
—————————————————————————————————————  
1. Central concept  
Hymes (1972) introduced “communicative competence” to cover not only grammatical competence but also sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic abilities. Canale & Swain (1980) operationalised it into four sub-competences:  
   • Grammatical (forms)  
   • Sociolinguistic (appropriacy)  
   • Discourse (cohesion/coherence)  
   • Strategic (repair, paraphrase).  

2. How CLT addresses earlier limitations  
a) Structuralism & ALM: provided form but ignored use → CLT integrates form WITH communicative purpose via information-gap, problem-solving, role-play.  
b) Direct Method: offered orality but not interactional authenticity → CLT adds negotiation of meaning, turn-taking norms, functional language (“Would you mind…?”).  
c) GTM: emphasised written translation → CLT re-balances the four skills, adding listening/speaking while still valuing reading/writing through genre tasks.  

3. Role of learners  
• Active negotiators of meaning; expected to pool information, ask for clarification, and take interpersonal risks.  
• Individual needs and experiential content shape tasks (learner-centred syllabi, needs analysis).  
• Errors treated as natural by-products; peer-feedback and self-monitoring promoted.  

4. Role of teachers  
• Facilitator and needs analyst rather than sole knowledge transmitter.  
• Designer of communicative tasks with clear real-world outcomes (planning a trip, drafting an email).  
• Provider of focus-on-form moments: brief, reactive grammar explanation when communicative breakdown reveals need (“Why can’t I say ‘He enjoy’?”).  
• Evaluator using performance-based assessment (portfolios, role-play rubrics) in addition to discrete items.  

5. Remaining challenges  
• “Strong” CLT versions risk under-teaching accuracy; research suggests integrating form-focused instruction (Ellis 2016).  
• Large, exam-oriented classes may drift into pseudo-communication (ask-answer display questions).  
• Cultural contexts valuing teacher authority may resist the egalitarian interaction patterns of CLT; adaptation (e.g., structured information gaps, scripted roles) can mitigate.  

In sum, communicative competence reframes language mastery as the ability to deploy structures and lexis appropriately and strategically in real discourse. CLT, by foregrounding this competence, redresses the imbalances of prior methods while assigning new, more collaborative roles to teachers and learners.

instruction: How to process awk '{print $2}' with jq so that it would be {"result": "value1,value2,..."}?
output:
awk will give you one value per line, e.g.

$ awk '{print $2}' file
value1
value2
value3

If you pipe that into jq you can:

• read the stream as raw text (-R)  
• slurp it into one big string (-s)  
• turn the newline-separated list into a comma-separated list,  
• wrap the result in an object.

Shell command:

awk '{print $2}' file | \
jq -R -s '{result: (split("\n")[:-1] | join(","))}'

Produces:

{"result":"value1,value2,value3"}

Explanation of the jq filter  
- -R read each line as a raw string instead of JSON  
- -s slurp all the raw lines into one string  
- split("\n") → array of the lines  
- [:-1] drop the last empty element that follows the final newline  
- join(",") join the array with commas  
- {result: …} wrap the string in an object with the key “result”.

(If you prefer to avoid awk completely, jq can also extract the 2nd column itself:

jq -Rn ' [inputs | split(" ") | .[1]] | {result: join(",")} ' <file )

Rewrite this bash script to be more efficient #!/bin/bash

declare -a username_base
username_base=($(snmpwalk -v 2c -c $comm $host SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.9.392.1.3.21.1.20 | grep STRING | awk -F"SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.9.392.1.3.21.1.20." '{print $2}' | awk -F" " '{print $1}' | sed 's#[^.]*$##'))

count_username=${#username_base[@]}
echo "There are $count_username VPN users connected."
i=0
while [ ${i} -lt ${count_username} ]; do
username_oid=${username_base[$i]:0:-1}
username_dec=`echo $username_oid | sed 's/^[0-9]*.//' | sed 's/\./ /g'`
for x in `echo $username_dec`; do printf "\\$(printf %o "$x")"; done

vpn_agent=`snmpwalk -v 2c -c $comm $host SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.9.392.1.3.21.1.18.${username_oid} | awk -F"STRING: " '{print $2}' | head -1`
vpn_extip=`snmpwalk -v 2c -c $comm $host SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.9.392.1.3.21.1.10.${username_oid} | awk -F"STRING: " '{print $2}' | head -1`
vpn_intip=`snmpwalk -v 2c -c $comm $host SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.9.392.1.3.21.1.8.${username_oid} | awk -F"STRING: " '{print $2}' | tail -1`

output:
Below is a drop-in replacement that does exactly the same thing while

• running ONE SNMP request instead of 1 + 3 × users  
• avoiding forks to grep/awk/sed/printf inside loops  
• using bash-only string handling and associative arrays

On a box with a few dozen users the speed-up is usually
two orders of magnitude.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fast VPN-session inventory
#
# Needs bash 4+, snmp(bulk)walk                                   
#   $comm – SNMP community
#   $host – host to poll
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

set -euo pipefail

COMM=${comm:?missing community}
HOST=${host:?missing host}

BASE_OID=".1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.392.1.3.21.1"       # cVpnVacEntry
OID_USER=20                                     # user name (in index, not value)
OID_AGENT=18                                    # client agent
OID_EXTIP=10                                    # client public IP
OID_INTIP=8                                     # tunnel inner IP

##############################################################################
# Helper – translate dotted decimal ASCII (part after first ‘.’)
##############################################################################
decode_user() {
    local idx=${1#*.}                  # drop leading “session-id.”
    local chr username=""
    IFS='.' read -ra octets <<< "$idx"
    for chr in "${octets[@]}"; do
        username+=$(printf "\\$(printf '%03o' "$chr")")
    done
    printf '%s' "$username"
}

##############################################################################
# 1) Get the four columns in one single bulk walk
##############################################################################
mapfile -t SNMP_ROWS < <(
    snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c "$COMM" -On -Oq "$HOST" \
        "$BASE_OID.$OID_USER" \
        "$BASE_OID.$OID_AGENT" \
        "$BASE_OID.$OID_EXTIP" \
        "$BASE_OID.$OID_INTIP"
)

##############################################################################
# 2) Split the different columns into associative arrays
##############################################################################
declare -A AGENT EXTIP INTIP
declare -a INDEXES                                     # list of unique indices

for row in "${SNMP_ROWS[@]}"; do
    oid=${row%% *}            # everything up to first space
    val=${row#* }             # everything after first space
    val=${val#\"}; val=${val%\"}   # strip possible leading/trailing quotes

    suffix=${oid#"$BASE_OID."}     # e.g. 20.123.97.100
    col=${suffix%%.*}              # 20 / 18 / 10 / 8
    idx=${suffix#"$col."}          # 123.97.100 …

    case $col in
        $OID_AGENT) AGENT[$idx]=$val  ;;
        $OID_EXTIP) EXTIP[$idx]=$val  ;;
        $OID_INTIP) INTIP[$idx]=$val  ;;
        $OID_USER)  INDEXES+=("$idx") ;;   # we just remember which indices exist
    esac
done

##############################################################################
# 3) Show result
##############################################################################
echo "There are ${#INDEXES[@]} VPN users connected."

for idx in "${INDEXES[@]}"; do
    printf '%s, %s, %s, %s\n'  \
        "$(decode_user "$idx")"      \
        "${EXTIP[$idx]:--}"          \
        "${AGENT[$idx]:--}"          \
        "${INTIP[$idx]:--}"
done
```

What changed and why it is faster

1. **Single SNMP query** – `snmpbulkwalk` fetches the four required columns in one go; no per-user polls.
2. **No pipeline storms** – All text munging is done with Bash string slicing/arrays, so no `grep | awk | sed | cut` spawned thousands of times.
3. **Associative arrays** – keep the different columns keyed by their index, making look-ups O(1).
4. **Portable decoding** – the original “ASCII-codes-in-the-index” trick is kept but implemented in a tiny pure-bash function.

Simply save the script, make it executable and call it with
the same environment variables (`comm`, `host`) you used before.

4. Tie plot hooks to the “Current Trouble” and to whichever faction or landmark interests your players.

Three dice, seven short tables, infinite cities. Have fun populating your world!

instruction: write a program to play connect-4
A 50 y/o m present with painful toe since yesterday, the toe is swollen and red, sensitive to touch. no other joints are involved what is the differential diagnosis?
output:
Acute, very painful redness and swelling of a single toe (classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint) is a common presentation, but several distinct disorders can look alike during the first 24–48 h.  The main possibilities can be grouped as follows:

1. Crystal-induced arthritis  
   • Gout (monosodium urate crystals; podagra is the classic picture)  
   • Calcium-pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout)  
   • Basic calcium-phosphate or hydroxy-apatite crystal arthritis (rare in the toe)

2. Septic processes  
   • Septic (bacterial) arthritis of the MTP or inter-phalangeal joint (Staph. aureus, β-haemolytic streptococci, etc.)  
   • Cellulitis of the toe and peri-articular soft tissues  
   • Acute osteomyelitis of a phalanx or the metatarsal head  
   • Paronychia / felon / infected ingrown toenail that secondarily involves the joint capsule

3. Trauma / mechanical injury  
   • Acute fracture or bone bruise of the phalanx/metatarsal  
   • Ligamentous sprain or capsular tear with haemarthrosis  
   • Traumatic synovitis from repetitive micro-trauma (e.g., running, new shoes)

4. Other inflammatory arthritides  
   • Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis (“sausage toe”)  
   • Reactive arthritis (post-GI or GU infection)  
   • Early presentation of seronegative spondyloarthropathy or rheumatoid arthritis manifesting as a mono-arthritis  
   • Acute flare of osteoarthritis with effusion (“wear-and-tear synovitis”)

5. Vascular / miscellaneous  
   • Acute gouty tophus with super-added inflammation  
   • Ischaemic toe (arterial embolus or severe peripheral arterial disease)  
   • Chilblain/pernio, frostbite or cold-injury inflammation  
   • Bite or sting reaction (spider, insect, scorpion, marine sting)

Key next steps to separate these entities  
• Careful history: trauma, alcohol intake, diuretics, infection elsewhere, psoriasis, vascular history.  
• Physical exam: puncture wounds, nail infection, pulsations, pattern of swelling (joint-centred vs diffuse soft tissue).  
• Laboratory: CBC, ESR/CRP, serum uric acid (not diagnostic but supportive).  
• Plain radiograph to look for fracture, tophaceous erosions.  
• Urgent joint aspiration if an effusion is present – Gram stain/culture (rule out sepsis) and crystal analysis (polarised light microscopy).  
• Blood cultures if febrile.  

Bottom line: in a 50-year-old man the leading considerations are gout, septic arthritis and cellulitis; the exact diagnosis hinges on joint aspiration and culture/crystal analysis.

instruction:
How do I merge the following into a single pass call?
rk <- rk %>% filter(Peptide %in% pp) %>% collect() %>%
    separate(col="FragType", into=c("Product","FragZ"), remove=FALSE)
  rk[is.na(rk)]=0
output:
Use one pipe and do the NA-replacement with dplyr/tidyr instead of the base-R bracket assignment:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

rk <- rk %>% 
  filter(Peptide %in% pp) %>%                 # keep wanted rows
  collect() %>%                               # pull from the DB
  separate(FragType,                          # split FragType
           into = c("Product", "FragZ"),
           remove = FALSE) %>% 
  mutate(across(everything(), ~replace_na(.x, 0)))   # turn all NAs to 0
```

The last line (`mutate(across(...))`) replaces every NA in every column with 0, reproducing the effect of `rk[is.na(rk)] <- 0`, so the whole task is carried out in a single pipeline.

instruction: It is 1.00 o clock at night and I have to wait for 1.65 hours what time is it going to be after the wait is over?
output:
“1.65 hours” is a decimal-hours figure.  
To convert the fractional part (0.65 h) into minutes:

0.65 h × 60 min/h = 39 minutes

So 1.65 hours = 1 hour 39 minutes.

Starting time: 1:00 a.m.  
Add 1 hour 39 minutes:

1:00 a.m. + 1 hour  → 2:00 a.m.  
2:00 a.m. + 39 minutes → 2:39 a.m.

Therefore, after waiting 1.65 hours, the time will be 2:39 a.m.

instruction: i would like to build a magic the gathering deck. this deck contains 99 cards. How many lands should i play to draw on average 3 lands in my starting 7 cards hand. explain the calculus
output:
Let  

N  = total cards in the deck  = 99  
n  = cards you draw for your opening hand = 7  
L  = number of lands in the deck (what we want to find)  
X  = random variable “how many of those 7 cards are lands”

The draw is a hypergeometric sample (draws are without replacement).  
For a hypergeometric distribution the expected value (average) is  

E[X] = n · (L / N)

We want the average to be 3 lands:

3 = 7 · (L / 99)

Solve for L:

L = 3 · 99 / 7  
L ≈ 42.4286

Because L must be an integer we round to the nearest whole card:

• 42 lands → E[X] = 7·42/99 ≈ 2.97 lands (slightly under 3)  
• 43 lands → E[X] = 7·43/99 ≈ 3.04 lands (slightly over 3)

Most players would choose 43 lands to be safely above the 3-land average.

So put 43 lands (and 56 non-land cards) in your 99-card deck if you want to draw, on average, three lands in your opening seven-card hand.

instruction: code a framework for a multiple traveling salesman optimization in python using DEAP
output:
Below is a compact, self-contained framework that uses DEAP to solve the symmetric multiple-travelling-salesman problem (mTSP).  

• The depot is node 0 (fixed).  
• An individual is
  – a permutation of the non-depot cities and  
  – a list of break points that split that permutation into k salesman tours.  
• Fitness = total tour length (minimisation).  

You can drop this in a file (e.g. mtsp_deap.py) and run it directly.  At the bottom you will find a minimal demo that invents random 2-D cities, so no extra data files are needed.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Multiple-TSP with a simple GA written on top of DEAP.

author  :  you
license :  MIT
"""

import random
import math
from typing import List, Tuple

import numpy as np
from deap import base, creator, tools

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# USER–TUNEABLE PARAMETERS
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
N_CITIES      = 21          # including depot (id 0)
N_SALESMEN    = 3
POP_SIZE      = 300
N_GENERATIONS = 400
CX_PROB       = 0.9
MUT_PROB      = 0.3
RANDOM_SEED   = 42


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# BASIC TOOLS
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def euclidian(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.linalg.norm(a - b))


def distance_matrix(coords: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    n = len(coords)
    dmat = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            dmat[i, j] = dmat[j, i] = euclidian(coords[i], coords[j])
    return dmat


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# GENETIC REPRESENTATION
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
creator.create("FitnessMin", base.Fitness, weights=(-1.0,))
creator.create("Individual", list, fitness=creator.FitnessMin, breaks=None)


def random_breaks(num_cities: int, num_salesmen: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Choose num_salesmen-1 unique positions in the permutation at which the
    itinerary is split into routes.  Returned list is sorted ascending.
    """
    assert num_salesmen >= 1
    if num_salesmen == 1:
        return []
    return sorted(random.sample(range(1, num_cities), num_salesmen - 1))


def init_individual(icls, num_cities: int, num_salesmen: int):
    """
    Random permutation of 1..(num_cities-1) plus random break positions.
    """
    perm = random.sample(range(1, num_cities), num_cities - 1)
    ind = icls(perm)
    ind.breaks = random_breaks(num_cities - 1, num_salesmen)
    return ind


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# EVALUATION
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def evaluate(individual, dmat: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float]:
    """
    Returns total distance.  Depot is 0.  `individual` is only the permutation.
    Breakpoints are stored in individual.breaks.
    """
    perm = individual
    breaks = individual.breaks
    # Build segments
    segments = []
    prev = 0
    for b in breaks:
        segments.append(perm[prev:b])
        prev = b
    segments.append(perm[prev:])     # last salesman
    total = 0.0
    for seg in segments:
        if not seg:                  # empty route – salesman sits idle
            continue
        cur = 0                      # start at depot
        for city in seg:
            total += dmat[cur][city]
            cur = city
        total += dmat[cur][0]        # return to depot
    return (total,)


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# GENETIC OPERATORS
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def cx_mtsp(ind1, ind2):
    """
    Ordered crossover for the permutation + random 50/50 swap of break lists.
    """
    tools.cxOrdered(ind1, ind2)
    if random.random() < 0.5:
        ind1.breaks, ind2.breaks = ind2.breaks, ind1.breaks
    return ind1, ind2


def mut_mtsp(individual,
             indpb_perm=0.2,
             indpb_break=0.2) -> Tuple[creator.Individual]:
    """
    • With prob indpb_perm mutate the permutation using shuffle-indexes.
    • With prob indpb_break redraw breakpoints uniformly.
    """
    if random.random() < indpb_perm:
        tools.mutShuffleIndexes(individual, 2.0 / len(individual))
    if random.random() < indpb_break:
        n_sales = len(individual.breaks) + 1
        individual.breaks = random_breaks(len(individual), n_sales)
    return (individual,)


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TOOLBOX
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def get_toolbox(dmat: np.ndarray, num_salesmen: int):
    toolbox = base.Toolbox()
    num_cities = len(dmat)

    toolbox.register("individual",
                     init_individual,
                     creator.Individual,
                     num_cities,
                     num_salesmen)
    toolbox.register("population", tools.initRepeat, list, toolbox.individual)

    toolbox.register("evaluate", evaluate, dmat=dmat)
    toolbox.register("select", tools.selTournament, tournsize=3)
    toolbox.register("mate", cx_mtsp)
    toolbox.register("mutate", mut_mtsp)

    return toolbox


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# DEMO / MAIN
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def main():
    random.seed(RANDOM_SEED)
    np.random.seed(RANDOM_SEED)

    # Generate random 2-D points (first one is depot at origin for clarity)
    coords = np.vstack(([0., 0.],
                        np.random.rand(N_CITIES - 1, 2) * 100.0))
    dmat = distance_matrix(coords)

    toolbox = get_toolbox(dmat, N_SALESMEN)
    pop = toolbox.population(n=POP_SIZE)
    hall_of_fame = tools.HallOfFame(1)
    stats = tools.Statistics(lambda ind: ind.fitness.values[0])
    stats.register("avg", np.mean)
    stats.register("min", np.min)
    stats.register("max", np.max)

    # Run GA
    pop, logbook = algorithms_ea(
        population=pop,
        toolbox=toolbox,
        cxpb=CX_PROB,
        mutpb=MUT_PROB,
        ngen=N_GENERATIONS,
        stats=stats,
        halloffame=hall_of_fame,
        verbose=True)

    best = hall_of_fame[0]
    print("\nBest distance :", best.fitness.values[0])
    print("Permutation   :", best)
    print("Breaks        :", best.breaks)
    pretty_print_solution(best, N_SALESMEN)


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# HELPER : very small wrapper around eaSimple to keep main() readable
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def algorithms_ea(population, toolbox, cxpb, mutpb, ngen,
                  stats=None, halloffame=None, verbose=__debug__):
    """
    Thin wrapper around DEAP's eaSimple so we can call it with named params in
    main().  You can replace this by any DEAP *ea* algorithm (eaMuPlusLambda,
    eaMuCommaLambda...) without changing the rest of the code.
    """
    return tools.eaSimple(population, toolbox, cxpb, mutpb, ngen,
                          stats=stats,
                          halloffame=halloffame,
                          verbose=verbose)


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# HELPER : show the final routes nicely
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def pretty_print_solution(ind: creator.Individual, num_salesmen: int):
    perm   = ind
    breaks = ind.breaks + [len(perm)]
    start  = 0
    print("\nRoutes:")
    for i, br in enumerate(breaks):
        segment = perm[start:br]
        start   = br
        route   = [0] + segment + [0]
        print(f"  Salesman {i+1}: {route}")


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from deap import algorithms    # imported late to keep header tidy
    main()
```

How to use / tweak:

1. pip install deap numpy  
2. Adjust N_CITIES, N_SALESMEN, and GA parameters near the top.  
3. Provide your own coordinates instead of the random demo if you wish:
   replace the creation of `coords` with `coords = np.array([...])`.  
4. Run:  `python mtsp_deap.py`

From there you can
• swap `tools.eaSimple` for `tools.eaMuPlusLambda`,  
• add elitism or 2-opt local search in `mut_mtsp`,  
• track additional statistics, etc.  

This code is meant as a clear starting point rather than an industrial-strength solver, but everything you need to experiment with mTSP inside DEAP is in place.

instruction: Two trains, train A and train B, are driving toward each other. They start 10 km from each other. Train A runs at 10 m/s and train B at 5 km/h. An insect flies back and forth between both trains at 50 km/h. What distance will the insect fly before both trains touch each other?
output:
1. Put every speed in the same units  
   • Train A: 10 m/s = 10 × 3.6 = 36 km/h  
   • Train B: 5 km/h (already km/h)  
   • Insect: 50 km/h  

2. How long until the trains meet?  
   They approach one another, so the closing speed is  
   36 km/h + 5 km/h = 41 km/h.  

   Time = distance / closing speed  
         = 10 km / 41 km/h  
         = 10/41 h ≈ 0.244 h  
         ≈ 14.6 min ≈ 878 s.

3. How far does the insect fly in that time?  
   Distance = insect speed × time  
            = 50 km/h × (10/41 h)  
            = 500/41 km ≈ 12.2 km.

Answer: the insect travels about 12 km (≈ 12,200 m) before the trains touch.

instruction: how to train a vision transformer deep learning model in tensorflow
output:
Below is a complete, end-to-end recipe for training a Vision Transformer (ViT) image-classification model in TensorFlow 2 / Keras.  
The same scaffold works for any dataset; to keep the example reproducible we will use CIFAR-10 (32×32 RGB). Feel free to swap in a larger dataset such as ImageNet or a folder of your own images.

────────────────────────────────────────
0.  Environment & dependencies
────────────────────────────────────────
```bash
pip install -U tensorflow tensorflow-addons tensorflow-model-optimization
# (optional) pip install tensorflow-datasets  keras-cv einops
```
This guide assumes TF 2.10+ or TF 2.15-GPU.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Hyper-parameters
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
IMG_SIZE        = 72          # the picture will be resized to 72×72
PATCH_SIZE      = 6           # one patch = 6×6 pixels  ➜  (72/6)**2 = 144 patches
NUM_PATCHES     = (IMG_SIZE // PATCH_SIZE) ** 2
EMBED_DIM       = 64          # dimension of the linear projection of each patch
TRANSFORMER_LAYERS = 8
NUM_HEADS       = 4
MLP_UNITS       = [128, 64]   # hidden units in the MLP blocks inside the encoder
DROPOUT_RATE    = 0.10
BATCH_SIZE      = 256
EPOCHS          = 30
LEARNING_RATE   = 5e-4
WEIGHT_DECAY    = 1e-4
NUM_CLASSES     = 10          # CIFAR-10
```

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Data pipeline
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow_datasets as tfds

def preprocess(sample):
    image = tf.image.resize(sample['image'], (IMG_SIZE, IMG_SIZE))
    image = tf.cast(image, tf.float32) / 255.0          # [0,1]
    label = tf.one_hot(sample['label'], NUM_CLASSES)
    return image, label

(ds_train, ds_val), ds_info = tfds.load(
        'cifar10',
        split=['train', 'test'],
        as_supervised=False,
        with_info=True)

AUTOTUNE = tf.data.AUTOTUNE
ds_train = (ds_train
            .map(preprocess,  num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE)
            .shuffle(10_000)
            .batch(BATCH_SIZE)
            .prefetch(AUTOTUNE))

ds_val   = (ds_val
            .map(preprocess, num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE)
            .batch(BATCH_SIZE)
            .prefetch(AUTOTUNE))
```
(Optional) add `tf.image` augmentations (`flip_left_right`, `RandomRotation`, `RandAugment`, etc.)

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Custom layers: Patch extraction & encoding
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
class PatchExtractor(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, patch_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch_size = patch_size

    def call(self, images):
        batch_size = tf.shape(images)[0]
        patches = tf.image.extract_patches(
            images=images,
            sizes=[1, self.patch_size, self.patch_size, 1],
            strides=[1, self.patch_size, self.patch_size, 1],
            rates=[1,1,1,1],
            padding='VALID'
        )                                   # shape: (batch, n_patches_h, n_patches_w, patch_size*patch_size*3)
        patch_dim = patches.shape[-1]
        patches = tf.reshape(patches, [batch_size, -1, patch_dim])  # (batch, NUM_PATCHES, patch_dim)
        return patches

class PatchEncoder(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, num_patches, embed_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.projection = tf.keras.layers.Dense(embed_dim)
        self.position_embedding = tf.keras.layers.Embedding(
              input_dim=num_patches, output_dim=embed_dim)

    def call(self, patches):
        positions = tf.range(start=0, limit=tf.shape(patches)[1], delta=1)
        embedded   = self.projection(patches)
        return embedded + self.position_embedding(positions)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Transformer encoder block
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
def transformer_encoder(x, embed_dim, num_heads, mlp_units, dropout):
    # Layer norm → multi-head attention → skip-connection
    x1 = tf.keras.layers.LayerNormalization(epsilon=1e-6)(x)
    attention_output = tf.keras.layers.MultiHeadAttention(
            num_heads=num_heads, key_dim=embed_dim, dropout=dropout)(x1, x1)
    x2 = tf.keras.layers.Add()([attention_output, x])

    # Layer norm → MLP → skip-connection
    x3 = tf.keras.layers.LayerNormalization(epsilon=1e-6)(x2)
    for units in mlp_units:
        x3 = tf.keras.layers.Dense(units, activation=tf.nn.gelu)(x3)
        x3 = tf.keras.layers.Dropout(dropout)(x3)
    x_out = tf.keras.layers.Add()([x3, x2])
    return x_out
```

────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Build the ViT model
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
def build_vit(
        img_size      = IMG_SIZE,
        patch_size    = PATCH_SIZE,
        num_patches   = NUM_PATCHES,
        embed_dim     = EMBED_DIM,
        num_heads     = NUM_HEADS,
        transformer_layers = TRANSFORMER_LAYERS,
        mlp_units     = MLP_UNITS,
        dropout       = DROPOUT_RATE,
        num_classes   = NUM_CLASSES):

    inputs = tf.keras.Input(shape=(img_size, img_size, 3))

    # 1) split the image into patches and embed
    patches     = PatchExtractor(patch_size)(inputs)       # (B, N, P^2*3)
    encoded     = PatchEncoder(num_patches, embed_dim)(patches)

    # 2) transformer blocks
    for _ in range(transformer_layers):
        encoded = transformer_encoder(encoded,
                                      embed_dim,
                                      num_heads,
                                      mlp_units,
                                      dropout)

    # 3) classification head
    representation = tf.keras.layers.LayerNormalization(epsilon=1e-6)(encoded)
    representation = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool1D()(representation)
    outputs = tf.keras.layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(representation)

    return tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

vit_model = build_vit()
vit_model.summary()
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6.  Optimizer, scheduler & compilation
────────────────────────────────────────
AdamW (Adam with weight decay) + cosine decay is common for ViTs.

```python
# learning-rate schedule: warm-up 10% → cosine decay
training_steps = (ds_info.splits['train'].num_examples // BATCH_SIZE) * EPOCHS
warmup_steps   = int(0.1 * training_steps)

lr_schedule = tf.keras.optimizers.schedules.PolynomialDecay(
        initial_learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
        decay_steps=training_steps - warmup_steps,
        end_learning_rate=0.0)

def lr_warmup(step):
    return tf.cond(step < warmup_steps,
                   lambda: LEARNING_RATE * (tf.cast(step, tf.float32) / tf.cast(warmup_steps, tf.float32)),
                   lambda: lr_schedule(step - warmup_steps))

optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.experimental.AdamW(
            learning_rate=lr_warmup, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY)

vit_model.compile(optimizer=optimizer,
                  loss='categorical_crossentropy',
                  metrics=['accuracy'])
```

────────────────────────────────────────
7.  Train
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
history = vit_model.fit(ds_train,
                        epochs=EPOCHS,
                        validation_data=ds_val,
                        callbacks=[
                            tf.keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint('vit_ckpt', save_best_only=True),
                            tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)
                        ])
```

────────────────────────────────────────
8.  Evaluate / inference
────────────────────────────────────────
```python
test_loss, test_acc = vit_model.evaluate(ds_val)
print("test accuracy:", test_acc)

# predict on one image
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
for img, _ in ds_val.take(1):
    pred = vit_model.predict(img[:1])
    print("predicted class:", np.argmax(pred))
    plt.imshow(img[0]); plt.axis('off'); plt.show()
```

────────────────────────────────────────
9.  Training from a pre-trained checkpoint (optional but recommended)
────────────────────────────────────────
Instead of training from scratch, use a ViT backbone from KerasCV or TensorFlow-Hub and just add a small classifier on top.  
Example with Hub:

```python
import tensorflow_hub as hub

url = "https://tfhub.dev/sayakpaul/vit_b16_fe/1"   # feature-extractor (ViT-B/16, ImageNet-21k pre-training)
backbone = hub.KerasLayer(url, trainable=False)     # freeze, then fine-tune if desired
inputs   = tf.keras.Input(shape=(224,224,3))
x        = backbone(inputs)                         # (None, 768)
outputs  = tf.keras.layers.Dense(NUM_CLASSES, activation='softmax')(x)
model    = tf.keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer=optimizer, loss='ce', metrics=['acc'])
```
Unfreeze `backbone.trainable = True` for the last few epochs with a low learning rate for full fine-tuning.

────────────────────────────────────────
10.  Tips & tricks
────────────────────────────────────────
• ViTs need relatively large datasets or strong augmentation.  
• Larger `PATCH_SIZE` ⇒ fewer tokens ⇒ lower memory but weaker locality; smaller patch ⇒ more GPU memory.  
• Mixed-precision (`tf.keras.mixed_precision.set_global_policy('mixed_float16')`) speeds training on modern GPUs.  
• Gradient-accumulation is useful when the whole batch cannot fit into memory.  
• Label-smoothing (e.g., 0.1) often helps.  
• For bigger ViTs (B/16, L/16) use 224×224 or 384×384 inputs and 12-layer / 24-layer encoders.  
• If training absolutely from scratch, schedule many more epochs (300–1k) and use `stochastic depth`, `token augmentation`, or `CutMix`.

That’s it—you now have a working Vision Transformer built and trained in TensorFlow/Keras. Happy experimenting!

instruction: How can we put together multiple pertained encoders or decoders to create a new model?
output:
Below is a practical cookbook for “lego-style” model building with the 🤗 Transformers library, i.e. how to take two (or more) already-trained encoders/decoders and wire them together into a brand-new model that can then be fine-tuned.

────────────────────────────────
0.  When is this useful?
────────────────────────────────
• You want a seq2seq model but prefer an encoder that is trained for your source domain and a decoder that is trained for your target domain (e.g. BERT-based encoder + GPT-2–based decoder).  
• You want to mix modalities, e.g. an image encoder (ViT) with a language decoder (T5/GPT-2) for image-captioning or VQA.  
• You want several encoders feeding a single decoder (multi-source NMT, retrieval-augmented generation, etc.).  

────────────────────────────────
1.  One-to-one pairing (Encoder ↔ Decoder)
────────────────────────────────
For most text-to-text or vision-to-text tasks you can rely on the “ready-made” wrapper classes the library already provides:

• Text ↔ Text      EncoderDecoderModel  
• Vision ↔ Text    VisionEncoderDecoderModel  
• Speech ↔ Text    SpeechEncoderDecoderModel  

They handle all the plumbing (cross-attention layers, weight tying, generation utilities, etc.).

Step-by-step example: BERT encoder + GPT-2 decoder
--------------------------------------------------
```python
# 1. Choose/check the checkpoints
enc_ckpt = "bert-base-uncased"
dec_ckpt = "gpt2"

# 2. Load/patch the decoder config so it can be an actual *seq2seq decoder*
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
dec_config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(dec_ckpt)
dec_config.is_decoder = True                       # let HF know it is used as a decoder
dec_config.add_cross_attention = True              # mandatory for encoder-decoder attention
dec_config.vocab_size = 50257                      # same as GPT-2
decoder = AutoModel.from_pretrained(dec_ckpt, config=dec_config)

# 3. Build the pair
from transformers import EncoderDecoderModel
model = EncoderDecoderModel.from_encoder_decoder_pretrained(
             enc_ckpt, None,                        # encoder stays untouched
             decoder_model=decoder,                 # our patched decoder
             tie_encoder_decoder=False)             # can be True when vocabs align

# 4. A single tokenizer or two?
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(dec_ckpt)
tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token                      # GPT-2 has no PAD by default

# 5. Mandatory generation attributes
model.config.decoder_start_token_id = tok.bos_token_id or tok.eos_token_id
model.config.eos_token_id           = tok.eos_token_id
model.config.pad_token_id           = tok.pad_token_id
model.config.vocab_size             = model.config.decoder.vocab_size
```
The new model behaves like any seq2seq model (`model.generate(...)`, Trainer, PEFT, etc.).

────────────────────────────────
2.  Multi-source encoders  → one decoder
────────────────────────────────
Sometimes you want to fuse two or more encoders (e.g. “document encoder + retrieved-paragraph encoder” feeding the same decoder).  There is no stock class for “n-encoders-to-one-decoder”, but it is only ~40 lines of code.

Sketch:
```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoConfig, PreTrainedModel

class MultiEncoderDecoderConfig(PretrainedConfig):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.is_encoder_decoder = True                   # for generation

class MultiEncoderDecoder(PreTrainedModel):
    config_class = MultiEncoderDecoderConfig
    def __init__(self, encoders, decoder, fusion="cat"):
        super().__init__(MultiEncoderDecoderConfig())
        self.encoders = nn.ModuleList(encoders)
        self.decoder  = decoder
        self.fusion   = fusion
        
        # Hidden-size alignment
        hidden_sizes = [e.config.hidden_size for e in encoders]
        self.proj = nn.Linear(sum(hidden_sizes), decoder.config.hidden_size)
        
    def forward(self,
                encoder_inputs,         # list of dicts, one per encoder
                decoder_input_ids=None,
                **generate_kwargs):
        # 1. Run every encoder
        encoder_hiddens = []
        for enc, enc_kwargs in zip(self.encoders, encoder_inputs):
            encoder_hiddens.append(enc(**enc_kwargs).last_hidden_state)
        
        # 2. Concatenate (or average, attention-pool, etc.)
        fused = torch.cat(encoder_hiddens, dim=-1)
        fused = self.proj(fused)
        
        # 3. Pass through the decoder (as “encoder_hidden_states”)
        return self.decoder(
            decoder_input_ids=decoder_input_ids,
            encoder_hidden_states=fused,
            encoder_attention_mask=None  # build mask if needed
        )
```
Usage:
```python
enc1 = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
enc2 = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roberta-base")

# Decoder must accept cross-attention:
dec_conf = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("gpt2")
dec_conf.is_decoder = True; dec_conf.add_cross_attention = True
dec  = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2", config=dec_conf)

model = MultiEncoderDecoder([enc1, enc2], dec)
```
You can now fine-tune the whole system end-to-end, or freeze encoders and train only the decoder and `proj`.

────────────────────────────────
3.  Vision-to-Text example
────────────────────────────────
```python
from transformers import VisionEncoderDecoderModel, AutoProcessor

model = VisionEncoderDecoderModel.from_encoder_decoder_pretrained(
            "google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k",  # image encoder
            "gpt2")                              # text decoder (patched as above)

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k", 
                                          tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2"))
```
Fine-tune on image-caption pairs. The library’s `VisionEncoderDecoderModel` already handles shape projection from 2-D image tokens to 1-D language tokens.

────────────────────────────────
4.  Tips & gotchas
────────────────────────────────
• Hidden-size mismatch?  
  – Either set `config.encoder.hidden_size == config.decoder.hidden_size`, or add a projection layer (see section 2).  

• Different vocabularies?  
  – Keep separate tokenizers; tie weights only if the vocabularies match.  

• Generation helpers fail?  
  – Make sure `config.is_encoder_decoder = True`, `is_decoder = True`, `add_cross_attention = True`, and you have set `decoder_start_token_id`, `eos_token_id`, `pad_token_id`.  

• Large decoders (GPT-J, OPT) often drop the `position_ids` shift required when running as a decoder. Patch their config with `use_cache=True` and watch out for positional embeddings.  

• Speed/Memory: you can freeze encoders, train only the lightweight fusion/projection and the decoder (`for p in encoder.parameters(): p.requires_grad=False`).  

• Licensing: confirm that the individual checkpoints’ licenses are compatible before redistributing the merged model.

────────────────────────────────
5.  Where to look next
────────────────────────────────
• Official examples:  
  – `examples/research_projects/bert2bert`  
  – `examples/legacy/pytorch/seq2seq/`  
• Library docs: `EncoderDecoderModel`, `VisionEncoderDecoderModel`.  
• PEFT (LoRA, adapters) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the composite model.  

With the patterns above you can mix and match virtually any combination of pretrained encoders/decoders—text, vision, audio—while still inheriting all of 🤗 Transformers’ training, generation and inference utilities.

instruction: What is the most efficient way to uniformly sample a point inside a right angle triangle?
output:
Suppose the right-angle triangle has its right corner at P0 and the legs end in P1 and P2  
(e.g. P0 = (0,0), P1 = (b,0), P2 = (0,h) ).  
Generate two independent U(0,1) numbers r1 , r2 and do one inexpensive test:

1. r1 ← U(0,1)  
   r2 ← U(0,1)

2. if r1 + r2 > 1            // point fell in the upper half of the unit square  
      r1 ← 1 – r1            // reflect it through the line r1+r2 = 1  
      r2 ← 1 – r2

3. The barycentric coordinates inside the triangle are then  
        w0 = 1 – r1 – r2 ,   w1 = r1 ,   w2 = r2            (all ≥ 0, w0+w1+w2 = 1)  
   and the Cartesian point is  
        P = w0·P0 + w1·P1 + w2·P2
      (for the axis-aligned case that is simply P = ( b·r1 , h·r2 ) ).

Why it is uniform
• The unit square is cut by the line r1+r2 = 1 into two congruent right-angle triangles.  
• Reflecting a point that lands in the upper triangle into the lower one is an
  area-preserving, one-to-one mapping, so every differential patch of area in
  the target triangle receives the same probability mass.  
• No sample is rejected, so every draw succeeds; the algorithm needs only
  2 uniform deviates, 1 comparison and a few arithmetic operations.

Cost
– two random numbers  
– one conditional branch and two subtractions (no square roots)  
– a few multiplies/additions to form the final coordinates.

This is as efficient as it gets: 100 % acceptance, O(1) time, and only elementary arithmetic.

instruction: I need a python script that connects to a qbittorrent client using the api and removes a specified tracker from all torrents
output:
Below is a small stand-alone script that logs in to a running qBittorrent Web-UI, scans every torrent, and deletes a tracker you specify.

Save it as (for example)  remove_tracker.py, make it executable and run it:

$ python3 remove_tracker.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -u admin -p your_webui_password \
      https://the.tracker.you.want.to/remove/announce

If the tracker is present in several torrents it will be deleted from all of them in a single API call.  
(If nothing matches, nothing is changed.)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Remove a given tracker from every torrent that contains it in a qBittorrent client.

  python3 remove_tracker.py -p <password> <tracker_url>

Options (all have sensible defaults except the password):

  --host HOST        Web-UI host, default 127.0.0.1
  --port PORT        Web-UI port, default 8080
  -u, --user USER    Web-UI username, default 'admin'
  -p, --password PW  Web-UI password   (required)
  tracker_url        The exact tracker URL to remove, e.g.
                     'https://tracker.example.org:443/announce'
"""
import argparse
import sys
import requests


def login(session, api_base, username, password):
    r = session.post(f"{api_base}/auth/login",
                     data={"username": username, "password": password})
    if r.text != "Ok.":
        sys.exit(f"Login failed: {r.text.strip()}")


def torrents_with_tracker(session, api_base, tracker_url):
    """Return a list of torrent hashes that contain tracker_url."""
    wanted = tracker_url.rstrip("/")
    hashes = []

    for t in session.get(f"{api_base}/torrents/info").json():
        t_hash = t["hash"]
        trackers = session.get(f"{api_base}/torrents/trackers",
                               params={"hash": t_hash}).json()
        if any(tr["url"].rstrip("/") == wanted for tr in trackers):
            hashes.append(t_hash)

    return hashes


def remove_tracker(session, api_base, hashes, tracker_url):
    hash_param = "|".join(hashes)                 # pipe-separated, per API spec
    data = {"hashes": hash_param,
            "urls": tracker_url}                  # newline-sep if more than one
    r = session.post(f"{api_base}/torrents/removeTrackers", data=data)
    if r.status_code != 200:
        sys.exit(f"Removal call failed: {r.text.strip()}")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Remove a tracker from all torrents")
    ap.add_argument("--host", default="127.0.0.1")
    ap.add_argument("--port", default=8080, type=int)
    ap.add_argument("-u", "--user", default="admin")
    ap.add_argument("-p", "--password", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("tracker", help="Tracker URL to remove")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    api_base = f"http://{args.host}:{args.port}/api/v2"
    s = requests.Session()

    print("Logging in …")
    login(s, api_base, args.user, args.password)

    print("Scanning torrents …")
    hashes = torrents_with_tracker(s, api_base, args.tracker)

    if not hashes:
        print("No torrent contains the given tracker — nothing to do.")
        return

    print(f"Removing tracker from {len(hashes)} torrent(s) …")
    remove_tracker(s, api_base, hashes, args.tracker)
    print("Done.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Notes / requirements
• Works with qBittorrent Web API v2 (the default in every recent qBittorrent release).  
• Uses only the standard `requests` package (`pip install requests` if you don’t already have it).  
• The tracker comparison is done on the full URL after stripping a trailing “/”; modify the equality test inside `torrents_with_tracker()` if you want fuzzy matching (e.g. host-only).

instruction: write a python script that reads from stdin and extracts all watch?v= hrefs and prints youtube watch urls
output:
Below is a short, self-contained program that reads any text/HTML from STDIN, pulls out every value of an href= attribute that contains the string ​watch?v=, normalises relative links to full YouTube “watch” URLs and prints one URL per line.

save as  extract_youtube.py
────────────────────────────────────────
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
import re
import html
from urllib.parse import urljoin

YOUTUBE_ROOT = "https://www.youtube.com/"

def main() -> None:
    # Slurp everything that arrives on STDIN
    data = sys.stdin.read()

    # Undo HTML entity escaping ( &  →  &  etc.)
    data = html.unescape(data)

    # Grab the contents of every href="…"
    href_re = re.compile(r'href\s*=\s*["\']([^"\']+)["\']', re.I)
    hrefs = href_re.findall(data)

    seen = set()                      # avoid duplicates

    for href in hrefs:
        if "watch?v=" not in href:    # not a YouTube watch link
            continue

        # Turn relative “/watch?v=…“ or “watch?v=…” into full URL
        if not href.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            href = urljoin(YOUTUBE_ROOT, href.lstrip("/"))

        if href not in seen:
            print(href)
            seen.add(href)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
────────────────────────────────────────

usage
$ cat somepage.html | python3 extract_youtube.py
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oHg5SJYRHA0
…

The script relies only on the Python 3 standard library, so it works anywhere Python 3 is available.
